## Isekai Project F

### Chapter 1: Prologue: The End of Equations

#### Scene 1

The city outside was quiet, covered in a layer of fog and neon light. Inside the research tower, rows of computers blinked, and the smell of metal and ozone filled the air. Saitou sat alone in the control room, surrounded by monitors showing endless streams of data. It was late—too late for anyone else to still be working—but he couldn’t stop. The hum of machines was the only sound that kept him company. He thought of the world outside—the children playing in the streets, the families who depended on clean energy, the future he promised to make better. He smiled weakly, telling himself that all this effort would be worth it someday.

The steady hum of machines filled the room. Saitou barely noticed it anymore. His tired eyes stared at the glowing screen covered in numbers and symbols. Lines of formulas scrolled endlessly, but tonight, they felt heavier than ever.

“So… this is what it all means,” he whispered, voice dry and weak. The blue light from the monitor made his pale face look ghostly.

He had done it. His research worked. Humanity now had a new energy source that could power the entire planet forever. It was supposed to be a miracle.

At first, he didn’t think much when the project was transferred to another division—one filled with military contracts and classified funding. The official reports said it was for safety testing, but something about the sudden change felt wrong. His requests for updates were brushed aside with vague excuses. Security clearance levels changed overnight. Still, he wanted to believe it was routine.

Until one day, a young researcher from the defense team came to him, his expression pale and uneasy. “Dr. Saitou… there’s something I need to tell you.”

Saitou blinked, exhausted. “What is it?”

The young man hesitated before handing him a folder. “They’re modifying your equation.”

“Modifying it? For what?” Saitou frowned. “The stability field is delicate. If they tamper with the resonance balance, the system could—”

“—That’s just it,” the man interrupted nervously. “They say they found a way to invert it. If done correctly, it can… amplify energy beyond control.”

Saitou stared at him in disbelief. “That’s insane. You’d be creating a collapse. The output would be catastrophic.”

The young researcher nodded, his hands trembling. “I know. But the higher-ups… they called it an ‘opportunity.’ A new kind of power.”

For a moment, the room was silent except for the dull hum of the generators. Saitou’s throat went dry. He laughed softly, but there was no humor in it.

“Do they even understand what that means? That formula isn’t a toy—it could erase everything in its range!”

“I’m sorry,” the man whispered, stepping back. “I just thought you should know.” He left before Saitou could say another word.

Saitou sank into his chair, staring blankly at the folder. Inside were revised calculations—his equations rewritten with inverted parameters. Amplification instead of stabilization. Energy expansion instead of containment.

He imagined it. The resonance field breaking apart. A city erased in an instant. The world’s atmosphere trembling under an uncontrolled surge.

He felt sick.

“No… I can’t let this happen.” His voice shook as he opened his terminal and began rewriting his models, desperately trying to find a countermeasure. “If I can find a reversal formula, I can stop it… before anyone uses it.”

He didn’t know if anyone had actually tested it yet. Maybe no one would. But he couldn’t take that chance.

Days turned into weeks. Then months. He barely slept, barely ate. The lab lights stayed on through countless nights as he worked to undo the damage that hadn’t even happened yet.

“If they ever activate that formula,” he muttered, “the planet itself might—” He stopped, shaking his head. “No. I can’t think like that. I can still fix this.”

He pushed himself harder, running simulation after simulation. Each failed. The energy overflowed, destabilized, collapsed. Every outcome ended in ruin.

Sweat dripped down his temples as he typed faster. “Just once… please… let it work…”

Another error message blinked back at him.

He slammed his hands on the desk. “Damn it!”

His reflection in the dark monitor looked hollow, lifeless. “It’s not the math’s fault,” he whispered. “It’s the people who used it wrong… or maybe… the fool who made it in the first place.”

His head felt heavy. His vision swam. He hadn’t realized how long it had been since he last rested.

“Maybe… that’s why gods stay silent,” he muttered weakly. “They gave us reason… and watched us destroy ourselves with it.”

He reached out toward the glowing screen one last time. The formula shimmered faintly in front of him— beautiful, precise, and deadly.

Then everything went dark.

The sound of machines faded. His body slumped forward, fingers still hovering over the keys.

Then came a strange silence—too deep, too endless. He opened his eyes, but there was no floor, no ceiling. Only light. A bright, endless white that felt neither cold nor warm.

He floated in it, or maybe he was part of it. Time didn’t seem to move here.

“Where… am I?” His voice echoed softly, fading into the light.

“You are where all things end… and begin again.”

Saitou turned, but there was no one. Only shapes of light—shifting, flowing, like waves of pure radiance. They had no faces, no form. Yet he could feel their presence, calm and vast.

“Who… are you?”

“We are the watchers beyond the cycle. The ones who guide what remains when a world reaches its end.”

The words weren’t heard—they were felt, resonating directly in his thoughts.

Saitou’s heart tightened. “End? You mean… the world is gone?”

“Not yet,” the light replied gently. “But your path in it is. You have already fallen, Saitou. Your body lies still.”

He looked down. There was no body to see—only fading fragments of himself, dissolving into the brightness.

“Why am I here, then?”

The light pulsed faintly.

“Because your heart still clings to what you could not finish. You tried to undo what others would one day awaken.”

Suddenly, the light around him began to shift. Images formed in the air—visions of Earth, years passing in seconds. Towers collapsing, cities burning, skies shattering under waves of radiant energy.

“No…” His voice broke. “They actually used it…”

“Long after your death,” the Divine Being answered. “The formula you tried to reverse became the core of their weapon. What you feared… came true.”

Saitou fell silent. His mind couldn’t grasp it. The equation meant to save life had ended it instead.

“Then why am I here?”

“Because the cycle has not forsaken you. You sought to repair, not destroy. That intent cannot be erased.”

A gentle glow surrounded him, brighter now, wrapping him like sunlight through water.

“Your world has ended… but your story hasn’t.”

He wanted to speak, to ask for forgiveness, but his voice was gone. Panic filled his chest. The endless light around him felt suddenly cold.

“Wait… am I dead? Am I going to hell?” His voice trembled. “Please—please, I didn’t mean for it to happen. I just wanted to help. I just wanted to fix it!”

The light pulsed, calm but powerful.

“We know, Saitou. We saw the weight in your heart long before it broke. You carry regret, not malice.”

He fell to his knees—or whatever counted as ground here. His body shook, tears falling into the void. “Then… what happens to me now? If everything I did led to destruction, how can I ever be forgiven?”

“Forgiveness is not given. It is earned. But you will not find it in this place.” The light grew warmer, wrapping around him. “Your second chance awaits. A new life, far from this world. There, you may rediscover purpose—and perhaps the answer you sought.”

Saitou looked up, trembling. “A second… life?”

“Yes. A soul reborn, free of memory, free of burden. You will live again—not as punishment, but as hope.”

He clenched his hands. “Will I remember… any of this?”

“No. That knowledge would only bind you to despair.”

But as the light embraced him fully, the last thing that flickered in his mind was not fear—it was the memory of numbers, glowing faintly in the dark. Equations that refused to die.

And then, a sensation of warmth—followed by weight. Air filled his lungs for the first time. He gasped and cried out, his voice weak and high. Light blurred his vision, and muffled sounds reached his tiny ears.

He realized he was in someone’s arms. A woman’s voice—gentle, loving—whispered softly, though he couldn’t understand the words. He could feel warmth, hear faint laughter, and smell the faint scent of clean hay and herbs. It wasn’t the metallic air of the laboratory. It was… life.

‘I… was supposed to lose my memories,’ he thought. The words echoed clearly in his mind. He blinked, confused. ‘Then why do I still remember?’

He tried to move, but his arms refused to obey. His fingers twitched weakly. He tried to speak, but all that came out was a faint whimper.

‘No way… don’t tell me… I’ve been reborn?’

He could think, reason, remember—but his body was that of a newborn. He could only look up at the unfamiliar ceiling and the woman who smiled down at him, her eyes full of warmth. In that instant, Saitou realized he wasn’t in his old world anymore.

Somewhere beyond, unseen by mortal eyes, the Divine Beings watched. Their forms glimmered like shards of sunlight across the sky.

“This isn’t supposed to happen,” one voice murmured. “The cycle was meant to erase his past.”

Another replied, sharp and uneasy. > “His memory remains. The mortal mind should not endure across worlds.”

Yet amidst the murmuring light, one voice rose above the rest—the same gentle tone that had spoken to Saitou before. The other presences quieted, their glow dimming in uneasy stillness, as if bound by rules they could not break.

“Let it be.”

The other lights dimmed in hesitation.

“You are the only hope…”

The words echoed softly through the void before fading away, leaving only silence.

And so, under a new sky, in a peaceful town untouched by war, the man once called Saitou took his first breath as another.

Time passed slowly, and his awareness grew. He could hear voices—soft, gentle, and full of warmth—but the words made no sense. The language was foreign, distant, like a melody without meaning. He wanted to ask where he was, but when he opened his mouth, only a small murmur escaped. A baby’s sound.

‘My body won’t listen,’ he thought, trying to move his fingers. They only twitched. His limbs felt heavy, soft, uncoordinated. He realized, with growing disbelief, that he was trapped in the fragile body of an infant.

He cried without meaning to, his small lungs struggling as a pair of warm hands held him close. The woman’s laughter was gentle, comforting. Even though he couldn’t understand her words, he could feel the love in her tone.

‘Calm down… breathe… this is real,’ he told himself. ‘But why do I still remember? I shouldn’t… I was supposed to forget everything.’

The world around him was a blur of color and warmth. Yet within his tiny body, his mind remained clear and sharp—a strange contrast that filled him with unease.

He listened to the sounds of the room, the creak of wood, the faint rustle of wind outside. He wanted to study, to analyze, to ask questions—but all he could do was blink and gurgle softly.

Somewhere beyond, unseen and unreachable, the Divine Beings watched in silence once more, their radiance faint against the sky.

And in that quiet moment, Saitou—now reborn—took his first steps into a world he did not yet understand, his mind still carrying the weight of a life that should have been forgotten.

His second life had truly begun.

### Chapter 2: 1: The First Light

#### Scene 1

Days became weeks, and weeks slowly turned into months. The world around him began to make more sense—the soft colors, the sounds, the warmth of his home. His body grew stronger, though not enough to stand. For now, crawling was all he could do.

He pushed himself across the wooden floor, his small hands trembling as they pressed against the surface. Each movement felt clumsy and heavy, but it was progress. He could reach the small toys scattered near his bed, and sometimes, his mother would laugh softly when he tried to follow her across the room.

‘My mind’s sharp, but this body… it just won’t listen,’ he thought. Every small motion required effort. His muscles refused to obey as they once did. ‘I can analyze complex equations but can’t even walk properly. How ironic.’

Every night, just before bed, his mother would lift him gently into her lap near the window where moonlight pooled across the wooden floor. The world outside would fade into silence as she opened a small book and began to read, her voice calm and warm. The words were still foreign to him, but their rhythm, their rise and fall, fascinated him.

He sat nestled against her chest, feeling the soft beat of her heart as she spoke. Each sound she made echoed clearly in his mind. He didn’t understand the meaning yet, but he memorized the way the words flowed, how her tone softened at certain parts, how her lips shaped every syllable. When she closed the book, he murmured softly, repeating fragments of sound without realizing it, like a baby imitating a lullaby.

At first, she looked surprised, then smiled and kissed his forehead. “You’re such a clever little one,” she said in that language he barely grasped.

‘Clever, huh?’ he mused. ‘If only you knew I’m an adult trapped in this body.’

He spent every day listening to her voice and repeating the strange new words until they began to take shape in his mind. Sounds became patterns. Patterns became language.

Though he could not yet speak properly, he began to understand her stories—the tales of heroes, of stars, and of the Divine Beings who watched over the world.

Each night, as he lay in his crib, he stared at the ceiling and thought about those Divine Beings. The memory of their light, their voices, still lingered faintly in his heart.

‘If they sent me here,’ he wondered, ‘then there must be a reason.’

But for now, all he could do was listen, learn, and grow in this peaceful home far from the world’s chaos.

As months passed, the days blended into gentle routine. His once fragile arms grew steadier, and his small fingers finally obeyed his will. He could crawl freely now, exploring corners of the wooden house with quiet curiosity. Sometimes his mother would find him under the table, staring at reflections in the glass floor tiles like they were formulas only he could see.

‘I can move better now,’ he thought, dragging himself across the floor. ‘Still no strength to walk though. My balance is awful.’

He often stopped to catch his breath, resting against a chair leg. The rhythm of his heartbeat, the feel of air filling his chest—it all reminded him how real this new life was.

And then one morning, he realized something. ‘How long has it been? A few months? A year?’ He tilted his small head. ‘Wait… how do they even count time here? Days? Weeks? Is it the same rotation, the same stars?’ The thought lingered in his mind like an unfinished equation. ‘I’ll figure it out later… that’s a homework for me—Elrond.’

By the time his first birthday approached, the house began to stir with excitement. Selene prepared garlands of flowers while Aldric polished an old family crest to hang by the doorway. The air smelled faintly of baked bread and herbs, and the neighbors brought small gifts wrapped in colored cloth. In this small town, a child's first year was a celebration of life itself—a promise that the newborn had truly joined their world.

Elrond, meanwhile, could only watch the bustle from his crib, his curious eyes following every movement. ‘All this… for me?’ he wondered, amused. ‘It feels like some grand ritual. I suppose, in a way, it is.’

When evening came, the townsfolk gathered outside the Astrea home. Aldric stood tall, his voice proud yet gentle as he thanked everyone for coming. “Tonight we celebrate the first year of our son’s life,” he announced. “May his future be guided by light and courage.”

Selene stepped forward, holding Elrond close in her arms. The crowd quieted as the couple exchanged a glance filled with love and certainty.

“From this day forward,” Selene said softly, “we name him Elrond—Elrond von Astrea.”

A cheer rose from the townspeople, and the soft glow of lanterns filled the night. Music played, laughter echoed, and warmth spread through the small gathering. Elrond blinked, momentarily stunned by the sound. He had never experienced such pure joy before—not in his old world, not in his sterile lab.

Selene kissed his forehead. “Elrond,” she whispered, “our little light.”

He blinked up at her, tiny hands reaching for her face. For a brief moment, his analytical mind went quiet. All he felt was warmth, belonging, and a strange peace that words couldn’t describe.

‘Elrond von Astrea,’ he thought again, committing it to memory. ‘If this is truly my second life… then maybe I can do it right this time.’

Time passed quickly after that. The seasons shifted, and sunlight poured through the windows in longer streaks. Elrond’s once fragile legs grew stronger, his steps unsteady but full of determination. Each day he tried to walk further—from the crib to the chair, from the chair to the doorway—falling often, laughing softly each time he failed.

‘Finally,’ he thought, wobbling on his tiny feet. ‘My body’s catching up.’

His speech improved too. The nonsense babble of a baby slowly became small, understandable words. He could call his parents by name and respond to simple phrases. To any observer, he was just a clever child— but behind those innocent eyes, a calculating mind quietly measured the world around him.

Lately, his father had become busier. Aldric, Captain of the town guard, often returned late into the night, his armor dusty and his expression weary. Selene would wait by the window, her hands clasped together, eyes fixed on the path leading home.

One evening, Elrond sat on her lap as she stared into the darkness beyond the door. “He’s late again,” she murmured, her voice soft but trembling.

Elrond tilted his head, watching her. ‘Something’s wrong. She’s worried.’ He couldn’t speak much, not enough to ask what was happening. But he could sense the tension in her heartbeat, the way her hand absentmindedly stroked his hair.

He reached up and tugged gently at her sleeve, letting out a cheerful “Ma!” followed by a giggle. Then he clapped his hands and made silly noises, swaying side to side.

Selene blinked, then smiled despite herself. “You little rascal,” she said, kissing his forehead. “Trying to cheer me up, hm?”

He responded with another laugh, pretending to babble nonsense. Inside, though, he thought, ‘At least I can make her smile. That’s something.’

When Aldric finally came home that night, his steps were heavy. “The monsters are getting restless near the eastern woods,” he said quietly, setting down his sword. “We may have to increase patrols.”

Selene’s smile faded, but she nodded. “Just… come home safe.”

Aldric’s eyes softened. He leaned down to kiss her forehead, then lifted Elrond into his arms. “And how’s my little knight doing, huh?”

Elrond laughed again, tiny hands gripping his father’s armor plates.

As the fire crackled beside them, Selene exhaled softly, her worries easing just a little. Elrond, nestled between his parents, felt that same warmth return—a small, fragile peace he wished could last forever.

Time continued its gentle flow, and Elrond’s awareness deepened with it. As his steps grew steadier, he started to notice the patterns of light and dark, the changing air, the rhythm of daily life. Slowly, his logical mind began to assemble what his senses told him.

‘So the sun rises and falls in roughly the same pattern,’ he thought one morning while watching sunlight spill across the wooden floor. ‘Every cycle feels like twenty-four hours. Even the word they use—’ he paused, recalling a recent conversation he overheard—‘“year”… it’s the same. Seasons, months, days… this world follows the same count.’ He let out a small sigh. ‘So this really is… another Earth? Or maybe something closer than I thought.’

It was both comforting and eerie. The familiarity of time’s passage made him feel grounded, yet it also raised questions that lingered in the corners of his mind.

Another night came. The sound of boots on stone echoed outside before the door creaked open. Aldric stepped in, exhaustion painted across his face, monster blood still drying on his armor. Selene gasped softly, rushing to meet him.

“Aldric! You’re hurt—”

He shook his head. “It’s not mine.” His tone was firm, though his eyes were distant. “The monsters are acting strange. They’re moving in clusters now, like something’s driving them out of the deeper woods.”

Selene frowned, worry clouding her gentle features. “Driven out? By what?”

“I don’t know,” Aldric said, unfastening his gauntlets. “But if something larger is behind it, we’ll need to prepare. I’ve already sent a notice to the garrison. We’ll form a scouting unit at dawn.”

Elrond watched from Selene’s arms, his small hands gripping her sleeve. The air felt heavier than usual. Even as a child, he could sense the tension behind his father’s calm words.

Aldric continued quietly, his voice lowering. “The eastern wood’s magic stone was damaged in the last attack. It’s disrupting the barrier field.”

Selene’s eyes widened. “The stone? If that’s broken, the town’s defense will weaken.”

“That’s why I need you,” Aldric said. “You’re the only one who can repair the enchantment properly. We’ll go together.”

Selene hesitated. “An expedition, then.”

Aldric nodded. “Yes. We move in two days.”

That night, after Aldric had gone to rest, Selene sat by the fire in silence. Elrond, sensing her unease, climbed awkwardly into her lap. He babbled a string of cheerful sounds and patted her cheek with his tiny hand.

She smiled faintly, brushing her fingers through his hair. “You always know how to make me smile, don’t you?”

Elrond laughed softly in return, but behind his innocent eyes, his thoughts were elsewhere. ‘A magic stone that controls a barrier… this world’s structure really is built on magical theory. I need to remember every detail. There’s so much I still don’t understand.’

The fire flickered gently, casting shadows across the room. The night outside was calm, yet something in the air hinted that peace would not last forever.

The expedition day arrived under a pale blue sky. The crisp morning air carried a faint chill, and the streets of the small town buzzed with tension and movement. Soldiers from the Althein military unit had already gathered near the eastern gate—armored warriors, archers with quivers slung over their shoulders, and magicians in long robes etched with shimmering runes. Twenty-five in total, all ready to march into the woods.

At the front of the formation stood their leader, a tall man with sandy-blond hair tied neatly behind his head, his armor polished to a noble shine. His name was Commander Lucen Halberg, a noble of Althein known for his disciplined leadership and cautious temperament. His family crest—a silver hawk over twin swords—was engraved on his chestplate.

Aldric exchanged a firm handshake with him. “Commander Halberg, thank you for answering the request so swiftly.”

Lucen nodded. “If the eastern barrier stone is damaged, it concerns more than this town, Captain Astrea. We’ll proceed carefully. I expect your experience in the region will guide us.”

“I’ll take the lead team,” Aldric replied. “My wife, Selene, will handle the restoration. She’s the only mage here capable of repairing a core enchantment.”

As Lucen’s gaze shifted toward her, he paused briefly. Something in her face stirred a faint memory— familiar yet distant. Her calm poise, the refined way she carried herself, it reminded him of someone from the noble circles of Althein’s capital. He blinked once, concealing the recognition behind a courteous nod, deciding not to mention it.

Selene stood nearby, adjusting the straps of her satchel filled with magic tools and crystal shards. Her expression was calm, but her eyes betrayed quiet worry. “It shouldn’t take long once we reach the stone… as long as the damage isn’t too deep.”

Lucen said nothing for a long while. He looked ahead, his thoughts drifting. There had been stories— rumors of a young noblewoman who vanished years ago after swearing a binding Vow Magic with her house’s leader, made to ensure she would never reveal her noble origins after marrying a commoner. He wondered if this woman before him was that very person, now living quietly far from the capital’s watchful eyes.

Standing nearby was a young maid with chestnut hair tied in a simple braid, dressed neatly in a blue apron. Her name was Mira, a caretaker newly working in the Astrea household but already well-known and trusted among the townsfolk. She and Selene had known each other for some time, their bond built through shared work and quiet understanding.

Before they departed, Selene knelt down beside Elrond, who sat on the porch, holding a small wooden toy. He looked up at her, eyes wide and curious.

Selene smiled softly and stroked his hair. “Be a good boy, alright? Mama and Papa will be back soon.”

Elrond reached out his tiny hand, gripping her fingers tightly. He wanted to speak—to tell her to be careful —but his baby voice could only manage a faint, drawn-out “Ma…”

A warm laugh came from behind. “He doesn’t want to let you go,” Aldric said, crouching down beside them. “That’s my son.”

Selene’s eyes softened. “He’s grown attached to us quickly. We should hurry back before he cries himself tired.”

They both smiled, though worry lingered between them.

“Mira,” Selene said gently, “please look after him while we’re gone.”

The maid nodded, bowing lightly. “Of course, Lady Selene. I’ll keep him safe and happy.”

Elrond turned his gaze toward the soldiers assembling outside, their armor gleaming in the light. ‘So this world really does have its own military structure,’ he thought. ‘Knights, magicians, formations… it’s organized, not unlike Earth’s forces.’

As the horns signaled departure, Aldric placed a hand over his wife’s shoulder. “Let’s move.”

Selene gave Elrond one last smile. “We’ll be back before nightfall.”

He watched them go—his small hands gripping the edge of the porch rail—as the group marched toward the horizon where the forest loomed.

Mira knelt beside him, smiling gently. “Don’t worry, young master. Your parents are strong.”

Elrond only nodded faintly, eyes still fixed on the path. ‘Strong or not,’ he thought, ‘something about this feels… uneasy.’

The sound of marching feet faded into the wind, leaving behind the quiet hum of the village—and a feeling deep in Elrond’s heart that the peace of this town might not last much longer.

The expedition group began their march shortly after sunrise. Twenty-five members strong, composed of both the Althein military garrison and local guards, they rode in formation on horseback along the dirt road leading east. Armor clinked with every motion, the faint sound of hooves merging with the rustling wind. Their pace was steady, cautious. The eastern wood was notorious for its unpredictability—monsters that appeared from nowhere, bandits taking advantage of weak patrols—so the group kept their senses sharp.

Aldric rode near the front, his hand never far from the hilt of his sword. Behind him, Selene sat gracefully on her horse, a leather satchel of magical instruments secured at her side. The scent of damp earth and distant pine filled the air.

Commander Lucen Halberg rode beside her, the reins of his horse held loosely in one gloved hand. After a long silence, he finally spoke. “Forgive my curiosity, Lady Selene, but have we met before? Your face… it feels strangely familiar to me.”

Selene blinked, her expression remaining composed. “Perhaps in passing, Commander. I once lived in the capital… but it has been many years.” Her tone was polite but reserved.

Lucen tilted his head. “The capital, you say? Then it makes sense. I recall seeing someone much like you at one of the royal convocations years ago—though I couldn’t quite place which house she belonged to.”

For a moment, Selene hesitated. Her hand unconsciously brushed against the faint mark on her wrist—a small sigil, nearly invisible under her glove. “I… was once part of a noble family,” she admitted softly. “A rather high one, in fact. But I took a vow long ago never to speak of it again.”

At that, Lucen’s eyes widened slightly. “A Vow Magic…?”

Selene nodded faintly. “Yes. Bound by my own choice.” Her gaze turned forward, eyes reflecting the morning light. “Please forgive me if I can’t speak further, Commander. The vow ensures my silence.”

Lucen said nothing for a long while. He looked ahead, his thoughts drifting. There had been stories— rumors of a young noblewoman who vanished years ago after swearing a binding Vow Magic with her house’s leader, made to ensure she would never reveal her noble origins after marrying a commoner. He wondered if this woman before him was that very person, now living quietly far from the capital’s watchful eyes.

After traveling along the dirt road for hours, the sun climbed high into the sky before dipping toward the west. Half a day had passed, and the expedition finally reached the edge where the proper road ended, giving way to the tangled roots and towering trees of the eastern woods. The air here was heavier, filled with the earthy scent of moss and the faint hum of mana drifting through the forest.

Lucen raised his hand, signaling the group to halt. Horses pawed at the ground, snorting softly, their riders straightening in their saddles.

“We’ve reached the perimeter,” Lucen announced. “From here on, we proceed on guard. The monsters here aren’t to be taken lightly.”

Aldric nodded, scanning the treeline. “Agreed. It’ll take another half-day to reach the stone. We should move deeper before we rest.”

The commander looked at the sky—the light was fading to the soft glow of late afternoon. “Then we’ll make camp once we’ve reached the inner clearing. The sun will be down by then.”

The group moved forward once more, slower now, weaving through narrow paths between the thick trees. Leaves brushed against their armor as the sounds of wildlife faded into the deeper, uneasy silence of the woods. Even the birds seemed to avoid this place.

Selene rode quietly near Aldric, her gaze occasionally drifting to the forest’s shifting shadows. “The mana here feels… distorted,” she murmured.

Aldric nodded. “The monsters’ aggression must’ve disrupted the flow.”

By the time the sky began to darken, they found a clearing surrounded by moss-covered stones and ancient trees. Lucen signaled for the halt again. “We camp here. Set the perimeter spells and torches. Mages, ensure the barrier is stable.”

The soldiers dismounted, moving efficiently as tents were raised and fires kindled. The faint light of magic circles shimmered across the clearing, forming protective layers.

Aldric helped Selene down from her horse, his voice low. “We’ll start early tomorrow. Get some rest while we can.”

Selene nodded, brushing her hair from her face. “Understood.”

As the night settled, the rhythmic crackle of campfires and the low murmur of conversation filled the air. Somewhere in the distance, a faint howl echoed—too far to threaten, but close enough to remind everyone why they were there.

Even with the mana barrier raised, tension hung thick in the air. The faint shimmer of the protective spell wrapped the camp in a soft glow, but Selene knew too well that some creatures could still slip through the magical field. Their presence would distort the barrier’s mana flow—something she and the other mages had to monitor constantly.

Archers took positions along the perimeter, their keen eyes scanning the darkness beyond the torchlight. Warriors and guards took shifts patrolling in pairs, while the magicians kept the barrier stable from the center. The faint hum of mana and the rhythmic crackle of fire merged into a haunting harmony of vigilance.

Aldric moved from one patrol post to another, checking on his men. He met Lucen near the largest campfire at the center, where sparks danced upward into the night sky.

Lucen exhaled slowly, staring into the flames. “Even with the barrier active, I can’t bring myself to rest. The mana flow in this forest feels… alive. Too alive.”

Aldric nodded, removing his gloves and warming his hands by the fire. “I feel it too. The beasts here— something’s driving them closer to the surface. If a higher-tier monster is moving its pack, that could explain the recent attacks.”

Lucen’s gaze sharpened. “Then we’ll need to be ready. If it comes to that, the garrison will hold the line.”

Silence lingered between them for a moment, broken only by the crackling fire and the distant rustle of trees.

After a while, Lucen spoke again, quieter this time. “Captain Astrea… may I ask you something personal?”

Aldric looked up. “Go ahead.”

Lucen hesitated, his tone cautious. “Did you, too, make a Vow Magic? Like Lady Selene?”

Aldric blinked, then chuckled lightly. “No. I didn’t need to. I have no noble blood to hide.” He poked the fire absently with a stick. “Selene’s vow was something between her and her family’s head. It was a condition for her to be allowed to marry me.”

Lucen raised a hand gently, stopping him. “No need, Captain. Out of respect for Lady Selene and her family, I would rather not know the name. Let her past stay buried, as she wished. The story alone is enough.”

Aldric hesitated, then gave a quiet nod. “As you wish, Commander.” He stared into the fire, his voice softening. “Still… sometimes I wonder if she ever regrets it. The life she left behind was something most could only dream of. Power, luxury, recognition… all gone because she chose me.”

Lucen looked at him thoughtfully. “She never strikes me as someone who regrets her choices.”

A faint, conflicted smile crossed Aldric’s face. “No. She never does. She smiles every time I come home, no matter how tired I am. But I can’t help feeling that what she lost… was far too much.”

Lucen’s gaze softened. “And yet, in that smile, you find her peace—and yours.”

Aldric chuckled weakly. “Maybe. Or maybe I’m just trying to believe that.”

Lucen nodded in understanding. “You know, Captain… the reason I asked about Lady Selene’s vow wasn’t out of curiosity alone.”

Aldric glanced toward him. “Oh?”

Lucen gave a short, humorless laugh. “I once had a similar chance. There was someone I wished to protect —someone not of noble birth at all. A commoner.” He smiled faintly, his gaze distant. “She worked in my family’s estate, tending to the gardens. I thought I could change everything—defy the expectations of my house, break the chains of rank. I truly believed love would be enough.” He shook his head slowly. “But unlike you, I failed to make it happen.”

Aldric frowned softly. “Failed?”

“Yes,” Lucen replied. “My family refused to even hear of it. They said a Halberg could never disgrace his lineage by taking a commoner as his wife. I fought back, but I was too young, too bound by duty to oppose them. In the end, she was dismissed from our estate, and I never saw her again. Not long after, my family arranged my marriage—to a noblewoman I had never met.”

He paused, eyes distant, watching the fire’s embers drift upward. “She’s a good person, my wife. Kind and dutiful. But… the heart does not always follow the logic of bloodlines.”

Aldric listened quietly, his expression softening with empathy. “You sound like you still carry that weight, Commander.”

Lucen gave a quiet nod. “Perhaps. Or maybe I just envy those who found the strength to follow their hearts. You and Lady Selene… you remind me of what I couldn’t do.”

Aldric smiled faintly, though his gaze remained distant. “It wasn’t easy. We lost much to gain this peace. But I’d choose it again if I had to.”

Lucen returned the smile, weary but sincere. “Then I’ll drink to that once we’re home.”

The two men fell silent again, the fire crackling between them. Above, the moonlight filtered through the branches, silver and cold. The forest around them whispered softly, as if listening to their shared confessions.

Neither man noticed the faint ripple in the barrier’s glow—just at the edge of the clearing—where something large brushed against the mana field before slipping back into the dark.

It seemed to be a peaceful night after all. The guards kept their rotations steady, and the faint hum of the mana barrier stayed undisturbed. No monster breached the line, and even the usual sounds of the forest faded to a quiet calm. Lucen finally allowed himself to rest, handing command to the next watch before settling into his tent to wait for his turn at dawn.

Morning came, soft rays of sunlight piercing through the canopy above. Dew sparkled over the grass, and the cool air carried the fresh scent of the forest. One by one, the resting members stirred awake. Aldric, Selene, and the rest of the off-duty soldiers stepped out from their tents, stretching stiff limbs and greeting the new day with weary but ready faces.

Selene and a few of the magicians walked down to a nearby stream to wash their faces and gather water. The river shimmered faintly under the sunlight, reflecting the green hues of the forest. Aldric joined them a moment later, crouching to splash his face with the cold water. “A good sign,” he murmured, glancing at the still trees. “If the monsters were near, the water wouldn’t be this calm.”

Lucen approached, fastening his armor straps as he spoke. “Then we take it as a blessing. Once everyone’s packed, we move.”

After breaking camp and erasing traces of their presence, the group mounted their horses once more. Their formation tightened as they entered deeper into the forest, the path narrowing between dense walls of foliage. The morning light dimmed gradually, replaced by the emerald shade of the towering trees.

Hours passed in steady rhythm—the muffled thud of hooves on damp soil, the distant chirp of unseen birds, and the occasional hum of mana drifting through the air. By midday, they emerged into an open area bathed in filtered sunlight.

“We’re here,” Lucen announced, pulling his reins. Before them stood the site of the Eastern Magic Stone—an ancient formation surrounded by weathered stones and overgrown roots. A small wooden shelter stood nearby, half-buried under vines and leaves, built long ago to provide mages rest after their work.

The warriors dismounted, spreading out to secure the area. Some cleared away the plants covering the shelter while others checked the ground for tracks. One of the soldiers called out suddenly, his tone uneasy. “Commander! You’ll want to see this!”

Lucen and Aldric strode forward, Selene following close behind. What they saw stopped them cold.

The Magic Stone—the heart of the eastern barrier—was shattered. Not merely cracked or chipped, but destroyed completely. Large fragments lay scattered across the ground, their once-glowing surfaces now dull and lifeless. Deep gouges scored the earth around it, as if something massive had torn through the area with overwhelming force.

Aldric crouched beside one of the shards, running a hand over the smooth edge. “These aren’t the marks of tools,” he said grimly. “Something tore it apart.”

Selene’s eyes widened as she traced the lingering mana residue in the air. “The distortion… it’s enormous. Whatever did this wasn’t a normal monster.”

Lucen’s jaw tightened. “Then we’re not dealing with chance. This was an attack.” He looked to Aldric. “Form a perimeter. We’ll need to stay alert while Lady Selene examines the fragments. If this continues, the entire eastern defense line could collapse.”

Lucen then turned to Selene. “Lady Selene, how long can the residue barrier from this stone hold before it completely fades?”

Selene knelt beside one of the shards, her hand hovering above its surface as faint traces of blue mana drifted upward. “At this rate… perhaps a day, maybe two at most before the residual mana disperses. After that, the barrier protecting the town will fully collapse.”

Lucen frowned. “And to rebuild it?”

“It will take at least half a day to reconstruct the base formation, longer if the mana flow is unstable,” Selene replied. “But I can start now. We’ll need a new mana conduit and a stable channel core to rebind it.”

“Understood,” Lucen said, his tone sharpening. “We’ll make sure you have the time you need. Aldric, tighten the perimeter. Have your men check the perimeter for any mana fluctuations or heat signatures.”

Aldric gave a short nod and began issuing orders. “You heard the Commander! Spread out in pairs, keep line of sight. Archers, take high ground if you can. Magicians—support Lady Selene.”

The clearing shifted into disciplined motion. Warriors raised torches, magicians adjusted their staves, and the hum of detection spells filled the air.

Lucen looked to one of the senior magicians. “Conduct a wide-range scan of the forest. I want every trace of mana fluctuation within two kilometers identified. If there’s something large out there, I want to know before it finds us.”

The magician saluted and began chanting, his hands weaving intricate symbols as glowing circles expanded outward in waves of pale light. The air pulsed faintly with each surge, like ripples spreading across still water.

The rest of the squad fell silent, watching the forest beyond. The faint hum of mana grew stronger, accompanied by a slow, rhythmic vibration deep in the ground.

Lucen’s eyes narrowed. “Prepare for the worst. Whatever destroyed that stone may still be nearby.”

The magic scans spread slowly, rippling outward across the forest. Each pulse of mana shimmered faintly through the air, disappearing into the distance before returning as faint echoes of energy. The magicians maintained focus, their eyes closed, whispering incantations as the range widened.

After several minutes, one of the magicians suddenly opened his eyes, his voice tense. “Commander! We’ve detected movement—something big. I can’t identify the exact type, but it’s enormous. And… it’s not alone.”

Lucen turned sharply toward him. “How far?”

“Roughly one kilometer east, closing slowly,” the magician replied, beads of sweat forming on his forehead. “Smaller mana signatures are moving with it. Possibly a pack.”

Lucen’s jaw tightened. “Keep tracking its direction. Focus all detection spells on that sector.”

“Yes, Commander!” the magician replied, focusing again as glowing runes formed beneath his feet.

Lucen drew his sword, its silver edge glinting faintly in the dim light. “All units—prepare defensive formation. Four warriors will stay behind to guard Lady Selene and the magicians. Everyone else, form up on me.”

Aldric stepped forward beside him. “Understood.” He barked orders across the clearing, and the men quickly adjusted positions, creating a protective circle around the mages.

Meanwhile, Selene and the magicians began a secondary enchantment, their voices weaving in unison as ancient glyphs burned faintly into the ground. The air vibrated with power as they invoked the old magic of protection—the same spell used to safeguard towns and even kingdoms from monster incursions.

Selene’s voice was calm but resolute. “This stone was supposed to be indestructible,” she said under her breath. “Compressed mana lattice, ancient runic core—it shouldn’t break under any natural force. Which means…”

Aldric finished her thought grimly. “Something unnatural did this.”

Lucen nodded, his gaze locked toward the eastern tree line. “That’s why this mission fell to me. If something out there can destroy a magic stone, it threatens not just this town—but the whole eastern frontier.”

The chanting grew louder, the light from the barrier expanding in a radiant circle around Selene’s squad. The wind shifted suddenly, carrying a faint, guttural roar from the forest’s depths.

Lucen’s hand tightened around his sword hilt. “Positions! Eyes forward! Whatever’s out there—it’s coming.”

As the magic enchantment continued, the tension within the group grew thicker. The faint light from the spell circles cast long shadows over the ground, reflecting in the eyes of every warrior standing guard. The soldiers gripped their weapons tighter, waiting for the first sign of movement.

Selene’s team maintained their chant, channeling mana into the shattered fragments of the stone. Each verse resonated with ancient power, stabilizing the surrounding flow of energy. The air hummed, thick with pressure, as the barrier’s incomplete structure began to take form.

But this was also the dangerous part.

Lucen knew it too well—magic stones were natural mana conduits. While mages restored their energy flow, the stones emitted faint pulses of pure mana that spread through the environment like a beacon. Monsters, drawn by instinct, would often approach to feed from that energy. Normally, they stayed at a distance, wary of human presence. But if something larger lurked nearby, it would break that fragile balance.

The commander watched the forest edge, every sense sharp. “Stay alert. The restoration’s pulse will attract them,” he ordered quietly.

Aldric nodded, gripping his sword. “Understood. Keep formation!”

Selene continued her focus, sweat beading down her temple as she synchronized her mana with the others. The shattered pieces of the magic stone began to glow faintly again, threads of light weaving between the fragments.

From the front line, one of the archers whispered, “Movement at the edge! Shadows… too many to count.”

Lucen raised his hand. “Hold position. Do not fire unless I command it.”

The trees swayed under an unseen wind, leaves rustling in unnatural rhythm. The faint mana pulse from the partially reactivated stone resonated through the clearing, and the faint growls of beasts echoed in response.

Selene’s voice rose slightly over the hum of magic. “Just a little longer—we’re close to stabilizing the conduit!”

Lucen’s eyes narrowed toward the treeline. “Make it fast,” he said under his breath, “because they’re already coming.”

### Chapter 3: 2: Magic Stone Restoration

#### Scene 1

The atmosphere grew tense as the enchantments deepened. The faint glow of the barrier cast a silver haze across the clearing, while the rhythmic chants of magicians filled the air. Their words intertwined with the whisper of the wind, forming an ancient melody of power.

The offensive magicians began their preparation, forming a secondary layer of support spells. Circles of light appeared beneath their feet, each one humming with raw mana.

“Defensive enchantments first!” barked one of the senior mages. “Then strengthen the front line!”

Bright lines of sigils spread outward from the center. The Defense Spell wrapped the entire formation in a faint, translucent dome, thickening the air around them like an invisible wall.

Next came the Strength Enhancement Spell, an old combat rite known for pushing warriors to their physical limits. As the chant rose, faint crimson light began to cling to the soldiers’ armor and skin, the condensed mana amplifying their vitality and power. The pressure was heavy—every breath felt like inhaling fire.

Lucen felt the change immediately, his muscles tensing beneath his armor. “Remember to control your movements. This spell will make you stronger but slower if you overexert.”

The enhancement came with risk. Too much mana density in the bloodstream caused resistance—a slowing of reflexes, a dulling of speed. The magicians knew this, and so they tuned the spell to a cautious balance. But because they were casting for a large group, the precision equation for each person’s limit was lost. The enhancement had to remain general, a compromise between strength and stamina.

To balance it, the Agility Spell followed next. Blue light streaked through the air, mixing with the crimson hue. The warriors felt a sudden lightness in their limbs as mana flow redirected from muscle density to movement channels. The two spells—the embodiment of power and precision—needed to exist in harmony.

Too much strength would lead to exhaustion and broken form. Too much agility, and every swing would lose impact. The perfect equilibrium required instinct and control.

Lucen steadied his breathing. “You all know the principle—find your own balance. Don’t rely on the magic alone. Use your training.”

“Yes, Commander!” the soldiers responded, gripping their weapons as light pulsed faintly around them.

The air vibrated with combined mana fields, and the forest responded in kind. The ground shuddered as mana waves rippled outward—signals that something enormous was drawing closer.

Selene looked up briefly from her enchantment circle. “Lucen, the restoration field’s mana output is stabilizing, but the signal is still active. Monsters will sense this as free-flowing energy. We’re running out of time.”

Lucen’s jaw clenched. “Then we finish before they reach us. All units—prepare for engagement. Protect the magicians at all costs.”

The soldiers adjusted formation, weapons gleaming beneath the waning sunlight. The sound of steel locking into place echoed like a heartbeat against the low hum of magic.

And somewhere beyond the trees, a roar answered.

The roar echoed through the forest, low and thunderous, shaking leaves loose from the canopy above. The soldiers tightened their grips on their weapons as the sound grew closer—snarls and heavy footsteps reverberating through the woods.

From the shadows between the trees, a pair of glowing yellow eyes emerged, followed by a hulking silhouette. The creature stepped into the faint light of the barrier—a wolf, but nothing like the kind they had seen before. Its fur shimmered dark like obsidian, with streaks of silver mana running along its limbs. The beast’s size dwarfed even the largest of horses, its shoulder towering above a grown man.

The magicians froze, their chants faltering for a moment.

One of them whispered in disbelief, “An… Amarok.”

Lucen’s expression hardened. “An evolved beast. So it’s true.”

The Amarok let out a guttural snarl, its breath visible in the cooling air. Then, from behind it, smaller shapes moved—dozens of glowing eyes flickering through the treeline. Wolves of varying sizes stepped into view, their numbers growing with every heartbeat.

“By the gods…” muttered one of the soldiers. “There’s at least twenty—no, thirty of them.”

Aldric drew his sword, the steel catching the dying sunlight. “That explains it,” he said grimly. “This is why the monsters were pushed out from the deeper woods. They were fleeing this thing.”

Lucen raised his hand. “Form up! Archers, to the rear! Swordsmen, brace the front line! Magicians—continue the restoration, but be ready to reinforce the barrier if it breaks!”

The Amarok threw back its head and howled, the sound cutting through the forest like thunder. The smaller wolves followed, their collective voices forming a chilling chorus.

Selene’s voice trembled but remained steady as she refocused her magic. “We have to finish the restoration before they strike, or the barrier will collapse completely!”

Lucen stepped forward, blade raised. “Then we’ll buy you that time.”

The wolves’ glowing eyes tightened around the clearing, their growls rising as the Amarok led the charge.

The battle for the Eastern Magic Stone had begun.

Lucen charged forward, sword gleaming with enchanted light, drawing the Amarok’s attention instantly. The colossal beast snarled, its claws gouging deep trenches in the soil as it lunged toward him. Their blades of light and fang of darkness met in a shockwave that rippled through the clearing, shaking trees and scattering leaves.

The clash between man and monster erupted into chaos. Lucen moved with precision—each strike powerful and deliberate, his armor resonating with the faint hum of protective magic. The Amarok, however, was faster than its size suggested. It twisted aside from his blade, snapping its jaws at him with enough force to splinter a tree.

Lucen barely dodged, sliding across the ground before striking upward, leaving a deep cut along the beast’s foreleg. Blood hissed as it hit the soil, steaming with mana corruption.

Aldric quickly joined the fray, cutting through lesser wolves that darted at his flank. His movements were steady and efficient, each swing clean and deadly. The surrounding wolves fell one by one, but their numbers kept surging forward. Still, Aldric didn’t falter—his swordsmanship, honed from years on the frontier, was both disciplined and ferocious.

Lucen spared a glance amid the chaos, impressed by Aldric’s control and composure. “So this is the Shield of the South,” he muttered, blocking another swipe from the Amarok. “No wonder Lady Selene chose him.”

The Amarok howled again, forcing Lucen to focus. The sound shattered the lingering magic in the air, disrupting weaker enchantments as it reared up and slammed its front claws into the ground. A wave of shock tore through the battlefield, sending dust and broken roots flying.

“Hold the line!” Lucen roared. “Keep them away from the magicians!”

The soldiers responded with renewed vigor, forming defensive walls around Selene’s circle. Arrows of light and bolts of mana shot through the air, striking the smaller wolves to thin their numbers.

Selene, though tense, never stopped chanting. The broken fragments of the magic stone now pulsed brighter with every verse, responding to her effort.

Aldric intercepted a wolf that broke through the perimeter, cutting it down with a single swing before stepping beside Lucen. “Commander! Focus on the head—its mana flows are concentrated there!”

Lucen nodded sharply. “Then we end this together!”

The Amarok’s eyes flared with raw rage as both men advanced, their blades shining beneath the storm of mana.

Aldric broke formation, his instincts sharp. “Commander! I’ll draw its attention—prepare your strike!”

Lucen gave a quick nod. “Understood!” He stepped back, gathering mana around his sword, the runes on its blade igniting in a white-blue glow.

Aldric charged toward the Amarok, shouting a battle cry that echoed through the forest. The monstrous wolf turned its attention toward him, snapping its massive jaws. Each swing of Aldric’s sword deflected deadly swipes of claws and teeth. He moved with remarkable precision, ducking beneath one strike, rolling past another. His blade carved shallow cuts into the beast’s legs, angering it further.

The Amarok roared and lunged, its maw gaping wide. Aldric twisted aside, leaving deep gashes along its flank, the beast’s mana-rich blood spraying like burning mist. He could feel the tremor of its fury through the ground—but it was working. The Amarok’s attention was locked fully on him.

Behind them, Lucen completed his chant. Magic symbols erupted beneath his feet, forming a circle of radiant light. The ground trembled as his sword blazed brighter, heat distorting the air around it. As a seasoned spellblade, Lucen channeled both martial skill and high-level incantation into one devastating technique.

“Celestial Severance!” he roared, slamming his sword into the ground.

From the point of impact, a colossal blade of light surged upward, piercing through layers of soil and mana. The luminous edge extended like a spear of the heavens, tearing through the forest floor and driving straight into the Amarok’s body from below.

The blast of light consumed the clearing, the force throwing debris and ash into the air. The Amarok howled in agony as the radiant energy exploded through its torso, burning through flesh and bone. Yet, even impaled by divine magic, the beast refused to fall.

Its body convulsed as it unleashed a deafening final howl. The sound shattered focus across the battlefield —mages screamed as their concentration broke, and soldiers clutched their heads as the piercing resonance tore through their eardrums. The air grew frigid, frost spreading rapidly across the ground.

Lucen’s eyes widened. “It’s channeling its last mana!”

The Amarok’s howl transformed into a chilling wind, a mini-blizzard erupting from its core. Ice shards rained down in deadly bursts, slicing through tents and armor. Chaos erupted again—but amid the storm, one senior magician stood motionless, his spell already complete.

He thrust his staff forward and shouted, “Inferno’s Judgment!”

A pillar of fire burst from his circle, engulfing the Amarok in searing flames. The explosion illuminated the clearing in blazing orange, melting frost and vaporizing snow instantly. The ground cracked from the heat.

When the flames subsided, smoke billowed thick and heavy. The Amarok still stood—charred, trembling, its glowing eyes dimming but not yet extinguished.

Aldric’s voice cut through the haze. “Not yet!” He gathered his remaining strength, leaping high into the air with a burst of mana propulsion. His sword gleamed with a golden hue as he descended, shouting a final battle cry.

The blade sliced clean through the Amarok’s neck. A spray of dark blood followed as the beast’s head hit the ground with a thunderous thud.

Silence fell.

The soldiers lowered their weapons, staring in awe as the colossal creature collapsed. The oppressive mana in the air began to fade, replaced by the quiet hum of the recovering forest.

Lucen exhaled heavily, lowering his sword. “It’s over… finally.”

Selene’s hands trembled as she looked up from her circle, her voice barely above a whisper. “The restoration held through the fight. The stone… it’s stabilizing.”

Aldric landed beside Lucen, breathing hard but grinning faintly. “Guess that did it.”

Lucen smirked back, shaking his head. “Remind me never to doubt you again, Captain Astrea.”

Around them, the surviving soldiers began to lower their weapons, some letting out shaky laughs and sighs of relief. A few clapped each other on the shoulder, disbelief and gratitude mixing on their faces. For the first time since the expedition began, the crushing tension in the air eased slightly. They had survived the impossible, and that simple fact was enough to make even the hardest warriors smile.

The two men stood amid the aftermath, surrounded by smoke, ice, and the shattered remnants of battle.

The soldiers began tending to their wounds while magicians stabilized the remaining mana fields. The clearing smelled of ash and frost, a haunting reminder of the battle’s ferocity. Lucen gave orders to secure the perimeter, knowing they had only survived through sheer coordination and resolve.

Aldric sheathed his sword, glancing toward Selene, who continued to channel gentle streams of mana into the repaired stone. Its fractured surface now pulsed with life again—unstable, but glowing.

“Once we return,” Lucen said quietly, “we’ll need to report this to the capital. The appearance of an Amarok so close to civilization means something has changed.”

Aldric nodded. “And we’ll need stronger patrols around the perimeter. If that thing was just a vanguard…” He left the rest unsaid.

Selene turned to them, smiling faintly through her exhaustion. “For now, the stone is holding. But it will still take several hours before full stabilization. We’ll have to maintain the spell until then.”

Lucen nodded grimly. “Then we stay alert. No one relaxes until the mana flow stabilizes completely.”

Aldric looked around the battlefield where the wounded soldiers were being treated. “We’ve got about ten wounded,” he reported. “None dead, thank the gods—but some serious injuries.”

The magicians quickly moved between the injured, channeling healing magic and applying salves where their mana was too depleted to mend flesh. The soldiers who could still stand formed a wide perimeter around the clearing, weapons drawn, watching the dark forest.

Even as calm slowly returned, the air still hummed with unstable energy. The magic stone pulsed faintly, its light flickering in rhythm with Selene’s chant.

Lucen exhaled slowly. “Hold formation. If anything moves out there, I want it dead before it gets close.”

Aldric gave a short nod. “We’ll hold the line. Just keep that stone steady.”

Selene’s voice softened but remained firm. “Don’t worry. It will hold. Just a few more hours.”

The three of them stood beneath the faint glow of the half-restored magic stone, its pulsing light flickering across weary faces. Around them, the remaining soldiers exhaled in relief, tending to the wounded and murmuring quiet thanks that the nightmare was finally over. For a moment, the forest felt calm again—its shadows no longer menacing but still holding secrets beyond reach. Lucen, Aldric, and Selene exchanged a brief, wordless look—an understanding that though this battle had ended, something far greater was waiting beyond the trees.

After a couple of hours, Selene and the other magicians finally completed the restoration of the magic stone. The faint glow intensified until the crystal’s veins of mana shone steady once more, signaling stability. As the last verse of the chant ended, Selene’s legs gave out beneath her—her mana completely drained.

“Selene!” Aldric rushed forward, catching her before she hit the ground. She looked pale but smiled faintly, exhausted. “It’s done,” she whispered weakly. “The stone… it’s finally restored.”

Aldric held her close, relief washing over his face. “You did well. Truly.”

Lucen glanced at the glowing stone, its pulsing light spreading warmth through the clearing. “The barrier’s strengthening again. The worst is over.”

The soldiers, still alert, began to lower their weapons. Some sat on the ground, bandaging wounds or tending to their comrades. Ten men lay on stretchers, breathing but battered, their armor cracked from the earlier battle. The medics and magicians moved between them, administering what healing spells they could.

“Maintain the perimeter for another hour,” Lucen ordered. “Once the barrier stabilizes, we rest.”

The sky dimmed toward evening, streaks of orange filtering through the canopy. As the light softened, Aldric and Lucen oversaw the group setting up a proper camp beside the wooden shelter near the magic stone. It would be the safest place to rest—protected by the restored barrier’s reach.

Torches flickered to life, and the smell of cooked rations filled the air. The exhausted but relieved expedition members finally allowed themselves to breathe. The battle had ended, but the memory of the Amarok’s howl still lingered faintly in their minds.

Lucen sat by the campfire, his sword across his knees, eyes fixed on the now-peaceful glow of the magic stone. “We’ll leave at first light,” he said quietly. “But tonight—we rest.”

Meanwhile, back in town, on the day after the group left for the expedition, Elrond was being taken care of by Mira, the hired maid. During his parents’ absence, the little boy—now three years old—had grown curious and restless. With stable steps and boundless curiosity, he decided to explore the house further while Mira was busy with the morning chores.

Until now, he had never managed to reach the second floor where his mother’s study was. The staircase had always seemed daunting—tall, wooden steps that towered over his small frame. But today, with determination shining in his young eyes, Elrond began his climb.

He placed one tiny foot after another, gripping the railing with both hands. Each step creaked softly beneath his weight. His small legs trembled, but he pressed on. After what felt like an eternity, he reached the top.

Panting softly, Elrond looked down the hallway, noticing the faint smell of parchment and herbs drifting from the door at the far end. That was his mother’s room—the one she always kept closed.

Driven by curiosity, he shuffled forward and pushed the door open.

Inside, he was met with a sight that made his eyes widen. The room was filled with books, scrolls, and half- finished experiments. Crystals of various colors floated inside glass containers, faintly glowing. Papers covered the desk, filled with handwritten notes and strange diagrams. It looked messy yet oddly comfortable—a place that pulsed with life and knowledge.

Elrond stepped inside slowly, his gaze darting from one shelf to another. “So this… is where Mother works,” he whispered to himself, the faint echo of his voice mingling with the hum of magic in the air.

His fingers brushed against the edge of the desk, where a small crystal orb shimmered faintly. It reminded him of something—of formulas, energy flows, resonance patterns. His mind, though trapped in a child’s body, stirred with the logic of the man he once was.

‘Just like back then,’ he thought. ‘Only this time… it’s magic, not science.’

He smiled faintly, the memory of his past life flashing through his thoughts.

But he didn’t want to make the same mistake as in his past life. This time, he would do things differently— he would learn, grow, and become someone better. The thought filled him with quiet determination.

Elrond continued to look around, his eyes wide with wonder. Shelves lined every wall, overflowing with books and scrolls. He tried reading a few titles, but the words made no sense to him yet. The letters shimmered faintly with magic, written in the script of this world.

Still, he didn’t give up. He searched through cabinets and boxes, hoping to find something he could understand. Inside one of the boxes, buried beneath layers of parchment, he found a leather-bound book. The cover was rough, decorated with a faint insignia of crossed blades.

“A sword manual?” he murmured curiously. He opened the first page—it was filled with basic sketches and stances for sword combat. “This must be Father’s,” he thought, tilting his head. “But why is it here, in Mother’s room? Or maybe… she once wanted to learn, too.”

He closed the book carefully and set it aside by the door, deciding to read it later when Mira wasn’t watching.

His gaze drifted upward toward the tall bookshelf that stretched almost to the ceiling. There were dozens of books stacked neatly there, their titles faintly glowing under the light of floating crystals. Squinting, he began scanning each spine one by one until something caught his eye.

“The Basics of Magic,” he whispered first, spotting the title among several similar tomes—Basic Elemental Theory, Introduction to Mana Control, Foundations of Spellcraft, and Elemental Arts Primer. His heartbeat quickened as he realized how many different books about magic his mother kept here. Magic—he had always been fascinated by it. The first time he saw his mother conjure water to tend the plants or create a small flame to light a lantern, he had thought it was some kind of trick. But after seeing it again and again, he knew—it was real.

“I want to learn it too…” he murmured softly.

But the book sat high on the shelf, far beyond his reach. Elrond frowned, tapping his chin. With his three- year-old body, he barely reached the shoulder height of an adult, and the shelf towered twice that.

He began to look around the room for something to help—a stool, a crate, anything he could climb on. His eyes scanned the floor carefully until he spotted a small wooden chair tucked beneath the desk.

‘That should work,’ he thought, dragging it toward the shelf with effort. His small hands gripped the chair’s legs as he positioned it just beneath the row where the book sat.

He climbed onto it, wobbling slightly but steadying himself with the edge of the bookshelf. The glowing book seemed to call to him, its faint hum resonating with something deep inside his mind.

“Almost there…” he whispered, stretching his arm upward.

He reached higher, his small fingers brushing the edge of the book’s spine. “Just… a little… more…” he whispered, standing on tiptoe. The chair wobbled beneath him, creaking from the strain.

With one final pull, the book came loose—but the sudden release threw him off balance. “Ah—!” Elrond yelped as the chair tipped backward. He fell, hitting the floor with a loud thud.

The noise echoed through the house.

“Master Elrond?!” Mira’s voice came from downstairs. The sound of hurried footsteps followed, and within seconds, the maid burst into the room, her face pale with worry.

She gasped when she saw him lying on the floor, clutching his back in pain. “Oh heavens—are you hurt?” she cried, rushing over. She knelt beside him, gently lifting him into her arms. “Does it hurt badly? What were you doing up here?”

Elrond winced, trying to catch his breath. He couldn’t tell her he was reaching for a book on magic—it would sound strange, even suspicious for a child his age. Before he could respond, Mira’s eyes caught the faint glow of a crystal on the nearby shelf.

“Oh… I see,” she said softly, misunderstanding. “You wanted to reach this glowing crystal, didn’t you? It’s very pretty, isn’t it?”

Elrond hesitated for a moment, then nodded lightly. “Mm.”

Mira let out a small sigh, shaking her head with a faint smile. “You really are a curious one.” She brushed dust off his clothes and examined his back carefully. “You’re not crying… how brave. But that fall must have hurt.”

She placed her hand gently on his back, a soft light forming at her fingertips. “Don’t move, alright? I’ll heal you.”

A faint warmth spread through his body as Mira murmured a low incantation. The gentle magic mended the small bruises along his back, the pain fading into a tingling comfort.

“There,” she said with relief. “Good as new. But please, Master Elrond, don’t climb dangerous places again. You nearly scared me to death.”

Elrond nodded quietly, his eyes lowering in guilt. “Sorry, Mira…”

She smiled softly and patted his head. “Come on, let’s go downstairs. You should rest.”

As she carried him out of the room, Elrond glanced over her shoulder at the shelf one last time—the book on magic still glowing faintly, waiting for him.

Mira worried that this accident could get her into trouble with Aldric and Selene. With a nervous laugh, she tried to lighten the mood. “Master Elrond, let’s keep this between us, alright? No need to tell your parents about today, hmm?” she said playfully, though her tone carried a hint of genuine concern.

Elrond understood perfectly well—it had been his fault after all. He nodded firmly, giving a small smile. “Okay.”

Relieved, Mira let out a soft laugh. “Good boy. You’re really kind, you know that?” The tension in the air faded as both of them chuckled together, the earlier fright giving way to a moment of warmth.

As she stood, Mira picked up the glowing crystal she thought had caused the commotion. “So this little thing caught your eye, huh?” she said teasingly, showing it to him. Elrond, not wanting her to know his true goal, nodded enthusiastically. “It’s pretty,” he said, pretending to be delighted.

Mira smiled, completely convinced. “Then maybe I’ll put it somewhere you can see it safely next time.”

Time passed quietly after that. Mira brought Elrond downstairs and prepared a small meal—simple vegetable stew with bread. They ate together at the small kitchen table, Mira keeping a close eye on him the whole time. The warm food and soft chatter made the house feel peaceful again.

When they were finished, Mira wiped his face gently with a cloth and carried him to his bed. “You’ve had quite the adventure today,” she said fondly, tucking him under the blanket. “Rest well, young master.”

Elrond yawned, the day’s excitement catching up to him. “Good night, Mira…”

She smiled, brushing his hair aside. “Good night.”

As she dimmed the lamp and left the room, Elrond’s eyes drifted closed—but his thoughts lingered on that glowing bookshelf upstairs, and the secrets waiting within those books of magic.

Morning came softly, sunlight filtering through the curtains. Mira gently shook Elrond awake, her voice cheerful. “Good morning, young master. Time for breakfast.”

Elrond rubbed his eyes sleepily and yawned. The smell of warm bread filled the room, mixed with something creamy and rich. When he reached the table, he was surprised by the sight before him—a plate with milk, eggs, and thick slices of toasted bread.

He blinked. “This looks… fancy,” he murmured, a hint of excitement in his voice. Compared to his usual breakfasts with Selene—simple bread dipped in light broth—this felt almost like a feast.

Mira smiled proudly. “Breakfast should give you strength for the day. Eat plenty.”

Elrond nodded and took a bite. The bread was crisp, the eggs fluffy, and the milk fresh and cool. ‘She’s actually a great cook,’ he thought. ‘Mother’s meals are good too, but Mira’s… have a homely touch. Lighter, but richer somehow.’

As he ate, his mind began to wander. The taste of the food reminded him of something—how similar it all was to medieval cuisine from old history books. Wooden bowls, open flames for cooking, and everything made from scratch. Even the house itself reflected a simpler age.

‘If this really is Earth,’ he thought, ‘then it must be somewhere in the medieval era. Everything’s still so primitive—fire lamps instead of lights, toilets that just… go into the ground, and hardly anyone takes a proper bath.’

He grimaced at that thought, wrinkling his small nose. ‘Ugh… that’s kind of disgusting. I should fix that someday.’

He looked down at his glass of milk, determination flickering in his young eyes. ‘A proper bath system. Clean water, soap, something everyone can use. That’ll be my next goal.’

Mira noticed his expression and chuckled. “You look so serious while eating, Master Elrond. Are you thinking about something grand again?”

Elrond just smiled innocently. “Maybe.”

She laughed and ruffled his hair. “Then make sure you finish your breakfast before your big ideas take over, alright?”

He giggled, nodding eagerly, and took another bite.

Once breakfast was finished, Elrond lingered at the table, his curiosity bubbling up again. His eyes sparkled as he looked at Mira. “Mira, can you use magic?” he asked, his tone filled with innocent excitement, like only a three-year-old could manage.

Mira blinked in surprise, then laughed softly. “Magic? Oh, you mean what I used yesterday when you fell? Yes, a little.” She smiled warmly, setting her cup aside. “Most maids with proper training learn basic spells— small fire and water magic, and a bit of healing. It’s useful for housework and for taking care of people like you.”

Elrond’s eyes widened in amazement. “Wow! So you’re like a magician too?”

She chuckled at his enthusiasm. “Maybe a tiny bit. But I’m nowhere near the real magicians your mother works with. What I know is just the basics—making water boil faster, cleaning stains, healing small bruises. It’s all practical magic.”

She paused for a moment, her tone softening. “Actually, I learned magic a long time ago, when I worked as a monster hunter.”

Elrond gasped, his little hands gripping the table. “You were a monster hunter?!”

Mira nodded, her smile faint but tinged with nostalgia. “Mm-hmm. It was a dangerous job. We fought beasts outside the towns and escorted caravans. But… it wasn’t easy. I had a few close calls—bad ones. So I quit. I wanted a safer, steadier life, and being a maid turned out to be perfect for me.”

Elrond listened with rapt attention, his eyes wide and shining. To him, it sounded like a story out of one of the adventure books his mother read aloud. “That’s amazing! You’re so strong, Mira!”

Her cheeks reddened slightly as she laughed. “You really think so? Well, I guess I had my moments.” She leaned closer, lowering her voice playfully. “But don’t go telling anyone I used to punch monsters, alright?”

Elrond giggled and nodded eagerly. “I won’t! Promise!”

Mira smiled warmly. “Good boy. Now, why don’t we clean up the table before I tell you another story?”

Elrond hopped off his chair, eager to help her carry the dishes. His heart was filled with admiration—and a spark of inspiration. ‘Even Mira can use magic and fight monsters,’ he thought. ‘Then I can too… someday.’

After some time, Mira prepared to head out for shopping. She turned to Elrond, drying her hands on her apron. “I need to go buy some ingredients for lunch. Would you like to come with me, young master?” she asked with her usual bright smile.

Elrond hesitated for a moment, tempted to go. But then he remembered the books upstairs—the ones he hadn’t been able to read yet. The thought of exploring them again made his heart race. “Um… I think I’ll stay here,” he said after a pause, smiling awkwardly.

Mira frowned slightly. “Are you sure? I don’t want you getting bored—or doing something dangerous again.”

Elrond quickly waved his hands, assuring her. “I’ll be good! I promise! I’ll just play quietly.”

Her expression softened, though she still looked uncertain. “Alright, but please stay safe. I won’t be long.”

Once Mira left, Elrond waited until the sound of her footsteps faded outside before hurrying upstairs. His small feet pattered softly against the wooden floor as he reached his mother’s study again.

The books from before were still scattered on the floor from his earlier accident. Mira must have tried tidying them but hadn’t returned them to their shelves. Elrond knelt beside them, carefully picking up the ones he recognized. His eyes immediately found the familiar cover of The Basics of Magic.

He smiled faintly, clutching it against his chest. “Finally…”

He sat by the window where sunlight spilled across the desk and opened the first page. The handwriting was neat but slightly faded, filled with diagrams, symbols, and notes in a language he barely understood. At first, it was confusing—circles, terms, and strange characters that didn’t quite make sense. But Elrond was used to this kind of challenge. He began to read line by line, committing every word and symbol to memory.

His photographic memory worked effortlessly, imprinting the entire text into his mind. Even if he couldn’t grasp the meaning yet, he could review and analyze it later once he learned more.

“This world’s magic system…” he murmured softly, tracing a line of text with his finger. “It’s not that different from energy equations… maybe…”

He spent the next hour quietly reading, occasionally glancing toward the door in case Mira returned early. When his small arms began to ache from holding the heavy book, he decided to hide it away for later.

He stacked the books one by one, carrying them carefully to his room. Each trip up and down the stairs made him pant, but he didn’t stop. When the last one was in place, he wiped his forehead proudly.

“All done,” he whispered, satisfied.

By the time Mira returned from shopping, Elrond was sitting innocently in the living room, pretending to play with his toy blocks. The books were safe—and waiting for him to continue his secret study later.

Mira smiled when she returned and saw Elrond playing quietly on the floor. “Good job, young master,” she said warmly. “You behaved perfectly while I was away.”

Elrond grinned, proud of himself. “I told you I’d be good!”

Mira laughed softly. “That you did.” As she began setting down the groceries, she noticed him yawn widely and rub his eyes. “Oh my, someone looks sleepy,” she said with a teasing tone. “How about a small nap before lunch?”

Elrond hesitated but nodded. “Okay.” Outwardly, he seemed obedient—but inside, his thoughts were already wandering back to the books hidden in his room. ‘Just a little nap,’ he thought. ‘Then I’ll read more later.’

Mira patted his shoulder affectionately. “Such a good boy. Come on, I’ll tuck you in for a bit.”
