He followed her quietly to his room, trying to look as innocent as possible. After she helped him settle under the blanket, Mira smiled. “Rest now, young master. Lunch will be ready when you wake up.”

Elrond nodded, pretending to close his eyes. But even as sleep began to pull at him, a small, excited thought echoed in his mind—I’ll keep learning. No one can stop me from understanding this world.

Once Mira left and began preparing lunch in the kitchen, Elrond opened his eyes. His mind immediately returned to the book he had been reading earlier. Quietly, he slipped out of bed and tiptoed to his room, retrieving The Basics of Magic from its hiding spot.

He climbed onto his small chair and placed the book on his desk. “Let’s see…” he whispered, flipping through the first pages again. The text described something called mana—the life energy flowing within all living beings. To use magic, one had to sense that energy and learn to move it consciously.

Elrond frowned. “Feel the magic energy inside your body…” he repeated softly. “But it doesn’t say how it feels.” He pressed a hand to his chest, closing his eyes. He tried to focus inward, breathing slowly, waiting for something—anything—to happen.

At first, there was nothing. Only the steady beat of his heart.

‘Come on… if it’s energy, then it must move somehow,’ he thought. He pictured the way electrical currents flowed in circuits, or how heat moved through metal. Maybe it was similar—an invisible flow that existed but couldn’t be seen.

Minutes passed. He tried harder, concentrating until his head ached, but still—nothing. No warmth, no tingle, no spark. Only the steady beat of his heart and the sound of his own breathing filled the silence.

He frowned, frustrated. ‘So that’s it? I can’t even feel it?’ He sighed quietly. ‘Maybe it takes more practice… or maybe I just don’t understand how yet.’

He turned the page carefully. The next section explained that if someone managed to feel their mana— something Elrond still couldn’t do—then they could attempt to shape it and transform it into natural energy through focus and willpower. The book gave an example of what came next for those who could already sense it: beginners often tried simple spells like creating a small flame in one’s hand or a light splash of water.

Elrond squinted at the page, his brows furrowed in deep thought. The words were clear enough, but their meaning slipped just beyond his grasp. He read the lines again and again, as if repetition alone could make sense of it. After a pause, his gaze drifted to the example illustration beside the text—a crude drawing of a person holding a hovering flame.

He blinked at it curiously, tilting his head. “If I try water, it’ll just make a mess… maybe fire would be easier,” he muttered softly, thinking aloud as if weighing the idea but still not really understanding what it meant.

The next paragraph mentioned something about enchantments—phrases or sentences that guided intention and gave form to thought. The book noted that meaning mattered more than the exact words themselves. It gave an example of an old phrase: ‘Let warmth be born from my will, and let it take form as flame.’

Elrond traced the sentence with his finger, sounding out each word slowly. He didn’t really understand it, but there was something oddly calming about the way the sentence flowed. It felt more like poetry than instruction.

He stared at the line for a while, then whispered softly, imitating it in his tiny voice: “Let warmth be born… from my will… and take form as flame.”

Elrond kept staring at the page, trying to make sense of the words, but there was no clear answer. He quietly repeated the sentence again, as if saying it one more time would somehow make it work.

At first, the air stayed still—but then, just barely, something stirred. A faint warmth brushed against his fingertips, so light he almost thought he imagined it. His small hand trembled slightly as a dim spark flickered above his palm, fragile and wavering like the breath of a candle.

His eyes widened, and instinctively he whispered the chant again, this time with more focus. The spark reappeared—brighter, steadier. The warmth spread from his fingertips up through his arm, a strange pulse moving beneath his skin like the slow beat of a second heart. The air shimmered faintly as mana, though invisible, began to circulate within him for the first time.

The flame hovered gently above his palm—small, yet alive. Its light reflected in his wide eyes, painting them with faint orange hues.

“I can feel it…” he murmured, barely above a whisper. The sensation was new—soft and warm, yet powerful. It wasn’t just fire; it was his own energy, shaped by his will.

He watched it flicker for several seconds before it slowly faded into smoke once more, leaving behind a faint trace of heat.

Elrond stared at his hand in stunned silence, his chest rising and falling quickly. His heart raced—not from fear, but from exhilaration.

“So that’s… mana,” he breathed, almost reverently. A smile spread across his face, small but filled with wonder.

He had done it. He had felt it—his first true connection to magic.

Elrond couldn’t stop smiling. His whole body tingled with excitement. He clenched his small fists, feeling a faint buzz still lingering under his skin. “I really did it… I used magic,” he whispered to himself, his voice trembling with joy.

Still grinning, he opened the book again and reread the same lines. He wanted to memorize everything— the feeling, the warmth, the rhythm in his body when mana moved. “If I can do it once, I can do it again,” he told himself, his voice filled with determination.

He took a deep breath, placed his hand over the desk, and began chanting once more. The words came naturally now, his mind recalling the subtle sensation of mana moving through him. A tiny flame flickered to life again, weak but steady.

Encouraged, Elrond repeated the process several more times. Each time he did, the motion of energy inside him felt clearer, as though something dormant within his body was finally waking up. He didn’t understand why it worked, or what truly caused it—but it worked.

Soon the room filled with faint warmth and the smell of heated air. Small embers shimmered and vanished as he continued to conjure tiny flames again and again. He laughed softly, mesmerized by the sight.

But after a while, fatigue crept in. His breathing grew shallow, and his arms began to feel heavy. The warmth that had filled him moments ago now drained away, replaced by a dull ache spreading through his limbs. “Why… am I so tired…” he mumbled, trying to raise his hand again but finding it too heavy.

His knees gave out, and he stumbled onto the bed beside him. His head spun, the ceiling swaying in his vision. “Mana… it’s energy, right?” he murmured weakly. “Did I… run out?”

The world blurred. His eyelids drooped, and exhaustion overwhelmed him. “Maybe… just a quick nap…” he whispered before drifting into sleep.

When he opened his eyes again, two hours had passed. The faint smell of food wafted through the air, and a gentle voice called out from beyond the door.

“Elrond, lunch is ready.”

He blinked groggily, turning his head. Mira was standing by the door, smiling. “Come on, sleepyhead. You’ve been out for a while.”

He slowly sat up, rubbing his eyes. Despite the exhaustion earlier, he felt strangely refreshed—his body buzzing faintly with newfound energy. “Coming…” he said softly, climbing out of bed.

Downstairs, Mira had already set the table. Today’s meal was simple yet mouthwatering: tender meat simmered in tomato sauce, served with freshly baked bread.

“Eat up while it’s warm,” Mira said cheerfully.

Elrond nodded, taking a bite. The rich flavor of the sauce filled his mouth, and he couldn’t help but smile. ‘She’s really good at this,’ he thought. As he ate, a quiet satisfaction filled him—not just from the food, but from what he had accomplished earlier.

For the first time since coming to this world, Elrond truly felt alive.

After finishing his meal, Mira returned to her chores—washing dishes, sweeping the floor, and tidying up the rooms. Elrond watched her for a while, pretending to play near the table, but his thoughts were elsewhere. The urge to try magic again was too strong to ignore.

Once Mira became absorbed in her work, Elrond quietly slipped back to his room. The book still rested where he had left it, and he smiled faintly as he opened it again. He placed it on the desk and raised his small hand, recalling the faint warmth he had felt earlier.

At this point, Elrond was focused—fully immersed in the rhythm of magic. The spark in his hand flickered like a living thing, responding to his will. The more he repeated it, the more natural it became. He didn’t yet understand why it worked, only that it did—and with every breath, it felt like a step closer to mastering it.

### Chapter 4: 3: The Encounter

#### Scene 1

After finishing his meal, Mira went back to her chores—washing dishes, sweeping the floor, tidying every corner. Elrond watched her for a while, pretending to play, but his curiosity burned quietly beneath his calm expression.

When Mira was fully occupied, he slipped away to his room. The book still lay where he had hidden it. He placed it on the desk and raised his hand, trying to recall the faint warmth he’d felt earlier.

Whispering the same chant aloud each time, he repeated the simple fire spell. The warmth came faintly at first—unsteady and hard to maintain. He still didn’t understand how the mana turned into fire, but each attempt helped him notice small changes in how it felt. There was rhythm to it, though he couldn’t quite define it.

He tried again, voicing the chant softly each time, The first few felt awkward, but by the tenth time, the motion of mana no longer resisted him. When he reached the fifteenth cast, he realized he still felt fine. No dizziness, no fatigue like before.

He glanced at his hands, confused. ‘Last time, I was exhausted by now… why not this time?’ he thought.

Curiosity drove him to keep going. The sixteenth time, the small flame flickered brightly and hovered for a moment longer. Seventeenth. Eighteenth. Nineteenth. Each one came easier, the flame responding faster, smoother. When he reached the twentieth, a faint heaviness began to settle into his limbs.

He stopped briefly, rubbing his arm. “So that’s when it starts to drain…” he murmured. Still uncertain, he tried once more—the twenty-first time. As soon as the flame vanished, his knees buckled and the world tilted.

The familiar wave of fatigue hit harder this time, spreading through his entire body. His breathing slowed, and his vision blurred. ‘So… that’s my limit,’ he thought weakly before collapsing onto the bed.

His eyelids grew heavy, and despite trying to stay awake, sleep took him almost instantly.

A little while later, Mira walked quietly into Elrond’s room to check on him. She smiled softly when she saw him lying on the bed, fast asleep. His breathing was calm, and a faint trace of soot marked his fingertips. Assuming he had simply tired himself out from playing, she decided not to wake him.

The afternoon sun crept through the curtains, painting gentle light across the room. Time passed quietly, and by the time it was nearing noon, Mira returned to check again. To her surprise, Elrond was still sleeping soundly, barely stirring.

She frowned lightly and stepped closer. “You must’ve been really tired, little one,” she whispered. As she adjusted his blanket, something caught her eye—a book lying open beside him: The Basics of Magic, opened to the chapter titled Basic Mana Control.

Mira blinked. “Magic?” she murmured, curiosity mixing with disbelief. “Was he… trying to read this?”

Her gaze drifted between Elrond’s peaceful face and the book’s open pages, filled with neat, faded handwriting and small rune diagrams. She couldn’t tell if he understood any of it, but the idea made her chuckle softly. “Learning magic at your age, huh?” she said under her breath.

Leaning closer, she gently brushed his hair aside. “Young master Elrond,” she called softly, tapping his shoulder. “It’s nearly lunchtime.”

It took several gentle shakes before he stirred, rubbing his eyes slowly. “M-Miss Mira…?” he mumbled sleepily.

“There you are,” she said politely but kindly. “You’ve been asleep for quite some time. I was starting to think you’d never wake up.”

Elrond sat up slowly, blinking groggily. He noticed the open book beside him and quickly closed it before Mira could say anything more. “I was just… reading,” he muttered.

Mira raised an eyebrow, her tone composed but careful. “Reading, young master? That’s quite early in the day for studies.”

Elrond forced a nervous laugh. “Hehe… I guess I lost track of time.”

She gave a restrained smile and adjusted his blanket neatly. “You should rest properly next time, young master. It’s already well past noon.”

He blinked in surprise, realizing how long he’d slept. “Past noon? I didn’t notice…”

Mira nodded. “Yes. I thought it best to let you rest since you seemed so tired earlier. But you should come downstairs soon—tea and a small meal are ready.”

Elrond nodded quietly, following her as she turned toward the door. His mind, however, remained elsewhere —still lingering on the sensation of mana and the strange new power he was beginning to grasp.

As they left the room, Mira glanced at him once more. “That book beside you,” she said in a measured tone. “It wasn’t just for reading, was it?”

Elrond froze for a moment, realizing she might have noticed. He scratched the back of his head awkwardly. “Umm… I just wanted to see what it was about,” he said honestly. “Because you and Mother can use magic, and… I want to learn too.”

Mira’s expression softened slightly, though her words stayed proper. “That’s quite an ambition, young master. But magic is not something learned overnight. Please, take care not to overexert yourself.”

Elrond smiled faintly. “I understand, Miss Mira. I’ll be careful.”

“Good,” she replied with a small nod. “Now come downstairs, young master. Your tea will cool.”

Elrond followed her quietly, his thoughts not of guilt—but of quiet determination. ‘Next time,’ he thought, ‘I’ll learn even more.’

After their simple meal, Mira tidied up the table while Elrond watched her, still full of curiosity. As she worked, they talked casually—the kind of innocent conversation only a child could start.

“Miss Mira,” Elrond asked softly, “when will Father and Mother come back?”

Mira paused, thinking for a moment before replying with a gentle smile. “Most likely tomorrow, young master. The expedition should return by then.”

Elrond nodded, his tone curious again. “And… what about you, Miss Mira? What will you do when they come back?”

Her hands paused over the dishes for a moment before she spoke again, her tone gentle and patient. “Once your parents return safely, I’ll be heading back to the town center. I often help the mayor and take on household work where I’m needed.” She glanced toward Elrond, noticing his worried expression, and smiled faintly. “But you know, young master, this isn’t my first time working here.”

Elrond blinked curiously. “It’s not?”

Mira shook her head, her movements calm and deliberate as she wiped the dishes dry. “No, not at all. Your mother has asked for my help many times before—even back when she was expecting you. I helped around the house when she couldn’t move much, made sure everything stayed tidy and the meals were ready. In a way, I’ve been here since before you were even born.”

Elrond’s eyes widened in surprise. “Really?”

“Yes,” she said softly, nodding with a faint smile. “So don’t worry, young master. It’s quite normal for me to be called back when Lady Selene needs assistance. I come and go when I’m needed.” Her tone grew a little lighter, hoping to ease his concern. “This position now is just temporary, but you might see me again sooner than you think.”

Elrond frowned slightly. “Temporary? But you’re really good at everything! I think you should stay here.”

Mira chuckled softly at his sincerity, the kind of laugh that was polite but warm. “That’s kind of you to say, young master, but this was only meant to be short-term. Your mother and father hired me just to help while they were away.”

“But…” Elrond pouted a little. “You’ve been really helpful…”

She smiled gently, lowering her tone to something soft but still formal—something a child could understand. “I’m glad you think so. And don’t worry, young master, you can always visit me when you go to town. I’ll be helping around the mayor’s office or doing housework for other families.”

Elrond nodded quietly, still not entirely happy but accepting her answer. “Okay… but you have to promise to visit again too.”

Mira smiled at that, her eyes soft. “Of course, young master. I promise.”

The two shared a brief, comfortable silence before Mira resumed her chores. Elrond watched her quietly, a faint thought forming in his mind—that people like Mira, humble yet strong, were the kind of people who kept this world running.

Even though Elrond looked like a normal, curious child, his mind worked differently. He sincerely thought Mira was exceptional at her work. As he sat quietly at the table, he began counting all the good things she’d done—how she took care of him, cooked, cleaned, and kept the house running perfectly while his parents were away. The more he thought about it, the more he felt a small ache in his chest at the idea of her leaving.

‘It’s really sad,’ he thought. ‘She’s been here all this time, helping with everything… and tomorrow she’ll be gone.’

His eyes followed her as she moved gracefully through the room, tidying the dishes with her usual care. Then, in the middle of wiping the counter, Mira let out a soft, tired yawn she tried to hide behind her hand.

Elrond blinked, tilting his head. “Miss Mira,” he said innocently, “you look sleepy. Maybe you should rest.”

Mira immediately straightened and shook her head politely. “Ah, forgive me, young master. I shouldn’t show such lack of discipline in front of you.”

But Elrond only smiled, his tone soft but genuine. “It’s okay. You’ve been working a lot since morning. You should rest too, Miss Mira. If you get tired, who’s going to take care of things tomorrow?”

Her eyes softened at his words. The sincerity in his voice made her heart warm. “You really are kind, young master,” she said, bowing her head slightly. “But I assure you, I’ll be fine. I’m used to long days like this.”

Elrond pouted slightly, crossing his small arms in a childish gesture. “Still… I want you to stay healthy.”

That made her chuckle softly. “Understood, young master. I’ll take a little rest later. You have my word.”

“Promise?” he said, his tone light but serious.

“Promise,” she replied with a faint smile.

The room fell into a comfortable calm again, filled only by the sound of clinking dishes and the quiet hum of the evening air. For the first time that day, Elrond’s thoughts drifted not toward magic or mana—but toward gratitude for the people around him.

As the evening deepened, Mira continued tidying for a while longer before finally setting aside her work. “I think that’s enough for today,” she said softly, wiping her hands on her apron. “You should rest soon as well, young master. It’s getting late.”

Elrond nodded obediently, though his mind was elsewhere. Once Mira finished closing the curtains and extinguished the lamps, both of them bid each other good night and went to their rooms.

But for Elrond, sleep refused to come. Having already rested twice earlier in the day, he lay awake, staring at the ceiling. The thought of mana and magic returned to his mind again. ‘Maybe just one more test,’ he thought.

Quietly, he got up, lit a small candle, and opened his book once more. The familiar page about Basic Mana Control greeted him. Taking a deep breath, he whispered the chant again and conjured a faint flame. It flickered softly in his palm.

He whispered the chant softly, forming the small flame again in his palm. The fire flickered weakly at first, barely holding its shape before fading. He repeated it slowly, taking note of how each attempt felt within his body—the faint pulse of warmth, the rhythm that flowed from his chest to his fingertips.

He counted each try aloud, keeping track. “One... two... three...” The flame trembled but returned every time, slightly steadier than before. Ten, eleven, twelve—still no dizziness, no weakness. His hands began to move with more certainty, his breathing syncing with each cast.

When he reached fifteen, he paused, blinking in surprise. He felt fine. ‘Last time I was completely drained by now,’ he thought. ‘Did my body change?’

He rested for a short while, then continued. The sixteenth flame came brighter, the seventeenth warmer. By the twentieth, the casting felt natural, like breathing. The mana inside him moved more freely now, though he still couldn’t understand why it obeyed him.

‘So far, so good,’ he thought, his small voice echoing in the quiet room. He tried again and again—twenty- five, twenty-six, twenty-seven. Each cast left him a little warmer, but still steady. His confidence grew with each repetition.

At thirty, he stopped briefly to study his hand, watching the faint glow fade. “Still fine…” he whispered, almost smiling. ‘Maybe my idea’s right—the more I use it, the more it grows.’

He resumed chanting, the flames appearing quicker now, swirling softly before fading. His pace quickened, and soon he reached the count of forty. Sweat formed along his temple, but the rhythm of mana remained steady—fluid and controlled. His breathing deepened, each exhale syncing with the pulse of heat in his hand. “Forty-one… forty-two… forty-three…”

When he reached forty-five, a faint wave of dizziness brushed his senses. The candlelight wavered, and the flame in his palm flickered uncertainly. Still, he persisted. “Just a bit more,” he murmured, determination replacing caution.

Forty-six. Forty-seven. Forty-eight.

Each repetition sent ripples through his body—the mana flowed faster, smoother, like a river gaining strength after rain. His limbs trembled faintly, but he pressed forward, counting each breath until he reached forty-nine.

The flame that appeared this time was brighter and steadier. Elrond exhaled deeply, lowering his hand as the fire faded. “So that’s… the limit,” he said softly. But instead of stopping, he sat still for a moment, thinking.

‘If mana is energy,’ he reasoned, ‘then my body must adapt to it every time I use it. It’s not just recovering— it’s growing, expanding. Each time I push it, my capacity increases.’ His small brow furrowed in concentration as he considered the idea. ‘It’s like training a muscle… exponential growth with every use. But… is it safe?’

He took a slow breath, feeling the mana circulate through him. There was no pain, no strain—only warmth spreading naturally inside. Even though it was only his first day, his body already moved with the flow, familiar with it.

Encouraged, he whispered again, “One last time.”

The fiftieth chant left his lips steady and calm. A spark flared in his palm, brighter than before—then his vision blurred. The world spun gently, and his body lost strength.

‘So it’s true… fifty’s the limit,’ he thought weakly, sinking onto the bed. The faint warmth of mana still hummed under his skin as exhaustion overtook him completely.

Elrond slept deeply through the night, his body exhausted from overusing mana. When morning light filtered through the curtains, he was still fast asleep. Mira, already awake and preparing breakfast, eventually came to wake him.

“Good morning, young master,” she said softly, tapping his shoulder. “You’ve overslept quite a bit today.”

Elrond stirred, rubbing his eyes and yawning. “M-Miss Mira… morning…” he mumbled, still groggy.

“Come now,” she said kindly. “Breakfast is ready.”

He followed her to the dining area, still sluggish from fatigue. The scent of freshly baked bread and warm soup greeted him. They shared a quiet meal, chatting lightly about the morning chores and how bright the day was.

Not long after they finished, a sudden knock echoed from the front door. Mira wiped her hands and went to answer it, while Elrond peeked curiously from his chair. Standing outside was one of the neighbors, looking slightly out of breath but cheerful.

“Ah, good morning, Miss Mira!” the woman said. “I bring good news—Captain Aldric and Lady Selene have returned from the expedition! The group made it back safely. They’re currently in the central town wrapping up the report before heading home.”

Mira’s eyes lit up, relief washing over her face. “That’s wonderful news! Thank you for telling us.”

Elrond’s face brightened instantly. “Really?! Father and Mother are back?” he said with excitement that was half real and half performed. His heart beat faster, though he kept up his childish act, eyes wide with glee.

The neighbor nodded. “Yes, young master. They should be back by this evening, I believe.”

Elrond turned eagerly to Mira. “Miss Mira, can we go to the central town to meet them? Please?”

Mira hesitated for a moment, glancing at his hopeful face. “It may be crowded, young master. Are you certain?”

He nodded quickly, smiling brightly. “Yes! I want to see them!”

Mira sighed softly, then smiled. “Very well. We shall go. But promise me you’ll stay close, alright?”

“I promise!” he said cheerfully.

With that, Mira fetched their cloaks, and the two prepared to leave. As they stepped outside, the warm sunlight greeted them, and Elrond’s heart stirred with both excitement and unease—because deep down, he could feel that this reunion might mark the start of something far greater than he could yet imagine.

The walk to the central town wasn’t far—about thirty minutes if they took the main road. Mira carried a small satchel over her shoulder while Elrond, still brimming with excitement, insisted on walking beside her.

“Are you certain, young master?” she asked gently. “It’s quite a distance. You might get tired.”

Elrond puffed his chest with a grin. “It’s okay! If I get tired, you can carry me!”

Mira sighed softly, but there was a faint smile on her face. “Very well. But you must tell me right away if you feel tired, understood?”

“Understood!” he said cheerfully.

As they made their way through the cobblestone path leading toward the town, the scenery around them shifted from open fields to clusters of modest homes. Farmers waved as they passed by, and merchants rolling carts nodded in greeting. Children ran across the road, laughing and playing, while older townsfolk exchanged warm smiles at the sight of the young master walking hand in hand with the maid.

“Everyone here looks happy today,” Elrond said, looking around with wonder.

“They’re probably excited about the expedition’s return,” Mira replied. “It’s rare for a mission near the Eastern Woods to end without losses. The news must’ve lifted everyone’s spirits.”

They passed a flower vendor arranging bright wildflowers in small pots. The woman smiled warmly at Elrond. “Good day, young master! Off to see your parents, are you?”

Elrond blinked, a little surprised but smiling shyly. “Y-yes!”

Mira bowed slightly. “Good morning, ma’am.”

The vendor chuckled softly as they continued on their way. “What a polite young one,” she murmured to herself.

By the time they reached the outskirts of the central town, the faint buzz of voices could already be heard. People were gathering along the main street near the square, where banners of the local garrison fluttered gently in the breeze. The air was filled with cheerful chatter and relief.

Mira slowed her pace as they approached. “It seems everyone’s come to welcome them back,” she said softly.

Elrond looked around in awe. “Wow… there’s so many people!” he said, his tone full of excitement.

The townfolk exchanged stories about how the expedition succeeded and how the barrier stone had been restored. There were no grand decorations or parades—just warm smiles, handshakes, and quiet gratitude that their soldiers had returned safely.

A few of the townspeople noticed Mira and Elrond, greeting them warmly.

“Miss Mira! You’re here too?” one of the butchers called out.

“Yes,” she answered with a polite bow. “We came to see Lady Selene and Captain Aldric return.”

“Good to see you both safe,” another said kindly, nodding to Elrond.

Elrond returned the greeting with a bright smile, still pretending to be the innocent, cheerful boy everyone saw him as. But inside, he was quietly relieved—relieved that the parents of the life he now lived had returned safely.

As they stood among the townsfolk, Mira leaned slightly toward Elrond and spoke softly, her tone calm but filled with quiet admiration. “You know, young master, Lady Selene and Captain Aldric are both quite respected here in town.”

Elrond tilted his head curiously. “Respected? Like nobles?”

“Something like that,” Mira replied with a gentle smile. “They aren’t nobles by title, but their deeds have earned them nearly the same regard. The magic research your mother contributes, and your father’s work defending the outskirts, have both kept this town safe for years. Many here owe their peace to them.”

Elrond listened quietly, his small hands gripping the edge of his cloak. Her words stirred something warm inside him—pride. He looked at the gathered people, all smiling and relieved, and felt a strange sense of belonging.

‘So they’ve done all this… without power or rank,’ he thought. ‘They just worked hard for everyone.’

But as that warmth settled, another thought surfaced. He remembered his previous life—cold laboratories, endless calculations, and the faces of colleagues who worked beside him. Many of them had achieved things that truly helped people: medical breakthroughs, energy innovations, discoveries that improved lives. They weren’t perfect, but they pursued creation for good. Compared to them, he had gone too far— his own discovery twisted into a weapon. They built hope, he thought solemnly, while mine brought ruin.

His gaze dropped to the cobblestone beneath his feet. ‘I reached something far greater than most… but what’s the point if it brings ruin?’

He glanced toward Mira again, her expression serene as she greeted another townsman. ‘Mother and Father… they’re nothing like who I was before,’ he thought. ‘Maybe… this time, I can learn from them.’

A small, genuine smile tugged at his lips. “Miss Mira,” he said softly, “I think Father and Mother are amazing.”

She turned to him, her eyes soft with warmth. “Yes, young master. They truly are.”

He nodded, the pride inside him now settled with quiet resolve. ‘If I ever create something again,’ he thought, ‘I’ll make sure it helps people… like they do.’

The soft hum of chatter filled the square where the expedition group had already arrived and gathered. Some townsfolk chatted cheerfully with the returning members, while others helped unload supplies and tend to the horses. Aldric and Selene stood near the front, speaking with the town official, their armor still bearing the marks of the journey but their expressions calm and content.

Mira guided Elrond through the small crowd until they could see clearly. Around them, people talked in low voices, exchanging updates and light laughter. Soldiers rested nearby, some handing off supplies to the town guards while others chatted with familiar faces. People spoke softly, moving at their own pace, carrying on with quiet familiarity as if everything had simply slipped back into place. Elrond looked around, quietly watching how everyone moved and smiled, relieved that things were calm again.

With excitement, Elrond’s eyes darted through the crowd until he spotted his parents. Selene noticed him first—the moment their eyes met, her tired expression softened, and she waved gently. Mira gave a small bow of respect, then turned to Elrond. “Go on, young master,” she said kindly. “They’ve been waiting to see you.”

Elrond hesitated for a moment, glancing at the busy scene around them. “Is it okay if I go?” he asked shyly.

Mira smiled and nodded. “Of course. Go on.”

That was all the encouragement he needed. Elrond rushed forward, weaving between people until he reached them. “Mother! Father!” he called, his voice bright and full of energy.

Selene turned fully toward him, her armor catching the light. “Elrond?” she said softly, a smile tugging at her lips. When he threw his arms forward, ready to hug her, she stepped back slightly, her cheeks flushing. “Ah —wait, dear, I’m still dirty from the road. I might smell terrible.”

Elrond shook his head quickly, his eyes shining. “I don’t mind!”

That made her laugh softly, and before she could protest further, he wrapped his little arms around her anyway. Aldric, noticing the scene, approached with a grin. “Well, looks like someone couldn’t wait until we got home.”

Selene smiled warmly, ruffling Elrond’s hair. “He’s just happy, that’s all.”

Aldric looked to Mira and gave a brief nod of gratitude. “Thank you for watching over him while we were gone.”

“It’s always an honor, Captain,” Mira said with a polite bow.

Both Aldric and Selene shared a brief summary of what happened in the expedition—the restoration of the magic stone, the battle with the Amarok, and how the group managed to stabilize the eastern barrier again. Mira listened attentively, her expression one of relief.

“I’m glad everyone made it back safely,” she said sincerely.

Aldric exhaled, his tone thoughtful. “We were fortunate. It could’ve gone far worse.”

Selene nodded, brushing her hair back tiredly. “We’ll need to report to the commander and attend a meeting with the mayor and the nobles this evening. It might take us a while before we can return home.”

Elrond looked up at them, his expression falling slightly. “So… you’re not coming back yet?” he asked softly.

Selene knelt down, resting her hand gently on his shoulder. “Not tonight, dear. But we’ll be back soon. I promise.”

He nodded reluctantly, forcing a small smile. “Okay…”

Selene smiled tenderly. “That’s my boy.”

Just then, one of the soldiers approached and bowed. “Captain Aldric, Lady Selene—the Garrison Commander requests your presence at the town hall.”

Aldric sighed softly. “Understood.” He turned to Mira. “Could you look after Elrond a little longer?”

“Of course,” she said respectfully.

As Aldric and Selene walked away with the soldiers, Elrond waved, his small hand raised high. “Be careful!” he shouted.

Selene turned one last time and smiled. “Always.”

And just like that, they were gone again, leaving Elrond and Mira standing quietly among the thinning crowd.

Mira and Elrond stayed for a while in the central town after seeing Aldric and Selene off to the town hall. Some of the staff who worked there recognized Mira immediately and greeted her warmly.

“Oh, Mira, it’s been a while,” one of the clerks said with a smile. “Helping the Ardent family again?”

“Yes,” Mira replied politely. “Lady Selene called me to assist while they were away.”

They exchanged a few pleasant words before parting ways, and then Mira turned to Elrond. “Shall we take a short walk before heading back, young master?”

Elrond’s eyes lit up. “Can we? I want to see more of the town!”

With a nod and a small smile, Mira agreed. The two began walking through the streets of the central town. The place was lively but not noisy—vendors setting up stalls, children running with wooden toys, and shopkeepers chatting by their doors. The smell of baked bread, roasted nuts, and grilled meat drifted in the air.

At one of the stalls, Elrond’s eyes widened at the sight of freshly roasted meat skewers and candied fruits on sticks glistening under the sun. “Miss Mira! What’s that?”

Mira chuckled. “Simple street snacks, young master. Would you like to try one?”

He nodded eagerly, and Mira purchased a skewer of grilled meat and one of candied apples. The first bite made Elrond’s eyes sparkle—it was sweet, smoky, and unlike anything he’d ever tasted. “This is amazing!” he said, his voice full of innocent awe.

Mira smiled gently. “I’m glad you like it.” As they continued walking, a few of the townsfolk called out to Mira, greeting her with familiarity.

“Mira! Haven’t seen you since last month!” said a shopkeeper, waving.

She bowed lightly. “Good afternoon. It’s good to see you again.”

Elrond noticed how warmly everyone spoke to her, how naturally she blended into the crowd. He felt a small warmth growing in his chest—a sense of comfort. ‘Everyone here respects her,’ he thought. ‘And I’m surrounded by people like this… kind and good.’

That realization made him feel quietly grateful. His heart, once burdened with doubt from his past life, felt lighter.

After a few more stops and some playful chatter, they decided to head back home. The walk back took longer than before, but Elrond insisted on walking the whole way. “I’m fine, Miss Mira,” he said when she asked if he was tired.

“You’re sure? It’s quite a distance,” she said with mild concern.

He smiled brightly. “I’ll tell you if I get tired. Promise!”

She nodded, amused by his determination. The road back was quiet and lined with trees turning gold under the late afternoon sun. By the time they reached home, the sky had already shifted to shades of orange and pink.

Mira went straight to finish the chores she’d left undone before their trip. Elrond, however, went back to his own form of routine—training his mana again. He sat by his desk, whispered the chant, and began casting small flames repeatedly.

One, two, three—then ten, twenty, fifty. His progress from the night before showed clearly. The mana moved smoothly now, steady and strong. He pushed on, counting quietly under his breath.

When he finally reached a hundred, his vision wavered and his breath grew heavy. The warmth that once felt light now weighed on his body like a heavy blanket. “One hundred…” he murmured, smiling faintly in satisfaction before falling backward onto the bed.

This time, exhaustion claimed him completely, and he fell into deep sleep before the last light of sunset faded from the window.

Meanwhile, at the town hall, a heated discussion filled the meeting chamber. Around a large oak table sat the Garrison Commander Lucen, the town’s mayor, several senior magicians, and a few local nobles, each speaking over the other with growing intensity.

“The attack on the regional magic stone was no minor incident,” Lucen said firmly, his tone commanding enough to quiet the room for a moment. “If that barrier had fallen completely, the monsters could have reached the nearby villages. We can’t allow this to happen again.”

Aldric stepped forward slightly, his tone measured but grim. “If I may add, Commander—since the last few weeks, our patrols around the town’s own magic stone have reported a noticeable rise in monster activity. It’s not random either; it’s as if something is pushing them closer to the settlements. If the eastern magic stone had truly collapsed without warning while the town barrier weakened from constant strain, the result could’ve been catastrophic.”

Lucen gave a short, grave nod. “I can confirm that, too. The patrol reports I’ve reviewed align with Captain Aldric’s statement. Monster activity has grown denser along the outer ridges. It isn’t coincidence—it’s a pattern.” His gaze swept across the table, sharp and deliberate. “If both barriers were to fail, even briefly, this town wouldn’t stand a chance.”

A quiet unease rippled through the room. “We’re not just talking about another expedition,” Aldric continued. “We’re talking about the entire region being exposed if we don’t act fast.”

One of the nobles—a stout man in fine velvet robes—leaned forward with a frown. “And who do you expect to pay for this, Commander? Doubling patrols means doubling costs. The Garrison’s budget already drains half the seasonal levy. You can’t expect us to shoulder more tax!”

Another noble nodded in agreement. “He’s right. The eastern region isn’t even under constant threat. We can’t pour gold into paranoia.”

Selene, seated beside Lucen, folded her hands calmly. “With respect, my lords, this isn’t paranoia. We’ve seen firsthand how close we came to disaster. The residual mana imbalance in the region proves there’s still activity in the forest. Reinforcing patrols around both the town and regional magic stones is necessary.”

A murmur ran through the room. The mayor raised his hand to keep order. “Lady Selene is right,” he said evenly. “Safety must come first. But… the matter of cost is not insignificant.”

Lucen leaned forward. “If we coordinate better, we can manage with a rotation system—shared responsibility between the garrison and local guards. The cost wouldn’t be as severe.”

But the nobles weren’t convinced. “Even shared, it’s still an increase,” one of them snapped. “We already fund the defense lines through voluntary contribution. Enough is enough.”

Selene exchanged a glance with the senior magicians present, who nodded in quiet agreement before one spoke up. “If the patrols are reduced, the risk of another barrier breach rises. Should that happen, repairs will cost triple what prevention would.”

The words hung in the air, heavy with logic none could deny. Still, tension simmered until the mayor finally spoke again, his tone diplomatic but firm.

“Then we’ll adjust the budget,” he said. “I’ll open more land leases for agriculture and trade expansion. The profit from those leases can support the increased patrol without raising noble tax. It will ease your burden while ensuring our protection.”

The nobles exchanged glances. After a moment, one finally sighed. “If that’s how you intend to manage it, then… fine. But ensure the paperwork reflects it properly. We won’t tolerate hidden levies.”

“Of course,” the mayor replied, inclining his head respectfully.

Lucen gave a short nod. “Then it’s settled. The garrison will begin adjusting schedules immediately. Patrol expansion begins within the week.”

As the meeting settled, the heat in the room gradually faded. The nobles leaned back, satisfied enough, while Selene quietly exhaled. Aldric met her gaze and gave a small nod—relieved that the argument had ended with reason, not ego.

Lucen stood, his expression resolute. “We’ve seen how fragile the barrier can become. Let’s make sure next time, we’re ready before it breaks.”

The mayor smiled faintly in agreement. “Then may this meeting mark the start of a safer future for the town.”

The council members murmured their approval as the meeting drew to a close.

The discussion dragged on for hours as they refined the details of funding and coordination. Maps were spread across the table, quills scribbling on parchment as the mayor, Lucen, and the council debated logistics. They worked through each point—allocating resources, synchronizing patrol schedules between the garrison and local guards, and determining communication routes for emergencies. Every voice had something to add, every noble pushing to reduce their financial share while Lucen and the mayor pushed back, demanding balance.

By the time the final agreements were signed, the candles had burned low, casting tired faces in a soft amber glow. Lucen leaned back in his chair, rubbing his temples. “That took longer than I’d hoped,” he muttered.

The mayor gave a small chuckle, weary but content. “At least we reached an understanding. That’s more than I expected.”

Lucen nodded, turning to Aldric and Selene. “You two should head home. The report will be finalized tomorrow. I’ll stay the night here and return to the garrison in the morning.”

Aldric smiled faintly. “Understood, Commander. And… thank you for your support earlier.”

Lucen waved it off with a small grin. “We all saw what happened out there. You both did well.”

Selene inclined her head respectfully. “Your leadership helped hold the line. Thank you, Commander.”

They spoke briefly about the next steps before parting ways. When they reached the gate of the town hall, Lucen walked with them a little farther toward the main road. “Be careful on the way back,” he said, his tone softening. “You’ve earned your rest.”

Aldric chuckled. “You too, Commander. Try not to drown yourself in paperwork.”

Lucen smirked lightly. “No promises.”

He raised a hand as they departed. “See you again next time.”

Both Selene and Aldric mounted their horse, sharing the same saddle. The night air was cool and quiet as they rode along the familiar dirt road back toward their home. For a while, neither spoke, content to simply enjoy the calm after the chaos.

Then Selene smiled faintly, her voice low and gentle. “Do you remember the first time we met?”

Aldric glanced at her, brow raised. “When I was assigned to guard your carriage?”

She nodded. “You cut down two dire wolves before they could even touch the horses. I thought you were just another arrogant soldier then.”

He laughed softly. “And you scolded me for ruining your dress with blood.”

Selene chuckled. “You deserved it.”

They both laughed quietly, the tension of the day finally melting away. The rhythmic sound of hooves carried them through the dimly lit path, the moonlight glinting off their armor. By the time the familiar outline of their home appeared in the distance, both had fallen into a comfortable silence.

When they arrived, Mira greeted them at the door, bowing slightly. “Welcome home, Captain, Lady Selene.”

Selene smiled kindly. “Thank you, Mira. Is Elrond asleep?”

“Yes, my lady,” Mira replied. “He was full of energy earlier, but I believe the walk to town tired him out.”

“I see,” Selene said softly, stepping inside. “You’ve done well today. Please, rest once you’re finished here.”

Mira bowed again. “Of course, my lady.”

Selene made her way quietly to Elrond’s room. The boy was fast asleep, curled beneath his blanket. A small smile touched her lips as she leaned down and kissed his forehead.

But as she adjusted the blanket, something beside him caught her eye—a familiar book resting near his pillow. She picked it up, recognizing it immediately: The Basics of Magic.

Her brow furrowed slightly. “What’s this doing here?” she murmured, flipping it open to see the marked page. It was the chapter on Basic Mana Control.

A soft chuckle escaped her. “Trying to read already? He wouldn’t understand this yet…” Still, a faint sense of pride flickered in her chest as she held the book for a moment longer, then frowned slightly, conflicted.

After a brief pause, she decided to take the book with her. Quietly, Selene left Elrond’s room and climbed the stairs toward her own workspace. The familiar scent of parchment and ink filled the air as she entered her study. She walked to the bookshelf and returned The Basics of Magic to its proper place among her research volumes.

She lingered there for a moment, brushing a finger along the book’s spine. “What were you thinking, little one?” she murmured softly. “You wouldn’t understand this yet… or maybe you were just curious.”

A faint smile touched her lips again before she turned and left the study, heading back downstairs. On her way past Elrond’s room, she peeked inside one last time and whispered with a tender smile, “You really are full of surprises.”

With that, she quietly closed the door, the soft glow of moonlight resting over their peaceful home.

When morning came, sunlight peeked through the curtains of Elrond’s room. He stirred awake slowly, rubbing his eyes before sitting up. His gaze drifted to the desk—and his heart skipped a beat.

The book was gone.

He blinked, searching frantically around the room. Under the bed, behind the chair, even beneath the blanket. Nothing. It’s gone... did someone take it? he thought, panic rising in his chest. The memory of the faint flame in his hand flashed through his mind, and a cold dread followed. If someone saw me practicing...

He froze for a moment, then took a deep breath to calm himself. “Maybe... maybe I just moved it somewhere,” he muttered softly. Trying to act normal, he stepped out of his room and walked toward the main area.

The scent of breakfast filled the air. Selene was there, smiling gently when she saw him. “Good morning, Elrond.”

He blinked in surprise, trying to suppress his nervousness. “G-good morning, Mother.”

Outside, through the window, Aldric could be seen training with his sword as usual, each swing sharp and precise. Mira moved gracefully through the room, cleaning and setting the table.

Elrond ran toward Selene with a cheerful act, wrapping his small arms around her waist. “Mother!”

Selene chuckled softly, patting his head. “Good morning, my little one. I heard from Mira that you’ve been behaving very well while we were away.”

At her words, a twinge of guilt flickered inside him. Ah... she doesn’t know I fell from the chair two days ago... He laughed awkwardly but stayed quiet.

After a moment, he looked up at her. “Mother... what about Miss Mira? Is she going to stay?”

Selene smiled faintly. “Today might be her last day working here. She’s been helping us a lot, but she usually works at the town center.”

Elrond’s face dropped instantly. “Eh? But... but she’s really good! She can’t go! I don’t want her to leave!” he said, his tone rising with childish desperation.

Both Mira and Selene paused, surprised by his reaction. Mira looked away, flustered but touched. “Young master, please don’t say that. I’m very happy to hear it, but your mother will decide what’s best.”

Selene blinked, caught off guard by her son’s sincerity. For a moment, she thought quietly, then smiled softly. “Hmm... well, if you care that much, perhaps we can adjust something.” She turned to Mira. “How about this—you can work here on a scheduled basis? Perhaps three days a week. I usually have work on weekdays, so Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday should fit.”

Mira’s eyes widened slightly in surprise before softening with joy. “That would be wonderful, my lady. I would be honored to continue assisting the household.”

Elrond’s eyes brightened instantly. “Really? That means you’re staying?”

Mira laughed lightly. “At least for a few days each week, yes, young master.”

He grinned from ear to ear. “Yay!”

But as they talked, a thought stirred in Elrond’s mind. Monday... Tuesday... Wednesday? He repeated the words in his head, realizing the meaning. So this world has a concept of weeks too... The idea fascinated him— another small piece of the world falling into place, something familiar yet entirely new.

Selene, who was about to start on some morning chores, was stopped gently by Mira. “My lady, you should rest. You must still be tired from the expedition.”

### Chapter 5: 4: The Fateful Meeting

#### Scene 1

Elrond then decided to take a look at his father outside training with his sword. Aldric noticed him immediately and greeted him with a grin. He stopped his swings for a moment just to tease his only child. Elrond frowned and told him he was sweaty, which only made Aldric laugh louder and tease him even more. They played around for a bit until Aldric finally sat down to rest.

While catching his breath, Aldric glanced at Elrond with a playful smirk. “You know, one day, I want you to become a warrior too. Someone strong enough to swing a real sword beside me.”

Elrond’s eyes widened. “Really? I can be like you?”

Aldric chuckled. “If you train. And listen. And maybe stop running away every time I smell bad from training.”

“I only said that because you were sweaty!” Elrond pouted, then straightened proudly. “But… I want to be strong. I want to be like Father. Mira said you defeated the big wolf! The Amarok!”

Aldric froze for a moment, rubbing the back of his neck as his cheeks warmed. “Ah—well, yes, I struck the last blow, but that’s not something to brag about. Everyone fought just as hard. If Lucen hadn’t held its attention, or if the mages hadn’t weakened its legs… I wouldn’t have gotten that chance.”

Elrond leaned forward, eyes shining. “But you still did it! That’s amazing!”

Aldric laughed awkwardly. “You’re giving me too much credit, little one. It was teamwork—remember that if you ever swing a sword one day.”

After a little more chatting, Aldric stood up and dusted off his clothes. He told Elrond that he needed to go to the central town to see off Commander Lucen’s group as they returned to the garrison and to finalize the expedition report. He mentioned he had taken three full days off after the expedition, so he would be back home soon.

Selene remained upstairs doing her research work, and Mira was busy with her chores—making it the perfect time for Elrond to practice. Last time, he managed one hundred casts of his small fire spell. Today, his goal was two hundred. Even without the missing magic book, he remembered every word of the basic chapter he read.

The days that followed settled into a gentle rhythm. Each morning began with the soft creak of wooden floorboards as Mira moved through her chores, Selene vanished into her workroom, and Aldric shifted between house duties and short patrols. And in the middle of all that quiet movement was Elrond — practicing.

At first, his progress shot upward. One hundred casts became one hundred fifty, then two hundred. Each day ended with the faint glow of a dying flame in his palm and a small boy sprawled on his bed, drained but pleased. His mana flowed more smoothly the more he used it, becoming familiar in a way that felt almost instinctive.

Weeks passed. Leaves on the trees shifted from bright greens to darker tones. Mira would sometimes pause, watching him from the doorway as he trained, smiling gently at his determination. Selene began noticing faint traces of soot on his sleeves but assumed he’d been playing near the cooking hearth. Aldric occasionally peeked in on him, amused by how focused his son seemed while sitting cross‑legged on the floor, chanting under his breath.

As the weeks turned into months, Elrond felt something shift. When he reached three hundred casts in a single day, the exhaustion hit him differently. Not sudden—just a slow, creeping heaviness. He sat on his bed afterward, staring at his hands.

‘So I’m slowing down…’ he thought. ‘Or maybe… this is where real training begins.’

He pushed again the next day. And the next.

Four hundred. Four hundred thirty. Four hundred fifty.

By then, the familiar surge of rapid growth had faded. The increase in his mana capacity felt smaller now— small steps instead of leaps. It frustrated him at first. He would lie awake, thinking about what he was missing, how he could improve, what angle he hadn’t considered.

But he wasn’t discouraged.

‘Even if it’s slower… I’m still growing,’ he told himself quietly. ‘I just need a different approach now.’

For the first time, Elrond began treating mana as something to study—not just something to push.

A couple of months after he first started practicing magic, Elrond—now five years old—sat in his room surrounded by his scattered books. Every one of them was accounted for.

Except one.

He had reread everything he had collected—simple stories, beginner manuals, even a basic herb guide. But The Basics of Magic, the most important one, was nowhere to be found.

He searched the living room, checking under the chairs and behind the shelves. Nothing.

He checked the kitchen, even though he doubted a magic book would end up near pots and bread rolls. Still nothing.

He checked the storage room, pushing aside baskets and old tools. Dust filled his nose, but no book.

Finally, he opened the door to his parents’ bedroom and peeked inside. It was tidy—too tidy for anything to go missing without someone noticing. The book wasn’t there either.

He stood in the hallway, staring at the wooden floor.

There was only one place left.

Upstairs.

The place his mother worked. The place he normally wasn’t supposed to enter.

Elrond stared at the staircase, his small hands curling slightly with determination.

“Time to find it…”

As Elrond stood there thinking about the missing magic book, another thought weighed on his mind. His limit—four hundred fifty casts. His mana wasn’t just increasing; it was recovering faster than before. No matter how much he pushed himself, he no longer collapsed the way he used to.

‘At this rate… simple fire magic won’t work anymore,’ he thought, brows furrowing. ‘I need something harder. Something stronger. The book… I need the next level.’

His determination sharpened. Today, he had to find it.

The next morning felt different.

A stillness settled over the house. Mira wasn’t humming, and the kitchen held no movement at all. Only the soft creak of the floorboards greeted Elrond as he stepped out of his room, the early morning light spilling faintly across the narrow hall.

The scent of reheated bread and lightly fried eggs lingered in the air, drifting from the dining table where a simple breakfast had been set out. Aldric stood beside it, already halfway into his patrol gear, tightening straps and buckles with methodical precision. His armor glinted dully under the morning light, his cloak draped over the back of a chair, and his sword leaned nearby—silent, but ready.

“Father? Where’s Mother?” Elrond asked quietly.

Aldric let out a slow breath as he clicked a buckle into place. “Still upstairs. She worked through the night again,” he said with a faint frown. “I told her to rest, but she’s as stubborn as ever.” He ruffled Elrond’s hair gently. “Eat something. I need to head out before the gate closes.”

Elrond nodded, though his chest tightened. “...Be safe, Father.”

Aldric offered a reassuring grin. “Always.” Then he swept up his sword, swung his cloak over his shoulder, and stepped outside. The door shut behind him with a hollow thud.

Stillness returned.

Elrond stood there for a moment, staring at the untouched food. The thought of Selene staying awake all night tugged at something deep within him—a memory he tried not to dwell on. A cold, sterile room. Paper after paper scattered across desks. Colleagues dozing off mid-thought, waking again, pushing themselves past limits that eventually swallowed them whole.

He shook the image away.

‘She’ll hurt herself if this continues…’ he thought, his hands curling slightly at his sides.

He forced himself to take a small bite of bread—just enough to chase away the morning emptiness—before heading for the stairs.

The wooden steps creaked softly as he climbed. When he reached the door to Selene’s workroom, he hesitated. He half‑expected to hear her voice, perhaps the quick scratch of a quill on parchment or the clink of bottles being moved.

But when he cracked the door open, the room greeted him with silence.

The chair by the desk was empty.

He pushed the door wider. Still no sign of her. The candles on the desk had burned down to uneven stubs. Papers lay scattered across the surface—magic formulas, diagrams, half-finished calculations—the sort of work she rarely left unattended.

Then he noticed a figure slumped behind the door.

“Mother…?”

Selene sat curled against the wall, her head resting awkwardly on the wooden paneling. A few strands of hair clung to her cheek. Her breathing was soft but shallow, and she looked like she had simply stopped working mid‑movement and sleep claimed her where she was.

Elrond’s heart sank. ‘She really… worked until she collapsed.’

His mind flickered with memories he didn’t want—late nights in a past life, exhausted bodies falling asleep at desks, the slow breaking of people who pushed themselves too hard.

Quietly, he went back downstairs and fetched a blanket. When he returned, ready to cover her, something on the desk caught his eye.

Papers littered the surface—intricate diagrams of mana flow, notes scrawled in a rush, calculations so dense even he couldn’t follow them yet. A few sheets had slipped onto the floor, forming a messy pile beside her chair. It wasn’t chaotic… but it wasn’t far from it.

His gaze lifted to the bookshelf.

There.

The Basics of Magic.

Back in its original place.

Relief washed through him, loosening a breath he didn’t realize he’d been holding. “So you were the one who took it back, Mother…” he murmured.

He reached out and brushed a finger over the spine gently, almost reverently, before pulling his hand away. ‘Later,’ he thought. ‘I’ll study it properly later… the right way.’

He turned back and draped the blanket around Selene’s shoulders, careful not to wake her.

But the light movement stirred her anyway.

Her eyelashes fluttered faintly before her eyes opened—hazy, unfocused. “...Elrond?” she whispered.

Elrond knelt beside her with a small, gentle smile. “Good morning, Mother.”

Selene blinked slowly, trying to piece together where she was. Her gaze darted around the workroom; then realization struck. “I… fell asleep here?” She touched her cheek, eyes widening. “Oh no… I didn’t mean to— this is so irresponsible, I—”

“It’s okay,” Elrond said softly, tugging lightly on her sleeve. “Breakfast is on the table. Father already left for patrol.”

Selene stared at him for a moment, her expression softening. She let out a breath—a tired, shaky one— then placed a hand gently on his head. “Thank you… my sweet boy.” Her voice wavered. “And thank you for the blanket.”

“You looked cold,” he replied simply.

She smiled faintly, pushing herself carefully to her feet. “I’ll wash up and come downstairs soon. Wait for me, alright?”

He nodded.

As Selene left the room, her steps still unsteady, Elrond turned back to the bookshelf.

This time, there was no hesitation.

Ready.

But now that Selene had gone downstairs, Elrond allowed himself to move freely. He approached the shelf with a quiet, deliberate step, stretching onto the tips of his toes to grasp the familiar spine of The Basics of Magic. The moment his fingers closed around it, a strange calm settled over him—like reclaiming something that had always belonged in his hands. He held it close for a second, then slowly lowered himself onto the cool wooden floorboards of Selene’s workroom.

He opened the book with care, flipping through the early pages he already knew by heart. His eyes traveled past the simple flame techniques until they landed on a section he had never dared to approach before.

Advanced Fire Manipulation — Sustained Flame.

The explanation wasn’t written for children—it carried weight, demanding patience and precision. It explained how fire could be nurtured, fed by a constant flow of mana rather than a momentary spark. How shape, heat, and duration could be controlled through disciplined focus. The incantation that followed felt heavier as well, each word crafted to stir mana into a steady current.

Elrond read the chant once, then again, letting it settle into the rhythm of his breathing.

“Flame that answers my call, gather and grow—become the fire that follows my will.”

He whispered it under his breath.

A pulse of heat responded instantly. Mana surged through his arm—not wild or chaotic, but deliberate and firm—and a flame blossomed in his palm, larger and fuller than anything he had produced before. It danced and curled, its glow reflected in his wide eyes. The sensation of mana flowing steadily instead of bursting outward made his chest tighten with exhilaration.

He let the flame disperse and exhaled, his heart thudding with excitement.

There was more.

He turned the page.

Fireball Magic — Basic and Advanced Variations.

The description drew him in completely. The basic form involved compressing mana into a tight sphere before igniting it, releasing it as a projectile. But the advanced variation was on an entirely different scale— a dense, superheated mass that required careful calculation of mana density, ignition timing, and directional release. The diagrams detailed swirling layers of energy, ratios of mana concentration, and formation steps.

Elrond absorbed every line. His photographic memory captured the structure of the magic circles and the flow diagrams instantly. The incantation—long, intricate, and almost poetic—ran through his head as naturally as breathing by the third read.

He imagined the weight of the spell, the heat, the power of shaping something so volatile. A real fireball. His pulse picked up, the thrill of discovery compelling him to keep turning pages.

He didn’t notice the passing of time.

Nor did he hear the door open.

“Elrond…?”

The soft voice snapped through the quiet room. Elrond flinched and turned his head.

Selene stood in the doorway, still carrying the remnants of exhaustion in her expression—eyes half‑lidded, hair slightly tousled—but beneath the fatigue was something sharper. Surprise. Disbelief. Her gaze drifted from Elrond, to the book, then back to him, as if the image before her refused to arrange itself into something sensible.

“Elrond,” she said again, stepping inside slowly, “what are you doing?”

He swallowed and held the book a little tighter. “I… I was just looking around. I saw the magic book, so I…” His words shrank into silence.

Selene crouched down until she was eye‑level with him, her tired eyes narrowing with a confused blend of concern and curiosity. “Elrond… were you reading it?”

He froze. His breath caught.

Children his age didn’t read—not like this, not dense texts filled with diagrams and incantations. If he admitted it, would she think something was wrong with him? Would she take the book away entirely?

But she looked so exhausted… and he didn’t want to make her worry more.

So he nodded, barely above a whisper. “...Yes.”

Her sleepiness vanished in an instant.

Her eyes widened—not in fear, but in shock so deep it left her momentarily speechless. “Elrond… you can read this?” she asked, voice trembling between bewilderment and awe.

She looked down at the page he had open—one of the most complex early chapters—and then back at him, searching for any sign he was joking or imitating.

But she still didn’t know.

Didn’t know that he hadn’t just read it—

—but that moments before, he had already shaped its advanced flame spell perfectly in his own small palm.

Selene’s shock lingered for a long moment before she finally found her voice again. “Elrond… since when?” she asked softly, almost cautiously. “Since when could you read something like this?”

Elrond hesitated. His small fingers tightened around the book’s cover, and for a moment he looked down at his lap as though weighing his words.

But then he lifted his head.

“Since… since you read me stories before bed,” he said quietly. “The way you read them… I just remembered the shapes of the words. And the sounds they made.”

Selene blinked, her breath catching. “You… learned from that?” Her voice wavered as the meaning settled. “That was when you were barely three…”

Elrond nodded, a little shy but earnest. “Your voice makes it easy to remember. And… I liked those stories. So I wanted to know what the words looked like when you said them.”

A long silence followed.

Selene stared at him—truly stared—her tired eyes softening, her expression shifting slowly from disbelief… to something warm and bright.

“…Elrond,” she whispered, brushing a hand along his cheek, “you’re… incredible.”

Her heart thumped with a quiet pride she couldn’t restrain. A child reading at three? Understanding written text at five? It was beyond unusual—it was rare, unheard of. A genius hidden under her roof.

She swallowed back a swell of emotion and glanced at the book still opened on his lap. “Do you… understand what it’s saying?” she asked carefully. “Magic isn’t simple. Even adults struggle with the basics sometimes.”

Elrond shifted slightly, thinking. “I… understand a little,” he answered honestly. “The drawings help. And the parts you read to me make some parts easier.”

Selene let out a soft breath—half astonishment, half admiration. “A little…? Even understanding a little at your age is remarkable.”

She sat down beside him slowly, the wooden floor creaking under her weight. “Elrond… with talent like that, you might grow into a magician someday.” Her lips curved in a gentle, hopeful smile. “A real one. Maybe even better than me.”

His eyes widened, his heartbeat quickening at the idea.

“A magician…?” he repeated quietly.

Selene nodded. “If you want it. Magic isn’t easy—it needs patience, study, and discipline. But if you’re already this far at five years old…” She laughed softly under her breath, shaking her head in disbelief. “Then I can’t imagine how far you’ll go when you’re older.”

Elrond felt warmth bloom in his chest—an emotion tangled between pride, excitement, and a faint fear of discovery.

Because while Selene believed she had just found herself a prodigy… she still didn’t know that her five‑year‑old son had already mastered a spell many apprentices failed to perform even in their teens.

He lowered his eyes, hiding the small flicker of fire he still felt lingering in his palm.

“…Maybe,” he murmured.

But inside, the truth glowed brighter than any flame.

He already was one.

Still, Elrond kept it buried. Telling her he could cast simple fire magic—not once or twice, but hundreds of times—felt like crossing a line he wasn’t ready for. She was already exhausted. Already pushing herself. The last thing he wanted was to add worry on top of that.

So he took a quiet breath, lifted the book slightly, and changed the subject.

“Mother… um… Father said I can become a warrior someday,” he said, trying to sound casual. “With a real sword. He said I could be strong as him.”

Selene blinked, the shift in topic catching her off guard. Then, almost immediately, her expression softened, warmed, and brightened in a way that erased the last traces of drowsiness from her face.

“Oh, he did, did he?” she said with a small laugh. “Well… he is strong. And you admire him so much—it doesn’t surprise me.” She reached out and brushed his bangs aside lovingly. “You could be a fine swordsman, Elrond.”

Elrond nodded, a spark of excitement in his eyes. “He was so cool when he fought the Amarok. Mira said everyone talked about it.”

Selene’s smile widened. “Your father has always been reckless,” she said fondly. “But brave. And skilled.”

Then she paused—and her eyes shifted, glimmering with a new idea.

“But… if you combine swordsmanship with your talent for reading—your ability to understand magic…” She leaned closer, her voice gaining an eager lilt. “You could become something even more extraordinary.”

Elrond blinked. “Extraordinary…?”

“A spellsblade,” Selene said, the excitement growing in her tone. “A warrior who uses both sword and magic. Someone who moves like your father but casts like a magician.” She laughed softly, almost giddy. “Imagine it—my son, wielding a sword wreathed in flame or cloaked in wind! Oh, Aldric would faint from pride!”

Elrond couldn’t help smiling at her enthusiasm. It was infectious—sincere, bright in a way that made his chest feel lighter.

Selene clapped her hands together gently. “I must tell Aldric later. He’ll be thrilled.”

Then she stood slowly, brushing dust from her skirt. “Alright. I should get back downstairs and prepare things for the day.” She placed a hand gently on his head. “You may stay here for a little while longer if you want. Just… don’t tire yourself.”

“I won’t,” Elrond replied.

She gave him one last warm smile before heading toward the stairs, her footsteps soft and steady.

The moment the door closed behind her, Elrond exhaled.

Alone again.

And with the book open in his lap, he felt the familiar thrill rise in his chest.

He wasn’t just going to read.

He was going to master it.

Elrond drew a slow breath, settling himself more firmly on the wooden floor as the book rested open across his lap. He let his eyes trace the inked lines with a steadiness that didn’t belong on a five‑year‑old’s face. This time he wasn’t reading just to know the words—he wanted to understand the structure behind them, the logic hidden inside the chants he had memorized.

He flipped back and forth between the three fire incantations he knew: the basic spark, the sustained flame, and the fireball. Seeing only one at a time made them feel simple, almost obvious. But when he placed them side by side in his mind, paying attention to the order of the phrases and the way the wording changed, the difference between them became much clearer.

The first was the most familiar—the basic fire spell he had used since the beginning:

“Let warmth be born from my will, and let it take form as flame.”

The second was the sustained flame, written with longer, heavier words:

“Flame that answers my call, gather and grow—become the fire that follows my will and does not fade.”

And finally, the fireball incantation, the most complex of the three:

“Heat and power that answer my will, gather and condense at a single point—take the form of a burning star, and fly forth as a blazing spear of flame.”

These incantations were written in the ancient native tongue of this world—an old, ceremonial language no longer used in daily life. Modern speech sounded nothing like these phrases. The ancient words existed solely for spellcraft, crafted ages ago when magic was first formalized, and every syllable carried weight, rhythm, and intent that shaped mana itself.”

He read them again slowly, this time treating them not as separate spells, but as three stages of the same idea. The basic spell simply asked fire to appear. The sustained flame told it to stay, to grow, to follow. The fireball broke the process into steps: gather the mana, compress it, ignite, then release.

‘They’re all built from the same root,’ he realized, his gaze narrowing. ‘Same idea… different levels of detail.’

The basic fire spell was almost blunt in its directness—short phrases that pushed mana into a single sudden ignition. The advanced flame spell stretched those instructions outward, telling the fire not just to appear, but to stay, to grow, to follow, guiding the mana in a steady stream instead of a burst. And the fireball chant didn’t just ask the fire to burn or persist—it described a clear sequence: gather the mana, compress it, increase its density, ignite at the final moment, then release.

It reminded him of the way he used to break down reactions and physical processes—starting from the simplest form, then layering in energy, heat transfer, and the behavior of matter itself. The same idea expressed with more detail, more precision, and more understanding of how the world actually worked.

He rested his chin lightly on his fist.

‘So the incantations aren’t… magic words exactly. More like instructions. Or… a narrative that tells mana what shape fire should take.’

His mind churned with quiet intensity. Each chant felt like guiding rails for the subconscious—a way to give the body a clear path so mana would flow where it needed to without hesitation.

But Elrond had one advantage no child in this world should have.

He knew what fire actually was.

A simple chain reaction. Heat raising molecular motion. Fuel meeting air. Activation energy being crossed. Bond structures breaking apart and releasing stored energy as heat and light. And once that reaction began, it sustained itself as long as there was enough fuel and oxygen.

He traced a fingertip across the page slowly.

‘If mana is acting as the heat source… then all it needs to do is push the fuel—whatever’s in the air—past the activation point.’

It should work the same way it did in his old world. Heat something enough, and fire followed. If mana could behave as heat, and he understood how the reaction started, then maybe he didn’t need the chant to guide him. Maybe he just needed to recreate the conditions himself.

His gaze drifted down to his hand.

‘If I know exactly what fire needs to appear… then is the incantation really necessary?’

Elrond closed his eyes. He drew a slow breath, letting his awareness sink inward—not to his thoughts, but to the movement beneath his skin. Mana. The subtle current he had been pushing and prodding for months. But this time, he didn’t force it. He followed it.

He imagined the way it flowed through him—like warm currents rolling beneath the surface of water, soft but steady. He pictured it gathering, not explosively like the basic fire spell demanded, but smoothly, pooling in his palm as if guided by invisible channels.

His fingers relaxed. His breathing slowed.

He focused on the process.

Not the incantation. Not the imagery. Not the theatrics.

Just the science he remembered.

Fire—true fire—needed three things: Heat and oxygen.

Mana would be the heat source. The air itself provided the fuel—tiny particles, suspended oils, microscopic dust, and the ever‑present oxygen. All he needed was to push that air past its ignition point.

So Elrond visualized it.

He imagined the mana condensing into a point—compressing, tightening, raising the energy level of the air molecules directly above his palm. He pictured them vibrating faster and faster, colliding more intensely, until the bonds between them strained toward their limit.

He could almost feel it now. A tingling warmth in his palm—subtle at first, like the faintest brush of sunlight. Then it deepened, sinking past the skin, threading through nerves, traveling up the channels of mana he had slowly carved through constant repetition. A faint pressure followed, as if the air itself were gathering around his hand. A rising heat swelled inside his palm—not burning, not painful, but dense, concentrated, purposeful.

It reminded him of laboratory work from his past life—the sensation right before a chemical reaction reached its tipping point. That quiet, fragile moment where energy gathered, waiting for the smallest nudge to cascade into something unstoppable.

In his mind, the reaction unfolded with perfect clarity: – Air molecules vibrated faster as mana fed them energy. Heat climbed sharply, pushing suspended particles toward instability. Bonds strained toward breaking as the air neared ignition.

A spark without a spark. A flame without a chant. A reaction born purely from physics shaped by magic.

The moment the first molecular bond snapped—he felt it. A soft, almost imperceptible shift like the air exhaling.

Ignition.

A tiny fwip broke the silence, a sound sharper than a whisper yet gentler than a crack. A soft bloom of orange light burst into existence above his palm—no larger than a candle flame, but impossibly stable for something created with no incantation at all. It floated obediently, its edges curling and uncurling like a living creature testing its surroundings. The warmth brushed against his face, gentle and real.

His eyes snapped open.

“…I did it.”

The words slipped out unbidden, breathless.

He stared at the flame, disbelief washing through him in a cool, shivering wave. His heart pounded—not from exertion, but from the overwhelming realization pressing against his ribs.

No incantation. No ancient words. No ceremonial structure.

Just mana. And the fundamental laws of chemistry and physics. And understanding—true understanding— of what fire is.

His hypothesis, something scholars of this world never even considered plausible, had confirmed itself.

A shaky laugh escaped him, thin but overflowing with awe.

“So it is possible…”

The sensation swelling inside him was unmistakable. It was the same thrill he felt in his past life when experiments he designed—carefully, painstakingly, obsessively—finally aligned with reality. When theory met truth. When something impossible became possible under his own hands. A sharp clarity washed through him—an insight snapping into place with unmistakable certainty.
