Aldric’s usual morning weight was missing from the house. The sound of his boots, the clack of his practice sword—none of it reached Elrond’s ears.

Selene noticed his eyes open and set the book in her hand down on her lap.

"Father’s not here," Elrond said.

"He left before dawn," Selene said. "Multiple wyverns were spotted near the outskirts yesterday. That almost never happens. The patrol needed someone who can handle it if they get too close."

Elrond pushed himself up slowly. His limbs felt heavy in the way they always did the morning after mana fatigue, but the weakness was already fading.

Selene didn’t move from the chair. Her gaze stayed on him, sharp and quiet.

"How do you feel?" she asked.

"Just tired," Elrond said. "I’ll be fine after breakfast."

Selene reached out and rested two fingers lightly against the back of his hand. Warm mana stirred in her touch, tasting the flow inside him.

Her brow creased.

"Your mana is denser than it was last week," she said. "And higher than it was yesterday morning. That isn’t normal growth."

Elrond looked away.

"I’ve just been training," he said.

"Training doesn’t triple a pool in a year," Selene said mildly. "Not without something else." She tilted her head slightly. "Mira carried you home last night. Again."

A small knot tightened in Elrond’s chest.

"I just pushed a little too far," he said. "It’s not a big deal. I’m getting used to it."

"Pushing too far until you can’t walk back on your own is a big deal," Selene said. Her voice didn’t rise, but the edge in it sharpened. "This isn’t the first time, Elrond. Every time it happens, your mana spikes."

Her fingers stayed on his hand.

"Putting this together, it looks like you’ve been aiming for mana fatigue on purpose," she said. "Some mages only whisper that it might force a pool to grow, but no one treats it as fact. With you, the jumps are too clean to ignore. Is that what you’ve been testing?"

Elrond’s mouth went dry.

He could have lied again, but the way she was looking at him told him she had already built the shape of the answer in her head.

"…Every time I hit that point," he said quietly, "it gets bigger. I recover, and there’s more mana than before. If I stop now, it’ll slow down. I don’t want that."

Selene’s eyes softened for a moment, then hardened again.

"So you keep breaking yourself on purpose," she said. "Because you like the result."

"Because it works," Elrond said. "I’m getting used to it. I know where the edge is now. I haven’t collapsed in a long time. Yesterday was just…" He searched for the word. "Necessary."

Selene leaned back slightly in the chair, studying his face.

"You’re seven," she said. "And you’re already talking about ‘necessary’ damage to your own body."

Elrond held her gaze.

"If I want to stand where Father stands," he said, "I can’t stay where it’s safe."

For a long moment, Selene said nothing. The only sound in the room was the faint scrape of a branch against the window outside.

She finally drew in a quiet breath.

"We are not finished with this," she said. "But for now, you’re not leaving this house until I’ve checked your body and your mana properly. We’ll talk about your training again after that." Selene stood.

"Lie back," she said. "I’ll check you properly now."

Elrond eased down against the pillow again. Selene placed one hand lightly over his sternum and the other between his shoulder blades. Warm mana slipped from her into him in a thin, steady stream.

She started with the body. Her probing mana traced along his bones and joints, checked for tears in muscle, for bruised channels where mana flowed. Everything came back clean. No cracks. No burned-out pathways. No hidden damage from the collapses.

Her mouth tightened.

"Your body is fine," she said softly. "Too fine, considering what you’re doing to it."

She shifted the focus of her mana, pulling back from his limbs and sinking into the core of his chest instead.

The first sweep skimmed the surface. A dense layer of mana pressed against her probe like the top of a deep well. She tested the edge, trying to feel past it, but the bottom refused to show.

‘That’s already more than a normal child,’ she thought. ‘More than most adults.’

Selene drew a slow breath and changed methods. A simple surface read wasn’t enough.

She formed a small, precise circle in her mind—one designed to measure depth, not just presence—and let her mana spiral down along with his.

The pressure built in her senses.

Layer after layer of mana brushed past her probe, each one thicker than the last. It kept going—down and down—until her own control started to strain at the edges.

Her breath caught.

‘This can’t be right,’ she thought. ‘At his age…’

She pushed a little further.

The resistance on the far side of Elrond’s pool felt familiar—not in shape, but in scale. She had only felt anything like it a handful of times in her life, standing in the presence of those far above her own rank.

A Great Mage Sage. One of the few at the top of the mage hierarchies, whose mana alone could tilt a battlefield.

The comparison lodged in her mind and refused to move.

Her knees hit the floor beside the bed before she realized she’d lost strength in her legs. Her hands slipped away from Elrond’s back and chest as she pulled back all at once, breaking the contact.

Elrond pushed himself up on his elbows.

"Mother?" he asked.

Selene stared at her own hands for a moment, fingers curling slowly into her palms.

‘A child’s body,’ she thought. ‘And a mana pool brushing the edge of a Great Mage Sage. No wonder the rumors about fatigue training look true on him.’

She let out a short, uneven breath and forced herself back onto her feet.

"Nothing is broken," she said. "Your channels are intact. Your body is holding, somehow. But your mana…" She paused, searching for a word that didn’t exist. "Your mana is already at a scale most mages never reach, even at the highest ranks."

Elrond swallowed once.

‘So it really is that big,’ he thought.

Selene did not say anything more for a while. The room settled into a fragile, heavy quiet.

For today, the house stayed still. Mira wasn’t due to come by. If she had walked in on that examination, the secret of Elrond’s chantless magic would not have stayed buried for long.

Selene finally looked up from her hands.

"One more thing," she said. "Do not tell anyone about this. Until I say otherwise, your mana stays between us. Do you understand?"

Elrond hesitated, then nodded.

"I wasn’t planning to tell anyone anyway," he said. "Not even you."

Selene’s eyes narrowed a fraction.

"Not even your own parents," she said. "So mean…" Her lips pushed out in a small, exaggerated pout that didn’t match the weight of what she had just sensed. "Keeping something this big from your own mother? That’s totally unfair."

Elrond felt a vein of annoyance flicker under the tiredness.

‘Such a trouble…’ he thought. Another thought slipped in. ‘Wait a second. From my side, she’s the kid here.’ Selene was twenty-four. Saitou had died at twenty-nine. Add seven years in this life on top of that and, in his head, he was thirty-six—twelve years older than her. The math was so dumb it almost made him laugh.

He dropped his gaze to the blanket and tugged at the edge of it with one hand.

"Sorry," he said. "I was just… scared it would cause trouble. And that you’d be mad if you found out I did something stupid again."

Selene let out a breath that was almost a sigh.

"I am mad," she said. Then she reached out and flicked his forehead with one finger, not hard enough to hurt. "But not because your mana is big. Because you decided to hide this from me and break yourself on purpose without saying a word."

She rested her hand on his head for a moment.

"Don’t do that again," she said. "If you’re going to do something dangerous to yourself, you tell your mother first. No more secrets about your training."

Her tone eased a little at the end.

Elrond gave a small nod.

"Okay," he said.

He hesitated, then drew in a breath.

"Actually… there’s one more secret," he said. "About my magic. It’s easier if I show you."

Selene’s eyes narrowed again.

"Such a trouble…" she muttered. "Fine. Show me. But if this is another way you’ve been breaking yourself, I’m tying you to the bed for a week."

A few minutes later, they stood at the edge of the yard. The training field lay open in front of them, the far trees marking the border.

Elrond stepped forward, lifted his hand, and focused.

No words left his mouth.

A tight, bright fireball formed above his palm—clean, stable, the size of his fist. He flicked his wrist. The fireball shot across the yard like an arrow, slammed into a tree at the far end, and burst in a sharp, contained explosion that left a black scorch mark on the bark.

Selene blinked once. Twice.

Elrond lowered his hand.

"How is it?" he asked.

Selene looked at him. Then at the distant tree. Then back at him.

"What," she said. Then louder, "WHAT?! When did you chant the spell?"

"I didn’t," Elrond said.

The answer landed harder than the explosion. Selene’s legs went out from under her for the second time that day. She dropped to her knees in the packed dirt and covered her face with both hands.

"I know you’re amazing," she said weakly through her fingers. "But I didn’t think it was to this level…"

Elrond scratched his cheek, a small, helpless smile tugging at his mouth.

Before long, they were back inside. Selene sat at the dining table, elbows on the wood, staring at nothing in particular. Elrond set a glass of water in front of her.

"Here," he said. "Are you okay, Mother?"

She took the glass with both hands, drank, and set it down. The dazed look in her eyes cleared, replaced by something sharp.

She reached out and gripped his shoulders.

"Listen carefully," she said. "You never tell anyone about this. Not your friends, not the other mages, not anyone in town. Only me and your father. Understood?"

Elrond blinked.

"Only you and Father," he repeated. "Got it."

Selene held his gaze for one more heartbeat, then let go.

A bright smile broke across her face, sudden and unrestrained.

"Our son is this amazing," she said, almost bouncing in her seat. "This is unfair to the rest of the world."

By the time Aldric came home, the sky outside had already turned orange. The front door opened with a familiar creak, followed by the heavy sound of his boots in the entryway.

“I’m back,” he called.

Selene stood up at once. A bright smile spread across her face as she walked over to him, the earlier shock now settled into a quiet, bubbling happiness.

“Welcome back,” she said.

Aldric blinked at her expression.

“…What happened?” he asked. “You look way too happy for a normal day.”

Selene’s smile widened.

“I’ll tell you inside,” she said, tugging lightly at his sleeve. “It’s about Elrond.”

The day ended with the three of them at the table, Selene talking, Aldric listening with a furrowed brow that slowly turned into stunned silence, and Elrond sitting there with a small, helpless smile he couldn’t quite hide.

### Chapter 8: 7 - New path

#### Scene 1

Morning light slipped through the thin curtains and drew a pale line across Elrond’s ceiling.

He lay on his back and stared at it, hands folded over his chest. His shoulders still remembered the weight of Selene’s grip from yesterday. His ears still remembered Aldric’s stunned silence.

Nothing dramatic had followed after he showed them the chantless fireball. No thunder from the heavens, no Divine Being descending, no sudden invitation from the royal capital.

Just his mother sitting down very slowly. His father rubbing his temples in the doorway.

"One more time," Aldric had said last night at the table, voice lower than usual. "No chant. You’re sure?"

Elrond had nodded.

Aldric’s fingers had tightened around his cup until the wood creaked. He hadn’t said anything clever or wise. He just kept staring, as if the image of his son throwing that silent fireball refused to line up with the years of common sense inside his head.

Even now, Elrond could picture his father blinking a few times, looking almost… lost. As if he might wake up back on patrol and laugh that it had all been a dream.

‘Casting without a chant… of course they reacted like that,’ Elrond thought.

He turned his head on the pillow and watched dust motes drift in the beam of light.

Being able to shape a spell without speaking was rare enough to be called a story, not a skill. Most mages he had read about needed long, formal chants for anything above basic fire. Some geniuses could cut them shorter with practice. A handful of monsters in human form could skip them entirely.

Those monsters had names.

‘Demon Lords,’ he recalled.

On the demon continent, the strongest among the demonic races were said to twist mana as easily as breathing. Their magic didn’t wait for words. It moved the moment they willed it. Stories said that when a Demon Lord raised a hand, cities vanished before their lips even parted.

Compared to that, his little fireball was nothing.

But the method was the same: intent first, voice optional.

Humans almost never reached that level. The ones who did filled history books—great magi with titles instead of family names. Their portraits usually came with notes like "rumored to cast without chant" or "developed unique silent-activation technique".

Elves were listed in the same category, but it wasn’t quite the same.

‘Elves don’t truly use chantless magic,’ Elrond reminded himself.

They still chanted. They only moved the chant from their tongue to their mind. Every syllable, every structure, recited silently along a fixed route inside their thoughts. To anyone watching, it looked like pure willpower. In reality, it was a different kind of discipline.

Some humans had copied that trick—compressing chants into internal whispers instead of spoken words. Faster, less obvious, dangerous if the mind slipped even once.

What Elrond did felt different.

He didn’t recite anything, inside or out. No hidden chant, no memorized formula. He pictured how fire behaved, how heat crawled, how air changed, and then he pushed mana along that image until reality followed.

Last night, Selene had assumed it was a Divine Blessing.

"Maybe this is your gift," she had said, half in awe, half in panic. "A blessing that lets you ignore chants entirely."

Aldric hadn’t argued. For a moment, both of them stared at him as if some god had written a label across his forehead.

Then Elrond explained.

He talked about counting casts until he collapsed, about tracing each spell step by step, about training until the chant became a nuisance instead of a guide. He described how he pictured the spell’s structure, how he broke it apart and rebuilt it without words.

Selene had listened with her hands pressed to her mouth. Aldric hadn’t blinked much.

By the end, they both looked less like parents witnessing a miracle and more like people watching a child drag a boulder uphill every single day.

"So it isn’t a blessing," Selene had whispered, almost to herself. "You forced it open."

"You should’ve told us sooner," Aldric had added, voice rough. Not angry. Just tired.

Elrond exhaled slowly on his bed.

A massive mana pool. Chantless casting. Both parents knew now that none of it had fallen from the sky. No god had handed him an easy road. He had just walked further than most people tried.

One in a million—that was probably still generous. Most chantless users in the world were monsters or legends. Demon Lords on a faraway continent. Dead great magi whose spells only survived in worn-out tomes. A few elven archmages who only looked chantless from the outside.

And then there was him.

A boy lying in a small room in a frontier town, staring at the ceiling while morning light crept across the plaster.

‘No Divine Blessing, huh,’ he thought.

His lips curled in a faint, wry smile.

‘Good. That means the result is mine.’

He pushed himself up, feet touching the cool floorboards, and listened for sounds from downstairs. Selene in the kitchen. Mira moving through the hall. Aldric, maybe, already gone on patrol.

Today would be the same as yesterday.

A couple of days passed, and Elrond’s routine settled back into something that looked normal from the outside.

Morning sword in the yard with Aldric; afternoon magic under Selene’s eye in the workroom. The difference now was simple: he no longer needed to pretend he was weaker than he was.

As long as he stayed inside the fence, he could give it his all.

He still checked the gaps between the planks whenever he raised his hand. Neighbors walked past from time to time, carrying buckets or baskets. A wooden sword swing was one thing. A stray fireball climbing into the sky was another.

On that morning, the sun was already high enough to warm the packed dirt when Aldric lowered his wooden practice sword and narrowed his eyes.

"Again," Aldric said.

Elrond drew in a breath and ran through the familiar steps.

Strength Enhancement. Agility Enhancement.

Words left his mouth in a short, practiced chant. Mana moved, clung to his muscles, settled in his legs. His body grew heavier and lighter at the same time.

He stepped in. The next exchange was clean: three strikes, one parry, a pivot, a low sweep he barely dodged.

Aldric stopped first.

He rested the sword against his shoulder and watched Elrond’s stance.

"You can skip the chant for fire," Aldric said. "Why not for this?"

Elrond straightened and let the enhancement fade. The weight left his limbs in a slow breath.

"For chantless magic, I need to know exactly how the spell works," he answered. "Fire is simple. Heat, ignition, air. I understand what changes."

"Strength and Agility are different. I know the theory, but I don’t know what really happens inside. I tried a few times using only the image in my head. Nothing came out."

Aldric’s gaze dropped to Elrond’s arms.

"Theory is just a story until your body agrees with it," he said. "Maybe you’re thinking too far away from yourself."

Elrond blinked.

"Before you cast, feel it properly. Grip it. Remember it. Then cast the enhancement and check again. Not with your eyes. With your hand. With how it moves."

He paused, searching for the right words.

"Don't make it complicated," Aldric said. "Just remember how your arm feels now, then see what's different after the spell, because sometimes I can feel it."

Something clicked.

Elrond’s brows lifted a fraction. His lungs forgot their next breath for a heartbeat.

‘…I never checked,’ he realized.

He had counted casts. Counted failures. Counted the seconds spells lasted. But he had never once stopped to ask his own body how it felt.

He swallowed and stepped back, out of striking range.

"I’ll try now," he said.

Aldric only nodded and lowered his sword.

Elrond held out his left arm. He squeezed his forearm with his right hand, pressing his fingers into the flesh.

Soft. Warm. His fingers sank in easily. A child’s arm, thin but still more padding than muscle.

‘Weak grip strength. No real hardness yet,’ he noted.

He released his arm, drew in mana, and spoke the shortest version of the Strength Enhancement chant he knew.

Light crawled along his skin and sank inward.

He squeezed the same spot again.

This time his fingers met resistance almost immediately. The surface felt tighter, as if the meat under the skin had pulled itself into a dense bundle. The shape hadn’t changed, but it pushed back against his grip.

‘Different,’ he thought. ‘The tension is higher. Fibers packed together. The spell isn’t just "making me stronger". It’s forcing the muscle to hold more load.’

The magic faded. Warmth left his arm.

He kept his eyes on his own hand and built the image in his mind from the ground up: the soft forearm from before, the denser one from after, the mana pressing in like an invisible band.

No chant.

He drew mana again, guided it into that picture, and pushed.

Heat spread from shoulder to fingertips.

His forearm tightened under his skin.

Aldric’s fingers twitched on his sword hilt.

"…Did you just—" he began.

Elrond clenched his fist and pulled it up in front of his face. The motion came with a faint lag from extra weight, the same lag he felt when using the spoken spell.

He loosened his hand and let out a breath he hadn’t noticed he was holding.

"It activated," he said quietly.

No words. No chant. The enhancement held.

Aldric let out a slow breath he had been holding somewhere deep in his chest.

"Good," he said. The corner of his mouth twitched up. "Don’t get carried away with it yet."

The strength magic bled out of Elrond’s arm. His body settled back to its usual lightness.

He rolled his shoulders once, then glanced down at his legs.

‘If Strength tightens the muscle like that… then Agility should be doing something to how heavy I feel when I move,’ he thought.

He dropped the wooden sword to his side and lowered himself to the ground.

"What are you doing?" Aldric asked.

"Checking," Elrond said.

He set his hands on the packed dirt and started doing push-ups.

The first few were easy. By the tenth, his arms began to shake faintly. His chest brushed the ground a little harder each time.

He stopped, locked that weight into his memory, and pushed himself back to his feet.

‘That’s the baseline,’ he decided.

He drew in mana and spoke the chant for Agility Enhancement. Light slid down his spine and pooled around his hips and ankles. He dropped to the ground again and set his hands where they had been before.

One push-up. Two. Three.

His body rose and fell with less effort. The ground felt farther away. There was a faint sensation as if something under his ribs was helping lift him.

‘Lighter,’ he thought. ‘It’s not just making me faster. It’s taking some of my own weight away when I move.’

He finished the set, exhaled, and stood.

The magic faded. The familiar heaviness of his small frame returned.

Elrond closed his eyes for a moment and rebuilt the picture: his body pressing against the dirt before the spell, the easier rise after, the strange support under his muscles.

No chant.

He gathered mana at his core and pushed it along that image, toward his legs and feet.

A soft rush wrapped around his calves.

The yard seemed to tilt for an instant as his sense of weight shifted.

He took a single step forward.

His foot hit the ground faster than it should have. The move felt the same as before—just… lighter, as if the world had loosened its grip on him by a small notch.

He opened his eyes.

"It worked," he said. His voice came out a little higher than he expected.

He took two quick steps, then three, circling once in front of Aldric. The air pressed against his skin in a way he recognized from every chanted Agility spell he had ever used.

He stopped and turned back, cheeks lifted.

"I did it, Father," Elrond said.

Aldric stared at him for a heartbeat.

Then his face broke into a wide grin.

He laughed once, short and rough, and scrubbed at the corner of his eye with the back of his wrist as if wiping away sweat that wasn’t there.

"…Yeah," he said. "You did."

His voice caught on the last word.

Elrond watched him, chest still rising and falling from the small burst of movement.

‘He’s happy,’ he realized.

Not just because the spell worked. Because the hint had helped.

Aldric set his sword tip on the ground and leaned on it lightly.

"If you’re going to keep pulling ahead like this," he said, "then I’d better keep up. Otherwise I’ll lose my job as your teacher."

He was smiling when he said it.

Morning after morning, Elrond kept stepping out into the yard at Aldric’s side.

Wooden swords. Dust kicked up from the same packed lines. Strength and Agility spells layered over his muscles until the weight and lightness felt familiar instead of strange.

In the afternoons, Selene claimed him.

She filled a small table near the back door with opened grimoires, ink-stained notes, and a small stack of fire-attribute crystals. By the time they finished each day, the air above the practice stones in the yard carried a faint smell of heated stone and boiled ink.

"Today—Fire Pillar," she had said the first time, tapping the heading on a page.

It was a step above his usual fireball. Not just a lump of flame thrown forward, but a column that had to rise straight and hold its shape.

Selene wasn’t a combat mage. She reminded him of that more than once.

"I can teach you the structure and the chant," she said, palm resting on the grimoire. "But I don’t use this on battlefields. I only ever needed it for experiments."

That was enough.

Elrond memorized the chant, but his attention stayed on the description beneath it: the way mana gathered in a line, how ignition started from the ground up, how the pillar was supposed to maintain heat evenly from base to tip.

Out in the backyard, he stepped onto the training circle Selene had carved into the packed dirt. The first time he cast it with the full chant, a narrow column of fire roared up from that circle. It wavered. The top bent slightly in the breeze.

"Good," Selene said, squinting at the way it burned. "The shape is there. The heat is still low."

They repeated it until his throat went dry.

He logged every detail—the way the ground warmed under his feet, the sound of air rushing upward, the thickness of the flame compared to his arm.

Then, later, he tried without speaking.

He pictured a vertical line from the circle at his feet up into the sky. He filled that line with heat in his mind, stacked it with the rushing sensation he had felt, and pushed mana along it. A pillar of fire climbed up.

Water followed the same pattern.

Selene turned the page to a spell labeled Water Cannon. The diagram showed compressed water bursting forward in a straight shot.

"This one is more dangerous if you point it the wrong way," she warned. "Aim toward the yard wall. Not the house."

He learned the chant. He learned the structure: compression, release, direction.

Spoken, the spell spat a thick, high-pressure stream of water that slammed into the far wall and left the stone dripping.

Unspoken, once he had mapped the way his mana tightened and snapped free, the same spell answered his will with a silent rush.

Fire Pillar. Water Cannon. Again and again, until both came as easily as breathing.

Once the chantless versions stopped feeling special and started feeling normal, he began to combine them.

He stood in the center of the yard one afternoon with three empty circles etched into the dirt around him.

He raised his hand.

One pillar of fire surged up from the first circle.

He shifted his focus.

A second pillar roared to life on his left, then a third on his right, each born from a separate thread of mana he held like cords between his fingers.

Heat rolled over his skin. The air flickered.

He twisted his wrist.

The three pillars leaned inward, bending without breaking, their tops curving toward an invisible point above the center of the yard. Flame licked at an empty space as if trying to swallow something that wasn’t there.

It looked a little like a drawing he had stared at in one of Selene’s thicker books.

Inferno.

A very high-rank spell listed deep inside an expert grimoire. The description said its flames erased everything they touched. Stone turned to glass. Metal flowed. Nothing living survived.

Selene couldn’t cast it. Most people couldn’t even store enough mana to attempt it.

Elrond held his three pillars in place for a few breaths, then let them collapse. The flames thinned and broke apart, fading into rising heat.

‘No comparison,’ he thought.

His pillars were bright, but not blinding. The heat made his skin prickle, not blister. The air wavered, but the ground under his feet stayed solid instead of glowing.

Inferno in the book was something else entirely—hotter, denser, a single mass of fire that didn’t just burn the surface but chewed through whatever stood inside it.

All he had done was stack basic pillars and shape them into a crude cage.

Still, when he closed his eyes, he could imagine the next step: more pillars, tighter spacing, higher temperature. The structure was there, waiting.

He opened his eyes to the clear sky above the yard and let out a slow breath.

‘One day,’ he thought. ‘The real thing.’

The next morning, the yard was quiet.

The wooden swords still leaned against the wall, but Aldric’s spot in the center of the packed dirt was empty.

Elrond stood there anyway, fingers brushing the worn grip of his sword.

Selene stepped out from the back door, tying her hair up as she walked.

"Your father had to leave early," she said. "There’s been an increased alert. More wyvern sightings outside town."

Elrond turned to her.

"Wyverns? Here?"

"Reports from the patrol," Selene replied. "And there’s word a noble family will be passing through today. House escort, carriages, the whole thing. The patrol team has to make sure nothing happens while they’re inside our walls."

She smiled a little, but it didn’t quite reach her eyes.

"So Aldric gets to run around before breakfast instead of after."

Elrond’s fingers tightened around the sword hilt, then loosened.

He had been looking forward to the morning spar.

Selene glanced at him, then at the faint shadows under his eyes.

"You’re disappointed," she said. "But… this might be a good chance for you to rest."

"Rest?" he repeated.

"You’ve been training every day for weeks," she said. "Morning sword, afternoon magic, sneaking extra practice whenever you think I’m not watching. If you don’t stop sometimes, your body will complain before your mana does."

He opened his mouth to argue, then shut it again.

When he counted back in his head, there really weren’t any empty days.

‘She’s right,’ he admitted to himself.

He let go of the sword and exhaled.

"All right," he said. "I’ll take today off."

"Good boy," Selene said. "In that case, you’re helping with chores. We’re making something special for dinner."

"A feast?" he asked.

"If everything goes well," she said. "Your father will be exhausted when he comes back. We might as well welcome him properly."

To make the most of his day off, Elrond stayed close to the house.

He carried laundry baskets, fetched water, wiped tables, and peeled vegetables at the kitchen bench while Selene moved between the stove and the cutting board.

Mira arrived a little later than usual, breathless from walking quickly.

"Sorry I’m late," she said, bowing her head. "The town gate was noisy this morning. Lots of movement."

"We heard," Selene replied. "More monsters, more work for the patrol. We’re preparing a lot of food, so I’m counting on you."

"Yes, milady," Mira said, then glanced at Elrond with a small smile. "And the young master is helping today too, I see."

Elrond stood on a small stool to reach the counter properly, hands dusted with flour.

"Mother said I can’t train, so I’m working," he said.

Mira laughed softly.

"That’s very you," she said.

The three of them settled into a rhythm.

Knives tapped against the board. Water hissed where it boiled. The kitchen filled with the smells of meat, herbs, and baked bread. Every so often, Selene would reach over Elrond’s hands to adjust his grip on the knife or steady a bowl he was stirring.

It wasn’t often that all three of them were in the kitchen at once.

Usually, at this hour, Elrond would be outside trading blows with Aldric while Selene worked in her study and Mira handled the house.

For a while, the only sounds were cooking and quiet conversation.

Then something different slipped in from outside.

A distant clatter. Hooves on stone. The faint ring of metal on metal. Voices, sharper than the usual morning chatter of neighbors.

Elrond paused with the ladle halfway to a pot.

"…Do you hear that?" he asked.

Mira looked up from the vegetables.

"The street’s louder than usual," she said.

A few heartbeats later, someone knocked on the front door. Not the quick, light knock of a neighbor. Three firm blows. Solid. Selene wiped her hands on her apron.

"I’ll—"

"I’ll get it," Elrond said.

He set the ladle down, hopped off the stool, and hurried through the hall. The knock came again just as he reached the door. He pulled it open.

It was Aldric. For a moment, Elrond’s mind went blank.

His father stood in the doorway in full armor, helmet tucked under one arm. Scratches marred the metal. His cloak hung heavy, dark patches drying along the hem. A streak of deep red crossed his cheek and ran down to his jaw.

The smell of iron hit Elrond a beat later.

"Father—"

His heart lurched. He stepped forward and grabbed at Aldric’s sleeve, eyes darting over the plates of armor, searching for a cut, a gap, any sign of fresh blood.

Aldric caught his wrist gently with his free hand.

"I’m all right," he said. His voice was tired but steady. "This isn’t mine. Wyvern’s."

Elrond’s shoulders sagged all at once.

Now that he focused, he could see the color properly—thicker, almost black in places where it had dried. The scent was harsher than human blood, sharp enough to sting his nose.

He swallowed.

"…Wyvern?" he repeated.

Aldric released his wrist and stepped a little to the side. Only then did Elrond notice the people behind him. The street in front of the house was crowded.

Town guards in dented armor stood in small clusters, some leaning on spears, others supporting comrades with bandaged arms. Behind them, a group of strangers waited near a large carriage—polished wood, reinforced wheels, luggage stacked on top. Servants and maids in matching colors stood close, eyes flicking between the house and the road.

On the carriage door, a crest was painted in clean lines. Even without knowing all the details, Elrond recognized the name when Aldric spoke it.

"This carriage belongs to House Alfrost," Aldric said. "They were on their way back to Arbalest after finishing some noble business."

Selene and Mira had come up behind Elrond by then. Selene’s gaze went to the blood on Aldric’s armor first, then to the guards and the crest.

"What happened?" she asked.

"Wyvern attack, just outside the southern road," Aldric said. "One big one leading a pack. We arrived before they broke through to the carriage, but…"

His jaw tightened for a moment.

"We lost a few men holding the line. Some others are injured. They’re being treated at the central clinic now."

Elrond looked past him at the patrol members.

These were the same men who sometimes ruffled his hair when he passed the gate, who joked about Aldric’s lectures and complained about night shifts.

Now some of them sat on the edge of the street, faces pale, armor cracked, bandages showing under loosened straps. Aldric followed his gaze.

"Wyverns shouldn’t be this close to town," he said quietly. "Seeing one at all is rare. Lately we’re getting sightings every other week. And now they’re attacking carriages like they’re being pushed toward us."

He looked back at Selene.

"This one was A-class for sure. The pack made it worse. If we’d been a little later…"

He didn’t finish the sentence.

Elrond pictured a carriage crushed under claws and fangs, fire and scales tearing through wood and cloth.

Aldric’s gauntlets creaked as he flexed his fingers.

"Anyway," he said, forcing a breath out, "we managed. It was a hard fight, but the carriage is safe. House Alfrost will be staying in town for a while until we’re sure the road is clear again."

He shifted his weight and glanced past Elrond into the house.

"Sorry to bring work home," he added wryly. "But we need a place to talk and clean up before the next decisions are made."

Elrond stepped back from the doorway to make space, heartbeat finally slowing. Only then did he notice someone else stepping forward from the group near the carriage.

A man stepped forward from the group near the carriage.

He wore a dark travel cloak over light armor, the fabric trimmed in the same colors as the crest on the carriage door. Black hair with faint silver streaks fell to his shoulders, neat even after battle. When he smiled, the lines at the corner of his eyes deepened in a way that made him look both dangerous and easy to talk to.

He stopped a step away from Aldric, then turned his attention to Selene.

He placed a hand over his chest and bowed.

"Lady Selene von Astrea, I presume. I am Wilhelm Alfrost."

Selene’s hand tightened slightly on her apron.

"…Alfrost?" she echoed.

Wilhelm straightened, the smile still there.

"On behalf of House Alfrost," he said, "I came to offer my thanks. To you, and especially to Captain Aldric." He glanced at Aldric’s stained armor. "Without your lead, today’s outcome would have been… very different."

Aldric shifted his grip on the helmet under his arm.

"We only did our duty," he said. "The patrol moved as a unit."

"And that is exactly why I’m here," Wilhelm replied. "Duty or not, you stood between my family and an A-class monster. House Alfrost pays its debts."

His tone was light, but the weight behind the words was clear enough.

He glanced at the street, at the guards and servants waiting around the carriage.

"If possible," he added, "may we continue this inside? I don’t want to block the road longer than we have to."

Selene stepped back from the doorway.

"Of course," she said. "Please, come in."

Wilhelm entered first. Two of his attendants followed—one older servant with a notepad tucked under his arm, one maid carrying a small leather case. The rest of the group stayed outside with the carriage and the wounded.

The house suddenly felt smaller with a noble inside.

Elrond moved aside to let them pass, back pressing lightly against the wall as Wilhelm’s cloak brushed by. Up close, the man carried the same faint metallic smell as Aldric, mixed with a sharper scent of some kind of oil or potion.

Wilhelm caught his eye for a moment and gave him a quick, easy grin.

"You must be Elrond," he said.

Elrond straightened.

"Yes, sir," he said.

"A good name," Wilhelm replied. "We’ll talk another time."

He followed Selene into the living room.

Since it was clearly an adult discussion, Elrond stayed near the hall entrance only long enough to see where they sat—Wilhelm on the sturdier wooden chair, Aldric opposite him, Selene at the side.

Then he slipped back toward the yard, wooden sword still leaning by the back door where he had left it.

Outside, the noise of the street dropped to a dull murmur.

Elrond picked up the sword and walked to the side of the house where the fence cast a slanted shadow. He set his feet in the familiar stance and began to swing—not full drills, just controlled cuts to keep his hands busy while his ears stayed open.

The front window was cracked for air. Voices leaked through in fragments when the breeze shifted.

Inside, Wilhelm folded one leg over the other and rested his elbows lightly on the armrests.

"First," he said, "let me say this clearly. Thank you, Captain Aldric. From House Alfrost, from the lord I serve, and from me personally."

"You don’t need to—" Aldric began.

Wilhelm cut him off with a small wave of his hand, still smiling.

"If I don’t, my sister will scold me for a week," he said. "She’s fond of those children in that carriage."

Selene’s eyes softened for a moment.

"So your family is on the road with you," she said.

"My elder brother’s children," Wilhelm replied. "We were returning to Arbalest after a tiresome round of noble affairs. I expected boredom, not wyverns."

His smile thinned.

"I’ll admit it," he went on. "When that big one dropped out of the clouds, I had trouble keeping the formation clean. Their scales turn blades, their breath melts shields. On an open road with carriages to protect, things get messy."

Aldric’s jaw worked once.

"You held the front until we arrived," Aldric said. "We only picked up where you left off."

Wilhelm huffed a short laugh.

"That’s a polite way of putting it," he said. "From where I was standing, your orders and your timing cut the chaos in half. You saw the distance, the angles, the risk of breath attacks… and you still pushed in."

He tilted his head, studying Aldric with open curiosity.

"No flashy spell circles. No noble crest. Just a captain from a frontier town stepping up like a veteran commander."

Aldric looked away for a heartbeat, gaze dropping to his own hands.

"I’ve been in a few fights," he said.

"I noticed," Wilhelm replied.

He leaned back in the chair and snapped his fingers once. The older servant stepped forward with a small pouch.

"Which brings us to the second reason I’m here," Wilhelm said. "Reward."

Aldric’s expression tightened.

"That isn’t necessary," he said. "The town guard was only doing its job."

"And House Alfrost is only showing proper gratitude," Wilhelm said. He didn’t raise his voice, but he didn’t soften it either. "Refuse if you like, but I’ll just give it to your men directly."

Selene’s eyes flicked between them, lips pressing together.

"The patrol unit is already being paid by the kingdom," Aldric said. "Anything more is—"

"A matter between my house and the ones who saved our lives," Wilhelm said. "Not the treasury."

He nodded to the servant.

"One hundred gold coins," he said. "Seventy for your team to divide as you see fit. Thirty for you."

The servant opened the pouch just enough that the inside caught the light. Even from the hall, the dull gleam of stacked coins was clear.

Aldric froze.

"…One hundred?" he said.

The number left his mouth like it weighed something.

In the yard, Elrond’s swing faltered.

He had been half-listening, half-counting his breaths. The words "one hundred gold" snapped him back sharply. The wooden sword dipped before he caught it again.

‘That’s insane,’ he thought.

In his old world, one gold coin of this kingdom’s standard size could buy enough food to feed a family here for months. If he converted it roughly in his head, it landed somewhere around six thousand dollars. About one million yen.

One hundred coins meant a small fortune. Thirty coins for one person was… absurd.

Inside, Aldric shook his head.

"That’s too much," he said. "I can’t accept that kind of—"

"You can," Wilhelm interrupted. "And you will."

He leaned forward slightly, the easy smile sharpening just a touch.

"You lost men today," he said quietly. "Some won’t walk again. Some won’t hold a spear. You’re telling me you’ll look them in the eye and say House Alfrost tried to help, but you turned it down because your pride didn’t like the amount?"

Aldric’s mouth closed.

Selene’s fingers curled in the fabric of her skirt.

Wilhelm’s tone lightened again.

"Give the seventy to your unit," he said. "Call it battle hazard compensation, extra equipment funds, whatever lets you sleep at night. As for your share…"

He shrugged.

"Use it to fix your roof," he added. "Or buy your son a proper training sword when he’s old enough not to cut his own foot off."

Aldric let out a breath he hadn’t realized he was holding.

"…You’re very pushy for a guest," he said.

Wilhelm grinned.

"It’s my best quality," he said. "My brother handles the quiet dignity. I handle the rest."

A moment passed.

Aldric finally reached out and took the pouch.

He weighed it in his hand. The coins clinked softly against each other.

"Thank you," he said. "On behalf of my men."

"Good," Wilhelm said. "Now I can go home without my sister accusing me of being ungrateful."

Outside, Elrond kept his swings slow so the sound of wood cutting air wouldn’t drown the voices.

Hoofbeats shifted on the street. A few guards near the carriage had turned away from the door to watch him through the gate. Their faces looked tired, but a couple of them still managed to smirk when his wooden sword blurred through a series of clean cuts.

Elrond lowered the blade and rested it on his shoulder for a moment, catching his breath.

Movement at the carriage window drew his eye.

Two small faces peeked out between the curtains.

A girl and a boy, close in age, both dressed far better than anyone in this part of town. The girl’s dark hair spilled over her shoulders, glossy even in the shade of the carriage. The boy’s features resembled hers enough that Elrond guessed they were siblings.

He met the girl’s gaze first.

She stiffened, eyes widening a fraction when she realized he had noticed her. For a second, they just stared at each other.

Elrond lifted one hand and gave a small wave.

The girl flinched, cheeks coloring, and jerked back out of sight. The curtain twitched as she pulled it closed a little.

A second later, the boy leaned into the same space and looked out.

His posture was relaxed, chin propped lightly on his hand where it rested on the window frame. When he saw Elrond, he gave a small, lopsided grin and raised his fingers in a lazy half-wave.

Elrond’s grip on the wooden sword eased.

He smiled back and returned the gesture.

The boy’s grin widened for a heartbeat before he, too, pulled away from the window. The curtain fell back into place.

Elrond stayed where he was, the faint echo of their faces still clear in his mind.

‘Nobles,’ he thought. ‘So those are the kind of kids who ride in carriages guarded by A-class monster bait.’

He tightened his hands around the sword hilt again.

The front door opened with a soft creak.

Elrond slowed his swings and listened.

Boots crossed the hall. Voices moved closer to the entryway—Wilhelm’s smoother tone, Aldric’s lower one, the lighter steps of attendants behind them.

Elrond lowered the wooden sword and rounded the corner of the house just as the front door opened fully.

Wilhelm stepped out first, his half-cloak adjusted, armor clean now but still carrying faint scratches from earlier. His servants followed a step behind.

Aldric came after them, one hand resting near the small of his back as if he hadn’t quite shaken off the weight of the fight.

He walked Wilhelm toward the street, then stopped halfway to the gate.

His gaze slid to the waiting carriage, to the crest on its door, to the window where two children had just disappeared behind the curtain. Something in his expression shifted.

"So that’s why you paid us this much," Aldric said quietly. "Because of what’s inside that carriage."

Wilhelm’s smile sharpened, but the warmth didn’t leave it.

"Exactly," he said. "I don’t put prices on people, Captain. But I do pay properly for the lives my family still has because of you."

He turned his head, following Aldric’s line of sight. His gaze landed on Elrond. Elrond straightened instinctively, wooden sword still in hand.

Wilhelm’s eyes flicked to his stance, to the scuffed dirt under his feet, to the clean arc marks in the ground where he had been swinging.

He smiled.

"Your fencing form is very good for someone your age. Clean cuts. No wasted movement. You must have put in a lot of work already."

Elrond blinked once.

"I’m still learning," he said.

"That’s what good foundations sound like," Wilhelm replied.

He glanced at Aldric.

"You’ve raised a dedicated one," he said. "With talent like that, he should be standing in Arbalest’s Royal Academy, not just this yard."

The words dropped into the air like a stone into still water. Elrond’s fingers tightened around the wooden hilt. Selene had stepped into the doorway without him noticing.

Aldric’s shoulders went stiff.

"The… Royal Academy?" Aldric repeated.

"There’s no law saying only nobles can attend," Wilhelm said lightly. "It’s more a matter of entrance exams, sponsors, and whether someone has the backing to handle the politics. From what I’ve seen today, your son has the talent to qualify."

His gaze slid to Selene.

"And you," he added. "If anyone can navigate the capital’s paperwork and strings, it would be you, Lady Selene."

Selene’s breath caught. Her fingers dug slightly into the wood of the doorframe.

"…You know who I am," she said.

Wilhelm’s smile softened.

"House records run deep," he said. "I make it a habit to know which brilliant noble researchers vanish from the capital one day and reappear at the edge of the kingdom with a new surname. Don’t worry. I have no intention of dragging you back."

Selene didn’t answer. Her eyes flicked to Elrond, then back to Wilhelm.

"I only mean," Wilhelm went on, "that if you ever decide your son should see Arbalest and its academy, you’re not starting from nowhere. House Alfrost remembers those who protect it—and those it once failed to keep."

He let that hang for a moment, then eased back a step.

"For now, consider this just a recommendation," he said. "From an uncle who doesn’t like wasting talent when he sees it."

He turned toward the carriage and gave Aldric a final nod.

Wilhelm climbed into the carriage. The servants followed. The door shut with a solid click.

A driver’s call cut through the street. Hooves started forward. The carriage of House Alfrost rolled away toward the town’s center, guards falling into formation around it, armor clinking softly as they moved.

Silence settled over the front of the house once the wheels turned the corner. Elrond stared after the carriage until it disappeared, the faint echo of Wilhelm’s words still ringing in his head.

‘Royal Academy,’ he thought.

He looked back at Aldric and Selene. Both of them were still standing where Wilhelm had left them. Selene’s face had gone pale. Aldric’s brows were drawn tight, as if he had just been handed a problem bigger than the wyverns.

Selene was the first to move.

“…Let’s go inside,” she said.

Her voice sounded normal, but her hand stayed on the doorframe a moment longer than usual before she turned away. Aldric followed her into the house. Elrond came after them, still thinking about Wilhelm’s words.

They sat at the table they always used for dinner. The pouch of gold sat between Aldric and Selene like another person.

Elrond climbed into his usual seat and kept his hands on his knees. He listened.

Aldric tapped a finger against the pouch, then stopped.

“First thing,” he said. “We use most of this on the patrol. That was the deal I accepted.”

Selene nodded.

“Seventy coins to your unit,” she said. “Equipment, compensation, maybe some to the families of the men who died.”

Aldric’s jaw tightened, but he agreed with a short grunt.

“And the rest?” he asked.

Selene glanced at Elrond, then back at the pouch.

“Wilhelm didn’t just give us money,” she said. “He gave us a problem.”

“You mean the academy,” Aldric said.

Elrond’s shoulders twitched.

Wilhelm’s recommendation still echoed in his head. It felt less like praise and more like a hand pushing his back toward the capital.

‘He understood everything so fast,’ Elrond thought. ‘Like he could see straight through me.’

Aldric leaned back, folding his arms.

“With what Elrond can do now… he’d pass any basic requirement,” Aldric said. “He can read. He writes better than half the patrol. His magic and swordsmanship are…”

He trailed off and let the sentence hang. Selene looked down at her hands.

“He’s ready on paper,” she said. “That part isn’t the problem.”

Aldric studied her face.

“You’re thinking about your old house,” he said.

Her lips pressed into a thin line.

“If we use my name to get him into the academy,” she said slowly, “they’ll notice. Word will reach the capital. The moment my birth name appears on any document, someone will start digging.”

She met his eyes.

“That would be suicide for me,” she said. “For all of us.”

The room went quiet.

Elrond shifted in his chair. The word clung to the air. He understood what she meant. Not death on a battlefield. Something slower. Being dragged back into a life she had already chosen to abandon.

“So we don’t use your name,” Aldric said.

Selene nodded once.

“If he goes, he goes as himself,” she said. “As Elrond von Astrea. No strings to my past. No special treatment.”

Her gaze moved to Elrond.

“He passes on his own ability,” she said. “Or he doesn’t go at all.”

Elrond swallowed.

“In other words,” Aldric said, “we prepare him, but we don’t lean on anything except what he can do.”

Selene made a small sound of agreement. Elrond stared at the pouch for a moment, then raised his hand a little.

“Um,” he said. “Is… that money enough for the academy?”

Selene and Aldric both looked at him. He straightened his back.

“I mean,” he added, “for the fees. And living there.”

Aldric exhaled through his nose.

“It’s more than enough,” he said. “You could live in the capital for ten years with that amount if you’re careful. Tuition, food, lodging… all covered.”

Ten years. Elrond’s chest tightened. The number turned into a picture in his head: a long road, a city skyline, an academy tower.

“So we can really do it,” he said. The words slipped out before he filtered them. “Then I’m ready to enroll now.”

He leaned forward, eyes bright. Selene lifted a hand.

“Stop,” she said. “There’s no way a seven-year-old is getting into the Royal Academy.”

Elrond froze.

“…How old, then?” he asked.

Selene glanced at the ceiling as she thought.

“Fifteen,” she said. “Around that. The academy takes students for three years. Most people finish at eighteen, then choose their path—knight, court mage, merchant, researcher.”

Fifteen. Inside his head, something reeled.

‘What? That old?’ he thought. ‘In my previous world, five-year-olds were already going to school.’

He slumped back in his chair.

“Three years only…?” he muttered.

Selene heard him.

“The academy isn’t like town schools,” she said. “It’s not for teaching letters from the start. It’s for polishing people who already know how to read and count and use basic magic.”

She rested her elbows lightly on the table.

“There are other schools,” she added. “Places in bigger towns that teach reading, writing, arithmetic. Most nobles send their children there early. Merchants do the same if they can afford it.”

She looked at Elrond and smiled faintly.

“You don’t need those,” she said. “You’re already past that level.”

Elrond scratched his cheek.

“…So for me, it’s just the academy,” he said.

“If you still want it when you’re old enough,” Aldric said.

Elrond’s answer came out without hesitation.

“I do,” he said.

He sat there for a moment, letting the new timeline sink in.

‘Fifteen, huh,’ he thought. ‘Eight more years. That’s a long time to train. And only three years of school after that…’

It felt short compared to his old world. Here, those three years carried all the weight.

Aldric finally pushed back his chair.

“All right,” he said. “Decision for now: most of the gold goes to the patrol. The rest we save. If the day comes when you’re ready for the academy, the money won’t be the thing stopping you.”

Selene nodded.

“We’ll treat it as preparation,” she said. “Not a promise, but a door we can open if we choose.”

Elrond watched them, the shape of his future sitting in a small leather pouch on the table.

That night, the house filled with the smells they had worked on that morning.

Roasted meat. Fresh bread. Stew rich enough that even Aldric raised his brows when he tasted it. The table was more crowded than usual—extra plates, extra dishes, Mira moving back and forth with a satisfied look on her face.

Aldric sat at the head of the table, now in clean clothes, hair still damp from washing away wyvern blood.

Mira lifted her cup.

“To Captain Aldric’s safe return,” she said.

Selene bumped her cup lightly against his.

“And to the patrol who came back,” she added. “And to the ones who didn’t.”

They drank in quiet.

Elrond raised his own small cup of watered juice.

“To Father,” he said. “Who beat a wyvern and still came home in time for dinner.”

Aldric laughed, the sound low and a little hoarse.

“What a coincidence,” he said. “You planned a feast on the same day a wyvern tried to eat my patrol.”

Selene smiled.

“I told you,” she said. “We were preparing to welcome you back properly.”

Elrond took a bite of meat. It tasted better than usual. Maybe because of the seasoning. Maybe because of the way Aldric’s hand felt solid when it ruffled his hair between courses.

The day that had started with canceled training ended with a celebration of survival and a new road he could see in the distance.

Somewhere beyond that road, the Royal Academy waited.

### Chapter 9: 8 – The Decision

#### Scene 1

Eight years later.

The treeline ended in a jagged line of stumps and churned earth. Beyond that, fresh fields stretched out in uneven squares, soil turned over and marked with simple wooden stakes. Men with shovels and carts had been working here until an hour ago.

Now only the patrol remained.

An Amarok lay in their path, fur bristling, eyes burning with cold light. Its bulk blocked the half‑finished road like a fallen boulder, claws sunk deep into the broken ground. The first one Elrond had ever heard about had appeared near the eastern magic stone. This one had come from the opposite direction—out of the deeper woods that bordered the new farmland.

Elrond stood a few steps ahead of the front line, breath steady, hand resting on the hilt of his sword.

He was fifteen now.

When he turned thirteen, he had begged Aldric to let him join the patrol—at least as a watcher at the back line. It had taken weeks of quiet pressure, early‑morning training, and evening drills before Aldric finally agreed.

“Only to observe,” Aldric had said.

For the first few months, that was all Elrond did. He walked at the rear, memorized every formation, and watched how veterans reacted when monsters broke through the trees or bandits tried their luck along the trade road.

Observation turned into warning shouts.

Warning shouts turned into well‑timed spells.

By fourteen, he was standing where he stood now—close enough that a single mistake would put teeth and claws in his reach.

“Frontline, brace!”

Aldric’s voice cut through the growl rolling across the clearing.

Shields rose. Spears leveled. The mage squad stepped back and widened their stance.

Elrond drew a slow breath and called up the spells that had become as familiar as his own heartbeat.

Strength Enhancement.

Agility Enhancement.

He spoke the chants out loud, letting his voice fall into the same rhythm as the other mages in the line. Mana wrapped around his muscles, sank into his bones, and settled there like an extra weight and an extra spring layered over his skin.

Four times strength.

Four times agility.

The same limit Aldric used when he fought alone.

Elrond’s body didn’t buckle under it anymore. His breathing stayed smooth. If anything, it felt like he was still holding back.

He kept his expression calm and his stance simple. No one here needed to know that he could have skipped the words and reached the same result with a thought. Chantless magic was a secret that stayed inside the house fence and the woods.

Not on patrol.

“Little Captain,” one of the men behind him muttered. “You’re up today, right?”

“Don’t call me that on duty,” Elrond replied without turning.

The Amarok’s growl deepened. Its paws dug into the dirt, cracking the packed soil. Frost crawled along the ground under its claws, thin and sharp, clinging to the remains of cut roots.

“Remember,” Aldric said. “We’re not protecting a stone this time. We’re clearing land. No retreat path behind us. We finish it here.”

Elrond nodded once.

‘No barrier. No backup mages from the capital. Just us.’

The first Amarok he’d heard about had needed a commander, multiple squads, and complex formation magic. This one had walked right into their expansion zone as if the half‑made fields belonged to it.

It lowered its head.

It charged.

The ground shook.

“Hold!” Aldric shouted.

The front line did not move. The mages began their own chants—defensive barriers, support spells, layered over the men with shields.

Elrond stepped out of formation.

“Elrond!” someone barked.

“I’ll take the first cut!” he answered.

He ran straight toward the Amarok.

Wind tore at his cloak. The beast’s eyes locked on him, yellow light narrowing into a killing focus. Its breath smelled of blood and cold metal. Each of its strides crushed half‑rotten stumps like brittle twigs.

Elrond opened his left hand.

“Flame, wrap my blade.”

Fire gathered at his palm and leaped to his sword in a thin, controlled line. The steel caught, heat racing down its length until the edge burned bright, wrapped in a tight coat of orange.

Heat met the chill leaking from the Amarok’s body.

Steam hissed where they touched.

Elrond dropped his stance. Enhanced muscles pushed off the torn ground, sending him forward in a burst.

‘Front leg first. Kill the speed.’

He slid in under the Amarok’s reach, boots scraping against frozen soil. Claws slashed over his head, close enough that a few strands of his black hair tore free.

His sword flashed.

Flame‑coated steel bit into the Amarok’s front leg just above the joint.

There was resistance for a heartbeat. Then the fire ate through the frozen mana clinging to its fur, and the blade punched through.

Blood erupted—thick, dark, and steaming.

The Amarok howled and stumbled. Its massive body lurched, weight dropping onto its remaining legs.

Elrond did not stop.

He pivoted, letting the beast’s own momentum carry its bulk forward past him. As it tried to twist and bring its head around, he stepped in close to its flank.

‘Second leg. Then the tendons on the side. Don’t get greedy.’

He swung again, strength magic driving the cut. The sword traced a burning line along the back of the Amarok’s other foreleg. Muscle and tendon parted. The beast crashed down, shoulders smashing into the dirt hard enough to shake loose clods of frozen soil.

Its hind legs scrabbled to push it back up.

Elrond gathered a second layer of heat at the tip of his blade—the same control pattern as a fireball, packed tight and flat.

He drove the sword along its side and carved a line across its ribs. Flame spilled into the wound.

The Amarok roared. Frost burst outward in a sudden wave, coating the nearby stakes and stumps in white. Elrond narrowed his stance and braced against the pressure, cloak snapping around him.

“Now!”

Aldric’s order cut through the cold.

The waiting patrol moved at once.

Spearmen rushed in from the flanks. They drove their weapons into the Amarok’s exposed side and shoulders, pinning it in place. The beast thrashed, snapping at them, but every time its head swung toward one, two others drove their spears deeper from the opposite angle.

“Offensive squad!”

The lead mage finished his chant and thrust his staff forward.

A compressed fireball shot over Elrond’s shoulder—a proper one, big enough that the heat stung his cheek as it passed. It slammed into the Amarok’s back and exploded, fire washing over matted fur and crackling frost.

The blast didn’t kill it.

It stunned it.

The Amarok’s body jerked. For a moment, its movements lost all rhythm. Its legs kicked without pushing. Its head sagged, jaws snapping at empty air.

Aldric stepped in.

He had been holding back until then, guarding the line, watching for the opening he needed. Now he poured power into his legs and shoulders, his own enhancements flaring.

He leaped.

For an instant, his shadow crossed over Elrond’s eyes.

Then Aldric’s blade came down.

The sword cut through the Amarok’s neck in a single, clean arc. The force of the blow carried him all the way through, boots skidding when he landed.

The beast’s head hit the ground with a heavy thud.

Silence followed.

The frost‑bitten air hung still for a few breaths. Then the men exhaled—short laughs, curses, rough shouts cutting the tension.

“It’s down!”

“Check the flank! Make sure there’s no second wave!”

“Someone watch for strays from the pack!”

Elrond lowered his sword. The flame around the blade thinned, then vanished. Steam rose from the cuts along the Amarok’s side where his fire had burned deep.

His heart hammered, but not from fear. His breathing stayed steady. Mana still sat in his core like an unused reservoir.

He flexed his fingers once around the hilt.

‘I barely touched my limit.’

Boots crunched over frozen dirt behind him.

“Show‑off,” one of the spearmen said as he walked past, grinning. “Leave something for the rest of us next time.”

Elrond gave a small shrug.

“You were slow,” he said.

The man laughed and clapped him once on the shoulder before moving on.

Aldric wiped his sword on a patch of unburned fur and sheathed it. He walked over, helm tucked under his arm, breath fogging in the cold air.

“Well done,” he said. “You didn’t overextend.”

Elrond glanced at the severed legs and the long burn across the Amarok’s side.

“I had more room,” he said. “If I pushed to five times—”

“No.”

Aldric’s tone hardened for a moment.

“Four is enough until your body finishes growing,” he said. “You can’t treat your bones like spell circles. If they break, they don’t reset.”

Elrond closed his mouth and gave a short nod.

“…Understood.”

He knew Aldric was right. Every time he stacked his enhancements past four, his joints ached afterward. His tendons pulled tight and stayed that way for days. Numbers meant nothing if his body failed mid‑swing.

Still, every battle like this confirmed the same thing. As he was now, this town no longer pushed him to his limit.

The rest of the patrol had already fallen into post‑battle routine. Two men began checking for stray wolves at the edges of the trees. Others moved around the carcass with practiced hands, cutting away usable fur and harvesting fangs, claws, and anything that could be sold or turned into equipment.

“Captain,” one of the mages called out. “The frost around the wound looks cleaner than last time. Less corruption.”

“Good,” Aldric said. “That means the barrier is doing its job even out here.”

He turned back to Elrond.

“Take a short rest,” he said. “Then help with the harvest. We need the core.”

Elrond nodded and stepped back from the corpse.

He sat on a half‑cut stump at the edge of the clearing and let his enhancements fade. The sudden loss of power made his limbs feel oddly light and ordinary, like he had stepped out of someone else’s body and back into his own.

He watched the patrol work.

Ten years ago, the story of an Amarok had been something he heard secondhand—a monster from a battlefield he never saw. Now he was the one taking its legs apart while older men joked about who would have to drag the core back to town.

By the time they finished carving out the core and tying the Amarok’s legs for transport, the sky at the edge of the woods had begun to pale.

They hauled the spoils back to town.

The patrol hut sat a short walk from the main gate, its walls stained by years of smoke and mud. Light leaked from the shutters. Someone had already lit the lamps and dragged out extra benches.

The moment they stepped inside, the men started talking at once.

“First Amarok in years and we walk away without losing a man.”

“Better than the last time, that’s for sure.”

“Don’t jinx it. Drink first.”

Barrels were rolled out. Cups were slammed down. The smell of cheap alcohol mixed with sweat and damp leather, thick and familiar.

Aldric ended up in the middle of it without trying.

He stood near the far wall, one hand on a table, helm set aside. The men clustered around him in a loose half‑circle, waiting for his word like they always did after a big fight.

Elrond took a seat at a table near the side wall with a wooden cup of grape juice in his hand. Someone had pressed it into his fingers as he came in.

He took a sip and watched.

Aldric raised his cup.

“Listen up,” he said.

The voices in the hut quieted.

“Today went smoothly,” Aldric said. “Not because the Amarok was weak. Because everyone did their job. Shields held. Spears pinned. Mages didn’t overreach. No one tried to be a hero and get themselves killed.”

A few men chuckled.

“We had room to go all out,” he went on. “No magic stone at our backs. No town wall behind us. Just an open field we wanted to claim. That made it easier than the last time.”

He let that hang for a moment.

“But don’t forget what we were up against,” he said. “An Amarok is still an Amarok. Relax tonight. Remember that tomorrow.”

He tipped his cup back and drank.

The hut erupted again—laughter, boasts, someone clapping Aldric on the back hard enough to rock him forward.

“Captain, that last swing—!”

“Did you see the kid? Went for the legs like he was born to it.”

Elrond hid his face behind his cup for a moment as a few glances turned his way.

‘Focus on Father,’ he thought. ‘He’s the one they’re celebrating.’

It stayed like that for a while. They traded stories about the charge, argued over who had landed which hit, and cursed the frost clinging to their boots.

Eventually, the barrels ran low and the noise softened. One by one, men pulled on cloaks and drifted out into the thinning night.

Aldric caught Elrond’s eye and jerked his chin toward the door.

“Let’s go home,” he said.

The sky had shifted from black to deep blue by the time they reached their street. A faint orange line cut along the horizon behind the roofs.

Warm light spilled from the windows of the Astrea house.

The door opened before they reached it.

Selene stood there, lamp in hand. Mira hovered a step behind her, apron on, hair tied back.

“Elrond. Aldric.”

Selene’s shoulders dropped a little in relief as she took them in from head to toe.

“You’re late,” Mira said. “Or early. I haven’t decided yet.”

Something small moved at Selene’s feet.

A little girl was crawling across the floorboards, chasing the edge of Selene’s robe with both hands. Soft chestnut hair framed her round face. Her amber eyes blinked up at the two figures in the doorway.

Celica von Astrea.

Three years old.

“Brother,” Elrond said.

He stepped inside, crouched down, and scooped her up.

Celica wriggled once in his arms, sniffed, then wrinkled her nose.

“Sweet,” she mumbled.

She pushed at his chest with both hands and twisted around, reaching back toward Selene.

Elrond froze.

“…I don’t smell that bad,” he said.

“You reek of cheap sweets and sweat,” Mira said. “That hut always does. Don’t hug the child until you’ve washed.”

Elrond let Celica slip from his arms back into Selene’s hold.

He looked away and took a quiet sip of air through his nose.

‘…It’s not that strong,’ he thought.

“Come in,” Selene said. “You’ll catch a cold standing there.”

They stepped fully inside. Selene closed the door against the thinning night air.

Mira moved to the hearth to stir the pot hanging there. The smell of warm soup drifted through the room, cutting through the scent of outside.

Aldric set his sword and helm aside and stretched his shoulders once.

“Good work,” Selene said. “Both of you.”

Aldric gave a small nod.

“It went well,” he said. “We’ll file the full report after we sleep.”

Elrond unbuckled his sword belt and hung it on the familiar peg near the door.

His fingers hesitated on the leather for a heartbeat longer than they needed to.

“Father. Mother.”

Both of them looked at him.

Elrond straightened.

“I’m ready,” he said. “For the Royal Academy.”

The words dropped into the quiet room like a stone into still water.

Selene blinked.

“…Now?” she asked.

“For the next admission exam,” Elrond said. “The one in a week.”

Selene’s hand tightened slightly around Celica’s waist. The little girl, oblivious, grabbed at a lock of her hair.

“I thought…” Selene started, then stopped.

Elrond waited.

“I thought you might have forgotten,” she said quietly. “It’s been years since we talked about it.”

“I haven’t,” Elrond said.

He met her eyes.

“I wanted to be strong enough first. Today proved it. I won’t get stronger by staying here.”

Aldric’s gaze didn’t waver.

“You’ve been thinking about this for a while,” he said.

Elrond nodded once.

“Since the wyvern,” he said. “Maybe before that.”

Aldric let out a slow breath through his nose.

“The capital is different from this town,” he said. “Crowded. Loud. If you pass the exam, you’ll be living there for years. You’ll see nobles, politics, things you don’t deal with here.”

“I know,” Elrond said.

He didn’t, not fully. He had only what he’d read in books and what he remembered of cities from his previous life. But the weight of the decision didn’t scare him. It settled over his shoulders in a way that felt right.

Aldric’s mouth quirked at the corner.

“Then I’ll say this,” he said. “Don’t pick fights you don’t need. Don’t show everything you can do just because you can. Watch first. Move later. The capital has teeth sharper than any monster.”

Elrond nodded.

“…Understood,” he said.

Mira set bowls on the table, listening without speaking. Her eyes flicked between the three of them.

Selene shifted Celica to one arm and reached out with her free hand.

“Elrond,” she said.

He stepped closer.

“Before we decide anything,” she said, “I’ll ask you one more time.”

Her fingers closed gently around his wrist.

“Are you sure?”

Elrond didn’t look away.

“Yes,” he said. “I’m sure.”

No hesitation rose up behind the word. Selene’s shoulders eased by a fraction.

“All right,” she said.

Aldric gave a small nod.

“The carriage leaves in two days if we want you there with time to spare,” he said. “If there are too many passengers or stops, it might take that long to reach the capital. We’ll talk to the coachman tomorrow.”

The decision was made.

But Aldric set one last condition.

“Before you leave,” he said, “we’ll have one more match. No holding back. If you can’t stand against me when I’m serious, you’re not ready for what’s waiting out there.”

Real swords.

Real intent.

The fight would end the moment a killing blow would have landed—a cut to the neck, a stab to the chest, a strike that would have shattered a skull if it followed through.

They chose the woods behind the house.

The yard where they usually trained was too small now. Their sparring had long since spilled past the fence, footwork dragging them over uneven ground and between trees when Aldric wanted to push his son’s balance.

This time, they would need space.

—

Morning mist hung low between the trees.

The woods behind the Astrea house were quiet, dew clinging to leaves and spiderwebs. The air bit a little at the lungs when drawn in too fast.

Aldric stood in a small clearing, sword in hand. Just the blade he had carried through more battles than he could count.

Elrond faced him a few steps away, his own sword held in a familiar guard.

Selene watched from the edge of the clearing with her back against a tree, arms folded. A faint white barrier circle glowed under her feet—thin, just enough to deflect stray splinters or shards of bark.

“Last chance to say you’ve changed your mind,” Aldric said.

Elrond’s grip tightened around the hilt.

“I haven’t,” he said.

Aldric nodded once.

“Then enhancements,” he said. “Full power.”

He drew a breath.

“Strength Enhancement. Agility Enhancement.”

Mana roared through him like a second pulse. He layered the spell deeper, past the comfortable numbers he used on patrol.

His muscles swelled under his shirt, not in size but in density. Veins stood out faintly along his forearms. The air around him felt heavier, pressed down by the weight of concentrated mana.

Elrond followed.

“Strength Enhancement. Agility Enhancement.”

He pushed to fivefold. Heat and pressure flooded his limbs. Tendons pulled tight from the inside. His bones creaked—barely audible, but he felt it. Pain pricked along his knees and ankles in thin, sharp lines.

‘It hurts,’ he thought. ‘But I can hold it.’

His breathing didn’t break. Selene’s brows drew together slightly at the edge of the clearing, but she did not speak. Aldric raised his sword. They both began in the same stance.

Blade held low and to the side, tip angled slightly toward the ground. Feet set shoulder‑width apart. Weight centered, ready to shift in any direction.

Aldric had taught Elrond this guard years ago.

Now they mirrored each other.

“Begin,” Aldric said.

They moved at the same time.

Steel met steel in the center of the clearing.

Aldric’s first swing came in diagonally from Elrond’s right—a classic opening, meant to test response, not to kill. Elrond didn’t try to answer it with power.

He caught the blade with the flat of his own and let the force roll along his arms into his legs. His boots slid half a step on the damp earth.

Aldric stepped in, footwork tight and efficient. He didn’t waste a single movement. Every shift of his weight set up the next strike.

Horizontal cut at the ribs. Thrust at the shoulder. Short, brutal chop at the thigh.

Each blow was simple. No flashy spins, no unnecessary flourishes. The danger lay in how his timing and angles kept shifting, never quite the same twice, a style sharpened on real battlefields.

Elrond met him with the same sword forms he had drilled thousands of times.

When Aldric swung for his ribs, Elrond slanted his blade to bleed off force and turned his body with the strike. When the thrust came for his shoulder, he shifted his front foot back just enough that the point slid past his coat.

For the first dozen exchanges, neither of them tried anything clever.

They felt each other out.

Sevenfold vs fivefold.

Even with the extra enhancement, Aldric was faster. His blade reached center first. His steps carved the rhythm. Elrond’s arms throbbed after every block.

They circled through the trees.

Aldric pressed him toward a thicker patch of trunks, testing how Elrond handled restricted space. Elrond slipped sideways between two trees, sword close to his body to avoid catching it on the bark.

“Too tight,” Aldric said.

His blade came up in a sharp uppercut aimed at Elrond’s chin.

Elrond ducked under it, dropped his weight, and pivoted on his back foot. The tip of the sword scraped bark as it passed where his head had been a heartbeat earlier.

He brought his own blade up in a rising cut toward Aldric’s ribs.

Aldric twisted his torso and let it pass, slapping the flat of Elrond’s sword aside with a short, brutal parry.

“Good,” he said.

They broke apart.

Elrond’s lungs burned; fivefold was barely holding, every part of his body screaming at him to ease off.

He dragged in a sharp breath. “Six,” he muttered, and the enhancement surged—weight and heat slamming into his limbs, pain spiking through his joints until his vision narrowed—but he forced his stance to hold.

Aldric’s eyes narrowed at the sudden spike in mana. “Six? That’s reckless. Your body can’t hold that for long,” he said, but Elrond only reset his grip and sank lower into his stance.

Selene’s fingers tightened where she crossed her arms, yet she still didn’t speak.

They clashed again. Aldric chained three quick steps together—step in, half step to the side, full step around —each shift carrying a different cut.

Each step carried a different cut. First a low slice toward the shin, then a slash for the elbow, then a thrust that would have gone through Elrond’s heart if it landed.

Elrond’s mind broke the sequence down even as his body reacted.

‘Low. Elbow. Heart. Pattern one.’

He blocked the low cut with the edge of his blade angled down, hopped back from the elbow slash, and twisted just enough that the final thrust grazed his sleeve instead of his chest.

They passed each other, dirt kicking up behind them as they turned.

Elrond countered, mirroring Aldric’s footwork—step in, half step, full step—letting his blade drop in a low feint toward the shin before snapping across for a real cut at Aldric’s side.

Aldric caught it on his own sword and shoved, using raw strength to blow through Elrond’s form. The impact shuddered up Elrond’s arms and into his shoulders.

He slid back across wet leaves.

“Still relying too much on my patterns,” Aldric said. “Make your own.”

Elrond gritted his teeth and pushed back in.
