They went on, Aldric throwing out new sequences—high thrust, low cut, shoulder chop—and Elrond letting each one crash into his guard once before the pattern settled in. The second time it came, his blade was already there: a simple block, a turn of the wrist, a half step off line.

Sevenfold enhancement drove Aldric’s strikes like hammers. Sixfold let Elrond move fast enough to stay just ahead of being crushed.

The trees blurred around them as they moved, boots digging divots in the damp soil. Once, Aldric vaulted off a low stump and came down in a descending strike that split bark when Elrond twisted away.

The ground shook under the impact, pain shooting through Elrond’s joints as his vision pulsed at the edges, but he held on.

“Reckless,” Selene muttered at the edge of the clearing, the barrier under her feet flickering once before it settled again.

In that moment something clicked in his head—he had seen enough.

Every time Aldric shifted his weight to his back leg, a certain pair of cuts followed. Every time his shoulder rolled a certain way, the next strike always came from the same angle. He was still faster, still stronger—but his experience had carved grooves in his movement.

Patterns.

Elrond began to move inside them.

He met the next sequence half a beat early, blade already in position. Aldric’s sword rang against his and glanced aside instead of driving through.

Aldric’s brows drew together as they traded three more strings of attacks. By the third, his strikes no longer crashed against Elrond’s guard but into the exact points Elrond led them to, and in that instant the balance shifted—Aldric felt it.

He pulled nothing back. There was no spare power left to hide. He poured all of it into clean, lethal angles, trying to crush through with skill and weight.

Elrond’s guard did not crumble.

He tightened every movement, wasting no swing, no step. His world shrank to the line of Aldric’s shoulders, the flex of his fingers on the hilt, the way his hips started to turn a fraction of a second before each cut.

The next opening came in a flash.

Aldric lunged.

Straight thrust aimed at Elrond’s throat—a line they had drilled a thousand times with wooden swords.

Elrond dropped his head and shifted to the side, just enough that the blade slid past his ear.

He stepped inside Aldric’s reach, closing the distance in a single, sharp step.

His left hand snapped out and locked around Aldric’s sword wrist, shoving it off line with a twist that broke the thrust. At the same time, his right hand brought his own blade up in a smooth, practised arc.

The edge stopped a breath away from Aldric’s exposed neck.

If he had followed through, the cut would have gone cleanly across the carotid.

Silence slammed down over the clearing.

Aldric’s eyes widened. For a heartbeat his body stayed coiled around the failed thrust, muscles still driving power into a strike that no longer had a target.

His chest rose and fell once, sharply.

A fifteen‑year‑old had broken his line and taken his throat.

Elrond’s arms shook from effort and strain, the enhancement burning in his muscles like molten iron, but the blade did not waver. He held the position, jaw clenched, sweat running down his face.

Selene let out a breath she hadn’t realized she was holding. The faint barrier at her feet dimmed, reacting to the way her shoulders finally loosened.

Aldric slowly relaxed his grip on his sword. The tension bled out of his shoulders in stages, as if his body needed time to accept what his eyes were seeing.

“…That’s it,” he said quietly.

Elrond lowered his blade.

The sixfold enhancement collapsed. Strength bled out of his limbs in an instant, leaving behind throbbing joints and a bone‑deep ache that made his legs feel hollow.

His knees dipped.

Aldric reached out and caught his shoulder before he could drop.

His hand was steady. His gaze wandered for a moment to the empty space where the blade had hovered at his neck, then back to Elrond’s face.

He studied him in silence—a boy breathing hard, sweat‑soaked, eyes still clear despite the strain.

Then Aldric huffed out a short laugh under his breath, half disbelief, half pride.

“I lost,” he said. “Cleanly.”

He let out a rough, breathless laugh, the sound breaking halfway through. “Hahaha… to think I’d say that to my own son,” he added, and the words tasted strange in his mouth.

Elrond swallowed. “…Thank you,” he said.

Aldric squeezed his shoulder once, then let go. “You’re ready. Go show the capital what an Astrea can do,” he said. “And remember—this isn’t your limit. It’s just where you’re starting from.”

Elrond straightened as much as his aching body allowed. Pain tugged at every joint, but his back stayed straight. “Yes,” he said. “I will.”

Aldric rolled his shoulder once, forcing his voice to stay steady.

“Go get patched up,” he said. “We still have to get you on that carriage.”

Elrond let out a slow breath he hadn’t realized he was holding. His grip finally loosened on the hilt.

“…Got it,” he said.

He turned toward the path back to the house. The enhancement had faded, leaving only aching joints and heavy legs, but his steps stayed steady as he walked away between the trees.

Selene watched him go, eyes following his back until the last glimpse of his coat disappeared behind the trunks.

Only when Elrond’s footsteps had faded did Aldric’s legs finally give way.

The sevenfold enhancement, the strain of holding back nothing, and the weight of losing to a fifteen-year- old crashed down on him at once. He took the last few steps to Selene and dropped to one knee in front of her.

His sword point bit into the dirt as he leaned on the hilt. His free hand found her sleeve and held on.

“Hahaha…” The sound came out hoarse this time. “I really lost, Selene. I wasn’t holding back at all.”

Selene looked down at him, eyes soft. She set her hand on his head, fingers sliding into his hair, steady and warm.

“You did,” she said. “And you did well.”

Some of the tightness in his chest eased at that. He closed his eyes for a heartbeat, let himself breathe, then pushed back to his feet.

Selene stepped a little closer, her sleeve brushing his hand.

“He’ll be fine,” she said. “You saw it. Our son won’t break that easily.”

When he looked toward the path Elrond had taken, the surprise hadn’t vanished, but it sat beside something else—quiet pride and a quiet, stubborn hope. One day that back would be broader than his. One day people far beyond this town would shout Elrond’s name.

“Let’s go home,” he said.

Tomorrow, they would put Elrond on a carriage bound for the capital.

Now, he was ready to go.

After that last fight, Elrond spent the rest of the day on his feet.

He went back to the central street to say farewell to the patrol. The men who had watched him grow from a quiet kid at the rear line into a front‑line fighter slapped his back, gripped his hand, and told him not to embarrass them in the capital.

“Come back stronger,” one of them said. “Or at least send a letter if you start wearing a fancy coat.”

Elrond gave a small nod and a thin smile, committing every face to memory.

From there, he walked through the town.

He stopped by the neighbors who had brought food when he was small, by the shopkeepers who always pretended not to see him slip an extra glance at their goods, by the aunties who tugged his cheek when he passed their door. They were not close, not in the way friends were, but they had been there for as long as he could remember in this life.

Last was the forge.

Heat and the smell of metal hit him as soon as he stepped inside. The blacksmith’s son looked up from the anvil, soot on his face, hammer in hand.

“You’re really going?” the boy asked.

Elrond nodded.

“Yeah.”

“Tch.” The boy clicked his tongue and set the hammer down. “Don’t break that sword before you become famous, all right? I still want people to ask who made it.”

“…I’ll try not to,” Elrond said.

They shared a short, awkward laugh. It wasn’t a deep friendship, but it was something. When Elrond stepped back out into the street, the weight of leaving settled a little heavier on his shoulders.

—

The next morning, the carriage station was already busy.

Wheels creaked. Horses snorted and stamped. People clustered in small groups—families, merchants, travelers—saying their own goodbyes. Some tried to keep their faces straight. Others didn’t bother hiding the tears.

Elrond stood with his family near the side of the platform.

Aldric in his worn coat instead of armor. Selene with Celica in her arms. Mira just behind them, apron replaced with a plain cloak. A few of the relatives who had helped look after him over the years stood nearby, offering last‑minute advice he only half heard.

The carriage station was where farewells happened. No one expected anyone to hold back here.

Elrond tried anyway.

He kept his expression calm as he checked his bags one last time, as he listened to Aldric repeat the coachman’s instructions, as Selene smoothed a wrinkle in his collar that didn’t need smoothing.

But the quiet hurt in his chest made it hard to breathe.

‘Second life or not,’ he thought, ‘they’re still my family.’

He looked at his father’s rough hands, at Selene’s tired eyes, at Celica’s small fingers clutching the edge of her mother’s cloak.

This wasn’t just a house he had stayed in.

It was home.

“Write if you can,” Selene said. “It doesn’t have to be long. Just enough so we know you’re all right.”

“I will,” Elrond said.

Mira stepped forward and thumped a small wrapped bundle into his hands.

“Dried meat and some sweets,” she said. “Don’t eat it all in one day.”

Celica reached out toward him.

“Brother,” she said.

Elrond bent down and hugged her gently, careful of the dust on his coat.

“I’ll be back,” he said.

He didn’t know when. But he said it anyway.

“Passengers for Arbalest, board up!” the coachman called.

The shout cut across the station.

Aldric gripped Elrond’s shoulder once, hard enough that it almost hurt.

“Go,” he said.

Elrond nodded.

He turned, handed his luggage to the coachman, and climbed into the carriage. The wooden steps creaked under his boots. He took a seat by the window and looked out.

His family stood there in a small cluster—Aldric straight‑backed, Selene with one hand raised, Celica pressed against her leg, Mira wiping at the corner of one eye with the back of her hand.

The carriage jolted as the driver snapped the reins.

The wheels began to turn.

As the station slowly slipped backward, Elrond’s throat tightened. He blinked, but the heat behind his eyes didn’t fade.

By the time the carriage rolled past the edge of town and the houses began to fall away, tears had gathered at the corners of his eyes.

It felt, for a moment, like they might never meet again.

He didn’t look away until the town’s rooftops had shrunk to a distant line and vanished behind the curve of the road.

Only then did he sit back, wipe his face with his sleeve, and let out a long, shaky breath.

“New chapter, huh…” he murmured.

His old life was long gone.

Elrond’s new one had just begun.

### Chapter 10: 9 – Destination

#### Scene 1

The capital of the Althania Kingdom, Arbalest, was still far beyond the horizon.

From his seat near the carriage window, Elrond watched his hometown shrink into the distance as the carriage followed the road north. Wooden fences, familiar rooftops, and the training field where he had crossed blades with Aldric all slid slowly out of sight.

He let the rattling of the wheels fade into the background and reached instead for the memories of ink and parchment.

Arbalest.

The name belonged to both the city and the royal house that ruled this kingdom. It was a name he had seen written again and again in Selene’s books, ink pressed deep into yellowed pages.

The House of Arbalest. The royal family of the rebuilt Althania.

Three hundred years ago, there had been another royal bloodline. The old Althania kings had ruled from a different capital, a different palace, under a different crest. That line ended during the great war between humans and demons. Even after the demon race had lost their Demon Lords to the Heroes of the past nearly two hundred years before, their remaining armies were still strong enough to pour south. In that invasion, the Althania royal family was slaughtered. The capital burned, the crown vanished, and the kingdom that shared his new homeland’s name became a half-ruined country without a ruler.

Human scholars later called that span of time the Crownless Years—years without a king for Althania, and, on the demon side, years without a Demon Lord to unify their race.

In those years of confusion, when monsters roamed near roads that had once been patrolled and tax collectors stopped visiting the outskirt towns, three noble houses moved first.

Arbalest. Roosevelt. Alfrost.

Later, historians would name them the Founding Families of Althania. Back then, they were simply the lords who refused to let their lands be carved apart.

They rallied the scattered nobles from the frontier territories, including towns like the one Elrond had just left behind. They pulled veteran knights out of half-collapsed garrisons, recalled retired commanders, and scraped together an army from every village and border fort that could still raise a spear.

Even that wasn’t enough to push the demons back.

The tide only turned when the last descendants of the Hero’s party joined them—men and women whose blood still carried the blessings that had once killed a Demon Lord. Alongside them marched the holy

knights of the Western Church, armored in silver and white, their banners marked with the sun-shaped crest Elrond had seen in illustrations.

With those forces combined under a single banner, the humans began to fight their way north.

They reclaimed towns, then cities, then fortresses that had once been thought lost. Roads that had been abandoned for decades were cleared of monsters and opened again. The remaining demon army was slowly forced back toward their own territory on the northern continent.

The books did not describe that final retreat in detail. They did not need to. The name everyone used for it said enough.

The Demon Massacre.

According to the records Selene had given him, the demon hosts fell back across the wasteland that marked the boundary of human lands. They tried to regroup there and dig in, but they were not the only ones with grudges.

The elves moved in from the other side.

While the demons focused on the humans pursuing them from the south, elven forces attacked from the north and east. Their mages cracked the sky with light. Their archers reached into the gaps of demon armor from distances human archers could not match. The demon army was caught between enemies and crushed.

Some writers claimed that the sands of that wasteland were soaked in demon blood.

Elrond closed his eyes for a moment and let the carriage sway carry him. He had turned those sentences over again and again while reading. The numbers were impossible to ignore—populations halved, entire clans erased. Whatever the demons had done before, the result on the page still felt more like a calculation than a story.

The demons survived, but the blow to their strength was severe. First the previous defeat of a Demon Lord, then the massacre in the wasteland. Two disasters in close succession had cut away a large portion of their potential growth.

After that, they did something that even the human historians had not expected.

They changed the shape of their rule.

Instead of a single Demon Lord ruling over the entire demon race, they divided authority. Multiple Demon Lords took control, each holding dominion over a different region of demon territory. Each had their own army, their own capital, their own way of dealing with humans and other races.

According to the scholars, that change was deliberate. A single Demon Lord could fall to a single Hero’s party. Multiple Demon Lords, spread across different lands, were harder to wipe out at once. Humans could

build many kingdoms, crown many rulers, and raise many new Heroes. The demons, at last, had chosen a system that could respond to that.

To human scholars, that decision was nothing more than a logical response to repeated defeat.

After the Demon Massacre, the war on the central continent finally stopped moving forward. Human kings, dukes, and elven lords chose to face each other across tables instead of battlefields. They signed a peace treaty that bound their realms to treat one another as allies against the demon race, not rivals.

The demons had no seat at that table. What remained of their forces withdrew to the far north of the continent, beyond a stretch of wasteland and burning desert that ordinary armies could not easily cross. Past that barrier, the land turned cold and pale, with snow-covered plains and little in the way of farmland or forest. That was where the Demon Lords now ruled—the distant north, cut off from the central lands by heat and sand.

In the south, Althania slowly regained its peace.

At one point, the nobles who had fought under Arbalest's banner tried to give their new king a different kind of reward. They proposed changing the kingdom’s name itself to Arbalest, in honor of the family head whose strategies and leadership had held the country together.

He refused.

According to the histories Elrond had read, the head of House Arbalest accepted only one part of their suggestion: renaming the capital in his family’s honor. The kingdom, he insisted, would remain Althania. The name belonged to the royal family that had been slaughtered in the war, and to the people who had died with them defending the old crown.

Some of the surviving branch members of the Althania line agreed with that decision. The books said they thanked Arbalest for his restraint and his refusal to erase their house entirely.

From there, the kingdom began to rebuild in earnest. House Arbalest took the throne as the new royal family of Althania. Roosevelt, Alfrost, and the other great houses filled the upper ranks of the court, serving as high ministers and pillars of the restored state.

That peace had lasted for almost three hundred years.

Only now, in the generation Elrond was born into, were the first problems beginning to surface.

In the present era, the kingdom was ruled by King Aldren von Arbalest II.

The numeral had been adopted under his father. In reality, Aldren was the thirteenth king to wear the crown since the head of House Arbalest first took the throne of Althania.

He had earned authority long before he ever sat on that throne. As a prince, Aldren led border campaigns, oversaw the rebuilding of ruined provinces, and forced stubborn nobles to accept reforms that cut into their

comfort. The records in the palace archives described a man who believed that stability was built with two hands: one holding a sword, the other holding the law.

He preferred clear rules over court games. He was principled, pragmatic, and quietly intimidating. From the beginning, he had taken after his father in that.

Years before Elrond was born, during a decisive campaign, Aldren was struck by a curse-borne sickness that the Royal Academy later classified as the Ashen Pulse.

There was no cure.

Most days, the illness lay dormant, letting him carry out his duties as if nothing were wrong. But it could flare without warning. When it did, his heartbeat stuttered, his limbs grew heavy, and his light-attribute magic turned unstable. A severe flare could stop his heart outright.

By the time he reached his late forties, Aldren understood that the disease would not give him the luxury of a gentle old age. He had to decide clearly who would inherit the Arbalest throne.

He had three children who could inherit: Lucien, Darius, and Claire.

By law and by decree, Lucien had been named as the next king. Darius refused to accept that. His resistance did not come as open rebellion, but as constant pressure in council, in noble gatherings, and in the small shifts of loyalty that turned into trouble at court.

That reality was the reason Lucien became the heir not just by birthright, but by preparation.

Aldren did not raise him to inherit "someday." From the moment the Ashen Pulse proved it could strike on any night, Lucien was treated as a king-in-training. He was brought into council sessions earlier than tradition allowed. He was taught to read noble motivations, to weigh reforms against the risk of revolt, and to command soldiers without wasting their lives.

Aldren’s personal lessons were blunt. End conflicts before they turned into wars. Concede small victories to prevent greater rebellions. Keep the crown legitimate, even when parts of the court turned hostile.

To the people who watched them closely, Lucien became a reflection of what Aldren wanted the next reign to be: disciplined leadership with restraint.

At the same time, the very sickness that shaped Lucien’s education created the kingdom’s most dangerous tension.

The possibility of a sudden royal death sharpened every noble’s sense of opportunity. Some houses pushed harder for influence, favor, and positions that would matter in a rushed succession. That pressure fed the rise of factions.

On the other hand, Darius had already begun gathering like-minded nobles around him. Talented and ambitious, he refused to accept a future in which his brother’s legitimacy closed every path above him.

Where Lucien spoke for continuity and measured reform, Darius called for sharper control and faster change. The nobles who agreed with him would harden over time into what the court began to call the Second Prince Faction.

On that point, Aldren and Lucien moved in step.

He understood that leaving Darius’s camp unchecked would eventually tear the court in half. To keep the royal succession from being swallowed by raw power struggles, he accepted the nobles who gathered around him and shaped them into what would later be named the First Prince Faction. Their purpose was simple: protect the legitimacy of the crown, support stable governance, and keep the kingdom from sliding into a contest of force alone.

Aldren watched both sides.

He did not despise Darius’s ambition or Lucien’s caution. He simply understood what could happen if the Ashen Pulse stopped his heart on the same day the balance between those two factions broke. Even on the calmest days of court, the sick beat in his chest was a quiet reminder that succession was no longer a distant concern, but the fault line beneath the peace Althania had enjoyed for three hundred years.

Claire, the youngest of the three royal children, had already stepped away from the line of succession.

In the official records, her abdication was framed as a political choice. She was the only princess and still young; more than that, her ties within noble society were thin. By the time she reached academy age, most of the great houses had already let themselves be courted or charmed by either the First Prince or the Second Prince.

Stepping aside did not remove her from the board. It changed how she could be used.

Roosevelt and Alfrost remained publicly neutral between the two princes. In council and at banquets, their representatives listened more than they spoke, weighing offers without committing. Everyone in the capital understood what that meant. Whichever side Claire eventually chose to stand beside would almost certainly pull those two pillars with her. If that happened, the careful balance of power in the court would not survive.

Claire understood that as clearly as anyone.

Because of that, she watched her own steps with more care than either of her brothers. Every visit, every shared meal, every friendly conversation with a noble house could be read as a signal. From that point on, she could not afford a careless move.

Out of his thoughts, a sharp click of the tongue pulled Elrond back to the inside of the carriage.

On the bench opposite him, a woman in a warrior’s outfit sat with one arm hooked over the backrest. She watched the road behind them through the small rear window, lips twisting as the last glimpse of the town vanished from sight. She clicked her tongue again and looked away, as if the sight of another tearful farewell had been nothing more than a tired routine.

"Every stop, it’s the same," she muttered, low enough that she probably thought only her companion could hear. "Crying, waving, clinging… you’d think no one ever came back from the capital."

Beside her, a robed mage holding a staff rested both hands on the carved wood and followed her gaze for a moment. Then the mage’s eyes slid toward Elrond.

He had glanced up without meaning to.

Their eyes met. The mage woman’s expression tightened in brief alarm. She dipped her head at once.

"My apologies," she said. "Rina’s manners are rougher than they should be in shared space. Please don’t take it to heart."

She turned toward the warrior. "Rina, apologize. He heard you."

Rina clicked her tongue a third time, this one sharper, but Elrond raised a hand slightly.

"It’s fine," he said. "Really."

He added a small, polite smile to make the words reach properly.

In his previous life, he had seen that kind of traveler more than once—people who had ridden too many carriages, left too many stations, and stopped treating anyone else’s parting as special. He was not about to get angry over it.

Seeing that he wasn’t offended, the mage woman let out a quiet breath.

"If you insist," she said. "Still, it was rude of us to complain in front of someone we’ve just met."

She straightened a little in her seat. "I’m Lysette Farrow."

Now that he was looking directly at her, Elrond could see the details that the first glance had missed. She was in her mid-twenties, with ash-blonde hair gathered into a loose side braid over one shoulder and calm gray eyes behind thin-rimmed glasses. Her robes were travel-worn but neatly kept, a deep blue trimmed with silver embroidery at the cuffs that marked her as a formally trained mage.

"Elrond, from the southern frontier," he replied. "It’s a pleasure to meet you, Miss Lysette."

Lysette smiled, faint but genuine, then gestured toward her companion.

"This is Rina Calder. Don’t mind her face. She’s kinder than she looks, just… not in the mornings."

"Oi," Rina said, but she didn’t deny it.

Up close, Rina looked to be around the same age as Lysette, maybe a little younger. A lean, sharp-eyed swordswoman, she had short, tousled black hair and a faint scar running along her left cheek. The

annoyance in her eyes didn’t feel cruel, just rough around the edges, like someone who had burned through her patience somewhere on a long road.

Lysette shifted her staff to one side so it wouldn’t bump against Elrond’s knees.

"We’re adventurers," she explained. "We were traveling from another rural region on the outskirts when our previous carriage decided we were too much trouble to keep on. They dropped us at the last town and told us to walk the rest of the way."

Rina snorted. "They said our luggage was ‘unsafe’ for normal passengers. It’s not like anything exploded."

"Nothing exploded because I kept three layers of sealing on it," Lysette said under her breath. Then she looked back at Elrond. "In any case, we had to make our way on foot until we reached your town. This carriage was the first one heading toward the capital that would take us."

Elrond listened, keeping his expression mild. Adventurers being kicked out of a carriage for carrying something dangerous was the kind of story that would have sounded absurd in his old world. In this one, it fit a little too well.

"I see," he said. "Then I’m glad you managed to catch this one."

Lysette’s shoulders eased at his tone, and even Rina’s expression softened by a fraction.

"It was quite a walk to reach your town," Lysette added after a pause. "About half a day along the road by the woods. That stretch is known for monsters and bandits."

Rina rolled one shoulder. "Nothing showed up. Word travels."

"That’s because you were there," Lysette said. "Most things with any sense avoided us." She said it lightly, almost joking, but she did not take her eyes off Elrond as she spoke.

Elrond blinked.

Half a day on foot, at night, on a forest-side road with only the two of them. In his old world, that would have sounded reckless at best. Here, it was just another reminder of how people lived beside danger when they had no other choice—and how much work someone like Rina must have done to make that kind of journey feel routine.

"It was just the two of you?" he asked.

"Usually," Lysette said. "We’re like a core team. The rest of the party changes from town to town. We hire local adventurers wherever we go, use temporary members instead of dragging a big group across the kingdom."

She rested her chin lightly on the top of her staff.

"It’s easier on supplies that way. Less baggage, more flexibility. And you build more connections if you work with the people who already know the area."

Rina smirked. "And if someone turns out to be useless, you just don’t hire them again at the next town."

Lysette sighed, but there was no real heat in it.

Elrond nodded. It was an efficient approach, one that made more sense the longer he thought about it. A small, stable pair, surrounded by shifting support—lighter, cheaper, and harder to pin down.

Lysette studied him for a moment, as if weighing whether to ask something more personal.

"What about you, Elrond?" she said at last. "You’re not just going to the capital to sightsee, are you?"

Her tone was light, but her eyes were sharp behind the lenses of her glasses.

"I’m heading there to attend an academy," he said.

He left it there. The words "Royal Academy" stayed on his tongue. Saying it out loud in a cramped carriage full of strangers felt like inviting questions he didn’t want to answer.

Lysette’s gaze slid briefly to the sword at his side.

"A sword academy, then? Or some kind of martial school?" she asked.

Elrond gave a small shrug.

"Something like that," he said.

That seemed to satisfy her for the moment. The conversation drifted to safer topics—road conditions ahead, rumors about monster nests being cleared, the price of food in the capital compared to the frontier. Rina contributed a comment now and then, mostly to complain about bad tavern beds and stingy clients.

Time passed. The carriage rocked steadily along the road.

Before long, the driver called out that they were approaching the first town on the route.

It was busier than the settlement Elrond had left behind. When the carriage rolled through the gate, he saw rows of merchant stalls, wagons lined up along the main street, and shop signs painted bright enough to catch the eye even through the morning haze. The air smelled of fried batter, leather, and too many people trying to move in the same space at once.

The carriage stopped in a small yard behind an inn. The driver announced a short break before departure— half an hour to stretch legs, eat, or arrange baggage.

Elrond stepped down, feeling the stiffness in his knees ease as his boots touched solid ground.

"I’ll take a short walk," he said, more to himself than anyone else.

He stayed close enough to see the carriage yard whenever he turned his head. There was no point in wandering deeper into the town when they would be leaving so soon. Even so, the simple act of breathing air that wasn’t full of dust and other people’s breath felt strangely refreshing.

When the driver’s whistle cut through the noise, Elrond returned to the carriage.

After leaving that bustling town behind, the carriage slowly filled. At each stop along the road, more passengers climbed aboard—merchants with ledgers tucked under their arms, a pair of craftsmen carrying carefully wrapped tools, a woman with two sleeping children leaning against her side.

By the time the sky began to pale toward dawn, the seats were crowded. Elrond shifted to make room where he could and turned his face toward the narrow slice of sky visible through the window.

A thin line of gold edged the horizon.

Near him, Rina and Lysette had finally surrendered to exhaustion. At some point during the night, they had ended up leaning into each other, shoulders pressed together, heads tilted at awkward angles against the rattling of the carriage.

It looked uncomfortable.

Even so, after half a day of walking before they had even reached his town, the sleep was clearly needed. Elrond watched them for a moment, then looked away to give them their privacy.

Day cycled to night again as the caravan pressed on.

When darkness settled and the drivers judged the road unsafe to travel further, the line of carriages pulled off to the side of the highway and made camp. A group this size rarely traveled alone; counting quickly, Elrond saw at least six other carriages forming a loose circle with theirs, creating a small temporary camp in the open field.

Lanterns were lit. A fire was built near the drivers’ wagons, and warm chatter rose as they shared food and stories from other routes.

Elrond ate a simple meal from his own provisions, then returned to the carriage.

The wooden bench had never been designed as a bed, but he had slept in worse places during patrols. He settled against the wall, adjusted his cloak as a blanket, and let the rhythm of distant voices and crackling fire fade into the background.

His eyes closed.

The caravan would move again at first light.

Morning came.

By the time Elrond opened his eyes, the carriage was already moving again. The wheels rattled over the road, carrying them further north as the season crept toward winter. A faint chill clung to the air.

He drew his thick wool blanket out of his pack and wrapped it around his shoulders. The rough fabric scratched slightly against his neck, but the warmth was welcome.

Outside the window, leafless trees stretched along the roadside, their bare branches clawing at the pale sky. Patches of frost clung to the grass where the sun had not yet reached.

It was a familiar sort of scene.

In his previous life, he had never visited the countryside. His world had been a string of crowded stations, office towers, and narrow city streets.

'So this is the kind of view I might have seen in rural Japan.'

Nothing notable happened on the second day of the journey. The caravan rolled forward at a steady pace. Passengers talked quietly among themselves, traded small pieces of dried fruit or bread, and dozed when conversation ran out. A few simple songs passed through the carriage once or twice before fading into tired silence.

By nightfall, the caravan stopped at a town near the border.

This settlement stood close to the line that separated Althania from the neighboring country of Radras. The streets near the main gate were crowded with wagons and merchant groups, many of them bearing Radras-style clothing or accents.

Most of the merchants in Elrond’s carriage disembarked there, their journeys turning toward Radras. The two countries had shared a strong alliance in trade and defense for centuries; this town was one of the places where that connection was most visible.

The carriage emptied until only three passengers remained: Elrond, Lysette, and Rina.

They decided to rest in the town for the night. Elrond found an inn near the carriage yard, paid for a modest room, and let himself sink into a real bed for the first time since leaving home. The mattress was thin and the pillow lumpy, but compared to a carriage bench, it felt like luxury.

The next morning, the caravan formed up again on the road heading directly toward Arbalest.

The journey was smoother than Elrond had expected.

Part of him had assumed there would be at least one attack along the way—a monster straying too close to the highway, or a bandit group foolish enough to target a caravan of this size. Instead, the day passed

quietly. From time to time, they crossed paths with other caravans, small escorted wagons, or what looked like merchant-funded expeditions.

'Traffic density as a safety measure. The more people on the road, the fewer chances anything has to try its luck.'

He had heard that there were shorter routes to the capital, narrow paths that cut through forest or hills to save time. Caravans like this did not use them. Wide, well-traveled roads meant slower progress and more tolls, but also better patrol coverage and fewer surprises.

By the third day, the road had thinned out again.

At each stop behind them, carriages had peeled away, leaving their passengers in the towns they had chosen as destinations. By the morning of the third day, only three carriages remained from the original group.

There were no more scheduled stops ahead.

The remaining three wagons departed together after a brief check of wheels and harnesses. The final stretch of the journey passed without incident, the miles folding away under bright, cold sunlight.

By the time the sun reached its highest point in the sky, the driver’s voice rang back from the front.

"Arbalest ahead!" he called. "The capital’s in sight!"

Elrond leaned toward the window.

In the distance, the city finally revealed itself.

Arbalest was enormous, wrapped in towering white walls that rose out of the landscape like a man-made cliff. Watchtowers punctuated the line of stone at regular intervals, their tops bristling with pennants and the glint of metal in the sun.

To Elrond, it was the exact shape his mind supplied when someone said the words fantasy capital—a city he might once have seen only on a book cover or a game screen in his previous world, now standing solid on the horizon.

As the carriages drew closer to the city, their pace slowed.

Elrond shifted on his seat and leaned toward the window.

A long line of people and wagons stretched out before the main gate. Each carriage rolled forward in turn, stopping briefly as its wheels passed over a magic circle carved into the stone of the roadway. Faint light pulsed along the lines of the inscription with every crossing.

He watched, eyes narrowed in interest.

Lysette noticed almost immediately.

"It’s a simple detection circle," she said. "They use it to check for dark magic, curses, or objects that carry unknown energy."

'Is this like a metal detector?'

When their turn came, the circle flared brighter under the carriage.

For a moment, Elrond felt his own mana ripple faintly inside his body, like water disturbed by a passing wave.

'It’s probably just recording it.'

The light faded. The guards glanced at the readings on a small crystal set beside the gate, then waved them through.

The carriages passed under the shadow of the gatehouse and into the capital.

A warm clamor rose up to meet them.

Guides, runners, and informants waited just beyond the entry lane. As the carriages rolled to a stop in the receiving yard, voices called out at once—offers of cheap inns, safe storage for luggage, city tours, and directions to guild branches or noble districts.

Elrond stepped down after the driver dropped the footstool.

Lysette and Rina climbed down on the other side, adjusting their gear out of habit. For a moment, the three of them stood in the same small pocket of space, the flow of travelers splitting and rejoining around them.

"Thank you for the company," Elrond said, inclining his head slightly. "The road would have felt longer without it."

Lysette smiled.

"We should be the ones saying that," she replied. "If you ever need information in the capital, ask for Lysette Farrow at the guild bulletin. Someone will know where to find me."

Rina crossed her arms and gave him a short nod.

"Don’t die before you graduate from… whatever that academy is," she said.

"I’ll keep that in mind," Elrond answered.

He meant it when he told himself he would remember them. If they worked out of this city as often as it sounded, there was a fair chance their paths would cross again.

They parted there, each pulled in a different direction by their own errands.

Elrond stretched his back, feeling his spine crack pleasantly after too many hours on the bench. Then he started walking.

The main street leading inward from the gate was broad and neatly laid with pale stone. Buildings of two and three stories lined both sides—shops on the ground floor, residences or offices above. The architecture was clean and deliberate, a mix of sharp angles and gentle arches that gave the district an orderly feel.

Even without asphalt, the road was smoother and cleaner than many of the streets from his previous world.

He followed the central avenue.

According to the maps and notes he had studied, the Royal Academy lay further in, along the main line that cut straight toward the heart of the city. Around it, the noble estates and royal institutions formed a district that most people simply called the central ward.

As he walked, the buildings grew grander. Guard patrols in polished armor passed by at regular intervals. The flow of people shifted from merchants and travelers to better-dressed townsfolk, clerks, and the occasional noble entourage.

Ahead, a wide street branched off from the main avenue.

An archway of carved stone marked its entrance. Beyond it, Elrond could see a row of manicured trees and the silhouettes of taller, more refined buildings. Two pairs of guards stood on either side of the arch, watching the traffic.

People were still allowed to pass through freely. There were no chains across the road, no shouted challenges.

'Then what’s the point of the guards and the separation?'

He slowed his steps.

He still had time before the academy’s entrance procedures began. Walking straight into a district that clearly belonged to nobles and royal institutions, while carrying all his luggage, felt careless.

For now, he turned away from the arch and circled back toward the area near the gate.

He found an inn that sat just off the main road—a sturdy stone building with clean windows and a modest signboard. The common room smelled of stew, wood smoke, and freshly scrubbed floors.

The innkeeper, a broad-shouldered man with gray at his temples, looked Elrond over once as he approached the counter.

"Room?" the man asked.

"Yes," Elrond said. "One person. A few nights, for now."

The innkeeper named a rate, and it was lower than Elrond had expected for the capital. 'Cheaper than I thought it would be.'

"First time in Arbalest?" the innkeeper asked. "Most folk don’t come this way unless they have business. You here for work, family, or something else?"

"I’m here to enroll in the academy," Elrond said. He kept his tone casual.

The man’s eyebrows rose a fraction. "Academy, huh," he said. "We get a lot of you this time of year." He reached for the slate beside his hand, scratched something out, and wrote a new number beneath it.

"That was the normal price," he said. "This is the rate for students or exam takers who stay a while. Cheaper if you pay in blocks. You lot don’t eat much and you don’t break the furniture. Good business to keep you close."

Elrond blinked once. 'An innkeeper who thinks in long-term customers. That’s convenient.'

"In that case," he said, "I’ll pay for a few nights in advance."

He counted the coins out carefully. His father had pressed ten gold pieces into his hand before he left.

Later, in the small room on the second floor, Elrond set his pack down and ran the numbers again in his head. 'If I live carefully, this should be enough for around three years in the capital.' It wasn’t a fortune, but it was a solid foundation.

The room was simple: brick walls, a wooden floor, and a single bed pushed up beside a window that overlooked the busy street below. A wooden door in the corner separated off a tiny toilet space. Next to it, the “bathroom” amounted to a bucket and a hand pump for water.

Outside the window, he could see a narrow hanging rack bolted to the outer wall—just enough space to dry clothes if he needed to wash them himself.

It wasn’t as comfortable as his room back home, but for a single person in the capital, it was more than enough.

Elrond shrugged off his outer clothes until he was down to his thin white underclothes. He checked the small steel box stove in the corner, then rested his hand lightly against the metal and pushed a trickle of fire magic inside. The runes along its surface glowed faintly as the heater came to life.

Warmth began to seep into the room.

He lay back on the bed and stared up at the plain ceiling.

'Now I’m on my own.'

That thought didn’t unsettle him.

'It’s fine. I’ve done this once already. Nothing’s going to go wrong.'

At some point, his eyes drifted closed.

He woke when the sky outside the window had only just begun to pale.

His stomach growled before he even sat up.

Elrond pulled on his clothes and headed downstairs with the vague idea of taking a short walk and finding something to eat outside. Just as he reached the door, the innkeeper called out from behind the counter.

"Oi, student. Breakfast’s included if you’re staying here. Every morning, first bell to second bell."

Elrond paused with his hand on the door handle.

"Really?" he asked.

"Room rate covers it," the man said. "Bread, stew, and something hot to drink. It’s not much, but it fills the gap."

'So lodging and one meal a day for that price. That’s better than I thought.'

"Thank you," Elrond said. "I’ll come back for it."

Even so, curiosity tugged him outside.

He stepped onto the street and followed the flow of late-afternoon foot traffic. After a short walk, he spotted a small tavern already crowded with people, light and steam spilling out through the open door.

'A lot of customers at this hour. The food’s probably decent.'

Inside, the noise wrapped around him at once—voices, clinking cups, the scrape of chairs. He found a space at the counter and ordered beef soup, bread, and a drink.

When the bowl and plate were set in front of him, he took a cautious bite. The taste was solid—nothing remarkable, but warm and properly seasoned.

The bill came to seven silver.

It matched what he had expected for a capital city, but his mind automatically moved to numbers.

If one gold coin was worth a thousand silver, then ten gold meant ten thousand silver. Spread over three years…

'Roughly a thousand days if I round it. I have about ten silver to spend per day if I don’t want to go under. Better to aim for nine.'

Seven silver for one meal didn’t leave much room.

He let out a quiet sigh and finished the last of the soup.

'It’s fine. First day.'

On the way back to the inn, he stopped at a stall and bought bread and beef jerky for two silver. It would do for a late snack if he got hungry at night—or as a backup breakfast if he needed to skip eating out.

Back in his room, he set the food on the small table beside the bed and sat down.

'Yeah… I can live like this.'

The ceiling above him was the same plain surface as before, but the numbers in his head still felt uncomfortably tight.

'If I find a part-time job, even something small, I won’t have to watch every coin for three years straight.'

The thought settled into place alongside his other plans for the capital.

Academy entrance day finally arrived.

Elrond woke before dawn out of habit. Back home, this was the hour he usually spent crossing wooden swords with Aldric in the yard. Skipping that rhythm now made his body feel off, so he stepped outside instead and ran.

The streets were quiet at that hour, only a few other early risers moving through the pale half-light. He kept his pace steady until sweat prickled across his back, then looped back toward the inn as the first color crept into the sky.

By the time the sun began to rise, he was climbing the stairs again.

As he turned the corner toward his room, he saw a small figure standing in front of his door. A young girl in a simple apron and dress balanced a tray with bread and a covered bowl. She flinched when he appeared at the top of the stairs; from the way she glanced at the door, she had been about to leave the food on the floor and slip away.

"Ah—sorry," she blurted. "I thought you were still asleep, sir."

"It’s fine," Elrond said. "You’re with the inn?"

She nodded quickly.

"Lila," she said. "I help with breakfast and cleaning."

"I see. Thank you, Lila." He took the tray from her. "I’ll bring it back down when I’m done."

Her shoulders relaxed at his tone. She bobbed a small bow, then hurried back down the hall to whatever chore came next.

Elrond carried the breakfast inside and set it on the small table. Bread, stew, and a warm drink—simple, but enough to settle the hollow feeling in his stomach. He ate without rushing, letting his breathing return fully to normal.

When the dishes were empty, he set them neatly aside and opened his pack.

Today was not a day for travel clothes. He pulled out the best set he had—clean, well-kept, but not ostentatious—and checked it quickly for loose threads. After that, he went through the bundle of documents Aldric and Selene had helped him prepare: proof of his birth in this life, the necessary certificates from the local church and town records.

Everything was in order.

He drew in a slow breath, then let it out.

'Time to go to the Royal Academy.'

He fastened his sword at his side, adjusted the fall of his cloak, and stepped out of the room.

### Chapter 11: 10: Noble’s Life

#### Scene 1

Five years before Elrond stepped onto the road to the capital, another morning began in Arbalest.

In the royal district, where wide streets were lined with tall stone walls and carefully trimmed trees, one mansion stood with the Alfrost crest above its gate. That estate housed the main branch of House Alfrost.

Inside, behind the second-floor balcony windows, a ten‑year‑old girl sat quietly on her bed.

Emilia Alfrost had already woken before the servants’ knock. She sat with her back straight, hands resting on her lap, eyes turned toward the glass doors that opened onto the balcony. Beyond them, the morning light spilled over the tiled roofs of neighboring mansions and the faint outline of the palace in the distance.

The handle of her bedroom door turned with a soft click.

“Lady Emilia.”

Eira stepped inside, closing the door behind her with practiced care. Her ash-brown hair was tied in a neat braid, apron unwrinkled, steps measured.

Emilia glanced over her shoulder.

“Good morning, Eira,” she said.

“Good morning, milady.”

Eira stopped a precise distance from the bed, hands folded in front of her.

“Breakfast will be ready soon,” she said. “Your father and Lord Gilbert are already awake. I recommend you wash and dress within the next fifteen minutes.”

She paused, then continued without needing to check a list.

“Today’s schedule: morning sword practice with Lord Julian Roosevelt in the east courtyard. After that, magic training with Lady Vespera in the upper practice hall. In the late afternoon, you will accompany Lord Caelen and Lord Gilbert to a diplomatic meeting with House Silveria.”

Emilia’s fingers twitched slightly on the blanket.

“Silveria… that’s logistics and procurement, isn’t it?” she asked.

“In any case,” she said, “your father requested your presence. You are to observe and follow his lead. No formal statements are expected of you.”

Emilia drew in a quiet breath and nodded.

“Understood. I’ll get ready.”

Eira inclined her head.

“I will prepare your clothes,” she said. “Please wash your face first. The water is already warm.”

She moved to the wardrobe without another word. By the time Emilia’s feet touched the floor, Eira had already laid out a pale dress suitable for family breakfast and pulled fresh ribbons from the drawer.

Emilia crossed the room, splashed her face with the water waiting in the basin, and watched her reflection steady in the surface.

‘Sword in the morning, magic after… then politics,’ she thought. ‘Nothing unusual.’

Her heart felt a little heavier than usual anyway.

The dining room of House Alfrost was long but not cold.

Sunlight fell through tall windows onto polished wood. A single long table ran down the center of the room —the same one they used every morning for breakfast—though they only ever occupied the seats near the middle. Servants moved along the walls in quiet lines, placing bread, eggs, fruit, and tea with efficient motions.

At the center seat, Lord Caelen Alfrost sat with a cup of tea near his hand, gloves removed and resting beside the saucer. His posture was straight, his expression calm as always.

Emilia entered with Eira a step behind her.

“Good morning, Father,” she said, stopping beside her usual chair.

Caelen’s gaze shifted to her.

“Morning,” he replied. “Sit.”

She obeyed, smoothing her skirt before taking her seat. Eira stepped back to the wall, joining the silent line of staff while still watching the room.

Emilia lifted her cup, then lowered it again before taking a sip.

“Father,” she said. “About the meeting with House Silveria this afternoon…”

Caelen’s brows moved just enough to show mild surprise.

“You’ve been informed already,” he said.

“Eira told me,” Emilia replied. “What exactly will they be discussing? Is it about the southern supply routes, or…?”

He studied her face for a moment.

“You don’t need to worry about the details,” he said. “You are attending as an observer. For today, all you have to do is watch, listen, and follow my lead.”

Emilia lowered her gaze to her plate.

“…Yes, Father.”

Footsteps sounded at the doorway.

Gilbert Alfrost walked in with the easy stride of someone who had already finished a full set of morning drills. His dark hair was tied back, the collar of his shirt slightly open, a towel still draped loosely around his neck.

“Morning,” he said, pulling out the chair on Caelen’s other side.

“You’re late,” Caelen remarked.

Gilbert grinned as he sat.

“I was with the training captain,” he said. “We were going over formation changes and lost track of time.”

He reached for the bread, then glanced at Emilia.

“So,” he said, “what are we doing this afternoon?”

Caelen gave him the same look he had given Emilia moments earlier.

“The same thing I just told your sister,” he said. “We’re meeting House Silveria this afternoon. You’re both coming with me. Just watch and follow my lead.”

Gilbert let out a quiet breath and glanced at Emilia.

"You asked about it first?" he said.

Emilia answered with a small nod.

Breakfast continued without stiff ceremony. Caelen asked about Gilbert’s drills, about Emilia’s last magic lesson with Vespera, about minor details of the household. Servants refilled cups and replaced empty plates as needed.

For all its titles and obligations, the Alfrost household did not feel like a cage.

Caelen asked questions instead of barking orders, and when a servant slipped, he corrected it once and let it go. Gilbert joked with the kitchen staff the same way he joked with Emilia, trading small comments as plates moved across the table. No one was forced to bow at every step; they bowed when it mattered and spoke normally the rest of the time.

Most of the people in the mansion had already worked there for years. They stayed because they knew that as long as they did their jobs well, House Alfrost would treat them with respect and never act like it owned their lives.

Emilia listened to her father and brother trade short reports and lighter remarks. Every so often, Gilbert would nudge the conversation toward her on purpose.

“And Emilia’s sword work?” he asked at one point, glancing over the rim of his cup. “Has Julian made her scarier than last month yet?”

Emilia’s back straightened a little.

“I’m not scary,” she said.

“You’re scarier than you think when you get serious,” Gilbert said with a short laugh. “If someone insults your friends, you look ready to cut them down.”

He wasn’t guessing. At a spring garden gathering the year before, a visiting young noble had called Cestina a “fake Alfrost” within earshot of the staff. Emilia had stepped between them before anyone else could move, hand on the hilt of her practice sword and voice so flat and cold that the boy turned pale and backed away. The adults had smoothed it over afterward, but Gilbert had not forgotten the look on her face.

“That’s not—”

She stopped when Caelen’s gaze shifted toward her again.

“Caring about your friends isn’t wrong,” Caelen said. “Just learn when to step back.”

Emilia nodded in acknowledgment, fully aware that striking another noble without clear cause would stain Alfrost’s name—especially if there were no witnesses to what had really been said.

She still remembered the boy in the garden. Even with her father’s warning, she knew she would step forward again if she had to.

Gilbert leaned back slightly, satisfied, as if he had gotten the reaction he wanted out of both of them.

Time slipped by in the small sounds of breakfast—the scrape of chairs, the soft pour of tea, the low exchange between a footman and the cook’s aide at the far door. Plates that had arrived full left the table empty.

As the meal drew toward its end and servants began clearing the far side of the table, Gilbert tapped his fork once against his plate.

“By the way,” he said. “That blonde girl who keeps visiting—who is she exactly?”

Emilia looked up.

“Cestina,” she said. “Cestina Ludwell. She’s my best friend.”

Emilia answered that way on purpose. After hearing nobles talk about Cestina as a branch-family asset and even a possible body double, calling her “best friend” in front of her father and brother was her way of insisting that Cestina stood with her, not as something the house could move around as it pleased.

“Ludwell…” he repeated. “That’s one of our branch families, isn’t it?”

Emilia nodded.

"Yes," she said.

House Ludwell had come under Alfrost after losing their lands overseas, and from then on they served as one of Alfrost’s branch families.

Gilbert turned toward Caelen.

“Father,” he said. “Is it wrong to take someone from a branch family as a bride?”

Gilbert rarely asked anything about marriage. The question had been sitting in his head ever since Cestina’s last visit.

Caelen’s hand stilled on his cup. The faint steam rising from the tea curled in the space between them.

“…That’s a bit sudden,” Caelen said.

Gilbert didn’t look away.

"It’s been on my mind," he said.

Caelen set his cup down.

"As long as there’s no direct blood relation, it isn’t forbidden," he said. "Some houses even prefer it. It keeps trust and responsibility close."

Gilbert’s grip on his cup finally loosened, and he took an actual sip of tea; if Caelen had called it improper, every glance he’d stolen at Cestina since that garden visit would have turned into something he had to bury and never speak of again.

Once Gilbert decided on something, he almost never backed down. Thinking about how beautiful she was, like the main character of a story, made it clear to him that it had been love at first sight.

“So Cestina might become Emilia’s sister one day,” he said, looking back at his sister.

Emilia stiffened, staring at him. She couldn’t believe Gilbert was seriously thinking about marrying Cestina.

“…Sister?”

“Imagine it,” Gilbert said. “Your best friend at this table every morning, telling you not to skip meals.”

Color rose along Emilia’s ears.

“That’s not funny,” she muttered.

“I think it’s very efficient,” Gilbert said.

Caelen set his cup down with a faint click. The small sound cut through Gilbert’s amusement more effectively than a raised voice.

“Gilbert,” he said.

Gilbert glanced his way.

“There is one more thing you should know about that girl,” Caelen said. “At least the reason she ended up by Emilia’s side.”

Gilbert straightened in his chair.

“Yes, Father,” he said.

“When House Ludwell came to us, Cestina’s face drew too much attention,” Caelen said. “People mistook her for an Alfrost daughter more often than they did Emilia herself. Because of her looks and the way she carried herself, it was decided that she would serve as Emilia’s body double.”

Emilia’s grip tightened around her fork, the metal biting into her palm as that old memory pushed its way back.

Gilbert watched her.

“Did you really agree to that?” he asked.

Emilia shook her head at once.

“Of course not,” she said. “I told them no.”

On that day she stood beside Cestina in front of the adults who argued about risk and duty, and every time they pushed the decision back at her, she gave them the same answer until they finally backed down.

Caelen nodded once.

“Since then, on paper, she stays near as your guard,” he said. “In this house, I know you call her something else.”

Emilia hesitated only a moment. There was really only one word she could use for Cestina.

“…She’s my best friend,” she said.

The word sounded simple. For Emilia, it held shared lessons, late talks after training, and all the times Cestina had stood next to her when things turned difficult.

Gilbert’s usual easy smile faded a little as he watched her.

“Beautiful, mistaken for Alfrost, and still sticking to you after that,” he said. “No wonder she stands out.”

Gilbert said it while reaching for another slice of bread. He dragged it once through jam, then took a bite like he had only asked about the weather.

Emilia stared at him. Her fork stopped above her plate, and she lowered it again without eating.

'Unbelievable', she thinks.

“You’re getting carried away,” she said to him out loud.

Gilbert set his fork down. The tines lined up neatly with the edge of his plate before he looked back at her.

“Really?” he said. “This from the girl who was head over heels for Julian Roosevelt five years ago?”

Gilbert always brought up Julian when he wanted to push her. It was the easiest way to make her lose her guard.

Emilia jerked her gaze up.

“That was different,” she said quickly. “I was a child back then. I’m not like that anymore.”

Her fingers caught the napkin and twisted it once. She pressed it flat on her lap and kept her hands there.

Gilbert smirked.

“A ten-year-old declaring she’s done with childish crushes,” he said. “That’s a new one.”

Emilia stared at him. Her fork stopped above her plate, and she lowered it again without eating. Her brows pulled together, and she gave him the same cold stare she had once turned on the boy in the garden.

Caelen let out a small laugh.

“Both of you,” he said. “Seek knowledge first before you start worrying about romance. There is plenty of time for that later.”

Caelen did not raise his voice or take sides; he brought the talk to a close with that one line, just as he always did whenever breakfast chatter started drifting toward arguments at this table.

Gilbert leaned back and gave a quick nod.

“Yes, Father,” he said.

Emilia lowered her gaze to her plate again. The food had gone cold at the edges.

'Why would you bring Julian up at breakfast.'

Along the wall, Eira shifted the stack of plates in her arms. One plate slid a finger-width; she adjusted it at once. The corner of her mouth moved, then went still.

After breakfast, Gilbert left the table first to change into his Academy uniform.

When Emilia passed through the entrance hall a little later, she found him by the door, fastening the last button on his dark jacket while a servant checked the line of his sword belt. The towel from earlier was gone; his hair was tied back properly now, not a strand out of place.

“I’m heading out,” Gilbert said when he noticed her.

Emilia stopped a few steps away and folded her hands in front of her.

“Make sure you listen in class,” she said. “Not only when they talk about sword work.”

Gilbert let out a breath that sounded close to a laugh.

“I’ll listen,” he said. “As long as the lecturer doesn’t read everything off the notes.”

A little deeper in the hall, Caelen stood with a steward, going over a sheet filled with tight handwriting. He only looked up when Gilbert’s voice carried across the room.

“Go,” Caelen said. “And remember it’s our crest they see when you speak, not only your face.”

“I know, Father,” Gilbert replied. “I won’t shame the house.”

He smoothed his jacket once more, then pushed the front door open.

Outside, a carriage waited at the gate with the Alfrost crest painted cleanly on the door. The horses stamped their hooves, harness rings giving small metal clicks as the driver checked the reins.

Emilia walked far enough to watch him board.

Gilbert climbed into the carriage without letting anyone fuss over him. Once seated, he leaned toward the open window and glanced back at the hall.

“I’ll see you this afternoon,” he called.

Emilia raised one hand in answer.

“See you,” she said.

The driver closed the door and took his place. With a light snap of the reins, the carriage rolled forward. For a short while, the crest rocked in and out of view as it followed the curve of the main road toward the palace district, then it slipped behind the line of houses and was gone.

The front hall settled into its usual stillness. The only sound left was the faint rustle of paper as Caelen turned the next page.

Emilia drew in a slow breath and let it out.

“I will go to the east courtyard,” she said.

Caelen did not stop reading, but his gaze flicked toward her for a moment.

“Warm up properly,” he said. “Do not waste Julian’s time by turning up half asleep.”

“I understand,” Emilia replied.

She dipped her head once in acknowledgment and turned away from the doors, her footsteps carrying her down the corridor toward the practice yard.

Outside, the air was cooler and carried the dry smell of earth and oiled wood.

The east courtyard was built for practice, not display. Most of the ground was packed dirt. A square of pale stone tiles lay in the center, marked with shallow cuts where blades had bitten too hard. A weapons rack stood along the wall with rows of wooden swords, their grips darkened by use.

Emilia crossed to the rack and picked up her usual sword.

The weight settled into her hand the way it always did. She rolled her shoulders once to shake off the stiffness from sitting, then drew the blade through a slow test swing. It stopped exactly where she pictured it stopping.

“Good,” she murmured.

She stepped onto the tiles and began her warm-up.

Forward step, straight cut. Return, guard. Side step, diagonal cut.

Her boots left faint marks where stone met earth, tracing loops around an opponent that existed only in her head. After each set, she pulled herself back into the first stance and checked her balance, just as Julian had made her do since she first learned the forms.

“You lean when you get impatient,” he had told her once. “If your stance breaks, everything falls with it.”

Her front foot started to drift, and the memory of that line snapped it back into place.

The courtyard stayed quiet. The only sounds were the dull thud of her steps, the soft rush of wood through air, and her own breathing. Somewhere beyond the wall, the kitchen staff called to each other; a trace of warm bread reached her and faded again.

By the third run, sweat had begun to gather along the back of her neck.

She drew another breath and reset her stance.

“Your front foot, Lady Emilia.”

The voice came from the edge of the tiles.

Emilia finished the cut she had already started, let the sword fall back into guard, and turned.

Julian Roosevelt stood at the entrance to the courtyard, cloak folded over one arm, wooden sword resting against his shoulder. His hair was tied back with a simple cord. His posture was straight, but not stiff.

“Good morning, Lord Julian,” Emilia said.

“Good morning,” he replied, walking closer. “You’re putting too much weight on your heel again. The moment someone forces you back, you’ll be slow.”

Emilia glanced down at her footing and shifted her weight forward, spreading it more evenly along the ball of her front foot.

“Like this?” she asked.

Julian watched her stance for a moment, then nodded.

“That’s closer,” he said. “We’ll fix the rest as you move.”

He set his cloak neatly on the weapons rack and stepped onto the tiles opposite her. The distance between them fell into place out of habit; neither of them needed to measure it anymore.

“Start from the first pattern,” Julian said. “Slow. Think about where the cut starts and where it ends.”

Emilia’s fingers tightened by a fraction around the hilt.

“Yes,” she said. “I’ll focus on the line.”

She stepped in and swung. The wooden blade followed the path she had in mind and stopped at the point she had chosen.

Julian’s eyes stayed on her feet and hands.

“Again,” he said. “Same line. Let your shoulder drop a little.”

Emilia let out a small breath and eased the tension in her upper arm.

They worked through the forms one by one.

Advance, cut, recover. Lunge, withdraw, guard. Lateral step, counter.

Julian’s corrections came in short lines and short gestures.

“Guard a little lower. You’re leaving this side open.” “Back foot a bit wider. You need somewhere to push from.” “Don’t lock your wrist. Let the blade carry its share of the weight.”

Each time he spoke, Emilia changed what he pointed at.

“It feels unstable like this,” she said once, trying to soften her guard without letting it sag.

“It only feels unstable because you used stiffness to hold everything up,” Julian replied. “You’ll find the balance. Again.”

Emilia clicked her tongue once and repeated the movement. This time, her guard settled and stayed there.

“That’s better,” Julian said. “You could block a cut from my height with that.”

Her breathing had grown heavy. The sword was not especially weighty, but holding every cut and guard in the right place pulled steadily on her arms and legs. Sweat crept down between her shoulder blades under her training clothes.

Her swings lost the extra movement little by little. Step, cut, return. Step, cut, return. Her pace slipped into his without her needing to think about it.

After a while, Julian rested his sword across his shoulders and watched her return to her stance one more time.

“Better than last week,” he said. “Your feet and hands are finally starting to move together.”

Emilia straightened a little.

“I’m glad,” she said. “I don’t want to fall behind Gilbert.”

A faint smile tugged at the corner of Julian’s mouth.

“That depends on whether you keep doing this when no one is here to watch,” he said. “Once more from the second pattern. This time, picture ice. One clear line. No extra pieces.”

Emilia drew in a slow breath.

“I understand,” she said.

She pictured a narrow lance of ice, sharp from base to tip, and moved through the sequence again.

Only after that run did Julian lower his sword properly.

“That’s enough for today’s forms,” he said. “Remember how your body feels right now. When you get tired, your guard is the first thing that falls apart.”

Emilia rolled her shoulders, working out the tightness, and shifted the sword into her other hand for a moment to let her fingers rest.

“I’ll remember,” she said. “Thank you for training me.”

Julian picked up his cloak.

“Lady Vespera will be less patient than I am,” he said. “Don’t make her wait, and don’t go in with your thoughts still stuck on your sword.”

“I’ll go straight there,” Emilia replied.

She watched him leave the courtyard, then turned toward the mansion.

After sword practice, she headed to the upper practice hall for magic training.

The Alfrost family is known for their strength in both magic and swordsmanship, and one of their most outstanding abilities is ice magic. Ice is a very difficult element to control because it is derived from water.

In this world, people’s understanding of such things is very limited—unlike the science of Elrond’s previous world. They only know that when water becomes cold, it turns into ice, and that’s the extent of their basic understanding. Without any real knowledge of temperature or deeper scientific principles, ice magic is quite hard to perform.

The air changed the moment she pushed the door open.

The hall was brighter and colder than the courtyard. Tall windows faced the inner garden and drew in pale light that stretched across the floor in long strips. Frost clung in thin rings and splashes where spells had landed before, old lessons still visible on the stone.

Vespera stood near the center with a thin staff in her hand, robe hem just above the floor. A small cluster of crystal charms at her belt chimed softly when she shifted her weight.

“You’re on time,” Vespera said with a small nod. “Good. I would be annoyed if Julian’s sword drills started stealing minutes from my lesson.”

Emilia stepped onto the ring marked by faint chalk lines on the floor.

From yesterday’s practice session, she was still struggling to form and hold the shapes she pictured in her mind. Casting ice magic at all was hard; forcing it to match a clear image was even harder.

“I came straight from sword practice,” she said. “Lord Julian kept the forms a little longer today.”

“That sounds like progress,” Vespera replied. “He does not waste his time on people he has given up on.”

She lifted her staff a little, pointing the tip toward the space in front of Emilia.

“You remember what I told you yesterday,” Vespera said. “Less force, more shape. Ice does not care how hard you glare at it. It only follows the picture in your head.”

Shaping ice like this was not really meant for battle. It was a training method, a way to make the caster pay close attention to how their magic moved. In real combat, no one expected ice to look perfect—only to form fast and hit exactly where it needed to.

Emilia nodded once.

“Yes, Lady Vespera. I will focus on the shape.”

She raised her hand and began to chant in the ancient form language used for magic.

“Water that answers my will, gather in my hand and grow still. Cast off your warmth, and take the form of the ice I draw in my mind.”

Cold gathered along the paths Vespera had drilled into her over and over until her fingers moved almost on their own. A spear of ice formed in front of her. It was straight, but the middle was still too thick and the surface uneven.

Vespera had already cast clairvoyance before the lesson began. Through that spell, she could see the flow of mana inside the spear as fine lines of light, all bunching up in the center instead of running evenly through the shape.

“Look at the center,” Vespera said. “You are stuffing extra mana into it because you are afraid it will snap.”

Clairvoyance was a very handy magic for training. It let the caster read how mana moved through a spell or a person without having to guess from the outside. The price was focus—once a mage held clairvoyance, it usually took so much attention that they could not safely handle another spell at the same time.

Emilia narrowed her eyes and drew the excess in.

“It feels fragile,” she said. “As if one hit would break it apart.”

“Good,” Vespera said. “You should be able to feel where it would crack. Now stop stuffing mana into the middle. Stretch what you already have along the edge. A spear needs a clear point and an even body, not a swollen center.”

Emilia drew a slow breath and did as told. In her mind, she pictured the extra thickness pressed into a thin layer running from base to tip. The bulge in the middle shrank; thin white lines of light that Vespera saw through clairvoyance spread out more evenly through the ice.

The spear narrowed and its surface smoothed without losing its point.

“Better,” Vespera said. “Now do it again. This time, end it yourself before it starts shaking. You decide when the spell is finished, not the ice.”

The spear broke into fine mist as Emilia released it. She lifted her hand and formed another.

First a spear again, then a flat shield the size of her torso, then a thinner strand of ice meant to bind. Each new spell followed the same routes through her body. Each time she pushed too much power, the shapes thickened—edges puffing up, centers growing heavy—and Vespera’s staff tapped once against the stone.

“You’re forcing mana into every open space again,” Vespera said. “Look at that shield. The rim is so thick it would shatter the moment someone hits it. For this exercise I only want a clear outline and a steady middle. Anything beyond that is just you trying to feel safe.”

Emilia let out a slow breath and cut the image down, trimming the excess in her mind until the shield was little more than a clean, thin disc.

“It is hard to stop halfway,” she admitted. “Once I start, I want to keep adding more until it feels like nothing can break it.”

“Everyone does,” Vespera said. “It feels reassuring at the start. It feels far worse when the spell collapses and drags your control with it. Learn how much ice you need for one strike, one block, one bind. Stop there. If you keep pouring mana in just to calm yourself, it will always be too much.”

They went through the drills again and again. Spear, shield, binding thread, then back to spear. Each time Emilia thought they might stop, Vespera named another pattern and had her rebuild the ice from the first line. The light on the floor shifted with them, long strips from the windows sliding slowly across the frost- marked stone as the hours passed.

By the time faint circles and lines of ice overlapped in a pale web across the floor, Emilia’s fingertips were numb and her arms felt heavy from the inside. The hollow tiredness in her chest from burned mana had spread into her shoulders and legs. Her last spear came out thinner than she meant, the point trembling even as she tried to hold it steady.

Vespera watched the way the edge wavered, then let her staff rest at her side.

“That is enough for today,” she said. “You finally pushed up to your limit and still kept the shape from falling apart. That is where you stop.”

Emilia bowed her head, her breathing still rough.

“I will watch it more carefully,” she said. “Thank you for teaching me.”

She left the practice hall with a towel over her shoulders and took the corridor back to her room. The sounds of the mansion felt softer after drills: low voices near the stairs, dishes clinking faintly somewhere in the kitchen, the swish of a maid’s skirt as she stepped aside to let Emilia pass.

By the time Emilia reached her room, the sun had already begun to lean westward.

She set the towel on the back of a chair and opened her wardrobe.

The final task of the day waited: accompanying her father and brother to the meeting with House Silveria.

Emilia chose a darker dress suited for formal visits, one that would not catch at her knees if she had to move quickly. The fabric rested heavier on her shoulders than her training clothes. She hung the practice wear aside and changed piece by piece, fastening each button and clasp with steady fingers.

As she closed the last clasp at her collar, a distant rumble of wheels and hooves reached her through the window.

Gilbert had returned from the Academy.

Emilia smoothed the front of her dress once, checking for creases she had missed, then stepped out into the corridor.

By the time she reached the entrance hall, Gilbert was already there in his uniform, speaking quietly with Caelen. Emilia moved to his side, matched her pace to theirs, and fell into place without needing a signal.

She was ready to leave at his side.

The carriage was already waiting in front of the mansion when they stepped out.

The Alfrost crest on the door caught the afternoon light as the horses snorted and shifted. Servants checked straps and wheels one last time while Caelen spoke with the driver in a low voice. Gilbert climbed in first, then offered a hand to Emilia. She took it, settled onto the seat across from her father, and smoothed her skirt.

Their destination lay away from the clean lines of the royal district.
