The further the carriage rolled, the more the view outside the window changed—wide streets giving way to busier roads, chimneys rising in the distance, the air carrying the faint bite of coal and hot metal. This was the industrial district of Arbalest, where foundries, warehouses, and counting houses stood shoulder to shoulder.

The building they stopped at was tall rather than wide, stone walls reinforced with iron beams, the Silveria crest carved above the entrance. The interior smelled of ink, parchment, and polished wood. Clerks moved like a steady current along the corridors, arms full of ledgers.

Emilia walked between her father and brother.

They were shown into a meeting room on the upper floor. A long table, narrower than the one at home. Tall windows. No decoration that did not serve a purpose.

Cassian Silveria was already waiting.

He rose from his seat with practiced ease.

“Lord Caelen,” he said. “Lord Gilbert. Lady Emilia. Welcome. It is an honor to host House Alfrost.”

Caelen answered with a nod and the polite greetings expected of his rank. They took their seats—Caelen at the center, Gilbert to his right, Emilia to his left.

Cassian laid out the ledgers himself: columns of numbers, lists of ore and finished weapons, timelines for delivery. Military orders had spiked again. Blacksmith workshops across the kingdom were asking for more iron, more steel, more fuel.

“The demand is… considerable,” Cassian said, tapping one of the pages. “Our current network is operating near its limits. As you can see, requests from the northern fronts alone—”

He slid another sheet across.

“Of course, House Silveria remains committed,” he continued. “However, in order to maintain the level of reliability you expect, we may need to adjust our fees to match the strain on our resources.”

Caelen rested his fingertips lightly against the table.

“You have routes to Radras, to the western ports, and to three inland mining towns that do not even appear in those ledgers,” he said. “Your ‘limits’ are flexible when the price is right.”

Cassian’s smile froze by a fraction.

“…Lord Caelen jests,” he said. “We simply wish to avoid disappointing the crown by overpromising.”

“You’re free to avoid overpromising,” Caelen said. “You are not free to rewrite our agreement in the middle of a demand spike.”

“The fees stand as they are,” he said.

A thin line formed at the corner of Cassian’s mouth before he smoothed it away.

“Very well,” he said. “If that is House Alfrost’s position, then we will, of course, honor the existing terms.”

He paused.

“…On one condition.”

Caelen’s gaze sharpened.

“A condition?”

Cassian’s eyes flicked, just once, toward Emilia.

“I have a son,” he said lightly. “Lucio. He is diligent, but… narrow. I was hoping Lord Caelen might allow an introduction. If House Alfrost and House Silveria were to deepen ties, it would open a larger window for us to support your military and your blacksmiths. Directly. Even beyond current contracts.”

On the surface, it sounded like a polite offer between houses. In reality, he was lining up Emilia herself as the price for keeping the old terms.

Emilia felt his gaze brush over her like something oily.

‘So that’s what you want,’ she thought.

Caelen’s jaw tightened for a heartbeat. His expression did not change.

“You are asking me to sell my daughter in exchange for a discount,” he said quietly.

Cassian’s hands lifted a little.

“Never,” he said. “I speak only of a diplomatic relationship. Children meet, houses talk, and if in the future—”

“No,” Caelen said.

The single word cut the air sharper than any raised voice.

“I would rather pay double than tie my child to a bargain table,” he said. “This family does not trade its blood.”

Cassian’s smile thinned.

“…Of course,” he said at last. “Forgive me if my wording overstepped.”

Caelen moved on to the next topic without pause.

“On that note,” he said, “let us speak of something else your people have been doing.”

Cassian blinked.

“…My people?”

“The southern mountain range,” Caelen said. “Near the old research posts.”

Emilia looked up.

She knew that place. A jagged line of peaks, crawling with monsters, where Alfrost knights escorted scholars to study mana traces and ruins.

“That land was purchased by House Silveria under a residential permit,” Caelen continued. “Yet guards report mining equipment, extracted ore, and repeated trespass into protected zones. Each time they ordered it stopped, the work resumed.”

Cassian’s smile vanished.

“I was not aware of any mining operations there,” he said. “I assure you, Lord Caelen, I never issued such an order.”

Caelen’s gaze did not soften.

“Whether you ordered it or not,” he said, “it is happening under your crest. The southern range is under Alfrost protection for a reason. Monsters gather there. The area is used for academic surveys. Any mining requires additional permits. You know this.”

A bead of sweat traced the line of Cassian’s temple before he wiped it away.

“In that case,” he said quickly, “it must have been my subordinates. If they discovered ore without telling me, they may have… acted on their own judgment.”

Emilia watched the way his fingers tightened around his pen.

Caelen’s voice stayed steady.

“Then here is their correction,” he said. “All mining stops. Immediately. The land will be restored as far as possible. If the monster population shifts because of this, your house will share the burden of dealing with it.”

Cassian’s lips moved as if he wanted to protest. No sound came out.

“…Understood,” he said at last. “We will shut everything down at once.”

By the time they stepped back out of the Silveria offices, the sky above the industrial district had begun to darken at the edges. Smoke from the chimneys blurred the late light.

Emilia climbed into the carriage first this time. The driver flicked a glance at Caelen; he gave a small nod.

A hooded figure sat in the corner of the carriage, cloak plain enough to pass for another guard’s.

Caelen took his seat across from Emilia and signaled the driver with a short nod.

The wheels began to turn.

Emilia rested her hands in her lap and watched the city slide past the window. The quiet weight in the corner was familiar enough that she didn’t need to check it.

They did not make it far before the first jolt hit.

The carriage rocked hard to one side as something struck the outer guard. A shout cut off halfway through, swallowed by a dull thud. The horses screamed. The driver swore and hauled on the reins.

“Down,” Caelen said.

Emilia dropped from the seat without thinking, pulling her legs close. Gilbert moved at the same time, taking position near the door.

The outer guards were already gone. She could no longer feel their presence through the faint rhythm of armored footsteps she had gotten used to on the way there.

The door latch clicked. Before it could open, Julian moved.

One moment he sat with his hood half-drawn. The next, his sword was already drawn as he turned toward the door, moving through the cramped carriage without brushing against Emilia.

The door slammed outward.

A figure in dark leathers came into view, only to be yanked off balance as Julian’s blade caught the inside of his wrist. The assassin’s knife spun away, clattering onto the road.

Another shape lunged from the side. The carriage shuddered under the impact.

“Two on the left, one on the roof,” Julian said.

Caelen’s hand was already on his own sword.

What followed was quick and ugly.

From her place on the floor, Emilia saw flashes—boots, blades, the edge of Julian’s coat as he stepped in and out of reach. Steel struck, withdrew, struck again. Each time, another attacker went down and did not rise.

It ended almost as fast as it had begun.

The horses snorted and stamped but did not bolt. The driver held them steady with white-knuckled hands.

Julian wiped his blade once on a fallen cloak and turned one of the assassins over with his boot.

The man was still breathing, barely.

Julian checked the pulse at his neck, then shifted his grip.

Caelen stepped down from the carriage. Gilbert followed, checking the perimeter for any sign of a second wave.

Emilia hesitated, then climbed out after them, keeping close to the carriage door.

The road around them was quiet now. A few crates had spilled from a nearby wagon when the attack started, but no civilians lay among the bodies.

Julian crouched beside the wounded assassin and gripped him by the front of his clothes.

“Who sent you?” he asked.

No answer came. The man’s throat moved once, but no sound followed.

Julian’s fingers tightened.

“Then I’ll ask differently,” he said, voice flat. “Who ordered this?”

The man’s eyes rolled toward him. For a moment, Emilia thought he would actually speak; her hand even lifted slightly before she caught herself.

Dark lines suddenly crept up the side of his neck, tracing a pattern under the skin.

His body jerked once. His breath hitched, then broke. The focus in his eyes vanished, leaving nothing behind.

Julian’s grip did not loosen immediately. He kept holding the front of the man’s clothes, as if he could still drag an answer out of a body that had already gone still.

“…Vow Magic,” he said at last. “A binding. Talk, and the curse kills you.”

Emilia’s stomach tightened.

She had read about that kind of spell in lesson books—a binding that killed you if you tried to break it. It was wmagic that turned an agreement into a trap you could not walk away from.

Two more survivors died the same way before Julian could pull anything from them; whatever names or ties they could have given died with them.

Caelen looked down at the dead for a long moment without speaking.

Gilbert stood beside him, jaw tight. In both their minds, the same name rose to the surface—House Silveria —but neither of them said it.

It was only suspicion. That made it useless in public and dangerous to voice.

“We have no witnesses,” Caelen said at last. “Nothing that would stand in a court.”

He turned to Julian.

“We’ll bring the bodies to the city watch,” he said. “They can record the incident.”

Julian nodded once.

“Understood.”

While the guards moved to gather the fallen, Emilia stepped back into the carriage and sat down. The seat felt colder than before.

‘They really tried to kill us,’ she thought.

Her hands curled into fists in her lap and stayed that way until the door closed.

Scenes like this were not new to her. Over the last few years there had already been several attempts on the Alfrost family, and somehow the blades and spells always seemed to tilt in her direction. The fear never vanished, but it no longer locked her body in place. She knew that if she broke down now it would only pull her father’s attention away from what mattered, so she kept her eyes open and made herself breathe—slow in, slow out—until her hands stopped shaking.

Word of the attack spread quickly. Doors opened along the street as people stepped out to stare at the shattered traces of the ambush: the gouges in the road, the splintered wood on the carriage frame, the dark patches where blood had already begun to dry. Some of the braver ones helped the guards lift the bodies, lining them up to be loaded onto a second wagon bound for the city guard settlement.

By the time the reports were finished, the numbers settled into ink. Two guards dead. Four more injured badly enough to be taken off duty. Eight assassins who would never stand up again.

All of that for one ride home.

The next day, a formal burial was held within the city. The fallen guards lay in plain coffins arranged in a straight row, each one draped with cloth bearing the Alfrost crest and the emblem of the city watch. Caelen stood at the front with the commander of the guard; Emilia and Gilbert took their place behind him.

### Chapter 12: 10: Noble’s Life – Part 2

#### Scene 1

The next day, a formal burial was held within the city. The fallen guards lay in plain coffins arranged in a straight row, each one draped with cloth bearing the Alfrost crest and the emblem of the city watch. Caelen stood at the front with the commander of the guard; Emilia and Gilbert took their place behind him.

The courtyard of the city watch had been cleared for the ceremony.

Flags hung from the stone walls, the Alfrost crest beside the emblem of the guard. Incense burned in shallow brass dishes near the coffins, its thin smoke mixing with the cooler air of the morning. Guards stood in two lines facing each other, armor polished, helmets held under one arm.

Beyond them, families filled the open space.

Some clung to each other. Some stood with their backs straight, faces set, as if holding their own grief in check out of respect for the dead. Children shifted at the edges of the crowd, eyes red from crying or wide and dry, not yet sure what to do.

The commander of the guard stepped forward first.

“We gather today to honor our own,” he said, voice carrying clearly across the courtyard. “They fell in the line of duty, protecting the lives placed under this city’s care.”

His words followed a pattern Emilia had heard at smaller funerals before—duty, sacrifice, service to the city and crown. Still, the row of coffins made every sentence feel heavier.

When the commander had finished, he stepped aside.

Caelen moved forward.

He did not raise his voice much, but the courtyard went quiet without anyone needing to be told.

“Your sons, brothers, and fathers stood between my children and those blades,” Caelen said. “Two lives were lost. Four more were dragged to the edge and pulled back.”

He let his gaze move along the coffins rather than up toward the crowd.

“They did their duty,” he went on. “And I will not pretend that makes this easier. It is always those who walk beside us who pay the price when someone reaches for a noble’s throat. That weight belongs to me as well. House Alfrost will provide compensation and support to these families, but more than that, their names will be recorded among those who laid down their lives in our service. We will not forget who stood in our place.”

It was not a long speech. It was the kind that made a clear promise and stopped there.

Emilia listened in silence, hands folded in front of her. She watched the faces in the crowd rather than the coffins: the woman pressing a hand over her mouth; the old man whose shoulders shook, though no sound came out; the boy gripping the sleeve of a uniform that no longer had anyone inside it.

She knew these guards by name. They had stood watch at the gates, ridden ahead of the carriage, carried messages through the city. They had bowed to her in the mornings and joked quietly with Gilbert when they thought she was out of earshot.

Now all of that ended in a single straight row.

A murmur moved through the families once the formal words were done.

“If only that young instructor had acted faster…”

“He’s supposed to be some prodigy, isn’t he? Then why—”

“Don’t say that here.”

The last voice was a hissed rebuke, but the earlier words still reached Emilia’s ears.

She followed the direction of their glances.

Julian stood at the far edge of the courtyard, a step behind the line of guards. He wore plain black, sword at his hip, hands joined neatly behind his back. His posture was as straight as it had been in the courtyard when he corrected her stance, but his gaze did not leave the coffins.

He did not flinch at the words. He did not try to defend himself. He simply stood there and kept watching the row of cloth-covered boards.

‘They think he was too slow,’ Emilia thought.

Her chest tightened.

She remembered the way the carriage had lurched, the way the door had flown open, the blur of Julian’s coat as he moved. She had barely had time to drop from the seat before the first assassin fell. Without him, there would have been more coffins in this courtyard—hers among them.

But the dead lying there were still real. The families’ anger came from a place she understood, even if their blame landed in the wrong direction.

One by one, relatives stepped forward to place small items on the coffins—folded letters, bits of cloth, a carved wooden charm. Some pressed their hands flat against the boards and stayed there until someone gently guided them back.

When it was her turn, Emilia moved with Caelen and Gilbert.

She stopped in front of the first coffin.

Up close, the cloth made the outline beneath look almost peaceful. She knew better. She bowed her head, fingers tightening around the small white flower she held.

“Thank you,” she said softly.

Her voice did not carry beyond the space in front of her. It wasn’t meant to. The words were for the guard who had once held the gate for her on a rainy day and pretended not to notice when she slipped past the line of waiting carriages.

She placed the flower near the folded hands embroidered on the cloth and stepped to the next coffin.

Each one held a piece of her daily life that would not be there anymore—a greeting, a joke, a warning at the training yard gate when she forgot the time. By the third coffin, her throat felt tight. She kept her shoulders straight.

Gilbert moved beside her, resting his hand for a moment on each board.

“Your families are here,” he said under his breath. “We’ll make sure they’re not left behind.”

It was not a vow he could sign alone, but it was his way of standing next to Caelen’s promise.

When they had finished their part and stepped back, the ceremony began to wind down. Some families stayed rooted in place. Others moved in small clusters toward the edge of the courtyard, eyes still drawn to the row of coffins.

As the crowd thinned, a woman in a worn dress broke away from the others and approached Caelen. Her hands shook as she bowed.

“My lord,” she said. “My husband… he was on the carriage team.”

Caelen faced her fully.

“I know,” he said. “He held his position until the end.”

“If…” Her voice caught. She swallowed and tried again. “If that instructor had cut them down sooner, would he still be here?”

The question spilled out raw. It hung there in the air between them.

Emilia’s breath stopped for a moment.

Caelen did not glance toward Julian. He kept his attention on the woman in front of him.

“Your husband died doing what only he could do at that moment,” Caelen said. “He held the front and kept the horses under control. Without that, my children would have been overturned on the road before any sword was drawn. The instructor did his duty. Your husband did his. The failure is mine for not crushing the hand that sent those assassins before they ever reached you.”

The woman’s shoulders shook. Tears spilled over as she pressed her hands to her face.

“I… I understand, my lord,” she whispered, though understanding clearly did nothing to lighten the grief.

Caelen gave a small nod to one of the nearby officers. The man stepped forward to guide her back toward her family, speaking quietly.

Emilia let out the breath she had been holding.

Caelen’s answer had not erased the blame hanging over Julian’s name, but he had not allowed it to settle there, either. He had pulled it onto his own shoulders instead.

Gilbert’s jaw unclenched by a fraction.

‘Father really is taking all of it on himself,’ Emilia thought. ‘Even though he was the one they were trying to kill.’

The ceremony came to its end. The coffins would be taken to their burial site after the families had time to say their last words. For now, people lingered in broken lines and small circles, voices low and uneven.

Caelen turned to his children.

“We’ll return home,” he said. “The watch will handle the rest of the rites.”

Emilia glanced once more toward Julian.

He still had not moved from his place near the edge of the courtyard. The commander stood near him now, speaking in a low voice. Julian answered with a short nod, gaze finally lifting from the coffins.

Emilia’s feet shifted before she even decided what to do.

“Father,” she said quietly. “May I speak with Lord Julian before we leave?”

Caelen considered her for a brief moment, then nodded.

“Do not keep him long,” he said. “He has his own report to give.”

“I understand.”

Emilia crossed the courtyard, the sound of her steps muted by the uneven stone. As she drew closer, the commander finished his sentence and stepped back, giving her a brief nod of acknowledgment before leaving them space.

Julian turned toward her.

“Lady Emilia,” he said. His voice was the same as always, but up close the shadows under his eyes looked deeper.

Emilia stopped in front of him and bowed her head.

“Thank you for protecting us yesterday,” she said. “If you hadn’t been there, we would have needed more coffins.”

It was a simple line, but it carried everything she could not say in front of the families.

Julian held her gaze for a moment, as if weighing whether she was being polite or honest. Then he inclined his head a little.

“I only did my duty,” he said. “The ones who fell did the same.”

Emilia’s hands tightened slightly at her sides.

“Even so,” she said. “I wanted to say it.”

Something in his expression eased by a hair’s breadth.

“…Then I will accept it,” he said.

Behind her, Gilbert called her name.

“Emilia. Father is ready.”

She turned toward the voice.

“I’m coming,” she answered, then glanced back at Julian once more.

“I’ll work harder,” she said. “So that next time, I’m not just someone you have to protect in a carriage.”

A faint, tired smile touched the corner of Julian’s mouth.

“Then don’t waste the training I give you,” he said. “That will be enough.”

Emilia nodded once and walked back to her father and brother.

As they left the courtyard, the faint sound of families’ voices and the smell of incense followed her out into the street.

#### Scene 2

The carriage ride back to the Alfrost estate passed in a quieter silence than usual.

Emilia sat beside Gilbert, hands folded on her knees. The city streets rolled by outside the window—market stalls, laundry lines across alleys, the distant outline of the palace. None of it seemed to touch the lingering weight in her chest. The scent of incense still clung to her clothes.

Gilbert leaned his head back against the seat and closed his eyes, but his jaw was still tight. Caelen had his gaze turned outward, watching the road ahead, as if measuring every corner where another attack might come.

No one spoke until the carriage pulled through the main gate and slowed to a stop in front of the mansion.

They stepped down one by one.

The front doors opened before they reached them. Eira and the other servants bowed, then moved aside to let them pass. The hall felt strangely still, as if the building itself were holding its breath.

Inside, two girls waited near the base of the main staircase.

Cestina stood a little straighter than usual, hands joined neatly in front of her. Her light hair was tied back, and she wore a simple dress in Alfrost colors. Beside her, Lisoletelle clasped the edge of her skirt, eyes flicking between Emilia and Caelen with undisguised worry.

They had arrived the day before, called in by the household staff as soon as news of the attack spread. But when Emilia had been helped back to her room, pale and exhausted, neither of them had dared to force their way in.

Today, they had come downstairs early and waited.

“Emilia!” Lisoletelle’s fingers tightened on her skirt for a moment before she caught herself. She dipped a quick curtsy. “Welcome home.”

Cestina followed with a smoother movement.

“Welcome back, Lady Emilia,” she said. “I am… relieved to see you standing.”

Emilia stopped a few paces from them.

“I made you worry,” she said. “I’m sorry.”

Her voice came out softer than she meant it to.

Lisoletelle shook her head at once.

“You were attacked in the middle of the city,” she said. “Of course we were worried.”

Cestina’s gaze moved over Emilia’s face, down to her hands, checking for any sign of lingering injury.

“If something still hurts, say so,” Cestina said.

Emilia let out a small breath.

“I’m fine enough, I’m just tired.” she said.

Lisoletelle’s shoulders relaxed a little, but not completely.

Gilbert stepped up beside Emilia, folding his arms loosely.

“So,” he said, looking between the two girls, “no one is going to ask how I am?”

Lisoletelle blinked.

“You look fine, Lord Gilbert,” she said. “You were standing just now.”

Cestina glanced his way.

“If you were hurt, you would not be walking around without a healer,” she said plainly. “You’re strong. You can protect yourself.”

Her words were matter-of-fact, not meant as praise. She simply believed he was less likely to die than the guards had been.

Gilbert’s grin faltered for a heartbeat. The corner of his mouth twitched upward again almost immediately, but Emilia saw the tiny hesitation.

On one side, being called strong by Cestina made something in his chest lift. On the other, the way she brushed off his condition so easily stung more than he expected.

“I see,” he said. “So I don’t even rate a ‘welcome back’.”

“You were standing next to Lord Caelen,” Cestina replied. “You were clearly alive.” She paused, then added, slightly stiffer than before, “Welcome back, Lord Gilbert.”

Gilbert cleared his throat.

“…That’s better,” he said.

He straightened a little, realizing something else.

“Come to think of it,” he went on, “I never introduced myself to you properly, did I?”

Cestina’s brows lifted just a fraction.

“We have met several times already,” she said. “But… no, not formally.”

Gilbert stepped half a pace forward.

He placed his right hand over his chest and inclined his head with the kind of formal grace he usually tried to avoid.

“Gilbert Alfrost,” he said. “Eldest son of House Alfrost. I have been receiving reports about your work from my father and from Emilia for years, Lady Cestina, but until now I have only met you as a guest who keeps stealing my sister’s time.”

He threw the last part in lightly, but his posture stayed sincere.

Such a formal greeting from Gilbert was rare. It showed that he had decided to treat Cestina not only as Emilia’s friend, but as someone whose presence in the house mattered to him as well.

Cestina pressed her lips together for a heartbeat, then stepped forward in kind.

She gathered the edges of her skirt and dipped into a deeper curtsy than the one she had given Emilia.

“Cestina Ludwell,” she replied. “Daughter of House Ludwell, a branch under House Alfrost. My family owes our current position to your house’s mercy and support. I will do my best not to bring shame to that name.”

Because her family stood below his in rank, she could not afford to treat his introduction lightly. Even so, a faint line appeared between her brows, a small sign that his teasing still bothered her.

Gilbert noticed the tightness in her expression and hurried to add:

“I’m the one who should be worried about shame,” he said. “If I do my job poorly, Lord Ludwell will start wondering why he ever entrusted his daughter to this place.”

Lisoletelle let out a small breath she had been holding.

“That won’t happen,” she said. “Cestina works harder than anyone I know.”

Cestina shot her a quick look.

“Liso,” she said quietly.

Lisoletelle’s shoulders jumped.

“Sorry,” she muttered. “I did not mean to speak out of turn.”

Caelen, who had been watching the exchange from a short distance, gave a small nod.

“Thank you for coming,” he said to Cestina and Lisoletelle. “Stay close to Emilia for a while.”

That was permission and acknowledgment in one. For branch families and trusted attendants, it meant they had a place here for as long as they kept their footing.

Emilia felt some of the tightness around her lungs ease.

“I’m fine,” she said. “Really. I was just… tired yesterday.”

Lisoletelle stepped a little closer, her worry not fully convinced.

“You could barely stand when they brought you in,” she said, voice lower now. “Eira told us to let you sleep, so we just sat in the corridor listening for any sound at all.”

Emilia’s gaze dropped for a moment.

“…I don’t remember that part very well,” she admitted. “Sorry.”

A servant approached quietly from the side.

“Lord Caelen,” she said, bowing. “Tea and light food have been prepared in the sitting room.”

Caelen inclined his head.

“Please escort Lady Cestina and Lady Lisoletelle to the sitting room,” Caelen said. “Serve them tea and something light to eat. I’ll join you there once I’ve finished speaking with the steward.”

He turned away down the corridor, the steward already moving to meet him.

Gilbert glanced toward the corridor that led to the sitting room.

“Let’s go inside,” he said.

Emilia stepped forward first.

“Let’s sit,” she said. “I’ll tell you what happened—at least the part I’m allowed to talk about.”

Cestina moved to Emilia’s right and Lisoletelle to her left, and the three of them walked toward the sitting room together.

After they all went inside, Caelen did not follow the others to the sitting room.

The steward walked with him down the opposite corridor, a leather folder tucked under his arm. They entered the study—a quieter room lined with shelves and a single broad desk—and the steward closed the door behind them.

Caelen stayed standing.

“Report,” he said.

The steward opened the folder and laid a thin stack of papers on the desk.

“The city watch finished their examination of the bodies, my lord,” he said. “Their healers and court magicians assisted.”

He drew out the top sheet.

“They checked everything,” he went on. “Clothes, skin, teeth, any markings. No crest, no guild brand, no tattoos we can trace. Makers’ marks on their armor and weapons were scratched off. Even the stitching on their gear was common work—nothing that points to a particular region.”

Caelen’s hand rested lightly on the back of his chair.

“And the cause of death for the captured ones?” he asked. “Not the obvious wounds. The others.”

The steward’s mouth thinned.

“As Lord Julian suspected,” he said, “they found traces of vow magic. A binding placed in advance. When the watch tried to question the survivors, the spell activated. The veins along the neck and chest blackened, the heart stopped. It was the same pattern every time.”

He hesitated.

“The magicians say the trigger wasn’t just on spoken answers,” he added. “If the targets showed signs of breaking under pain or pressure, the spell treated it as betrayal and killed them.”

Caelen’s jaw tightened.

“So they were never meant to be taken alive,” he said.

“Yes, my lord.” The steward lowered his gaze. “Even after a full examination, we have nothing that points to who hired them. It is as if they were made to die without leaving a trail.”

It wasn’t just the curse that bothered him. It was the intent behind it. These men had climbed into their own graves the moment they accepted the job.

“It seems they went into this knowing they would not walk away,” the steward said quietly. “Whoever trained them must have decided their lives were easier to spend than to protect.”

The idea was simple and brutal at the same time: an organization willing to burn skilled fighters like fuel and cut every thread that might lead back to them.

Caelen’s gaze moved down to the reports at last.

“Someone paid for their training, their gear, and the curse that killed them,” he thought. “And they’re confident they can replace every man they just threw away.”

He did not say the name forming at the back of his mind. Without proof, it would only drag his own house into a fight he could not touch yet.

“Has the watch filed the public record?” he asked.

“Yes, my lord,” the steward said. “The incident is recorded as an organized ambush by unknown parties. The details about vow magic are kept in the internal report only.”

Caelen gave a short nod.

“Good,” he said. “No need to teach the capital how to hide its sins better than it already does.”

He finally pulled one of the sheets closer and scanned the neat lines of script—time of attack, location, positions of the bodies, condition of the carriage.

“Have them send copies of the internal report to House Roosevelt’s archive,” he added. “Quietly. Julian will need the details if this happens again.”

The steward nodded, committing the order to memory and gathered the papers, leaving one copy on the desk.

He reached for the door handle, then paused. There was still one thing he had not reported.

“There is one more thing,” he said. “Some of the guard families… they are blaming Lord Julian for not saving everyone.”

Caelen’s expression did not change, but his eyes cooled further.

“Let them grieve how they need to,” he said. “Do not silence them. But if anyone tries to turn that grief into a rumor that reaches the Academy, bring me their names. I will speak to them myself.”

That alone told the steward how seriously Caelen took both the dead and the living he had left to protect. The steward bowed deeply.

“Understood, my lord,” he said.

When the door closed behind him, the study fell quiet.

Only then did Caelen allow his gaze to drop fully to the report, tracing the lines that turned eight dead men into neat columns of ink. The vow magic had done its work perfectly. The bodies on the page had no master, no banner, no name.

“That will not last,” he murmured.

He set the report aside and reached for a fresh sheet of paper.

There were still inquiries he could make that did not go through official channels.

In the sitting room, the air felt a little softer than the courtyard, but the weight of the morning still sat on everyone’s shoulders.

Emilia took the single armchair near the low table. Cestina and Lisoletelle sat on the sofa opposite her, skirts gathered neatly, while Gilbert claimed the end of the same sofa, turned slightly so he could watch Emilia’s face.

A tea set had already been laid out. No one reached for it at first.

Emilia rested her hands in her lap.

“...I’ll start from when we left the Silveria offices,” she said.

She walked them through it in order—how the carriage had rolled out through the industrial district, the way the street had looked normal until the first impact, the jolt when the guard outside was hit.

“The carriage lurched hard to the side,” she said. “The horses panicked, but the driver managed to keep them from bolting. Then the door shook—someone tried to force it open.”

Lisoletelle’s fingers tightened around the edge of her skirt.

Cestina watched without interrupting, her eyes following each small movement in Emilia’s hands as much as her words.

Gilbert cleared his throat once.

“I pulled Emilia down behind the seat as soon as it hit,” he said. “There wasn’t enough room to swing a blade properly in there. If one of them had gotten inside, her body would’ve been the first thing they saw.”

He did not raise his voice, but he made sure that part was heard.

Emilia glanced at him briefly, then continued.

“Before the door could open, Lord Julian moved,” she said. “He was already halfway up when the latch clicked. I didn’t even see him draw his sword. One breath he was sitting there, the next he’d taken the knife out of the first man’s hand.”

Gilbert shifted, leaning an elbow on the arm of the sofa.

“I kept my focus on the inside of the carriage,” he added. “If anyone slipped past Julian, they weren’t going to reach her.”

He spoke like someone making a simple correction to a battle report. The angle of his gaze, however, slid toward Cestina for half a heartbeat before returning to Emilia.

Emilia neither corrected nor praised him. She let his words sit there and moved on.

“After that, it was over quickly,” she said. “Two on the left, one on the roof. Lord Julian called their positions, and Father and the guards handled the rest. We stayed inside until they told us it was clear.”

Cestina’s eyes narrowed slightly.

“So you never left the carriage until the fighting was done?” she asked.

“Not until there were no more blades swinging,” Emilia said. “When we stepped out, most of them were already on the ground.”

Gilbert gave a short nod.

“Julian was the one who cut them down,” he said. “My job was to make sure Emilia didn’t get dragged out in the middle of it. I wasn’t about to swing at shadows and open a gap for them.”

Even though he hadn’t taken down a single assassin himself, his report made it plain that he had stayed where he was needed—shielding Emilia inside the small, cramped space instead of chasing after kills outside.

Lisoletelle let out a shaky breath.

“So the stories about ‘eight assassins’...” she said. “They weren’t exaggerating.”

“No,” Emilia answered. “Eight. Two of the guards died. Four were injured badly enough that they won’t work for a while.”

Silence pressed in for a moment.

Cestina sat back slightly, eyes lowering as she turned that over.

“That matches what the staff were whispering,” she said quietly. “Just with less panic.”

Emilia’s mouth moved in something that wasn’t quite a smile.

“I left the panic to them yesterday,” she said. “I was too tired to do anything with it.”

Gilbert gave a small snort at that. It broke the stiffness in the room for just a moment.

As Emilia continued, she added the details she had seen from her place on the carriage floor—the way the horses trembled, how the driver’s hands shook on the reins, the sound of Julian’s voice calling out numbers and positions as if he were in a drill hall instead of a street attack.

Each time she paused to search for the right word, Gilbert filled in a small piece from his own angle—where he had braced against the seat, how he had kept his body between Emilia and the door, the angle of the carriage when it had hit the broken cobblestone.

Cestina listened without interrupting, but the faint crease between her brows deepened each time Gilbert cut in.

It wasn’t that his comments were wrong. He simply had a habit of stepping over Emilia’s rhythm and dropping his own emphasis wherever he liked. To someone as sharp as Cestina, it felt less like clarifying the story and more like nudging the spotlight toward himself.

She did not say anything. Her eyes, however, slid toward him more than once in quiet irritation.

Eventually, Gilbert seemed to notice.

The next time Emilia paused, his mouth opened, then closed again. He let her finish the sentence before adding anything.

“All I’m saying,” he summed up at one point, “is that if they’d breached the carriage, it would have gone much worse. The ones who fell out there… they bought us the time we needed.”

This time, he left it there. No extra comment about his own position in the carriage. No pointed glance toward Cestina.

Bit by bit, he adjusted the way he spoke, testing how much he could say without earning that small, sharp look from her. Gilbert was smart enough to see that forcing his way into the middle of the story wouldn’t win him anything; instead, he began choosing his timing more carefully, slipping his contributions in where they actually added to Emilia’s explanation.

Lisoletelle’s shoulders slowly eased as the story reached the part they had already heard from the guards— how the bodies were taken away, how the report was filed, how the burial had been arranged.

When Emilia finally fell quiet, the teapot on the table had gone lukewarm.

Lisoletelle reached for it anyway, if only to have something to do with her hands.

“I still don’t like it,” she said, pouring tea into Emilia’s cup first. “But at least now I can picture what happened instead of imagining something even worse.”

Cestina nodded once.

“And you came back alive,” she said. “That is the part that matters to me.”

The way she said it left no space for argument. For her, everything else—the street, the numbers, the assassins—was only the path that led to this point, where Emilia was sitting in front of her instead of lying in one of the coffins they had just walked past.

Gilbert leaned back slightly, letting that settle.

A knock sounded at the door.

One of his attendants stepped inside, bowing first to Emilia and the guests and then to Gilbert.

“Lord Gilbert,” he said. “Forgive the interruption. The documents from the northern district have arrived. Your father requested that you review the letters and initial the minor approvals before evening.”

Gilbert clicked his tongue softly, more at the timing than at the work.

“Already?” he said. Then he let out a small breath and pushed himself up from the sofa. “Understood. I’ll come now.”

Even at fifteen, he was already handling parts of the load Caelen could not carry alone every day—reading reports, checking trade requests, making sure the smaller matters never piled high enough to become problems.

He turned back toward the girls.

“I’ll leave the rest of the details to Emilia,” he said. “If she starts skipping anything important, remind her I expect a full report later.”

His tone was light, but he left the warning as a joke rather than a command.

He let his gaze rest on Emilia for a moment, then on Cestina.

“I’ll see you both at dinner,” he said.

He gave them a small, easy smile—gentler than the ones he threw around in the training yard—then followed his attendant out of the room, the door closing softly behind them.

After that, only the three girls remained.

The quiet that followed was different from before. The worst of the story had already been spoken; what was left were the parts that didn’t fit into any formal report.

A couple of days passed.

By the time the last of the formal condolences had been given and the last of the guard families had gone home, the mansion had begun to move again. Patrol schedules were adjusted, new guards rotated in, and the staff slipped back into their usual rhythm. The grief did not disappear, but it folded itself into daily work the way all old wounds eventually did.

Cestina continued to visit.

On the first day after the burial, she arrived in the late afternoon, as she always did when lessons allowed. Emilia met her in the corridor outside the practice hall, Lisoletelle hurrying along a step behind with a stack of borrowed books.

Gilbert happened to be coming from the opposite direction, a bundle of reports tucked under one arm.

He slowed as they drew close.

“Welcome, Lady Cestina,” he said.

It was a simple greeting, nothing like the teasing from before. He added a small, almost formal smile and shifted the papers in his arm instead of reaching for anything more.

Cestina blinked once.

“Thank you, Lord Gilbert,” she replied. “I hope your work with the reports is going smoothly.”

It was the sort of polite line nobles exchanged in hallways, but the edge of irritation that had been in her voice before was gone.

Gilbert stepped aside to give them the path.

“Work can wait a little,” he said with a faint smile. “Enjoy your time here.”

He left it at that and walked on.

He had decided, after the sitting-room conversation, that pushing too hard only made her shut down. Short, harmless lines were safer than forcing his way into the middle of every scene.

The pattern repeated.

The next time Cestina visited, she and Emilia were in the inner garden, going over magic notes on a stone bench while Lisoletelle tried to sketch the shape of a spell circle by hand. The late sun turned the surface of the pond into a dull mirror.

Gilbert crossed the garden on his way to the training grounds, practice sword in hand.

He slowed when he saw them.

“Studying again?” he asked, stopping a comfortable distance away. “If you keep this up, the Academy won’t have anything left to teach you.”

Emilia looked up from her notes.

“We’re just reviewing what Lady Vespera gave me,” she said.

Cestina closed the notebook in her lap.

“Emilia’s spells are written into these notes,” she said. “If I don’t understand them properly, I can’t support her at all.”

Gilbert’s gaze rested on her for a moment.

“Emilia’s lucky,” he said. “Most people would just leave the notes to her and wait to hear how it went.”

It wasn’t flattery thrown out at random. For Gilbert, it was a simple admission that he saw how seriously Cestina treated Emilia’s training.

He let a faint smile touch his face—small, not flashy.

“If any of you get stuck on the Academy’s written work later,” he added, “you can send a page to my study. I’m usually buried in documents anyway.”

To anyone overhearing, it sounded like a casual offer to help with homework. For Gilbert, it was a safer way to stay connected—through shared workload instead of forced charm.

Cestina considered him for a moment.

“I will keep that in mind,” she said.

Her tone neither invited nor rejected. It was enough that she hadn’t brushed him off.

He lifted his practice sword slightly in a half-salute and moved on toward the training grounds.

Day by day, it settled into a quiet habit.

Whenever Cestina came to the mansion—whether for training, to accompany Emilia on errands inside the estate, or simply to sit with her between lessons—Gilbert made a point of trading at least a few words with her.

Sometimes it was in the corridor, when he crossed paths with the three of them on his way to the study.

“On your way to Emilia again?” he would ask.

“Yes,” Cestina would answer with a small nod. “She’ll complain if I keep her waiting.”

It stayed light on the surface, but it showed he knew exactly where she would be, and that she understood Emilia well enough to joke about it.

Other times it was in the dining room before a meal, when he arrived a little earlier than usual.

“I’m glad you could join us again today, Lady Cestina,” he’d say as he took his seat.

“Thank you for having me, Lord Gilbert,” she would reply. “The carriage nearly made us late.”

It was ordinary conversation, but repeated often enough that it started to feel like part of the house’s daily rhythm.

Gilbert never pushed past that. He did not corner her for long talks or demand her opinion on everything he said. He only left those small, easy exchanges behind him as he passed, accompanied by a gentle smile that never lingered long enough to be called staring.

He had decided that if he was serious about her, then the first thing he needed to do was stop being a nuisance.

Big gestures and loud declarations would only annoy Cestina and make her pull away. Keeping it small and ordinary—a few words here and there, a steady presence—was the only approach he thought she might actually accept.

And if, later, Cestina remembered anything about these days, he wanted it to be that he had spoken to her properly and looked at her as more than a convenient branch daughter.

Each time he caught her eye in the hall or over the table, he offered that same small, steady smile.

He did not know if it was enough to leave a mark.

For now, he was satisfied with something small. If, later on, Cestina remembered these days and thought of him as the brother who spoke to her properly and stayed close when he could, that was enough.

A few months passed.

By then, Cestina had grown used to Gilbert’s presence in the house without really noticing when it had started.

He was simply there.

Sometimes it was a greeting in the corridor when she arrived for lessons. Sometimes it was a short exchange before dinner. Sometimes it was just the sense that, somewhere in the estate, Gilbert was either in the training yard or bent over a pile of reports in his study.

It was no longer surprising when he addressed her directly. It would have felt stranger now if he hadn’t.

He had stopped with the louder jokes. Instead, he chose his words carefully whenever he spoke to her, sticking to things that were easy to answer—lessons, traffic, small irritations with paperwork. Cestina, for her part, responded with steady politeness that had slowly softened into something closer to habit.

One morning over breakfast, Caelen mentioned it as if it were a simple scheduling point.

“Gilbert will be leaving the city for a time,” he said. “There are matters in the outlying districts that require an Alfrost representative.”

Emilia’s hand paused over her cup.

“How long?” she asked.

“Two weeks, perhaps a little more,” Caelen replied. “He will travel with an escort and return once the inspections are done.”

Gilbert gave a small shrug, as if two weeks away were nothing.

“I’ll bring back something interesting,” he said. “Assuming the districts have anything worth bringing back.”

He said it lightly, but he still took the time to speak to the staff afterward, giving quick instructions to the steward and gate guards. By the time the carriage took him out through the main gate, half the house knew he would be gone for a while.

Cestina heard about it later that day.

She arrived at the mansion in the afternoon as usual, cloak dusted with the smell of the city streets. The entrance hall felt a little too quiet. There was no low murmur of Gilbert’s voice from the study door, no distant clack of practice swords from the yard.

Emilia met her at the base of the stairs.

“Sorry,” Emilia said. “I kept you waiting.”

“It was only a moment,” Cestina replied.

Her gaze flicked, almost without thinking, toward the door that usually led toward Gilbert’s study.

It stayed closed. No attendant stood outside it with an armful of papers.

They went about their usual routine—reviewing notes, walking through the inner corridors, talking in low voices about lessons and the funeral that had already begun to settle into memory. But each time they passed a place where Gilbert was usually present, Cestina found herself glancing around before she could stop it.

By the third day, the absence had settled enough that it began to bother her.

She sat with Emilia and Lisoletelle in the inner garden, the same stone bench as before, a notebook open on her knees. Emilia was halfway through explaining one of Vespera’s more confusing corrections when Cestina’s eyes slid toward the path that usually led to the training grounds.

Still empty.

She turned a page in her notebook with more force than it needed.

“Something wrong?” Emilia asked.

“No,” Cestina said too quickly. “I was just… thinking.”

She kept her gaze on the paper.

A breath later, she spoke again.

“Your brother hasn’t been here lately,” she said. “Did he get himself buried under paperwork or something?”

Her tone came out sharper than the words themselves. It sounded like someone complaining about a noisy person who’d suddenly gone quiet, not someone openly admitting they missed them.

Such a question from Cestina was rare. She usually ignored Gilbert’s comings and goings unless he was directly in front of her.

Emilia blinked.

“Gilbert?” she repeated. “He left the city. Father sent him to the districts. He’ll be gone for a couple of weeks.”

Cestina’s hand paused on the page.

“A couple of weeks,” she said. “I see.”

She clicked her tongue once, almost irritated with herself, and added quickly:

“It’s just… the corridors are quieter than usual. I thought he was just hiding in his study again.”

She said it as if she were merely observing a change in noise, not in a person.

Lisoletelle glanced between them, picking up the edge in Cestina’s voice but choosing not to comment. She bent over her own notebook and pretended to review a spell diagram that she had already memorized.

Emilia watched Cestina’s face.

Cestina’s expression didn’t change much—still composed, still neat—but there was a tightness in the way she held her mouth, and her eyes kept drifting toward the garden entrance even though she knew no one was coming.

‘She noticed right away that he wasn’t here,’ Emilia thought. ‘She doesn’t usually ask about him at all.’

A question rose in her chest before she could stop it.

Is she… actually worried about him?

Her tongue stalled on the words. If she asked and Cestina brushed it off, it would only make things more awkward. And if Cestina didn’t brush it off…

Emilia lowered her gaze back to the notes spread between them instead.

“For now,” she said, “let’s finish this part. When he comes back, he’ll ask what we’ve been doing, and I don’t want to admit we were stuck on the same page for two weeks.”

Cestina let out a short breath that could have been a quiet laugh.

“Fine,” she said. “We’ll finish it before he has a chance to be smug about anything.”

She did not say she was waiting for him. She did not have to.

Emilia turned the page and started explaining the next line of Vespera’s notes, but in the back of her mind, the unfinished thought remained.

She understood that something in Cestina’s feelings had shifted.

She simply did not yet have the courage—or the certainty—to ask what, exactly, that meant.

### Chapter 13: 10: Noble’s Life – Part 3

#### Scene 1

On one morning, two years after the assassination attempt, Emilia—now twelve years old—continued her usual daily routine.

She had breakfast with her family, went through her scheduled morning training, and then, as she did on most days now, moved to her father’s study.

Recently, Caelen had added something new to that routine: lessons in noble duties. Manners and etiquette were no longer the focus; Emilia had picked those up quickly and had already mastered that part back when she was seven.

Caelen asked Emilia to start reading various documents he had approved, along with the notes he had written on some of the reports he had reviewed in the past. From time to time, she would ask him why he had written certain comments in the formal documents, and Caelen would answer directly, explaining that even formal paperwork needed detailed information and that nothing should be missing, whether in writing or in data.

So each morning, after the ink on that day’s reports had dried, he would pull out older documents—a trade request, a patrol report, a tax adjustment—and spread them across the desk between them. The study smelled faintly of paper and sealing wax, with sunlight cutting across the shelves and turning the dust in the air into a thin haze.

“Read it as if you were the one signing at the bottom,” Caelen would say.

Emilia sat opposite him, feet just barely reaching the floor, tracing the lines of script with her eyes. On one report, a border village requested extra grain from the city stores. The numbers were neatly added; the totals matched.

Near the margin, Caelen’s handwriting sliced through the white space.

Reason for sudden increase? Weather? Troop movement? Crop disease? Specify.

“...Even though they wrote the amount correctly?” Emilia had asked the first time she saw a note like that. “Isn’t it enough if the numbers are right?”

“If I accept this without a reason, I don’t know whether I’m feeding soldiers, farmers, or smugglers,” Caelen replied. “And five years from now, no one will remember why the amount changed. A proper report lets someone understand the situation without dragging the writer back into this room.”

Such answers made it clear this was not just about reading neatly copied sentences. He was teaching her how a noble’s signature could move food, men, and coin without anyone drawing a sword.

On another day, he handed her a patrol log from the city watch. Most of it was routine—streets checked, gates secured, nothing unusual. Near the end, one line stood out.

No incident. Situation remains under control.

Caelen’s comment cut across it in the same precise script.

Under control from what? Name the cause. Name the risk.

Emilia frowned slightly as she read it.

“So even saying ‘no incident’ is not enough?” she asked. “They still have to write what almost went wrong.”

“If they bother to mention ‘control,’ it means something was slipping,” Caelen said. “If they don’t say what, I can’t tell whether they need more men, a different route, or a different officer.”

He did not raise his voice. He did not scold whoever had written the original line. He simply treated sloppy information as something that had to be fixed before it was allowed to touch their seal.

The more reports she read, the more she saw the same pattern.

Whenever someone cut corners on reasons, Caelen’s notes cut them open again.

Gilbert, on the other hand, was now seventeen, with one more year left before graduating from the Royal Academy. He had started thinking seriously about his future path—whether to become a royal knight, a holy knight, an adventurer, or even something simpler like an instructor. Of course, his father would naturally recommend the path of a royal knight, possibly leading a military unit or some role within the army. But Caelen gave both of his children the freedom to choose their own futures.

To most people watching from the outside, the choice looked simple.

A royal knight served directly under the crown—leading troops, taking missions, and standing at the front of whatever the kingdom decided to push against. A holy knight answered to the Western Church instead, guarding sanctuaries and escorting priests where they were needed. An instructor rarely left the capital at all, but spent their days shaping the next group of nobles and officers.

Gilbert knew all of that in theory. The problem was deciding which kind of burden he actually wanted on his shoulders.

Some evenings, when patrol reports and trade summaries were stacked high on Caelen’s desk, Gilbert stood by the window with a cup of tea in his hand and asked simple questions that did not feel simple at all.

“If I become a royal knight,” he had said once, “how much of my time will actually be spent on battlefields, and how much in rooms like this?”

Caelen did not pretend the answer was glorious.

“The higher you stand, the more time you spend planning and listening,” he replied. “When the border is unstable, you travel with your men. When it is quiet, you sit in rooms like this so it stays that way.”

He was not trying to push Gilbert away from the role. He was cutting off any illusion that the title meant endless heroics without ink.

Still, since Gilbert would most likely become the next head of House Alfrost, the royal knight path was the most likely choice. It was the one that fit most neatly with everyone’s expectations: a noble who could fight, command, and sign his name on orders without hesitation.

He sometimes discussed this with Caelen or Julian, since Julian himself had walked through multiple roles related to that world. Julian spoke of campaigns and classrooms with the same even tone; he did not romanticize either.

“With a sword, you see the result in front of you,” Julian had told him once. “With teaching, you see it ten years later, when someone you trained chooses what to do with lives that are not their own.”

Gilbert remembered that line more clearly than he wanted to admit.

Gilbert also occasionally talked about it with Cestina, with whom he had grown closer day by day. Now, the two of them seemed to genuinely enjoy spending time talking to each other. Even though Gilbert was five years older, he never talked down to her the way he sometimes teased his little sister, Emilia.

When he spoke to Cestina about his options, his tone shifted without him noticing.

He did not list titles to impress her. Instead, he asked simpler questions.

On one afternoon in the garden where the three of them usually gathered, only Gilbert and Cestina were sitting on the bench, talking about Gilbert’s future. Emilia was busy in the study, yet lately Cestina kept coming to this place anyway. At first she told herself it was just habit, but before she noticed it, she was choosing this bench because she wanted to see Gilbert.

“If I spend all my time in the capital, will I still be able to protect this house properly?” he asked.

Cestina had taken a moment before answering.

“If you never leave, you will not see what your decisions do outside these walls,” she said. “But if you are always away, you won’t see what happens inside them either.”

She had said it calmly, as if she were talking about balancing a ledger instead of someone’s life.

Gilbert had laughed under his breath.

“So either way, I don’t get to rest,” he said.

“That is what it means to stand there,” Cestina replied.

Talking to her felt different from talking to Caelen or Julian. His father spoke as someone who already carried the weight. Julian spoke as someone who had walked through several roles and kept the marks

from each. Cestina listened like someone standing at his side, looking at the same narrow paths from the same low wall.

Gilbert never said it out loud, but that was why he kept bringing the subject up with her.

In those quiet conversations, away from the academy drills and the formal meetings, it became easier for him to imagine a future where he was not carrying all of that weight alone.

Listening to her that day, Gilbert finally noticed the expression on Cestina’s face.

Her posture was as composed as ever, but her eyes were different—clear, steady, carrying a quiet hope that she did not put into words. There was a small, almost hidden softness at the edge of her mouth. It was not the polite mask of a branch daughter speaking to the heir. It was Cestina herself, quietly glad that he trusted her with worries no one else heard from him this often.

For a moment, he simply watched her.

“Cestina,” he said. “Thank you. For always listening to me like this.”

He chose the words carefully. It was not his habit to thank someone just for staying and listening.

Cestina blinked, a little surprised.

“I’m only listening,” she replied. “You’re the one who keeps bringing it to me.”

To her, that was enough. If he wanted to talk, she would be there to hear it.

Gilbert’s fingers tightened once on his knees, then relaxed.

He let his gaze move around the garden. The paths between the hedges were empty. No servants were crossing the stone walkways, no guards were posted close enough to overhear. The nearby doors were shut; the windows looking out onto this side of the garden did not hold any watching silhouettes.

Once he was sure of that, he drew a slow, deeper breath.

Cestina noticed the way his shoulders settled and the air between them turned heavier.

“Lord Gilbert?” she asked. “Did something happen?”

Gilbert straightened his back.

“There is one thing I have not been honest about,” he said. “If I keep walking around it, I will end up dragging it into every conversation we have.”

He had rehearsed this alone, in quieter rooms than this one. Saying it here, to her face, was different.

On that sunny afternoon, with all the dignity and courage he had, Gilbert decided to put it into proper words.

“Cestina,” he said. “When I think about my future, you are already in it.”

To him, saying she already stood in his future was harder—and more serious—than throwing out a simple “I like you.” It was the kind of line he would only use after deciding she was someone he could stand beside in public.

“I respect you,” he continued, “not just as Emilia’s companion or as a daughter of House Ludwell, but as someone who stands on her own judgment. You speak honestly even when it is inconvenient. You take Emilia’s training seriously when she would rather run away from it. When I talk about the path I might take, you listen as if it truly matters where I end up.”

His voice stayed low but firm, each word measured without a single stumble. He never once looked away from Cestina; that quiet steadiness was the only proof he offered that this was not a passing whim, but something he had already decided on.

“If I am to shoulder command, or whatever role I choose,” he said, “I would rather do it with someone beside me who can still speak to me like that. In my mind, that ‘someone’ has already become you.”

For Gilbert, that alone was the confession, not an attempt to impress her but a way to show how deeply she was already woven into the future he imagined.

Cestina’s composure faltered.

Color rose quickly into her cheeks and along the tips of her ears. The hand resting on Emilia’s notebook tightened until the leather cover bent under her grip. Her shoulders stiffened for a heartbeat, as if her body had forgotten how to sit with its usual calm.

She had received confessions before—simple “I like you” declarations, flowery praise of her looks, careful letters that treated her as a pretty ornament one could try to obtain.

None of them had sounded like this.

Those past confessions always spoke as if they were doing her a favor by choosing her. Gilbert’s words treated her as someone whose presence changed the shape of his future.

'Why does it feel like this', she thought, 'when he never even said the simple words?'

Even so, she did not answer right away. She lowered her gaze slightly, forcing her breath to settle.

“Lord Gilbert,” she said at last. “I… don’t dislike the thought.”

Her voice was softer than usual.

“But I still feel too young to decide something like that now,” she added. “I’m afraid that if I answer you now, it won’t be honest enough.”

She wasn’t dodging him; she was choosing the only answer she could give without betraying herself. The quiet between them stretched, broken only by the faint rustle of leaves beyond the hedge, while Gilbert let her words settle and released them in one slow breath.

“I understand,” he said. “Thank you for listen to my feeling.”

A thin ache spread across his ribs. He could already imagine how awkward things would become if he clung to it—Emilia’s study sessions, the garden talks, all of it turning stiff because he refused to let this go.

“In that case, I apologize for putting this on you,” he began. “Please forget—”

Cestina looked up sharply.

“Wait,” she said, cutting him off. “I never said you should take it back.”

Gilbert stopped mid-sentence.

Cestina straightened her back again, regaining the dignity she wore so naturally, though the color had not left her cheeks.

“I said I feel too young right now,” she went on. “That isn’t the same as rejecting you.”

Such a correction from her was rare. Normally, she let other people’s assumptions stand if they made things easier. This one, she refused to let slide.

Gilbert watched her, weighing every word.

“Then,” he asked quietly, “when you’re older and sure of your feelings, will you allow me to ask you again— properly?”

He didn’t dress it up as romance. For a noble heir, a future partner was both feeling and decision. He acknowledged that plainly.

Cestina drew in a small breath.

She turned her eyes away for a moment, toward the garden path, then back to him.

“When I am older,” she said, “and when I can answer without uncertainty… if you still feel the same, then ask me again.”

She held his gaze.

“That time,” she added, “I’ll give you a clear answer.”

She did not say “yes” outright. She didn’t need to. For Gilbert, this was already more permission than he expected.

Relief washed through him so sharply that he almost let the smile break fully across his face.

He kept it measured.

His shoulders eased, the tension in his jaw loosened, and a small, steady smile reached his eyes instead of stopping at his mouth.

“Very well,” he said. “Then I’ll wait for that day, and try not to make a fool of myself until it comes.”

He did not reach for her hand. He did not try to push for promises she hadn’t made. He simply accepted the line she had drawn and took his place just behind it.

Inside, though, something settled.

Before this, when he pictured his future—royal knight, instructor, or something in between—he had only known that he didn’t want to carry it alone.

Now, no matter which cloak he imagined on his shoulders, there was always the same quiet thought under it:

When she is old enough, and if she still allows it, I will ask her again—properly, and in front of whoever I need to.

.

...

.....

But Gilbert, even after deciding to wait, couldn’t leave the matter completely untouched.

That same night, House Alfrost hosted a dinner for the main branch and several of its closest branch families. The venue was Caelen’s city-side mansion near the palace—smaller than the royal district estate, but built around a long hall designed for evenings event exactly like this.

Light from crystal lamps spilled down over polished stone and white-clothed tables. Banners bearing the Alfrost crest hung between the pillars, and servants passed through the room with practiced ease, refilling glasses and changing plates as nobles moved from group to group.

Somewhere between greeting the Siegharts and exchanging a few polite words with the Ashfeldts, Gilbert’s earlier resolve shifted into a sharper idea.

If I am serious, he thought, then the adults should hear it from me directly.

He stayed beside Emilia and Caelen as they made their rounds, trading short courtesies with each family. Cestina walked half a step behind Emilia as usual, Lisoletelle shadowing the other side, the two of them listening more than they spoke.

When they finally reached the Ludwell family, Gilbert stopped thinking about the idea and simply acted.

Lord Armand Ludwell stood with his wife near one of the side tables, speaking quietly with another minor noble. He looked as he always did—formal, composed, the lines at the corners of his eyes carved by too many letters that had carried bad news.

Gilbert stepped forward and bowed with proper form.

“Lord Armand. Lady Maris,” he said. “Thank you for accepting our invitation tonight.”

Armand turned, surprise flickering for a moment before he answered with the smooth politeness of a man used to court.

“The honor is ours, Lord Gilbert,” he said. “House Ludwell is always grateful for the main family’s hospitality.”

They exchanged a few lines of light talk—health, recent workloads, a brief comment about the Academy. It was the kind of conversation that could have passed without leaving any trace.

Then Gilbert’s tone shifted.

“There is one matter I wished to raise while we are all present,” he said. “If I may be so forward.”

He did not raise his voice, but the weight in it made nearby conversations dim just enough. Caelen’s gaze slid toward him; Emilia seemed confused by her brother's behavior.

Armand stilled.

“…Of course,” he said. “If there is a matter in which Ludwell can be of use, I will listen.”

Gilbert drew a steady breath.

“Lord Armand,” he said. “This is not about contracts or patrol routes. It is about your daughter.”

Cestina’s shoulders jumped almost imperceptibly. Emilia turned her head toward her, then back to Gilbert.

Gilbert met Armand’s eyes directly.

“Lady Cestina has stood by Emilia for years,” he said. “She has served this house without complaint since the day you entrusted her to us. She speaks honestly when silence would be easier. She sees things Emilia and I overlook, and she keeps saying them even when it is inconvenient for her.”

He did not look at Cestina while he spoke. Addressing her father and stealing glances at his daughter at the same time would have felt cheap.

“Because of that,” he went on, “when I think of the future I wish to build—as a knight, as the next head of this house, or whatever shape my duty takes—I no longer picture it alone.”

Only then did he allow himself to glance toward Cestina.

“In that future,” he said, “I would like Lady Cestina to stand beside me. If you permit it, I wish to take her as my future wife.”

He spoke it as clearly as he had spoken his earlier confession—measured, deliberate, with all the dignity his upbringing had drilled into him.

The air around them felt like it had stopped.

For a moment, the lively noise of the hall seemed far away. Armand could only stare at Gilbert, as if the boy’s words had stopped him in place.

For a man who usually reshaped threats into quiet agreements, hearing such a direct request from the main heir knocked the air out of his practiced calm.

“…Lord Gilbert,” he said slowly. “That is… quite the request to make in a hall like this.”

Nearby, one of the relatives who had been standing close enough to listen almost dropped his glass.

Emilia put a hand over her face and let out a small sigh.

'What is my brother doing…' She did not say it out loud. Her expression alone made it clear.

Caelen lifted his hand to his mouth, knuckles touching his lips as if adjusting his posture. It was just enough to cover the smile that threatened to show.

Cestina, on the other hand, flushed so fast she almost forgot how to breathe.

“L–Lord Gilbert!” she burst out. “I already answered you this afternoon. W-Why are you saying it to my father now?”

Her voice was sharper than usual, the calm edges stripped away. It sounded halfway between outrage and panic.

“That is exactly why,” Gilbert replied, looking at her properly for the first time since he began. “You gave me an answer that mattered. If I intend to hold to it, the first person who should know—after you—is the head of your house.”

To him, this was not repeating the confession. It was aligning his words with the person responsible for her future.

Emilia exhaled through her nose.

“If anyone overheard only this part,” she muttered under her breath, just loud enough for Cestina to catch, “they would think you two are already in a lovers’ quarrel.”

Cestina shot her a quick glare, cheeks still burning.

“That is not—” she started, then broke off, because she could not deny how it sounded.

Armand drew a slow breath, pulling his focus away from the two girls and back to Gilbert.

His gaze slid briefly toward Caelen.

“Lord Caelen,” he said quietly. “Before I say anything further… are these words something you instructed him to speak? Or are they truly his own?”

There was more than formality in the question. For Armand, the difference meant everything. A demand from the main house left no room to refuse. An honest request from the heir still allowed him to look at his daughter first.

Caelen lowered his hand from his mouth and turned fully toward Armand.

“I did not instruct him,” he said. “In this house, choices like these belong to my children. If Gilbert speaks here, he does so on his own will.”

He answered without hiding behind his rank. By saying it that plainly, he left the decision with Gilbert and with Cestina’s side.

Armand bowed his head once, more out of respect than habit. When he lifted it again, the shock had not vanished, but something warmer had joined it.

“Then… as Cestina’s father and as head of Ludwell,” he said, “I cannot pretend this offer is anything but an honor.”

Gratitude sat heavy on every word. For a branch family that had once arrived with nothing but their name, being chosen openly by the main heir felt like having the ground beneath their feet confirmed once more.

He turned from Caelen back to his daughter, letting the weight of the decision follow his gaze and making it clear that, whatever honor lay in the offer, the final word would come from her.

“However,” he added, “it is also her life. Cestina.”

Cestina straightened as if called to attention.

She let out a small, quiet sigh as the memory of this afternoon’s confession rushed back—the heat in her face, the clumsy way she had answered—then forced herself to look at Gilbert first and only after that at her father.

“As I said this afternoon,” she began, her voice steadier now, “I still feel too young to decide everything.”

“But… I am not unhappy with what Lord Gilbert said,” she continued, the words catching slightly at the edges. “If this is about a promise for the future, and if he is prepared to wait until I can answer properly, then I will not reject it.”

Heat crept back into her cheeks as she heard how the words carried in the quiet around them; every nearby pause and shifted gaze reminded her that this answer, which had been only between them in the garden, was now laid open to the hall.

That was as far as she could go without betraying what she had said in the garden. She still refused to give him a yes, but she no longer closed the door in front of him.

Around them, a few nearby relatives exchanged quick glances over the rims of their glasses. To ears trained on contracts and marriage talks, “I will not reject it” already sounded dangerously close to a promise.

Gilbert let out a slow breath he had not noticed he was holding and inclined his head in answer.

“Then I will wait,” he said. “As long as it takes for you to be certain.”

Gilbert let out a long breath as the last word left him. The tightness that had been sitting in his chest since the confession in the garden that afternoon finally eased. Saying it in front of Armand felt completely different from saying it in the garden with just Cestina there; this time, it felt like he had asked for a future that might actually be allowed.

Armand closed his eyes for a moment. He could already picture Cestina one day carrying the Alfrost name, standing beside Gilbert and signing for Ludwell’s people with him. When he opened them again, his next breath came easier. He had found a future for Ludwell that did not mean throwing his daughter away to get it.

“In that case,” he said, looking to Caelen, “if House Alfrost has no objection, I would be honored to recognize this as an engagement in principle. When they both come of age—and if Cestina’s answer remains the same —we can formalize it in writing.”

Armand spoke clearly and without hesitation, already prepared to shoulder whatever responsibility the Alfrost name would place on Ludwell when the two of them married.

Cestina’s composure finally cracked. The embarrassment of hearing her own hesitant answer laid bare in front of the hall was already more than enough; when her father calmly spoke of her future marriage on top of that, the mask she always wore as a daughter of Ludwell could no longer hold.

“F-Father…!” she protested, a hand flying up to cover part of her face as heat rushed back into her cheeks. “You’re saying it like it’s already decided…”

Maris lowered her gaze to her glass, hiding a small smile against its rim as she watched them; after everything their family had been through, the sight of Cestina’s future tying to the Alfrost name made her believe Ludwell might finally be heading toward brighter days again.

“House Alfrost has no objection,” he said. “On the contrary, I welcome it.”

The words were calm, but they made it real.

“That is because,” Emilia said quietly, leaning closer to Cestina’s ear, “from the way you two talk, it already sounds that way.”

Cestina let out a weak sound that was not quite a groan and not quite a sigh. If she could have disappeared into the floor for a moment, she would have.

Armand, despite his daughter’s obvious embarrassment, did not retract his words.

“Then it is settled,” he said. “From this day onward, House Ludwell will regard you as Lady Cestina’s intended partner, Lord Gilbert.”

Gilbert bowed with proper manners, but inside his chest felt quietly full of joy. At the Academy he had never lacked girls who admired him from a distance, yet almost none of them were his type. Just knowing he had managed to secure even this small promise of a future with Cestina, the one girl he truly wanted, was satisfying enough on its own.

“I will not make you regret that trust,” he said.

Spoken by an Alfrost heir, those words weren’t sweet talk. To anyone listening, they already sounded like a vow.

Word of it spread through the hall in an instant. One after another, nobles turned toward them with their congratulations for the almost-formal engagement, and soon the word “congratulations” was coming from every direction. Gilbert and Cestina bowed together once more, a quiet happiness softening their faces as they returned each greeting.

And on that night, even without papers signed or dates set, Cestina Ludwell was spoken of for the first time as Gilbert Alfrost’s fiancée.

Emilia stood a little behind her father, watching her brother and Cestina surrounded by adults and soft congratulations. Her chest felt tight in a way she could not name.
