She felt happy for them, of course, yet at the same time something small and childish curled up inside her, whispering that Cestina might drift far away one day.

While the adults kept talking, Emilia edged back a step and lightly tugged at Lisoletelle’s sleeve.

“Liso,” she murmured. “If Brother and Cestina really get married in the future… what happens to us?”

Lisoletelle tilted her head.

“What do you mean, ‘what happens’?” she asked.

“Cestina will become even busier, right?” Emilia said. “She will learn how to be the next lady of the house. She will have to stand next to Brother at parties like this. If that happens… will she still sit with us in the study? Will she still sleep in my room on stormy nights? Or will she start saying, ‘I am sorry, I have duties,’ and leave?”

The words spilled out in a small rush, quieter than the music in the hall but clear enough for Lisoletelle to catch every one of them.

Lisoletelle let out a tiny breath and smiled.

“Lady Emilia,” she said, “no matter what changes around her, Lady Cestina never forgets what she holds dear. You know that better than anyone.”

Emilia bit her lip.

“But…” she started.

“Even if she becomes Lord Gilbert’s wife one day,” Lisoletelle continued, “she will still be your sword partner. She will still scold you when you try to run away from training. She will still flop onto your bed when she feels worn out. That part will not change. The place where she stands will simply grow a little wider.”

Emilia glanced back at Cestina.

Cestina stood beside Gilbert, face still bright red, bowing to yet another round of congratulations. When she raised her head again, her gaze searched the room for a moment and found Emilia.

For a brief second, Cestina’s shoulders relaxed. She smiled in the same way she always did.

The tightness inside Emilia’s chest loosened.

“…You are right,” she muttered. “If it is Cestina, she will not just vanish.”

Lisoletelle’s smile deepened.

“And if she ever tries,” Lisoletelle said, “we will simply drag her back.”

Emilia let out a small laugh at that picture.

“Then it’s fine,” she said at last. “But Cestina as my sister-in-law still feels weird… she’s my best friend.”

So she decided not to care about the title and keep her as her best friend forever. No matter how far Gilbert and Cestina moved ahead, she would keep chasing after their backs, so that when they turned around, they would still find her standing right there with them.

The next day, nothing in House Alfrost’s routine changed.

Breakfast was served at the usual time, training was held in the same courtyard, and Emilia still moved to her father’s study afterward to read through documents. Cestina and Lisoletelle appeared where they always did, at the times they always had. If someone had only watched their schedule from a distance, they would have said that House Alfrost was exactly the same as yesterday.

Only Emilia felt a little unsure of how to act.

She still called Cestina by name. She still spoke to her the way she always had. Yet each time she looked at her, a small voice whispered, Brother’s fiancée, and she had to push it aside so her smile wouldn’t turn stiff.

Later that day, when the three of them finally sat down together with no adults nearby, Lisoletelle was the first to speak.

“Cestina,” she said, lowering her voice just enough that it stayed between them, “how did that even happen?”

Cestina shifted her weight slightly on the seat, as if buying a heartbeat to gather her thoughts.

“…Last night?” she asked.

“Yes, last night,” Lisoletelle replied. “I knew Lord Gilbert was fond of you. That was obvious. But straight to engagement?” She shook her head. “I didn’t expect that at all. And you answered so calmly in front of your father… since when were things that serious?”

In the hall, it had all happened so fast—Gilbert spoke, Lord Armand answered, and Cestina replied before anyone could even breathe.

“It wasn’t without hesitation,” Cestina said.

She had already hesitated in the garden that afternoon, when Gilbert confessed and she had to decide how far she could answer without betraying herself.

“He already spoke to me in the garden that afternoon,” she went on. “Before the dinner even started. He said that when he thinks about his future, I am already in it. He said he respects me, not just as Emilia’s companion, but as someone who stands on her own judgment.”

The memory lined up clearly in her head; putting it into words again made her chest feel tight.

“I hesitated then,” Cestina said. “I told him I still feel too young to decide something so large. I told him that if he still feels the same when I am older, he can ask me again properly. I did not give him a ‘yes’ there, and I did not give him one in the hall either.”

In her mind, the real struggle had ended in the garden; what she told them now was only the shape of the answer she had forced herself to choose that afternoon.

“But he has been like that for years,” she admitted. “Always asking what I think. Always listening seriously. Always treating me as someone who belongs at his side, not just behind him. Little by little, without noticing when it started, I got used to that place.”

Hearing herself say it that plainly made her realize how long she had been letting his steadiness decide where she stood.

“So yesterday, when Father and everyone else were listening,” she said, “it probably looked like I agreed right away. I’d already been thinking that way for a long time.”

Her gaze slid briefly toward the corridor, where footsteps sometimes passed, then came back to Emilia and Lisoletelle.

“And now,” she added, “when Lord Gilbert goes off on those long trips, everything feels off.”

She went through the motions of her duties as usual, only now every quiet moment felt a little like waiting for someone who was not in the room.

Cestina began to blush, her cheeks turning bright red. She placed both hands on her cheeks in an attempt to hide her embarrassment. Upon hearing and observing this, Emilia began to adore her, finally seeing Cestina’s cute side, as she had always been so serious about everything. Emilia hugged her right away.

Cestina, still red-faced, hesitated for a moment before gently hugging Emilia back. Her usual composure was momentarily lost, and she pulled back slightly, surprised. At that moment, Lisoletelle joined them, wrapping her arms around Cestina as well, adding her warmth to the embrace.

“W-Why are you guys hugging me?” she asked, her voice faltering. Her usual calm was nowhere to be found as she tried to make sense of the sudden affection. Emilia’s smile softened as she gently pulled Cestina back into the hug.

“Because I finally see your cute side,” she said with a laugh, her tone light and teasing. Cestina’s eyes widened as the words settled in. She had always been so serious, so proper, that the idea of being seen as cute was a concept she’d never fully grasped. Her cheeks flushed deeper at the realization.

“I see it too,” Lisoletelle said softly, her voice full of affection. “Cestina, you're so cute.”

“I… cute?” she repeated, almost as if she couldn’t believe it.

Emilia nodded, pulling back slightly to look at her. “Yes, Cestina, you’re always so serious. But now I see it. You have your cute moments too.”

Cestina stood there, stunned for a moment, before a small, shy smile tugged at the corner of her lips. She couldn’t help but feel a flutter in her chest. The words were unexpected, but they warmed her in a way she hadn’t anticipated.

Emilia pulled back slightly, her arms still around Cestina, and smiled.

“No matter what happens, we’ll be there for each other, okay? Whether you’re by my side as a friend or... as family.”

Cestina nodded, the words settling deep within her. It was a promise, and in that moment, she knew she wasn’t alone. The future, no matter how uncertain, now felt like something she could face with confidence, knowing Emilia was there with her every step of the way.

### Chapter 14: 10 Part 4 - Noble's Life

#### Scene 1

Three years later, the way House Alfrost worked had changed more than the faces inside it.

Emilia was fifteen now. Gilbert had already passed into his twenties. In that time, the work that used to stop at Caelen’s desk had been split between them in clear lines.

Gilbert was now treated as Caelen’s second-in-command and as the next head of the family in everything but name. Most of the time, he started his day in the office wing of the mansion, going through the stack of reports that arrived from their own lands and from the branch families. Requests for escorts, disputes over land borders, lists of collected taxes, invitations from other nobles—clerks sorted everything by type and urgency before setting it in front of him. Gilbert checked what could be approved as it was, what needed more information, and what had to be carried up to Caelen because it touched on royal policy or the balance between noble factions.

When the paperwork thinned, his work moved out of the office and into noble society. On some days, he rode out to attend a coming-of-age ceremony or a promotion celebration in another house’s hall. On others, he stood in for Caelen at a gala dinner in the capital, taking the main family’s place at the table and exchanging measured words with lords and ladies who watched Alfrost’s movements very closely. At smaller, quieter gatherings, he joined talks about patrol routes, joint funding for road repairs, or security for trade caravans that crossed through several territories at once. Wherever Caelen could not appear in person, Gilbert became the one other nobles spoke to first, and the one they measured as the future of the house.

Caelen himself spent most of his days at the royal palace. As one of Althania’s strategic ministers, he now dealt with matters that did not fit into a single noble estate: troop deployments on the borders, negotiations with the Western Church, the budget for the Royal Academy, and reports about monster activity near key trade routes. His desk there was piled with maps and sealed packets from every corner of the kingdom. Only late at night did he return to the mansion, where the steward prepared a thinner, filtered stack of papers—cases Gilbert had set aside because they needed Caelen’s direct decision or because they brushed up against royal politics.

Emilia’s place sat between those two.

The lessons she had endured in Caelen’s office were no longer just exercises. Simple internal matters were now sent directly to her: small repairs within the estate, routine spending for supplies, minor adjustments to tax collection that followed already established rules. Clerks brought her slim bundles of documents with clear categories, and she checked whether the numbers matched the previous records, whether the reasons were properly written, and whether the total stayed within the limits Caelen and Gilbert had already set. If everything lined up, she signed and passed them on to be carried out. If something felt off— an amount that rose too quickly, a reason that was too vague—she marked it and moved it to Gilbert’s side of the desk.

Anything that involved negotiation between families, changes to long-standing contracts, or decisions that could shift how other nobles viewed Alfrost did not reach her at all. Those went straight into Gilbert’s hands, and from Gilbert, the heaviest ones were held back for Caelen. In this way, the work inside the house moved

in three layers: staff and clerks at the bottom doing the sorting, Emilia handling the simple and clear requests, Gilbert carrying the main load of noble duties, and Caelen stepping in only when it touched the kingdom itself.

Seen from outside, the Alfrost household looked unusually efficient for a house led by a single parent. Servants knew where to send each problem. Branch families knew that if they wrote a proper report, they would get a timely and reasonable answer. Requests did not pile up in the corridors; decisions went out almost as fast as new letters arrived.

Even so, mistakes still happened. A new clerk once misfiled a set of patrol reports after accepting a “thank- you gift” from a nervous village representative who wanted his case read first. The gift itself was harmless— dried fruit from the village—but the favor was not. The missing reports delayed a patrol rotation by a day, and when Gilbert found out why, the clerk was removed from office work and reassigned to field duty under the captain of the guard. The rest of the staff understood the message without needing it written down.

Part of it was simply talent. Caelen had always been sharp. Gilbert had grown into his role with a steady hand. Emilia, though still in training, absorbed new patterns in the work quickly and made fewer mistakes with each passing month. Between the three of them, the house was effectively run by people who treated complex matters like routine tasks.

Caelen was fully aware of that.

From the palace, he heard the way other nobles spoke about his children. At home, he saw how smoothly the mansion now operated even on days when he was barely present. It was not something he said out loud at council meetings, but when he looked over the reports that had passed through Gilbert and Emilia before reaching him, there was a quiet satisfaction in the way he set his seal to the final page. Even as a single father, he had managed to build a family that could stand beside him and keep the Alfrost name steady while he moved pieces on the kingdom’s board.

And on one of those “ordinary” days, with work flowing through its usual paths and everyone in their usual places, the next small shift in their lives began.

Royal Academy entrance exams were now close enough that even the servants had started counting the days.

For Emilia, however, her daily life had not changed much. She still woke early, took breakfast with her family, and went out to the courtyard for her usual training. Sword and magic practice came first, as always. The content had become heavier over the years, but the flow itself remained the same. After that, she moved to the office and faced the documents that now came to her instead of going straight to Caelen.

On good days, the pile in front of her stayed small. Today was one of those days.

Emilia worked through the documents in order, pressing her seal down one sheet after another until only the last page was left. She checked the total written at the bottom, compared it with the note she had made earlier, then set her seal to the corner. She straightened the thin bundle with both hands and passed it to

the clerk waiting by the door. He stepped forward, received it with a bow, and left the office with his usual quiet steps.

Emilia did not stand up right away. Her hands rested on the now-empty part of the desk. The faint smell of ink and dried paper lingered in the air. Light from the tall window fell across the shelves and stopped just short of her fingertips.

‘Royal Academy…’

Lately, she had heard those words again and again. They showed up in the schedules the steward prepared, in tutors’ small side comments, and in the letters Caelen received from the palace. Everyone around her spoke as if her enrollment was already decided. No one had asked what she thought about it.

‘I can already fight and help with Father’s work. Do I really need the Academy on top of that?’

She had pushed that question aside while she worked. Now that the desk was clear, it was the only thing left in her mind.

After gathering the document she had been checking and that now needed Gilbert’s approval, she left the room. The corridor outside was the same as always—polished stone floor, portraits of ancestors along the wall, windows looking down on the inner courtyard where guards passed in formation. A few servants crossed paths with her, each giving a small bow before moving on to their tasks.

Emilia headed toward the upper floor where Caelen’s private office and Gilbert’s room were located.

Gilbert’s door was half-open. That alone told her he was inside and working.

She stopped at the doorway and peeked in. Gilbert sat at his desk, sleeves slightly rolled, with papers arranged in neat stacks around his hands. Letters from branch families were piled on one side, copied palace reports on the other, and a thinner bundle bearing Caelen’s seal lay closest to him. An untouched cup of tea rested at the corner of the desk, its surface already cooled.

“Brother,” Emilia called.

Gilbert looked up from the document and set it aside, turning his chair toward her.

Emilia stepped into the room and closed the door behind her.

The desk was crowded with reports. His sword stood against the wall within reach, and his old Academy cloak hung over the back of a chair with the crest turned outward. Emilia’s eyes stopped on that crest for a moment.

“About the Royal Academy,” Emilia said. “There’s something I want to ask.”

She crossed the room and stopped in front of his desk. The memo sheets from the office were still in her hands, though she was no longer thinking about them.

“Is it really that important for me to attend?” she asked.

The way she said it didn’t feel right, so she put it into clearer words.

“Is the Royal Academy really that important for me?” she asked. “I already train every morning, and I’m helping with Father’s paperwork. It doesn’t feel like I’m wasting my days here.”

For her, that was all there was to it. She worked, she can fight, and she could see the results in front of her.

Gilbert said nothing at first. He watched her for a moment, then let his gaze slide toward the window where the light from the capital reached the inner wall, before turning back to her.

To him, the Academy was not just a building. It was training fields lined with students, lecture rooms packed with nobles’ children, and corridors where future officers and household heads had brushed past one another for years. All of that sat behind his eyes when he looked at his little sister, who had only seen the inside of Alfrost and the nearby city.

“The Academy is not only a place to improve magic and swordsmanship,” Gilbert said. “You are not being sent there just to sharpen your skills.”

Gilbert watched her for a moment, weighing his words.

“Emilia,” he said, “the Academy is where you face people who don’t already know how to treat you. Heirs from other houses, merchants’ children, invited students from far-off towns—some stronger than you, some weaker. Some will stare at the Alfrost crest and try to stand close. Some will test you on purpose. Some won’t care who your father is at all. You’ll have to decide for yourself who you trust, who you treat as a rival, and who you refuse to follow, no matter how high their rank is.”

The courtyard could teach her how to protect herself. Caelen’s office could teach her how to help family affairs. Neither could teach her what to do when the person across from her smiled, bowed politely, and still pushed in a direction she did not like.

The edge of the document sheets bit into her fingers once before she eased her grip.

“There are also things you will only hear there,” Gilbert continued. “Law as the royal courts actually use it. How the kingdom’s land and money are laid out. History for people who have to decide what to protect and what to give up. You’ll listen to priests, envoys, and nobles from other houses talk about the kingdom—and about Alfrost—when they think they’re only speaking to students. One day you’ll be the one sitting on this side of a desk, signing papers that send people moving. It’s better to make your first mistakes while they only cost marks and pride, not villages and lives.”

Emilia lowered her eyes to her hands.

She was confident in her swordsmanship, her magic, and her paperwork, but all of it still belonged only to Alfrost.

‘I really only know what Father teaches me here,’ she thought.

“If you stay only in this house,” Gilbert said at last, “you’ll always lean on Father, on me, on Cestina and Liso. That isn’t wrong, but your world will stop at us. At the Academy, you’ll meet people who choose to stand with you for their own reasons—and people who stand across from you. Once you carry the Alfrost name in front of them, you’ll need to know how to face both.”

Emilia lowered her eyes and drew in a slow breath before raising her head again.

She had wanted him to say that staying here was enough—that if she kept training in the yard and working in Caelen’s office, she could stand beside them without going anywhere else. Instead, his words had pointed to people and places she had never once faced herself.

‘If I stay here, I’ll be the only one who doesn’t understand,’ she thought.

“…I understand,” Emilia said.

Emilia looked down again. Until now, every step toward the Academy had been written into the household plans by someone else. When she raised her head, she had already decided what to answer.

“If the Academy is where all those people gather,” she went on, “then I should go. If I don’t, I won’t be able to keep up when you and Father talk about the kingdom.”

Once she put it into words, the question stopped feeling like someone else’s schedule and turned into a choice she had made herself.

Across the desk, Gilbert let go of the arguments he had been lining up in case she refused. He would not need them.

“Then go,” he said. “Look carefully while you’re there, and bring what you learn back home.”

He did not add anything more. That was his way of accepting her answer.

Only then did Emilia notice how hard she had been holding the papers. The top edge was creased where her fingers had dug into it.

Going to the Royal Academy was no longer just a line on the household plans. It had become something she herself had said she would do, with the sword and magic she had built here and the lessons from Caelen’s desk behind her. What waited past the Academy gates, she would find out only when she stood there.

Emilia shifted the memo sheets in her hands and finally looked down at them properly.

“…Ah.”

The top page was not just her notes. It was a formal report, its title line clearly marked: a request to adjust several trade routes, with a note that it required Gilbert’s decision before the reply could be sent. The corner near the seal had a faint bend where her thumb had been pressing into it the entire time.

“You brought work with you?” Gilbert asked. “And tried to strangle it in front of me?”

Emilia set the report on his desk, a little more carefully this time.

“I picked it up on the way here,” she said. “It was on the stack that needed your approval. I must have been holding it since I came in.”

Gilbert picked up the report, gave the first page a quick look, then glanced at the creased edge and let out a quiet, amused breath.

“It’s a one-way report,” he said. “We only need it long enough to read it and send a reply, and then it goes into the archive. As long as the ink is still on the page. But next time, try not to fight the paper before the merchants do.”

“It’s not like I was doing it on purpose,” Emilia said.

“Of course,” Gilbert replied. “Sit down. You’ve been squeezing it since you came in—what’s wrong with it?”

Before Emilia could pull out the nearby chair, the door opened without a knock.

“Lord Gilbert, do you have a moment—”

Cestina stepped inside as naturally as ever, then stopped when she saw Emilia standing by the desk.

“…Lady Emilia,” she said. “I’m sorry. I should have knocked.”

“It’s fine,” Emilia said at once. “I don’t mind. Especially from you.”

Cestina closed the door behind her and came in properly.

“I didn’t mean to interrupt,” she said. “If you’re in the middle of something important, I can wait outside.”

“We’re just looking at a trade report,” Gilbert said. “Nothing that will explode if it waits a few breaths.”

Cestina nodded and stayed near the side of the desk. She mentioned how noisy the corridors had been that morning and how the servants were running around more than usual, It was the kind of small talk she used when she was stalling before a request.

“Did you need something from brother?” Emilia asked.

Cestina’s gaze flicked toward her, then away.

“…It can wait until you’re done, Lady Emilia,” she said. “Your discussion with Lord Gilbert is more important than what I came for.”

Gilbert watched that small exchange. He understood perfectly well that Cestina had come to take him out for lunch, but for now he turned back to Emilia.

“You said it was a trade report that needs my decision,” he reminded her. “What’s wrong with it?”

Emilia focused on the papers again and pulled a folded memo from between them.

“I’ve checked seventeen logistics reports tied to this request,” she said. “Most of the proposed routes follow the usual paths. But two of them use roads I didn’t recognize when I compared them to the map.”

Gilbert took the memo from her hand.

“Two?” he asked.

“These,” Emilia said, pointing out the lines she had copied. “They cut through areas that aren’t listed as standard routes. And there were recent reports of bandits and monster sightings along those stretches. Patrols have been sent out, but I don’t know how safe it really is.”

Gilbert opened the attached map, spread it on the desk, and matched the notes to the drawn lines.

“The companies behind these requests are large and well-known,” he said after checking the names. “They’ve worked with us and with the crown for years.”

“So they wouldn’t choose carelessly?” Emilia said.

“Probably not,” Gilbert agreed. “If they’re using unfamiliar paths, they might have a reason. Merchants like these sometimes keep a route that only insiders use—a way they’ve tested quietly, without putting it on the common charts.”

He tapped one of the marked lines with his finger.

“But that doesn’t erase the bandit reports,” he added. “You’re worried that if we approve this without a word, it will look as if we ignored them.”

“Yes,” Emilia said. “If something happens, the first question will be whether Alfrost read the reports properly.”

“Then don’t approve it as if nothing is different,” Gilbert said. “Approve the request, but add a condition in the reply.”

“A condition?” Emilia asked.

“Write that House Alfrost agrees to their route adjustments,” Gilbert said. “At the same time, request—no, in this case, require—that caravans using these paths coordinate with us for a guard escort, at least for the next season. That way everyone understands we saw the risk and responded to it.”

Emilia thought about his wording for a moment and nodded.

“So we grant it,” she said, “but write that they have to ask for an escort and tell us when their wagons will be on the road.”

“Exactly,” Gilbert said. “If bandit or monster reports rise again in those areas, we’ll already be watching. If the season passes quietly, we can loosen the condition in the next term.”

Emilia gathered the report back into a neat stack.

“I’ll have the clerk draft it that way,” she said. “I’ll check the letter before it’s sealed.”

“Good,” Gilbert said. “And try not to leave your fingerprints in the margin this time.”

Emilia gave him a flat look that needed no explanation. Cestina’s mouth curved very slightly, as if she had been following the exchange more closely than she let on.

“With that done,” Gilbert went on, leaning back a little, “I’m hungry.”

At that, Cestina’s posture changed by just a fraction. Her shoulders loosened, and the hand that had been hovering near her sleeve finally settled at her side. Emilia noticed the shift.

Gilbert glanced her way, then at Cestina.

“Come to think of it,” he said, “I think the real reason Cestina came here was to ask me out to lunch date. Right, Cestina?”

Cestina froze.

Her eyes widened, and a faint color rose at the edges of her cheeks.

“Lord Gilbert,” she said. “You didn’t have to say it like that.”

“You came at the same time you always do,” Gilbert replied. “If it was about reports, you would have brought a file.”

Emilia blinked.

“So that’s why you disappear around midday so often,” she said. “I thought it was more work from the palace.”

Gilbert gave her a noncommittal look that admitted enough without saying it outright. Cestina looked briefly as if she wanted to deny everything on the spot, then settled for a slower answer.

“It’s just lunch,” she said. “If no one reminds you to eat, you don’t leave your desk at all.”

“Of course,” Gilbert said calmly.

Since Emilia was already there, the unspoken part of Cestina’s visit had nowhere else to go.

“…If you’re free as well, Lady Emilia,” Cestina said at last, turning toward her, “would you like to come with us? We weren’t planning anything special—just a short lunch outside before returning.”

Emilia tilted her head.

“You’re sure?” she asked. “I don’t want to disturb your date.”

“It’s not a date,” Cestina said at once. “It’s really just lunch. If you don’t come, I’ll only be listening to Lord Gilbert complain about reports in a different room.”

“That sounds accurate,” Gilbert said.

Emilia looked from one to the other.

“In that case,” she said, “I’ll come. I need to drop this report at the office and tell them how to write the reply. I’ll meet you both at the entrance.”

“Good,” Gilbert said, rising from his chair. “If we stay here much longer, someone will find another stack of work for us.”

Cestina let out a small breath that sounded closer to relief than annoyance.

“I’ll wait downstairs,” she said. “Lady Emilia, please don’t let him sit back down at the desk on the way out.”

“I’ll make sure he doesn’t,” Emilia said.

Cestina gave a small nod and left the office first, closing the door softly behind her.

Emilia watched the door for a moment, then turned back to Gilbert.

“Brother,” she said, “how is Cestina, really?”

Gilbert looked at her, a little surprised by the question.

“Why do you ask?” he said.

“Lately she talks to me like usual,” Emilia replied, “but sometimes she stops in the middle of a subject and changes it. It feels like there’s something she doesn’t want to say yet. Especially when the topic is… you.”

For Emilia, that was the part she could not read. Cestina had always shared her thoughts with her, so the parts she was hiding stood out all the more.

Gilbert leaned back slightly in his chair.

“As you can see, Cestina is naturally shy,” he said. “She wants to take proper care of me, but she doesn’t always want to show it in front of other people. Even if that ‘other person’ is you.”

“So she’s holding back on purpose?” Emilia asked.

“In her own way,” Gilbert said. “If she says too much, she’ll only embarrass herself and spend the rest of the day thinking about it.”

Emilia thought back to how Cestina had reacted earlier, flustered just from the word “lunch”.

“…Honestly,” Emilia said, “for someone like you, who never stops teasing people, Cestina might be the perfect match.”

Gilbert let out a short sound that was half a laugh.

“You’re saying that as my sister,” he said. “But you’re not wrong.”

He paused for a moment, then added:

“She was even worse four months ago, when I came back late from Lowaka.”

“Lowaka?” Emilia repeated. “The trip for that diplomatic meeting?”

“Yes,” Gilbert said. “On the way back, the roads were covered in snow. A storm came in, and the carriage had to stop. We moved when we could, camped when we couldn’t, and stayed in whatever village would take us in. By the time the roads cleared properly, I was about a week late.”

He spoke about it plainly, as if it had only been a minor delay in his schedule.

“When I finally returned,” he went on, “Cestina looked calm enough in front of the others. She only asked how the talks went and whether the road conditions would affect trade. But when we were alone, she started crying, grabbed my coat, and refused to let go for a while.”

Emilia’s eyes widened.

“Cestina did that?” she asked. “I can’t imagine her doing something like that.”

“She tried to stop halfway,” Gilbert said. “I told her we’re Alfrost, and a little snow won’t kill us so easily. It didn’t help. She knew that already. She worried anyway.”

Emilia pictured Cestina clinging to Gilbert like that and failing to hold back her tears. It was so far from the orderly, composed maid she saw every day that she needed a moment to fit both images together.

“…That really sounds like her,” Emilia said at last.

“And that’s exactly how she is,” Gilbert replied. “She’ll act as if she’s fine, right up until she isn’t.”

Emilia let that sink in for a moment.

“I’ll keep that in mind,” she said. “If she suddenly runs out of composure one day, I’ll pretend I never saw it.”

“That would help,” Gilbert said. “She’d probably appreciate that more than anything you could say.”

With that, Gilbert rose from his chair and reached for the sword resting near the wall. Emilia adjusted the grip on the report she still had to return to the office, and together they headed out of the room toward the entrance, where Cestina was waiting.

The carriage was waiting at the entrance, and the three of them climbed inside as if they had done this a hundred times before. The driver glanced back through the small window.

“Same place as usual, my lord?” he asked. “Or somewhere new today?”

Since Emilia was with them, Cestina answered before Gilbert could.

“Let’s go to that small place near the west market,” she said. “The one with the beef steak. Lady Emilia likes meat.”

Emilia blinked, then nodded.

“I don’t mind,” she said. “I’m just tagging along today anyway.”

For her, it was enough that they had invited her. The fact that Cestina had immediately picked a place based on what Emilia liked made it feel less like she was just an extra.

The carriage rolled out of the gate. Through the window, Emilia watched the familiar streets pass by. Cestina exchanged a few words with Gilbert about the morning’s work and the servants’ schedule, slipping easily between topics the way someone long used to the household would. She walked into Gilbert’s office without knocking, spoke to the staff as if she had always been there, and now she was the one choosing their restaurant.

‘Once she really becomes my sister,’ Emilia thought, ‘the house will probably be even more fun.’

She must have let that thought reach her face, because Gilbert caught her eye and gave her a small, knowing smile. He didn’t say anything, but it was clear he had guessed what direction her thoughts had gone.

The restaurant Cestina had chosen was not especially large. The outside was plain, and the inside was crowded with people in work clothes, the clatter of plates and low voices spilling out as soon as the door opened. Even so, the owner hurried over when he saw them and led them to a quiet room at the back, separated from the main area by a sliding door.

“They keep a section at the back ready for nobles or special guests,” Cestina explained as they sat. “The seats and tables are nicer here, but the food comes from the same kitchen.”

Emilia took her seat and glanced toward the main hall through the small gap in the door. The noise from outside reached them only as a softer mix of sound.

When the food arrived, the beef steak on Emilia’s plate was cooked just the way she liked it. The surface was seared, the inside still tender, and the sauce soaked lightly into the vegetables at the side.

“This is really good,” she said after the first bite. “Why haven’t you brought me here before now?”

Gilbert answered before Cestina could.

“She has,” he said. “Three times. You just don’t remember, because you were too busy attacking the plate.”

Emilia stared at him.

“Three times,” Emilia said. “Wow, three times… it’s crazy I forgot all of that.”

“Apparently so,” Gilbert said. “But you see, Cestina only brings someone to this place if they’re special.”

Emilia frowned and turned to Cestina at once. For her, having this place called “special” wasn’t something to let slide without hearing Cestina’s own answer.

“Is that true???!!” she asked.

Cestina shook her head a little too quickly.

“It’s really not like that,” she said. “I was just worried you might not like a crowded place, Lady Emilia. The entrance is noisy, and the tables outside are close together.”

“I don’t mind,” Emilia said. “If the food is good, I don’t care how noisy it is.”

Cestina looked at her for a moment, then let out a small breath.

“…All right,” she said. “If you and Liso want to come to places like this, tell me. I’ll bring you whenever we have time.”

Emilia nodded, satisfied.

“I’ll remember that,” she said. “Don’t regret saying it later.”

Gilbert watched the exchange with a faint smile and cut another piece from his own steak. For him, the scene only confirmed what he had told Emilia earlier: Cestina was already moving as if she belonged in the family; the rest was only a matter of time.

Not long after, they finished their meal and returned to the mansion. There was still leftover work waiting in the office, but as Emilia picked up her pen again, the knot of unease around the Royal Academy felt lighter. The entry day was only a few days away now, and for the first time, it no longer felt like a path someone else had drawn for her alone.

—

The next morning, Emilia headed to the training yard at the same hour as always. Julian was already there, wooden practice sword resting against his shoulder.

“So,” Julian said, once they had finished their first set of swings, “the Academy’s almost here.”

Emilia adjusted her stance and raised her sword again.

“Father and Brother keep saying that,” she replied. “It still just feels like tomorrow’s training.”

Julian stepped in to correct her guard, then fell back.

“For you, this is probably the last ‘tomorrow’s training’ I’ll be doing in the mornings,” he said. “Once you go to the Academy, your days will be in the academyt”

Emilia’s hands tightened slightly on the hilt. This part, at least, was easy to understand: the routine she knew would change.

“Don’t overthink it,” Julian added. “You don’t need to carry the whole kingdom on your shoulders from the first day. Just focus on yourself and what’s in front of you.”

He said it as someone who had seen plenty of noble children try to act like full-fledged knights the moment they stepped through the Academy gates, only to exhaust themselves for nothing.

“Besides,” he went on, “I serve there as an instructor too. If something happens, you can come to me. As long as it doesn’t break the rules, I’ll help.”

“Ok” she replied.

Emilia answered with a firm nod and finished the session as she always did, but now each swing felt a little like a farewell to these morning drills.

—

Her next lesson was with Lady Vespera.

The magic room was quiet, the usual practice targets stacked neatly to one side. There were no new spells to learn that day; the patterns of Alfrost’s ice magic had already been passed on, and Vespera was not a front-line combat mage to begin with.

“You’ve taken in most of what I can teach you,” Vespera said, watching Emilia run through a final sequence. “From here on, your growth will depend on how you use it yourself.”

Emilia let the last shards of ice vanish and turned to her.

“Then today is the last lesson?” she asked.

“The last formal one,” Vespera replied. “If you want to ask something later, my door is still in this house.”

She placed a hand lightly on the open grimoire beside her, then closed it.

“There is one thing I want you to keep in mind,” she said. “If the day comes when you must use your ice in a real fight to protect yourself, never reveal everything from the start.”

Emilia listened without interrupting. This was not about practice anymore.

“Magic that can end a fight quickly is valuable,” Vespera continued. “But if you show your full power immediately, a clever opponent will adapt, or flee and prepare a counter the next time. First, see how they move. Test their reach, their speed, their nerve. Keep something in reserve until you know what you are facing.”

For her, that was the difference between playing with power and surviving with it.

“I understand,” Emilia said.

“And stay sharp,” Vespera added. “Pride makes people careless. I’d rather you be bored than dead.”

Emilia stored those words alongside the spell structures in her mind and left the room with the weight of that “if” settled firmly beside her new magic.

—

During work that day, Emilia noticed the pile of documents on her desk was thinner than usual.

She finished one set, reached for the next, and found only a few pages waiting. After checking the stamps twice, she raised her head toward the clerk standing near the door.

“Is this all for today?” she asked. “There should be more internal requests at this time of month.”

The clerk bowed.

“Yes, Lady Emilia,” he said. “By Lord Caelen’s instruction, matters that can be postponed are being held back. With the Royal Academy entrance this week, you are to focus on that first.”

Emilia looked at the modest stack and understood immediately. It was not that the house had suddenly grown quiet; it was that the work had been redirected away from her.

“I see,” she said. “Then I’ll finish these properly.”

She did so in less than half the time her usual load required, checked the last figures, and handed the completed documents back. With nothing else waiting, she allowed herself to rest in her chair for a while, eyes wandering over the familiar shelves and window instead of another set of reports.

Right on time, there was a light knock, followed by the door opening just far enough to admit Lisoletelle.

“I’m coming in,” Liso said. “Are you buried under paper yet?”

“Not today,” Emilia said. “Father had most of it held back.”

Liso stepped inside with her usual easy pace and dropped into the chair opposite Emilia.

“Good, then” Liso said. “Because if you start reading during our conversation again, I really will sulk.”

Emilia hesitated for only a moment before bringing up what had been circling in her thoughts.

“The entrance exam is almost here,” she said. “Are you ready?”

Liso made a face on purpose.

“Ready to puke, maybe,” she said. “Every time I think about the written part, my stomach complains.”

Emilia couldn’t help letting out a small breath of amusement.

“You’ve been studying,” Emilia said. “I know you have.”

“I did,” Liso replied. “That’s why thinking about it makes me want to puke. If they ask about something I forgot, it’ll be even worse.”

Without noticing it, the two of them kept picking apart the topic: what kind of practical tests there might be, whether the examiners would be strict about noble etiquette, which other houses’ children they were likely to see. The light outside shifted slowly from afternoon brightness toward dusk.

Only when the sky beyond the window had turned orange did Liso stand up.

“I should go back,” she said. “If I stay out any longer, they’ll start teasing me that I’m hiding the exam results already.”

Emilia walked her to the corridor, and Liso headed toward the main entrance with a small wave. The room felt quieter after she left, but less heavy than it had that morning.

—

The next day, the mansion felt different.

There was no call to the courtyard at dawn, no stack of documents waiting in her usual office. The staff greeted her as always, but none of them handed her anything to sign. For once, her schedule was almost empty.

Emilia walked through the halls with no particular destination. Sunlight fell across the polished stone, and the sound of distant footsteps echoed back softly instead of being swallowed by the usual rush of work.

She stepped out into the garden.

Among the trimmed hedges and late-season flowers, she spotted Cestina sitting on a bench, a book open in her hands. Cestina was reading so intently that she did not notice Emilia until she was almost in front of her.

“You really fit into this household already,” Emilia said.

Cestina started slightly and closed the book halfway.

“Lady Emilia,” she said. “I’m sorry—I didn’t see you there.”

Instead of answering Emilia’s comment directly, she retreated to the safest explanation at hand: the book and the exam.

“It’s about agriculture,” Cestina said. “Production methods, soil management, crop rotation. There will be questions on it in the Royal Academy exam.”

“Just from the title, it sounds boring,” Emilia said. “Even if I’ve already studied that part.”

Gilbert had told her more than once that the written exam would not decide everything. The Academy valued practical skill and potential more than neat answers on paper, so she had treated those subjects as something to review rather than worry about.

“I’m not reading it only for the exam,” Cestina said. “If I’m going to help manage this house, I should understand how the land works too. Food doesn’t appear in the pantry by itself.”

For her, knowing how the fields were treated and how harvests were planned was another way of taking care of the family.

Emilia let that answer sit for a moment. It matched what she had seen from Cestina in small ways: the way she adjusted the kitchen schedule when unexpected guests arrived, or how she paid attention to which suppliers the steward favored.

“Hoo..” Emilia humming in agreement.

She looked toward the mansion, trying to change of atmosphere.

“I was thinking of visiting Princess Claire’s mansion,” she went on. “It’s been a while since I last went. Will you come with me?”

There was no hesitation in Cestina’s answer.

“Of course,” Cestina said. “If you are going to see Her Highness, I should accompany you.”

Emilia nodded once.

“I’ll tell the maids and the guards,” she said. “If Liso comes looking for me, they can say I went to Princess Claire’s mansion with you.”

With that settled, Emilia and Cestina headed out together, leaving the quiet mansion behind them for the road to Claire’s estate.

When they arrived at Claire’s mansion, the carriage passed through the front gate and stopped at the familiar entrance. The doors opened from inside, and Claire herself came to greet them.

“Emilia,” Claire said, letting out a small, relieved smile. “It’s been a while.”

Emilia stepped forward.

“I’ve been busy lately,” she said. “Today is the first time in a while I’ve actually had the freedom to come.”

Claire nodded as if that matched exactly what she had imagined, then turned to the maid standing just behind Emilia.

“Cestina,” she said. “You’re as beautiful as ever.”

Cestina’s expression softened for a moment, but she answered with proper formality. They were still in the entrance hall, with servants nearby and guards at their posts.

“You are too kind, Your Highness,” Cestina replied with a graceful curtsey. “Thank you for receiving us.”

After a few more simple words, Claire led them through the corridor toward the central garden.

They took their usual seats there, around the table set near the fountain. It was the same place they had always used when Emilia came to visit: a spot where they could talk without being completely cut off from

the mansion. Servants brought tea and light snacks, then withdrew. They spoke about small things at first— how the days had been in Alfrost, what the atmosphere in the palace was like this week—and let the time pass while the sun moved overhead. Later in the evening, they planned to move to Claire’s room as they always did, once the halls grew quieter.

Before long, another carriage arrived, and Lisoletelle came hurrying into the garden.

“Hi,” Liso said as she took a seat.

With that, the four of them were finally together again.

The Royal Academy entrance came up almost immediately, as if the topic had been waiting for them.

“So, about the exam—” Claire began.

“Can we not?” Liso cut in at once. “If I hear that word again today, I really will go home.”

The others exchanged a brief look and let the subject drop. There was no point dragging the exam into the one place they had chosen not to think about it.

From there, the talk turned to safer ground: small incidents in their houses, funny mistakes made by servants, the latest gossip about other nobles’ children. The details shifted from one topic to the next without any clear line between them. At some point, as the sky began to darken, they moved indoors to Claire’s room, just as planned. The table changed, the chairs changed, but the flow of conversation did not.

One story about something that had happened last year led to a memory from when they were younger, which then turned into a complaint about current duties, which then circled back to a promise to meet again after the exam. Each time a topic seemed to end, another one came up naturally, pulled out by a half- remembered detail or a casual “oh, that reminds me”.

By the time night had settled fully around the mansion, it felt as if there was no such thing as running out of things to say. Their voices rose and fell, sometimes bright, sometimes quieter, but never reaching a true stop. It was the same as it had always been between them: four people sharing the same space, letting the hours pass as if the next day’s worries were still far away.

By the time they finally decided to sleep, it was already late. The entrance exam was still waiting a few days ahead, but that day had belonged only to the four of them.

### Chapter 15: 11: What It Takes

#### Scene 1

Dead mana lay heavy in the deepest hall of the Threshold Vault.

The Threshold Vault was a place built for monsters who acted like strategists. No sound leaked in or out; the stone swallowed it before it could travel. The torches along the walls burned with colorless flame, not for light but as a visible sign of the wards carved into every surface. The black crystal at the center of the hall was less a decoration and more a seal and a focus, tying the place to other points in the world. Around it, seven high-backed seats formed a broken circle.

Those seats existed for the Seven Chaos Bringers. Only three were occupied.

"…compressing a century into one move," a low voice said. "You always did have a talent for bad manners, Kaer."

The woman on the left spoke first. She sat with one leg crossed over the other, gloved hands resting neatly on the armrests, as if this were a formal report and not a discussion about ruining a country. A narrow, smooth mask hid her face, marked only by a single downward notch where the mouth should have been. White cloth trimmed in pale grey wrapped her frame, with a small sigil at the shoulder: a circle cut cleanly in two.

Serem was the one who usually preferred long plans and clean records. When she called something “bad manners”, she meant that it ruined structures she had spent years setting up.

Opposite her, a hound-shaped mask turned slightly, its long jaw and narrow eye sockets catching the flat light.

"Bad manners?" the rougher voice answered. "He’s talking about turning an entire country into kindling just to see if the spark takes. That’s past ‘manners’, Serem."

Blunt claws tapped once against the armrest. Where the cloak parted at the neck, dark fur showed, moving with each slow breath. Gharum did not bother with subtlety. He was the one who handled direct destruction when they needed it, and his sense for risk came from long practice breaking armies in the open.

Gharum had always preferred open ground to stone halls. Even sitting, he carried himself like someone measuring where to move next if the floor turned into a battlefield.

Between them, the third figure leaned back in his chair, cloak the color of dried blood pooling around the legs. His bone-white mask was smooth, marked only by seven small notches along the edge and a single cut running from brow to chin.

Kaer watched them both for a moment before speaking. Among the Seven, he was the one who treated countries as pieces. For him, the question was never whether something was too large to risk, only whether using it once would move them closer to their shared goal.

"You say ‘country’," he replied, "as if it were not already busy tearing itself apart without my help."

His tone was almost bored. The other two knew he had been watching that same country for years, waiting for the right crack.

They all wanted the same thing in the end. After the Demon Lord was defeated by the Heroes of the past expedition team, it had not truly been destroyed. Its power scattered across time and dimensions, bound to conditions that could only be fulfilled through multiple, coordinated schemes. The three in this hall knew that better than anyone; each of them had built their own work around those scattered pieces. Their shared goal was simple: bring that power together again and raise a true Demon Lord from it.

Serem did not use the word “gambit” for show. To her, it meant abandoning the habit of treating each plan as a separate, low-risk operation and staking several years of work on a single move that could not be undone.

"Before, you were content to work slowly," she said. "Each of us handled our own part in different places. You never tried to tie several of those conditions into one event. Now you call it a gambit."

She was stating the change directly. Until now, their schemes had been planned for decades, even centuries, each one designed to satisfy a single requirement of the Demon Lord’s scattered power. Kaer was the only one proposing to make one incident in one kingdom carry several of those requirements at once.

Gharum’s voice lost any hint of amusement.

"So that’s it," he said. "You’re willing to gamble one kingdom’s worth of people just to speed those conditions along."

Gharum had destroyed nations himself, but always as the last step in breaking an enemy’s army or will. Kaer was different. To him, a country was a pool of lives that could be spent all at once if it pushed the Demon Lord’s revival forward.

In his view, staking an entire kingdom at once was precisely what made the plan elegant.

"They’ll die in pieces if we leave them alone," he said. "Famines, border wars, purges in the capital. If we use them now, the same deaths happen in a shape that actually serves us."

In Kaer’s mind, the number was never the problem. The only question was whether those deaths moved them any closer to raising a true Demon Lord.

"You said this plan needs a center," she said. "One point where our prepared conditions and the fighting overlap."

She was no longer talking about the kingdom itself, but about the single weight he meant to drop—the thing heavy enough to tug everything else they had set up out of its current orbit.

"There is a primordial dragon sealed on the northern frontier," Kaer said.

He spoke as if he were reading from a report. The seal had been in place longer than the kingdom’s current royal line, and every year it consumed magicians, soldiers, and coin just to keep the creature from stirring.

Gharum’s claws went still on the armrest.

"Most countries collapse before they can hold something like that," he said.

He had seen records of lesser calamities breaking loose. Those files were short and blunt: lost forts, burned supply towns, chains of command that never recovered.

Serem shifted slightly, her gloved fingers brushing the armrest.

This was how he always worked. If a place carried a risk no one else wanted to touch, that was the place he watched the longest.

Gharum’s cloak rasped against the stone as he leaned back.

"So that’s your idea." he said.

In his mouth, it was less a question and more a verdict on how far Kaer was willing to go.

#### Scene 2

Morning in Arbalest came with clear air and the steady noise of a city already at work.

Elrond had finished checking everything before the sun was fully up. His clothes were clean and properly fastened, his documents stacked in the order he had decided on, and the familiar weight of the sword at his hip sat where it always did. There was nothing left to adjust.

He descended the stairs of the inn and crossed the narrow front hall. The innkeeper looked up from wiping the counter and gave him a short, easy smile.

“Good luck, lad,” the man said.

Elrond returned the nod, offered a simple word of thanks, and stepped out through the door.

The street outside was already busy. Workers moved past in small groups, some carrying tools, others pushing carts. A few city guards walked their routes with practiced boredom, armour and

weapons in good order but faces relaxed. This district felt cleaner than the places he had seen when first entering Arbalest—more swept stone, fewer patched walls, fewer signs of wear.

He followed the main avenue, boots keeping to the edge of the flow. The buildings here rose a little taller, their fronts straighter, their windows fitted more neatly. After a while, the road split. A broader street branched off toward the Royal District, just as the map had shown.

At the entrance, a stone archway spanned the way forward.

Two soldiers stood at the sides of the arch, spears resting against their shoulders. They watched the street in that unfocused way that came from standing in the same place too many days in a row. People passed between them at a slow but steady pace. No one was stopped. No one was questioned.

Elrond walked through as well.

He straightened his back and walked with even steps. The documents stayed firm in his hand. If the guards truly did not care who came and went, then there was nothing to worry about. That was what the scene in front of him said.

Even so, a small knot of tension loosened only after he had gone a few steps past the archway. The sigh that escaped him was quiet enough that it vanished into the city noise, half relief and half the leftover habit of expecting gates to mean checks and trouble.

A few steps inside, the air changed.

The cramped buildings and mixed smells of the outer streets fell away. In their place, grand mansions lined the road, each with its own gate and clean frontage. A well-kept park spread out along one side, its trees and shrubs trimmed into orderly shapes. The sounds here were calmer—no shouting, just carriage wheels in the distance and footsteps on clean stone.

Elrond kept walking, letting his feet follow what his memory had already traced. The map he had studied back at the inn rose in his mind with the same photographic clarity as always, every street and turn exactly where it should be. First the main street, then the turn, then the final stretch toward the academy gate.

People in neat, plain uniforms moved between the estates—staff, clerks, servants, all going about work that had nothing to do with him. Most of them only gave him a brief look before going back to their work.

The Royal Academy was not far from the gate.

After his first turn, he saw it ahead: a large building set back behind tall white gates, its outline matching what he had been told to expect. Even from this distance, something about the scale and placement made it obvious. A person could have walked here without a map and still guessed, just from the way the street seemed to lead toward it.

As he drew closer, more details came into focus.

Several carriages were lined up outside, the kind that required more coin than most people in his hometown would see in a year. Polished wood, clean paint, small family crests worked into the panels or flags—it was not hard to imagine the kind of people who had stepped out of them.

There were many students waiting near the gate.

Some sat on benches, their travel cloaks folded neatly at their sides. Others stood in small clusters, speaking with parents or friends in low voices. A few went through their own bundles of documents, much like he had done earlier, but even that looked different when done in finer clothes.

Everyone seemed neatly put together.

Coats and dresses were cut from cloth that hung just so. Boots had been polished for the day. Even the simplest outfits had some small crest or decoration worked into them. Elrond wore the best clothes he owned, clean and properly fitted, but standing among them made every plain line of his shirt and the unadorned belt and sword at his hip feel suddenly obvious.

Nothing here felt familiar.

He had held a sword, run patrol routes, and cast spells until his mana ran dry. He had walked streets much closer to the edge of danger than this calm road to the academy gate. Those things would not change just because this part of the city was cleaner than what he was used to. Even if the others had finer cloth and polished crests, he still had a body trained to move, magic drilled into him, and a head full of things he did not forget. That was what mattered now.

So he waited with the rest of them, watching the closed gates and waiting for them to open.

He stood a little way back from the gates, behind the line of carriages and the crowd pressed closer to the entrance.

From there, it was easier to see the whole scene at once. The carriages. The people talking near them. The empty space beyond.

One thing stood out almost immediately.

For a place like the Royal Academy, he had expected more movement. More people arriving, more applicants, more noise. Instead, the line in front of the gate hardly seemed to grow at all. A few new faces every now and then, but nothing like what the name “Royal Academy” suggested.

He watched for a while longer.

No sudden surge. No line snaking down the street. Just… a steady state, as if most of the people who were going to be here were already here.

He couldn’t help wondering why.

Elrond pulled out the paper his mother had given him.

The Academy’s entrance information was written across it in neat lines—date, time, place, a brief note about what to bring, a reminder not to be late. He had already memorised all of it back home. Even so, he unfolded it carefully and read it again from top to bottom.

His memory was not the problem. With him, once something went in, it did not blur or fade. But “remembered correctly” and “interpreted correctly” were not always the same thing. Equations had taught him that much.

He checked the date. The hour. The place. The note about gather time before the exam itself.

Nothing seemed wrong.

The paper still matched the gate in front of him. The only thing that didn’t match was the vague feeling in his chest that there should be more people.

‘Then that’s just how it works here,’ he decided.

If the Academy was fine with this number, then that was all there was to it. He folded the paper along the same lines as before and slid it back where he had been keeping it.

“Are you enrolling as well?”

A voice spoke right beside him.

Elrond looked up.

A tall figure had walked straight up to him without him noticing. Dark-brown hair that looked like it had lost a brief fight with a comb, bright eyes that took everything in at once, and a kind of restless energy in the way he stood—like someone who was more used to moving than waiting.

The boy had thrown the question out without any greeting at all.

Elrond blinked once, then glanced to the left and right to make sure there wasn’t someone else behind him.

“Are you talking to me?” he asked.

“Yeah,” the stranger said, as if it were obvious. “You.”

A moment later, his expression tightened and he straightened up, suddenly aware of how abrupt he’d sounded.

“Sorry. That was rude,” he added quickly. “I’m Ryn Halber.”

The name came with a small, apologetic smile. Up close, he didn’t carry himself like the people near the carriages. No polished crest. No careful noble posture. Just a straightforward way of looking at him, like this was the most natural thing in the world.

“I came over because you don’t look like a noble either,” Halber went on. “Same as me.”

Elrond needed a second to process that.

“You’re not a noble?” he asked.

Halber shook his head at once.

“Nope. Just a normal guy from Arbalest,” he said. “My old man’s a guard. Mom runs a flower shop in the lower district.”

His father was a guard and his mother ran a flower shop, the kind of ordinary city life that only showed up in background panels when a story passed through a town. For a moment, Elrond’s brain supplied the phrase “NPC backstory” all on its own, pulled straight from the manga shelves of his past life.

The thought almost made the corner of his mouth twitch.

He realised a moment later that he hadn’t given his own name yet.

“Sorry,” he said. “Elrond. Elrond von Astrea.”

“Von Astrea…?” Halber repeated, tilting his head a little as if checking it against something in his memory. “Yeah, I’ve never heard a noble house with that name.” Halber said it without a hint of mockery, as if he were just stating a simple fact.

“And yes,” Elrond said, answering the first question properly this time, “I’m enrolling.”

“That’s good,” he said. “Really good, actually.”

He let out a small breath and glanced toward the gate.

“Every year, it feels like there are fewer of us,” he said. “Commoners, I mean. The Royal Academy’s still open to everyone on paper, but… status and all that.” He pulled a face. “People don’t like the idea of their kids ‘mixing down’, I guess. And if you’re from outside the noble circles, you hear enough stories to think twice before applying.”

“Stories?” Elrond asked.

“Rumours,” Halber corrected himself. “Stuff about nobles throwing their status around whenever they get a chance. Making things hard for people who can’t talk back. That kind of thing.”

He had heard pieces of that before. In quieter talks at home, in the way Aldric and Selene chose their words when the capital came up. “Royal Academy” was the sort of name that carried its own weight—pride, hierarchy, and the kind of distance that came with both. Bullying wrapped in etiquette would not be surprising.

Even so—

“I’ve met nobles,” Elrond said. “A few. None of them were bad people.”

Halber didn’t argue.

He just lifted one hand, palm up, and gave a small, lopsided shrug.

“Then maybe you just haven’t met the wrong ones yet,” he said. “Hopefully you won’t.”

Elrond couldn’t really deny that.

He let the answer sit where it was.

They talked a little more—nothing deep, just simple things. Where they had come from in the city. How early they had arrived. Whether the number of carriages looked normal or not. With each exchange, the space around them felt a little less like a place where only other people belonged.

The first sign that anything was changing came from the gate.

Metal groaned softly as the tall white leaves began to swing inward. A guard stepped forward and raised his voice, cutting cleanly through the scattered conversations.

“Royal Academy entrance examination applicants, you may now enter. Carriages will proceed first. Those on foot will follow in order behind.”

The carriages moved before anyone on the ground could.

The whole line creaked into motion, wood and leather shifting as one polished carriage after another rolled through the open gates, each leaving a short gap before the next. When the last one had vanished inside, the line of students on foot began to move as well.

While the carriages were rolling through the gates, Elrond had watched each one and spotted a crest he recognised from a carriage that had once visited his hometown—the mark of House Alfrost—and he found himself wondering if the child he had seen inside it back then was there again today.

Halber glanced his way and gave a short nod, the earlier energy settling into something more focused.

“Shall we?” he said.

Elrond answered with a nod of his own.

Side by side, they joined the flow of applicants and walked through the Academy gates together.

They passed under the gate and into the Academy grounds.

Just beyond the entrance, a guard was already waiting. He wore the academy’s colours over his armour and looked as if he had repeated the same instructions many times already that morning.

“Examinees, this way,” he called.

Elrond and Halber followed him along a short path and into a wide, semi-indoor hall that sat at the centre of the front building. The ceiling was high and open on the sides, letting in light and air, but the counters and desks inside were protected from the street by pillars and railings.

It didn’t work like the queues he had seen at the town guard.

There was no single line. Instead, several counters had been set up in a row, each with a staff member seated behind it. Applicants simply walked to any empty space. Names were checked, documents taken, and people moved on at their own pace.

Outside the open side of the hall, attendants moved between small tables, setting out trays of light snacks and glasses on polished stands. Nobles and their families were already being served. With the quiet conversations, the neat arrangement of food and drink, and the way people drifted between groups, it almost looked more like the reception of a social gathering than the start of an entrance exam.

Halber let out a low breath beside him.

“I’ll grab that one,” he said, nodding toward an empty counter on the left. “See you later, hopefully.”

“Right,” Elrond replied.

They split without much ceremony, each heading toward a different space. Elrond took a free counter closer to the centre. As he walked, he didn’t notice the way one of the staff farther along the row lifted her head and watched him with full attention, as if something about him had just stepped into focus.

He stopped in front of the clerk at his own counter and set his documents down, ready to explain who he was and what he was applying for.

“Excuse me,” a woman’s voice called from a little further down. “Could you come here instead?”

Elrond glanced sideways.

The voice belonged to the same staff member who had been looking his way earlier. She was seated two counters away, a ledger open in front of her. Light hair was tied back neatly, and her uniform sat without a crease out of place. Her eyes were clear and calm, but there was a sharpness behind them that reminded him of Julian.

The clerk in front of Elrond did not look surprised.

“Understood,” the man said at once. He gave Elrond a small nod, more of a gesture of apology than dismissal. “Please respond to Madam Roosevelt instead. She will handle your case.”

So she was someone important enough that the others didn’t question it.

Elrond picked up his papers again and walked over to her counter.

“Sorry,” he said. “I was just—”

“There’s no problem,” the woman said, shaking her head once. “Thank you for coming over.”

She straightened the ledger slightly and met his eyes.

“My name is Lacia Roosevelt,” she said. “I’m in charge of enrollment records. I’ll handle your registration personally.”

Her gaze didn’t linger on his face for long, but when it shifted down to the documents in his hands, there was a tiny pause—as if she were confirming something she had already noticed the moment he walked in.

“Elrond von Astrea,” he said, introducing himself in turn. “I can use both sword and magic. I’ve brought all the documents they asked for.”

He set the bundle down in front of her.

“I see,” Lacia said.

She spoke quietly, more to herself than to him, and began to go through the papers. Her eyes moved quickly. Once or twice they widened by a fraction, then smoothed back to normal as she continued reading. When she was done, she stacked the documents neatly, drew one of the Academy’s printed forms toward her, and wrote something at the top before pressing a small stamp into the corner.

Then she turned the form around and slid it across to him.

“This is your enrollment sheet,” she said. “Please fill in your personal details here—name, age, place of origin, and your parents’ information—and here, your current skills. Nothing that isn’t already in your documents.”

The form was simple.

The form was simple and mostly asked for things he had already written in his other documents: his name, his parents’ names and occupations, his hometown, his ability with sword and magic. When the space asked him to describe his level, he wrote both sword and magic as “intermediate” because he did not want to draw attention to himself. The chantless casting stayed off the form entirely, and since it never asked about mana capacity, he chose not to mention that either. A section at the bottom left room for “other relevant training”, which he kept brief on purpose, and once he had checked it all once more, he pushed the form back to her.

He finished quickly and pushed the form back to her.

“Thank you,” Lacia said.

She checked what he had written against the earlier papers, then reached into a side tray and took out a sturdy card a little larger than his hand.

She placed it on the counter between them.

These are the examinations you’ll be taking today,” she explained. “Written exam, magic exam, physical exam. Each section has a box for the examiner’s stamp.”

The card was divided into three clear fields, each with a heading and an empty square waiting to be marked. It was straightforward enough. Elrond picked it up and looked it over once, then nodded.

“I understand,” he said.

Lacia rose from her chair.

“Then we’ll start with the magic examination,” she said. “This way.”

He had thought the exams had to be taken in order, but apparently not, and with a staff member telling him to start with the magic examination, he simply went along with it.

He followed her out of the registration hall and along a corridor lined with high windows. On the other side of the glass, he could see part of the magic test area: enrollees standing in a line, each one stepping forward in turn to cast at practice dummies while robed examiners watched and made notes.

Lacia did not lead him to that line.

Instead, she stopped at a door set a little apart from the main space, opened it with a key from her belt, and gestured him inside.

The room beyond was plain and quiet, with a smooth floor, bare walls, a single practice dummy near the far wall, and enough open space for him to move while Lacia watched beside him.

They had the room to themselves.

Lacia stepped a little further in, letting the door close quietly behind them, and turned to face Elrond. The air felt still here, the sounds from the main test area on the other side of the wall reduced to a faint, distant echo.

Meanwhile, on the second floor of the same building, six figures stood behind a pane of glass that blended almost perfectly with the surrounding wall. From the hallway below it might have passed for stone; from here, it was a window. They were looking down into the room where Lacia and Elrond now stood.

The man at the front, closest to the glass, was Julian Roosevelt.

He watched in silence, arms folded loosely, eyes fixed on the scene below. The five staff members behind him did the same, each with their own notes and responsibilities, but all of them sharing one role with Lacia: they were the people who handled “special case” candidates, the ones Lacia’s clairvoyance picked out of the crowd. Today, Elrond was one of them.

Inside the room, Lacia began explaining the first part of the examination.

“First, we’ll test your control and focus,” she said.

She walked to a small table near the centre of the room and set something on it: a small egg, no larger than a quail’s. Then she gestured toward another table near the practice dummies at the far side.

“I’d like you to use magic to send this egg to that table as fast as you can,” she said. “It must land on the table without breaking. Think of it as a throw and catch using magic alone.”

Simple on paper. In practice, the egg’s shell would shatter the moment his focus slipped.

Elrond stepped up to the nearer table and looked once at the egg, then at the distance between the two tables. He drew in a breath, raised one hand slightly, and began to chant.

He shaped the first spell to push the egg forward, compressing the air in front of it and releasing it in a sharp burst. The egg shot away from the table, cutting through the air toward the far end of the room. Just before it reached the second table, he layered another chant over the first, slowing its speed, and followed it with a short wind spell that pushed back against its motion and caught it from the front.

The egg dropped the last hand’s breadth onto the wood with only a small, soft sound.

It did not crack.

Lacia’s eyes widened for a moment before she smoothed her expression again.

“Good,” she said. “Very good. Let’s move on.”

She cleared the first table and brought out a long, transparent tube with a small, light object already placed inside it. She fixed the tube upright on a stand so the object sat at the bottom, then turned back to him.

“For the next test, I want to see how well you can hold a steady output,” she said. “Use wind magic to keep this object floating at the same height inside the tube. Don’t let it rise too high or drop back down.”

Elrond nodded.

He positioned himself in front of the tube, lifted his hand, and began another chant, this one tuned for fine adjustment rather than force. A light current of air formed inside the tube, lifting the object from the base and holding it in the middle.

He adjusted it once, then held it there.

Seconds stretched. Then minutes.

The object did not sway or drift. It stayed at the same level, as if someone had fixed it there by hand. Lacia kept her gaze on the tube and on him, counting the breaths.

Ten full minutes passed without the object losing height or wobbling.

She made a small note on her paper and looked at him again, more carefully than before.

“Very well,” she said. “We’ll proceed to the next part.”

The following test was about power.

“This time, I want you to destroy one of the dummies,” she said, indicating the far side of the room. “Use the lowest-tier spell you can. Minimum rank, maximum effect.”

Elrond turned to face the nearest dummy.

He chose a basic small fireball spell, the kind written in the first pages of any combat primer. The words that left his mouth, however, came slower and more layered. As he chanted, he shaped the spell tighter and tighter, compressing the fire’s mana into a denser core instead of letting it expand outward.

Lacia watched his hand, the air in front of it, and the invisible path the mana was taking. The amount of power he was feeding into such a simple spell made her eyes narrow.

When the spell was ready, Elrond released it.

The fireball flashed across the room with high speed and struck the dummy squarely in the chest. The impact was followed by a burst that shook the air, a blast more like a small explosion

than a beginner’s spell. When the light and smoke cleared, the dummy was half gone, the upper part scorched and torn apart.

Lacia’s fingers tightened slightly around her pen.

Up on the second floor, one of the observers murmured under his breath before catching himself. Julian did not say anything, but the set of his jaw had changed; his attention had sharpened, if that was even possible.

Lacia finished writing her notes in quick strokes. There were still several intermediate checks on the list in front of her, but at this point they felt redundant.

“We’ll skip ahead,” she said quietly, more to herself than to him.

One question had fixed itself in her mind now.

Just how much mana does this boy have?

Even with her clairvoyance, the exact number would not come into view. She could see that his reserves were large—far beyond what was normal at his age—but not where they ended.

She led him toward the side of the room and opened a door he had taken for part of the wall. Behind it sat a mana measurement device: a large, bulb-like sphere mounted on a solid base, its top reaching nearly twice Elrond’s height. Two hand-sized slots were set into the front at about his chest level.

“For the final part of the magic examination, we’ll measure your mana capacity,” Lacia said. “Place both hands here and don’t let go until I tell you.”
