Elrond stepped up to the device and slid his hands into the slots.

For a moment, nothing happened.

Then he felt it: a steady pull, as if something were drawing a thin stream of warmth out of his arms. Inside the sphere, light began to gather, a clear blue glow that grew brighter as the seconds passed. His body trembled slightly, a reflex to the unfamiliar sensation of mana being pulled in a controlled line instead of spent through a spell.

Minutes went by with no sign of the device stopping its pull.

Under normal circumstances, the device would have already drawn a person’s mana down close to empty and begun returning it to them in a gentle cycle. That return never came. The light inside the sphere only grew thicker and brighter, as if it had no intention of stopping.

One minute passed, then another. By the time ten full minutes had gone by, Lacia’s expression had lost its earlier composure.

This was not how the measurement was supposed to look.

She watched the sphere for a moment longer, then raised her hand.

“That is enough,” she said. “You can take your hands out now.”

Elrond obeyed. The strange tingling in his arms faded little by little. Inside the sphere, the light stayed swollen and heavy for a while before it began to thin.

The device had not reached the bottom of his reserves. It had simply reached the limit of how much mana it could draw in a reasonable time. For someone like him, they would need a larger, stronger instrument if they wanted a proper number at all.

Only a few people ever pushed a standard device that far, and only a handful of those were anywhere near Elrond’s age.

Lacia exhaled slowly, then closed the panel and turned back to him.

“That concludes the magic examination,” she said. Her tone was steady again, but she added one more note on his card than usual before stamping the box for the magic exam. “Your result is a Great Pass.”

Elrond stepped back from the device and flexed his fingers once, feeling the lingering tingle fade from his arms.

On the surface, his face stayed flat.

Inside, a different feeling had already started to move.

‘No way… what am I supposed to do…?’ he thought, the line of his mouth barely changing, but the weight in his chest clearly troubled.

They left the device behind.

Lacia opened the door and stepped back into the corridor, letting Elrond walk out first. The lingering numbness in his arms was already fading, but the result of the test clung to the back of his mind in a way that felt heavier than any physical fatigue.

“The next part is the physical exam,” Lacia said. “This way.”

She guided him along the corridor to another door not far from the magic test area. As they stopped in front of it, she nodded toward the handle.

“The room is prepared. Please go in ahead.”

Elrond answered with a quiet “Yes,” pushed the door open, and stepped inside.

He didn’t see who appeared behind Lacia a moment later.

Julian came down the corridor from the other direction, his pace unhurried. Lacia turned, saw him, and without greeting or small talk handed over a single sheet from her clipboard.

It was Elrond’s current summary.

Magic — Intermediate. Sword Skill — Intermediate.

Julian glanced down at the lines once, resting his free hand lightly against his chin as if fitting the words to what he had just witnessed from the observation room. He stayed like that for a brief moment, then lowered his hand again.

“I’ll take this one,” he said.

Lacia gave a small nod.

“Understood,” she replied.

She opened the door Elrond had gone through and stepped in first this time, with Julian following.

The physical exam room was similar in size to the one used for magic, but even barer. The floor was the same smooth stone, the walls the same plain finish. The only things inside were a rack of wooden practice swords and, beside them, a smaller rack holding a few real blades in their sheaths. There were no dummies set up yet, no other equipment.

Lacia moved to the side of the room, taking a position where she could watch without getting in the way. Julian walked toward the centre, stopping at a distance that would be comfortable for a bout.

Elrond turned to face him properly when he realised he was not just another staff member.

Julian held the summary sheet in one hand.

“About your sword skill,” he began, his tone even. “Is it the same as what you wrote here?”

Elrond glanced at the paper, then back at him.

“It’s just like it says on the form,” he answered. “Intermediate.”

Julian’s eyes shifted to the card for the magic exam and the Great Pass stamped there, then back to Elrond.

“You also wrote ‘intermediate’ for your magic,” he said, tapping the edge of the summary once with his finger, “but looking at the results…”

He let the sentence trail off there. He didn’t need to finish it. The contrast between the modest word on the page and the performance they had just seen was obvious enough on its own.

From the look in Julian’s eyes, “Great Pass” and “intermediate” did not belong in the same line.

Elrond felt his throat tighten a little. He turned his gaze away for a moment, as if the far wall had suddenly become very interesting.

“…It’s just how I wrote it,” he said quietly, not really offering more than that.

Julian did not press the point.

Instead, he walked over to the rack of wooden swords and picked one up, testing its weight with an easy, practiced motion. Then he nodded toward the rack.

“Choose a wooden training sword,” he said. “I’ll be the one testing you for the physical exam.”

Elrond stepped up to the rack in turn and reached for a sword that matched the length he was used to, the decision already telling him this would not be a simple strength measurement.

Julian weighed the practice sword in his hand once, then looked back at Elrond.

“I should introduce myself properly,” he said. “Julian Roosevelt. For now, you can think of me as your examiner.”

He didn’t add anything else about who he was. His tone made it sound unnecessary.

Elrond gave a small nod.

He took a few steps back to open the distance between them and let his body fall into the stance Aldric had drilled into him—blade held steady, centre of gravity low, feet ready to move in any direction. It was the same stance he had used a thousand times on the packed dirt of the training yard.

Julian’s stance, by comparison, looked almost too simple. Sword in his right hand, point angled toward Elrond, left hand relaxed at his side, shoulders loose.

Lacia raised one hand.

“Begin,” she said, and brought her hand down in a sharp motion.

They moved at the same time.

Elrond pushed forward, testing the distance with a cautious first step. Julian’s answer came faster than he expected. The older man slipped into his range with a smooth shift of weight and brought his sword in from an angle that didn’t match Aldric’s usual patterns.

Elrond barely managed to meet it in time.

Wood rang against wood. The shock of the impact ran down his arm. Before he could fully reset his guard, Julian had already adjusted his wrist and sent the next strike in along a different line.

Elrond barely managed to block it.

He could follow the movement with his eyes. Matching it with his body was another matter. Julian’s sense of timing was different from Aldric’s—sharper, less forgiving—and every time Elrond thought he had caught the rhythm, the next step came half a beat earlier than he expected.

They traded several blows like that: Julian pressing, Elrond defending with a mix of blocks and last-moment slips to the side.

Then Julian’s free hand moved.

Elrond saw his lips form the beginning of a chant. Mana stirred around him, faint but distinct, gathering into his muscles.

…He’s casting enhancement magic?

A heartbeat later, Julian’s body answered the spell.

He came in again, and this time the difference was obvious. His speed jumped, his steps hit the floor with more force, and when their swords met, the strength behind his blows drove Elrond back. Elrond braced his stance and still felt his feet slide a fraction on the smooth stone.

Wait. Magic is allowed in this? Elrond thought, teeth clenched as he caught another heavy strike on his guard. You could have mentioned that…

The next exchange shoved him back another step.

If this kept up, he’d be pushed into the wall.

His body reacted before he could finish the thought.

Mana surged through his limbs, guided along familiar paths. He did not speak. No sound left his mouth. The pattern of the enhancement spell formed out of pure habit, without the frame of a chant, and settled into his muscles.

The change came in a rush.

Julian’s next strike no longer felt completely out of reach. Elrond’s arms met it with less strain; his legs answered the force by shifting him cleanly instead of stumbling. His eyes tracked Julian’s shoulders and hips, memorising the way they moved, and his body started to follow what his memory was already mapping out.

Block. Adjust. Step. Block again, a little earlier.

The gap between them narrowed. Julian’s eyebrows rose by a fraction.

He broke away suddenly, letting their swords slide apart, and shifted his stance.

The new posture was not the same simple guard he had used before. His feet moved to a different line. The angle of his blade changed. The next attack came in with a completely different style, like another fencer had stepped into his place.

Elrond noticed the change right away.

His first response was late. He blocked, but the angle was awkward, and the rebound almost tore the sword from his hand. The second blow forced him to dodge rather than meet it, and the third skimmed close enough that he felt the rush of air along his sleeve.

He gave ground and focused on seeing.

Step, cut, twist of the wrist, recovery. The pattern was new, but not unknowable. He let Julian press him for a few more exchanges, then retreated one more step, not to flee but to reset. When the next attack came, his sword was already moving to meet it.

The clash sounded cleaner this time.

Julian’s mouth curved into a small smile.

He lightened the pressure for a few breaths, as if satisfied with something he had just confirmed. Then the smile faded again, and he moved in a way that made the room feel smaller.

Elrond saw the first step.

The second blurred.

For an instant, Julian’s figure slipped out of his focus like a frame missing from a reel. Elrond turned, instincts screaming, and felt the presence at his back a fraction of a second before wood met wood again.

He managed to bring his sword up and block.

Julian did not stay with one style now. His movements turned less readable, mixing pieces of the earlier forms with something faster and more irregular. Angles changed in the middle of swings. Footwork broke patterns right as Elrond thought he had found the rhythm. Attacks came from lines that made no sense if you tried to connect them to one school.

Elrond did his best to follow, but the pace and unpredictability together began to pull him apart. His guard held for a few more exchanges under sheer reflex and training, then a feint drew his blade just a little too far out of place.

Julian’s wooden sword struck his with a sharp twist.

The impact tore the weapon from Elrond’s hand. The practice sword spun up into the air, slow only in comparison to the rush that had preceded it.

Before it even reached the peak of its arc, Julian had already stepped in. The tip of his own wooden blade stopped in front of Elrond’s face, close enough that he could feel the faint stir of air from the motion.

Lacia lifted her hand.

“That’s enough,” she said.

The tension broke.

Julian drew his sword back and lowered it, planting the tip lightly against the floor. One hand came to rest on the back of the hilt while he took a breath and looked Elrond over again, this time without the pressure of motion between them.

“Good work,” he said. “You learn quickly. Most people can’t adjust to a change in style that fast, let alone twice in one bout.”

His tone was matter-of-fact, not flattering.

“Your eyes and memory are doing a lot for you,” he went on. “You see something once and it’s already sitting in your body the next time it comes. You even forced me to stop playing around and take you seriously for a bit.”

Elrond’s shoulders dropped by a hair, some of the held tension leaving his posture. His lungs were working harder than he wanted to show. Mentally, the effort of tracking Julian’s movements had tired him almost more than the physical strain.

Julian turned his head slightly.

“Lacia,” he called.

She stepped a little closer, her gaze flicking briefly from Elrond to Julian.

“You saw it too, didn’t you?” Julian asked.

“Yes,” she said. “During the bout, Elrond activated strength and agility enhancement on himself. I never heard him chant.”

Elrond’s spine went stiff.

For a heartbeat, his mind went blank. Then it filled with too many bad ideas at once. He could claim he had whispered the chant under his breath. That she must have missed it in the noise. That it was some kind of artefact. None of them sounded convincing even in his own head.

He closed his eyes for a moment, trying to catch a single excuse that wasn’t obviously weak.

Julian spoke before he could find one.

“You don’t have to scramble for a story,” he said calmly. “You can be honest.”

Elrond looked up.

Julian’s expression was steady, not accusing.

“I understand why you wouldn’t want to show everything in front of a room full of strangers,” he continued. “But it’s just us here. Whatever you say now stays between Lacia and me. We won’t spread it around.”

The words sounded exactly like the kind of thing a shady character would say right before doing the opposite. Elrond’s past life and his manga memories agreed on that point very clearly.

Even so, nothing in Julian’s eyes or voice matched that pattern.

Elrond let out a quiet breath.

“…I can cast without chanting,” he said. “Not silent chanting. Actual chantless magic.”

Lacia’s eyes widened. Julian’s hand went back to his chin for a moment, thumb brushing the line of his jaw.

“I thought at first it might be silent chanting,” he said. “Like some of the elves use. But that was cleaner than that. You activated it on instinct in the middle of a fight, without chanting at all.

He and Lacia exchanged a brief look , an unspoken agreement passing between them that Elrond could not quite read.

Julian lowered his hand again.

“I’ve decided,” he said. “For the physical exam, you also receive a Great Pass. And on top of that—”

He paused just long enough for the words to land.

“—you’ll become my disciple.”

Elrond stared at him.

“…Huh?”

Julian didn’t seem bothered by the reaction.

“I’m not a bad person,” he said evenly. “Nothing strange is going to happen to you because of this. It just means I’ll take responsibility for training you properly.”

That is exactly the kind of line a suspicious character would use, Elrond thought, somewhere between numb and exasperated.

He glanced once at Lacia. She looked more thoughtful than alarmed, and there was no sign that she considered Julian’s offer dangerous. If anything, she seemed to treat it as a natural extension of what they had already seen from him.

Elrond swallowed, suddenly aware of how tense he was.

“…All right,” he said at last. “If you’re sure.”

Julian gave a small nod, as if that settled the matter.

“Good,” he said. “Then the physical examination is complete. Lacia?”

She stepped forward with his exam card in hand and stamped the box for the physical test, adding a note beside it similar to the one she had written after the magic exam.

“That concludes the physical exam,” she said. “You have a Great Pass here as well.”

The adrenaline of the bout faded, leaving behind a thin, buzzing fatigue. It felt like the entire session had taken turns peeling back layers he would have preferred to keep hidden. At least, for now, those layers were only exposed to two people—and both of them had promised to keep them quiet.

“All that remains is the written exam,” Lacia added. “I’ll guide you there next.”

Elrond nodded.

Mentally, he already felt like he’d done enough for the day, but there was no avoiding the last part. He followed Lacia back out into the corridor once more, leaving the empty room and its rack of wooden swords behind as they headed toward the final examination hall.

Lacia led him back toward the front of the building.

“The written exam is held with the other applicants,” she said. “From here, you can handle it on your own.”

She stopped at the entrance to another hall and gestured ahead. Elrond nodded once in thanks and went in.

Inside, the room was already busy. Rows of desks filled the floor in a gentle slope, facing a single long table at the front where the examiner sat. It looked more like a lecture hall than an examination chamber. Voices were low, more rustle than noise, as people took their seats or waited with papers in hand.

An assistant near the door handed Elrond a worksheet as he passed.

He glanced over the room, then chose an empty seat near the back, away from the small clusters of applicants who had come with friends or family. He set his card and the sheet on the desk, took the pen provided, and only then unfolded the paper fully.

He scanned the questions once from top to bottom.

Basic arithmetic—mostly sums and simple problems framed around trade, tax and prices. General magic knowledge—nothing beyond what appeared in introductory texts. Monster-related questions—habits, weaknesses, classifications he had already committed to memory.

He read a few twice just to be sure, but they were all things he had seen before.

‘So that’s all,’ he thought.

He lowered his head and began to write.

The room settled into a steady quiet, broken only by the scratch of pens and the occasional shift of a chair. Elrond moved down the page at his own pace, filling in answers as they came, pausing only when he needed to decide how short or long to make the wording. His memory did most of the work; he only needed to choose how to put what he already knew onto the lines in front of him.

By the time he reached the last question, his hand was starting to feel the repetition more than his mind did.

He checked the sheet once more from the beginning, making sure no boxes or lines were left empty, then stood up and walked it down to the front.

The examiner took the paper with a brief nod and set it on top of a small stack to one side. Elrond stepped back and returned to his seat to wait.

About fifteen minutes passed.

One by one, the examiner went through the completed sheets, marking them with quick, practiced motions. When he reached Elrond’s, his eyes moved a little slower for a few lines, then he picked up a stamp, pressed it to the corner of the page, and reached for Elrond’s entrance card.

He called Elrond’s name, waited for him to come down again, and returned the card.

A clear PASS mark had been added to the box for the written exam.

“That’s all for today,” the examiner said. “You may leave.”

The written test itself had not been difficult. Even so, as Elrond stepped out of the hall and back into the corridor, the full weight of the morning settled over him. From the gate to registration, then the magic examination, then facing Julian, and now this… all of it together had only taken around three hours, but his mind felt as if it had run twice that distance.

Lacia was waiting near the front, where he had first met her.

“Your examinations are complete,” she said. “The official results will be sent to your inn by tomorrow, addressed to you. Please keep your card safe until then.”

“I understand,” Elrond said.

“Thank you for your cooperation today,” she added with a small nod.

He thanked her in return, then turned and made his way out of the Academy grounds, passing once more through the white gates and back toward the streets he had walked that morning.

The walk back to the inn felt longer than it had in the morning. His legs still moved without any problem, but his head was crowded—mana tests, “Great Pass”, chantless magic dragged out into the open, and now being told he’d become Julian’s disciple after only one day. Lacia and Julian had pulled almost everything he was trying to hide out of him with just a set of exams, and that more than anything was what left him tired.

He ordered a meal from the first floor, then went straight up to his room to wait, not trusting himself to sit among the other guests and pretend to be relaxed. By the time a knock came at his door and the tray was set down on the small table, his stomach had only just remembered it was hungry.

He ate without rushing, one bite at a time, letting the warmth of the food steady him. The day’s exams—magic, the match with Julian, the written test—ran through his head in order whether he wanted them to or not, but the simple act of chewing and swallowing made them feel a little further away.

When the plate was finally empty, he pushed the chair back, lay down on the bed, and closed his eyes. This time, he did not stop himself from resting.

### Chapter 16: 12 – Day of Entrance

#### Scene 1

The palace treated the Academy season like a yearly state operation.

When the council finally arrived at the Academy part of the agenda, most of what they needed to decide had already been discussed beforehand. The long stone hall smelled of ink and wax. The table was filled with packets stamped with the Academy crest and the royal seal. King Aldren sat at the head of the table, his dark coat against the pale wood, and watched as the last of the papers changed hands.

Formally, he led the session. In practice, the court apparatus moved it.

Lord Chancellor Rehvain stood at the center of the table, the intake file open in front of him. His finger rested on a line of neat script as he read the summary, not as if he were discovering it, but as if he were guiding the room through something already agreed in smaller offices.

“Overall intake matches our projections,” he said. “Entrance examinations are underway, both written and practical. Scholarship candidates have been verified. We’re keeping the same distribution rules we approved at the start of the year.”

Further down the table sat Treasurer Maelia Corth, one hand resting on a closed ledger. She did not need to open it. The numbers for this year were already fixed in her head, and she had no intention of letting anyone move them.

“The money is where it needs to be,” she said. “The Academy stays within its current allotment. Scholarships for noble cadets, recommended commoners, and frontier candidates follow the existing ratios. If they want more than that, they wait until the next revision.”

Her tone made it clear the numbers were not up for argument today.

Minister Vannor Kehl of Internal Affairs had a thin folder marked with colored strips. He did not bother to open it.

“The discipline framework is set,” he said. “The revised code has been delivered to the Academy. They know what is expected and when it leaves their hands and lands in mine.”

Across from him, Queen Lysandra listened with her hands folded, eyes steady on Rehvain rather than on any of the individual ministers. Lucien did the same, the closed file in front of him untouched while he followed the sequence of reports.

Darius broke the line of calm with a small movement of his chair.

“If we’re treating the Academy as part of national treasure,” he said, “then we should stop talking about it like an ordinary school. The people who leave that place will be the ones posted to border forts and patrol routes where the monsters actually appear. If a student breaks under pressure here, where everything is controlled, they have no place out there, where towns depend on them to hold their ground.”

He didn’t raise his voice, but the edge carried.

At the other side of the table, Claire shifted one of her thin notebooks closer, though she did not open it.

“The Academy exists to teach before it sends anyone out,” she said. “If we talk about it as if its task is to see who can be thrown at the border and who cannot, then we are not training students, we are sorting lives into those we think we can afford to lose. I will be there this year as a student as well, in the same halls as the heirs, the scholarship children, and the ones from the frontier.”

“Demanding effort is one thing,” she went on, “but building a system that quietly expects certain students to be expendable is something else entirely. The Academy should be where they learn how to protect towns, not where we decide in advance whose future can be traded away.”

Her tone stayed even, the words directed at the ministers and the table, but the objection to Darius’s view was unmistakable.

Rehvain noted both comments with a slight tilt of his head, but he didn’t let the discussion drift.

“Internal Affairs has drawn the lines,” he said. “How hard the Academy pushes inside those lines is their responsibility. Where they step over them becomes ours.”

He turned a page.

“On wards and screening,” he continued, “the Court Mage has filed a full certification. Lady Vale?”

Seraphine Vale sat in the chair reserved for the Academy’s representative, the bundle of Academy papers resting by her elbow. Princess Claire sat further down the table, present as a royal daughter and as a student who would enter the Academy this year.

“The lattice around the grounds is stable,” she said. “We’ve extended coverage to the exam fields for opening week. Entry arrays will screen for demonic influence, tampered blessings, and foreign tracking marks from the first day. If a hostile element still reaches the grounds, it will not be because the barrier failed to detect it.”

Everyone around the table understood what that meant. Any attempt to push demonic influence or external control into the Academy through its students would land on the palace’s desk as a hostile act, not as something the school could quietly write off as a mistake.

Caelen Alfrost sat among the high nobles, outwardly at ease, but he weighed every report against a single worry in his head. He wanted to know which problems could still pass through all of these measures and reach the new first-years during the Academy entrance.

While Seraphine spoke about wards and screening and while Internal Affairs set its thresholds, he treated each line as another piece of that risk. The notes he kept now were meant for later, when the term had begun and he had to report which threats the council had seen coming and which ones they had ignored.

Further down, Cassian Silveria glanced once at his own thin packet and received a small nod from Rehvain.

“Lord Silveria, how are the Academy preparations report on your side?” Rehvain asked.

“Preparations were completed on time,” he said. “Dormitories, practice grounds, and exam rooms were ready on the dates agreed with the Academy. Weapons and training gear had already been delivered, and food stores had been assigned. If they had changed their plans at the last moment, they would have been the ones hurrying, not us.”

Seraphine rose from her chair again with the bundle of Academy papers in one hand. As the court mage and the one in charge of Academy affairs in this council, this part of the report was hers to give.

“From the Academy’s side,” she said, “intake numbers are within capacity. Written scores are being checked and managed carefully. Practical exams are ongoing. Dorm and track assignments are drafted and can be confirmed as soon as the last results arrive. Scholarship and tuition status are recorded in the ledgers, but we do not intend to divide treatment along those lines.”

She hesitated for a heartbeat, then continued.

“As for the rumors about noble–commoner bullying,” she said, “we’re not pretending they don’t exist. Orientation will include explicit conduct rules. First-year dorms will have tighter oversight. We’ve opened direct reporting routes to the administration office so complaints don’t vanish halfway up the stairs. We can’t promise there won’t be incidents, but we can promise they won’t be ignored.”

Claire’s gaze flicked toward them briefly, weighing whether that would be enough. Darius gave no visible reaction at all.

Rehvain closed the file in front of him, drawing a line under the reports for this term.

“The council acknowledges Treasury, Internal Affairs, Court Mage, and Academy reports,” he said. “The directives for the first term will be drafted on that basis and sealed today.”

Aldren’s hand moved toward the row of crystal seals at his side. Clerks along the wall straightened, ready to carry out stamped packets the moment they were marked.

“Thank you for all your work,” he said. “The Academy’s first term will proceed under these measures. See that your offices follow through.”

His gaze paused for a moment on Seraphine. Out of everyone in the room, she had carried the most on this entrance day, handling both the royal barrier and the Academy’s side of the exam.

He reached for the row of crystal seals at his side and pressed the first one to the waiting papers. Along the wall, the clerks bowed and moved to collect the newly marked documents.

With that, the session was concluded, and the day of the entrance exams went on outside the council hall.

#### Scene 2

On the other side of the capital, Emilia and all the girls (except Claire) were on their way to the Royal Academy entrance exam.

The Alfrost carriage, its door marked with the family emblem and a small house flag fluttering above, rolled into the queue in front of the Academy gates. They waited there with the other carriages until the iron bars finally began to move. When the guards signaled them through, the coachman guided the carriage past the gate and into the Academy grounds, then brought it to a stop in an empty space near the main hall entrance.

The area was already busy. Carriages arrived one after another, lining up along the path. Families who had come on foot filed in through a side lane. The air felt crowded even before anyone spoke.

Emilia stepped down first when the door opened.

Cestina followed, and then Lisoletelle, who hesitated for a heartbeat at the top of the small carriage steps before she forced herself to move.

Most of the faces they could see nearby were bright with anticipation. Liso’s was not.

"…My stomach hurts,” Liso muttered. “If I mess up the written exam, that’s it. They’ll mark me as a failure and I’ll have to write home that I couldn’t even get into the Academy.”

Cestina turned slightly toward her.

“Lady Lisoletelle, you’re thinking too far ahead,” she said, her voice steady. “It’s one test. They’ll look at your recommendation and the practical results as well.”

“You’ve been saying that all week,” she said. “It still feels like this test decides my whole life.”

“It doesn’t,” Cestina replied. “You go in, write what you know, and hand it in. That’s all you have to do today.”

Before Liso could start again, Emilia cut in.

“You can complain after we’re inside,” she said quietly. “For now, keep walking.”

SShe had noticed the way people were looking at them.

The voices were not loud, but they were easy to catch.

“Look at that Alfrost family.”

“It must be nice…”

“Is that blonde the Alfrost?”

For most of the people here, “Alfrost” was a name that belonged on reports about the frontier, not in front of the Academy hall. They knew Caelen’s house by reputation, not by faces. When they saw the crest on the carriage and then looked at the girls who stepped out, their eyes slid to the most striking one and stopped there. Cestina was a vassal’s daughter, not the main heir, but no stranger was going to sort out details like that in the middle of a crowd.

At the beginning, Emilia used to tense every time she heard that kind of mistake. But she let it pass. The people who needed to know who she was already did. Correcting every passing assumption in front of the hall would not change the exam, and it would not change her place in Alfrost.

“We’re blocking the way,” Emilia said. “Let’s go.”

She took the lead toward the hall doors, and the other two fell in beside and behind her.

Inside, the atmosphere changed from open crowd to controlled order.

The same kind of hall that Elrond had entered from the other side of the building spread out in front of them, with counters lined up along one wall where staff in Academy blue checked names and papers. Further inside, the space had been left open on purpose, and that empty center was already filling with small groups of nobles who treated the day as both exam and gathering, talking over drinks and light food while they waited for their turn.

It was ceremonial, but not quiet. The Academy had set it up as an intake hall, and the nobles standing under its ceiling were treating it as a place to be seen.

Not long after they stepped inside, a familiar voice called out.

“Lady Emilia.”

She turned her head. A small group of girls from other noble houses was gathered near a table where drinks and light food had been set out. One of them waved.

“You came early too,” the girl said. “Come sit with us for a bit. They say the written rooms won’t open yet anyway.”

Another laughed softly.

“It would be a waste not to talk when everyone is gathered here,” she said. “The exam is only one part of today.”

Around them, nobles were indeed treating it like a gathering. People stood in small clusters, chatting as if they were at a quiet party, cups in hand.

Emilia offered them a polite smile.

“Thank you for the invitation,” she said. “I should complete the entrance procedures first. If there is time after that, I will greet everyone properly.”

The girl who had called out to her gave a small shrug that said she had expected that answer.

“Then we’ll see you after you pass,” she said.

Emilia inclined her head once and turned away, heading straight for the counters. Liso and Cestina followed without comment.

At the reception, she gave her name and documents, received brief instructions, and moved on. The steps that followed matched what had been laid out in the letters and were the same as what another group of candidates was facing elsewhere in the Academy that day, starting with a physical exam, then a magical exam, and finally the written exam.

There was no need for surprises.

Emilia moved through each part in order. The examiners did their work, recorded what they needed, and sent her on. By the time she set down her pen in the written room and left her seat, all three sections were behind her.

The examiner had given each of them a small slip at the end of the written exam. One word was printed at the top.

Pass.

When she returned to the waiting area, Liso looked like she was holding herself together with sheer will.

“…It says ‘Pass,’” Liso said. Her voice was thin, but it came out. “I passed. I actually passed.”

Her shoulders shook once, half from relief and half from the stress that had finally let go.

Cestina checked the slip with a quick glance and nodded.

“That’s all you needed for today,” she said. “You passed the entrance. The exact score doesn’t matter anymore.”

Liso let out a small, shaky laugh.

“What if my score is at the bottom,” she said, “and they all look at me like I slipped in by accident?”

“As long as it says ‘Pass,’ you are a student the same as the others,” Cestina replied. “No one out there can see the number on this paper.”

Emilia looked from the slip to Liso’s face.

“You already know the result,” she said. “It says ‘Pass’. You were already accepted. You don’t have to keep worrying about the part that’s already over.”

Liso drew in a long breath, let it out, and this time some of the tightness left her shoulders.

“…Right,” she said. “Pass is pass.”

Cestina relaxed a little as well.

“Then all that’s left is to wait for the class placement,” she said. “We’ll see where they put us.”

Liso stared at the word “Pass” on her slip again.

“…What if they split us up?” she said. “What if they throw you into some upper class and push me down to the lower ones, and we barely even—”

Emilia cut her off before she could finish the thought.

“If they put us in different classes, I will arrange something,” Emilia said. “Worry about that when it happens. For today, you passed. That is enough.”

Liso closed her mouth. The complaint that had been forming died halfway, and she settled for gripping the slip a little less tightly.

The word “class” in the Academy had a very clear meaning.

First-year students were split by results into classes arranged in alphabetical order. A was the top, then B, C, D, E, and so on. The higher the letter stood, the better the overall result that group had shown in the entrance exams.

Above even Class A, there was one more layer.

S class.

Anyone could be placed there on paper. The Academy never wrote that it belonged to nobles only. But everyone knew that S class usually ended up filled with high-ranking nobles or students whose talent was so obvious that no one could complain.

Classes A, B, and C were mostly made up of nobles as well, with a few exceptional commoners mixed in.

A = very high overall results, mostly nobles with a few outstanding commoners. B = high results just below A, still mainly nobles, with more room for strong commoners. C = solid above-average results, a mixed group of nobles and commoners. D = average results, mostly commoners and children from trader families. E and below = lower results among those who still passed, almost all from commoner or trader backgrounds.

The lower classes were where most commoners and trader families’ children gathered. The teachers and the rules said that everyone in the building was a student of the same Academy.

In the Academy’s official stance, the class list was not meant to separate students by power, but to decide how they received their lessons, with the lower classes carrying heavier, slower drills so that everyone who graduated was supposed to reach the same standard.

#### Scene 3

The next morning, the results came.

Elrond did not go out for his usual run. His body woke up at the same time as always, but he turned over and stayed on the thin inn mattress instead. The exams were over. One late morning would not change his training.

A knock came at the door.

“Morning breakfast,” the inn girl called.

Elrond pushed himself up, ran a hand through his hair, and went to open the door.

She stood there with a tray as usual. On top of the covered dishes sat a neatly made envelope, clean white paper, written and stamped with the Royal Academy seal.

“Breakfast. And a letter for you,” she said. “Got it. Thanks,” Elrond said.

He took the tray and the envelope together and closed the door with his foot.

For a moment he stood in the middle of the room, looking at the seal. Then he set the envelope down on the table and uncovered the plates instead.

“…Food first,” he muttered.

He ate without rushing, more out of habit than calm. By the time the plates were empty and the last of the tea was gone, the envelope was the only thing left on the table.

Elrond picked it up.

The wax seal broke cleanly under his thumb. Inside was a single folded letter. The handwriting was careful and even.

'To Mr. Elrond von Astrea,

We extend our greetings on behalf of the Royal Academy of Arbalest.

After careful review of your performance in the entrance examinations held this term, we are pleased to inform you that you have been accepted as a first-year student of the Royal Academy.

In accordance with the excellent results of your examinations, you have been assigned to

First Year – S Class

As a member of this class, you will follow a curriculum that includes additional guidance and special arrangements where necessary.

A short orientation for S Class students will be held the day after tomorrow at the Royal Academy main camp ...'

He read the sentence twice to make sure his eyes were not skipping anything, then went on. The letter stated his assigned class.

S Class.

Elrond frowned slightly. The letter did not explain what that meant. For a second the letter in his hand and the exam room in his memory did not quite connect.

Then he remembered the small booklet Lacia had handed him before the exam day. The one with the basic explanation of the Academy’s structure.

He reached into his bag, pulled the booklet out, and flipped through the pages until he found the section on classes.

A, B, C, and so on. Then one more at the top.

S Class.

His eyes stopped on the short paragraph under it.

S Class was described as the place for special students recognized by the Academy’s expert examiners, the ones they judged to be outside the usual scale and worth grouping together under closer watch.

“…You have got to be joking,” he said quietly.

He sat back on the edge of the bed with the booklet in one hand and the Academy letter in the other.

He had only wanted to pass without trouble and enter the Academy as one more new student in the crowd. Instead, they had put him in the one class that would draw attention the moment anyone saw the list.

Elrond let out a slow breath.

Being treated as “special” was dangerous. It drew people’s attention, brought questions, and constant comparisons, and that only made it harder for him to stay low and hide what he needed to hide.

On the other hand, the decision was already made. The letter in his hand carried the royal seal. The Academy had looked at his results and placed him where they wished.

“…It cannot be helped,” he said.

He folded the booklet closed and put it back on the table next to the letter, then read the rest of the page.

Under the placement line, the letter continued with more instructions. Students assigned to S Class were told to attend a special orientation the day after tomorrow. The Academy wanted to confirm any particular needs and to explain what support they would provide for that group.

That part made him pause.

“Specific needs,” he repeated under his breath.

The phrase was vague, but it suggested they were willing to adjust things for S Class students if needed. That could mean time, access, or money.

A thought took shape.

“…Scholarship,” he said.

He had enough funds for now because of the patrol work and Alfrost’s reward, but the capital would eat money faster than his village ever could. If there was a chance to have the Academy shoulder more of that cost, he wanted to at least ask. The orientation seemed like the right place to bring it up.

He set the letter down carefully.

For today, there was nothing more he could do about the result. He had passed. He had a class. The next fixed point was the orientation.

Until then, he could rest.

He lay back on the bed for a moment, staring at the ceiling. The sounds from the street below drifted up through the window. The city was already fully awake.

He could spend the day walking the capital again and learning the layout a little better. He could also start looking for a simple part-time job that would not interfere with classes later, something that would let him stretch his savings as far as possible.

Those were problems he could work on quietly.

The fact that the Academy had stamped S next to his name would not change overnight, no matter how much he thought about it.

#### Scene 4

In the Alfrost house, the morning started with a knock on Emilia’s door.

She was still in her pajamas, half-wrapped in her blanket and not ready to deal with anything serious yet.

“Lady Emilia,” the head maid called from outside. “May I come in?”

Emilia pushed herself up, ran a hand over her face, and sat on the edge of the bed.

“You may,” she said.

The door opened. The head maid stepped in with her usual calm expression. In her hands was a single envelope on a small tray. The paper was thick and white, the Royal Academy seal pressed clearly into the wax.

“Your letter from the Royal Academy has arrived,” the maid said. “It was delivered to the house directly. I came as soon as it was checked.”

Emilia swung her legs over the side of the bed and stood.

“Thank you,” she said.

She took the tray, then the envelope, feeling the weight of the paper more than the tray itself. The maid waited just long enough to see that Emilia had it securely in hand, then bowed and stepped back.

“If you require anything, I will be outside,” the head maid said.

Emilia nodded, and the door closed again.

The room was quiet.

She broke the seal and unfolded the letter.

The words were formal and neat. They congratulated her on passing the entrance examinations and confirmed her admission as a first-year student of the Royal Academy. A little further down, they gave the part that mattered most.

She had been assigned to S Class.

There was a short line under that. It listed the other names that had applied under Alfrost and stated that they would also be placed in S Class.

There was no burst of surprise on her face, only a small exhale. It fit the way the exam day had gone and the way Cestina and Liso had performed, even with Liso’s nerves. Still, seeing it written with the Academy seal above the sentence made it feel heavier.

She folded the letter once and set it on the table beside her bed.

A few minutes later, another knock came, faster and less measured than the first.

“Emilia, are you awake?” Liso’s voice called.

Without waiting for a full answer, the door opened a crack. Liso slipped in, still in her own indoor clothes, and Cestina followed more politely behind her.

Emilia folded her arms across her thin pajamas, suddenly very aware of how unprepared she looked.

“I am awake,” she said. “Barely.”

It was obvious from her face that being visited while still in pajamas was not something she enjoyed.

Liso, still focused on the letter in her hands, did not notice at all.

Liso held out her letter. “Emilia, we were all placed in S Class,” she said.

Cestina lifted her own letter slightly.

“See,” Cestina said. “I told you that you did not need to worry so much.”

Liso puffed her cheeks, but her eyes were shining.

“I know you said that,” she replied. “I still thought they would throw me into some lower class because I missed one tariff question. But it really says S. Look.”

She almost shoved the paper toward Emilia.

Emilia glanced at the letter, then at the two of them, her expression tightening.

“Both of you!” she said. “Look at me. I am still in pajamas. Does this look like the time to burst into my room?”

Liso stiffened, the excitement on her face shrinking at once.

“…Right,” Liso said. “Sorry.”

Cestina let out a small breath that was almost a laugh, then thought better of it.

“We were too happy and forgot ourselves,” Cestina said. “We came straight here.”

Emilia rubbed her temples once.

“Go and wait in the living room,” she said. “I will come down after I am dressed. You can say everything you want there, not at my bedside.”

Liso opened her mouth as if to argue, then thought better of it.

“Fine,” Liso said. “But do not take too long. I have too many things to say about that exam.”

“We will wait,” Cestina said.

They both stepped back out into the hall. Emilia watched the door close behind them, then pressed her fingers briefly against her forehead.

She changed quickly into proper clothes, fixed her hair, and made sure she did not look like someone who had only just rolled out of bed with an Academy letter on her table.

When she entered the living room, Liso and Cestina were already there.

Liso was bouncing one leg restlessly on the sofa, her letter still in her hand. Cestina sat beside her with her own folded neatly on her lap.

Emilia sat down opposite them, resting her hands on her knees. “So the Academy really put us in S class together,” she said.

Liso leaned forward at once.

“It still feels strange,” Liso said. “I keep thinking they will come back and say they miswrote it and actually meant some lower class. The physical exam was fine, the magic part I barely survived, and the written exam was horrible. I almost left one page blank. Do you remember that question about the trade routes. And the one about tax law. Who writes questions like that for an entrance exam.”

Cestina let her talk herself out for a moment before answering.

“You answered them in the end,” Cestina said. “You finished all three parts. The Academy saw that and placed you here. They did not make a mistake.”

Liso sank back into the cushions.

“I still hate written exams,” she said. “If they tell us S Class has extra theory, I might cry.”

“We do not even know the schedule yet,” she said. “You are already quitting classes they have not shown us.”

Liso opened her mouth to argue, but Emilia spoke over her.

“Listen,” Emilia went on. “The exam is done. We passed. All three of us. And they put us in the same class. That much is real. Be happy about that first before you start fighting ghosts.”

Liso stared at her, then gave up and slumped again.

“…Fine,” she said. “I’m happy. I still plan to complain about that exam for the rest of the week.”

“That sounds exactly like you, Liso,” Cestina said, a small smile slipping out.

That finally pulled a short laugh out of Emilia.

“Complain as much as you like,” she said. “Do it as a student of S class. Not as someone who failed to get in.”

#### Scene 5

Elrond did not feel like going back to sleep.

After a while on the bed he got up, put his things in order, and left the inn. Since the letter had fixed his future for the next few years, the least he could do was learn the shape of the city he would live in. He stepped out onto the street and chose the main road that ran in the opposite direction from the Royal Academy.

The morning had already settled into its usual rhythm. Carts and carriages rolled past with steady noise, shopkeepers were opening shutters, and the mix of voices on the street grew thicker the farther he walked. He followed the road without turning off, letting it pull him away from the district he already knew.

Before long he reached a wide intersection.

The street opened into a small square built around a fountain, the water catching the light as it fell back into the stone basin. Stalls, shops, and restaurants surrounded the square. People crossed from one side to the other, some with baskets, some in travel clothes, a few in finer coats. Carriages cut through the flow whenever the guards at the corners let them pass.

It felt different from both his old world and his village. Not as overwhelming as a giant city from his past life, but far busier and more layered than his hometown. For a moment he simply stood there and watched it.

On one side of the square a signboard stood above the heads of the crowd. Elrond moved a little closer until he could read it.

The road to the right led to the library. The road to the left led to the Adventurer Bureau. The road straight ahead returned to the city entrance.

He frowned slightly.

“I walked straight through this place when I first came in,” he thought. “I did not even see it.”

It made sense. That day he had been focused on finding an inn and reaching the Academy on time. Now that his eyes were not tied to one goal, he was finally noticing what sat on the sides of the road.

For the moment, he turned right toward the library.

The street here was still fairly wide, but the noise thinned out as he walked. There were many small side streets and alleys that branched away between the buildings. Some of them looked like quiet back lanes, others were lined with small signs and looked worth visiting later. Elrond noted a few in his mind and stayed on the main road.

The shops began to change. There were more houses with small yards or balconies, and fewer large storefronts. Flower shops and handicraft stores sat between the homes, and occasionally an inn showed its sign, ready for travelers who preferred a calmer area.

After a while a different sort of building came into view ahead of him.

It was a large red structure with a wide front and an open gate. People went in and out in regular intervals. Most of them wore long outer robes over their clothes. The cut and color were similar from person to person, close enough that Elrond assumed they were some kind of uniform.

“Probably a magic school,” he thought, watching for a few moments from outside the gate.

Then he noticed a plaque fixed to the stone beside the gate, with clear letters that read *Arbalest Public Library*.

“…So it’s the city’s public library,” he corrected himself in his head. “Those robes are probably Academy uniforms. They’re just here to pick up or return books.”

He did not go inside yet. Now that he knew it was the public library, he understood he could come back whenever he needed a book or a quiet place to study. For today, he wanted to see more of the city before the light faded, so he fixed the red building and its open gate in his memory, then turned away and walked back toward the fountain square.

Once he returned to the first fountain square, he took the road opposite the library this time.

The air changed again in a few dozen steps. This district already felt more like a market. Traders were opening their doors, setting out crates and goods on stands. The smell of metal, leather, cooked food, and spilled ale mixed together. Taverns and equipment shops stood side by side. The people here walked with purpose and carried all kinds of gear.

After some distance the road widened into another busy intersection, this one packed with stalls. People stopped to argue over prices or to point out items they needed. At the end of this street stood a large building whose front wall was almost entirely open. There were no doors to separate inside from outside.

Elrond slowed.

From the street he could see the interior clearly. A long counter ran along one side where a receptionist spoke with people in turns. Tables and chairs filled the open floor, some occupied by people eating and

drinking, others by groups in the middle of discussions. It felt like a tavern that had been rearranged for work instead of only food.

He looked up and read the sign above the open front.

Adventurer Bureau.

He stood there for a while, watching people go in and out. Some wore armor, some light travel clothes, some just carried bags and weapons. A thought came to him without effort.

“If I need extra money or work later, this might be one of the places to ask,” he thought.

He did not step inside. For now he only wanted to remember where it was and what it looked like. Once he felt that he had seen enough, he moved on.

The intersection ahead sent streets in several directions. One of them ran toward the rear of the city, where the land seemed to rise. Elrond followed it.

The road sloped upward little by little. It was not steep enough to trouble the carriages that used it, but it was high enough that the houses began to fall away behind him. There were other people walking in the same direction, some alone, some in small groups.

The sun had started to drop toward the horizon.

“If there is a view from up there, now is the time to see it,” he thought.

He kept climbing until the road leveled out near the top of the hill.

From there, the city spread below him. Rooftops and streets formed a pattern he could finally understand as a whole instead of as scattered pieces. Beyond the far edge of the buildings, at the line where the land met the sky, he saw a faint strip that caught the light.

The ocean lay there, just visible as a thin band of color under the setting sun.

Elrond stood in a spot a little away from the main path and watched as the light shifted and the sky darkened. The capital felt different from this height, distant and quiet, even though he knew the noise still ran through its streets below.

“This is enough for the first day,” he thought.

He fixed the path in his mind, from the inn to the fountain square, from there to the library side, the red building, the Adventurer Bureau, and finally this hill. With that rough map settled in his head, he turned back toward the road that would take him down again and back to his room.

His first proper walk through the city ended there, for now.

### Chapter 17: 13 – Orientation

#### Scene 1

The day after tomorrow came faster than Elrond expected.

He woke before the sun was fully up and sat on the edge of the bed for a moment, staring at the folded Academy letter on the table. Orientation for S Class. The words had not changed in two days, no matter how many times he checked.

He washed, combed his hair, and put on the same best shirt he had worn for the entrance exam. It was not new anymore, but it was still the neatest thing he owned. After that he folded the letter once more, slipped it into an inner pocket, and patted it once to make sure it was there.

"Okay. Don’t forget to ask about the scholarship when there’s a good moment," he reminded himself.

With that decided, he left the inn and headed toward the Royal Academy again.

The streets to the Academy were familiar now, and his steps settled into the same rhythm as on exam day. The difference started at the gates.

Two days ago, the grounds had been filled with candidates, families, and staff. Today, the people moving through the entrance wore matching uniforms. Dark jackets, lined coats, skirts and trousers cut to the same pattern. They moved in small groups, talking as they climbed the steps and crossed the paths.

Upperclassmen, Elrond guessed. Students who already belonged here.

“As far as I remember, the entrance period is still going,” he thought. “So why are there this many students on the grounds already.”

The question lingered for a heartbeat, then he set it aside. Whatever timetable the Academy used for its older years, it had nothing to do with the appointment written on his letter.

He walked across the open yard and stepped into the main building.

The inside was almost a different place.

The long counters that had filled the hall on exam day were gone. In their place stood an open space that actually looked like a lobby. Benches and low tables lined the walls. The stone floor was clean and unmarked by extra screens or ropes. The air felt calmer.

Elrond had heard that the entrance exams were only held for two days, but it still surprised him that they had taken everything down and put the hall back into its usual shape so quickly.

The far side of the lobby opened into a garden court. Two days ago, nobles had taken that space over and used it as a place to talk and snack while they waited. Now the same space was quiet. A few students sat

under the trees, reading or writing. In one corner, two students practiced spell patterns with low voices and careful hands, their light barely visible in the daytime.

Elrond stood just inside the doorway and looked around.

Without the temporary counters, the room felt wider. It took him a moment to notice the reception that actually belonged here. On the far left side, against the wall, there was a fixed desk with shelves and ledgers behind it. A permanent sign hung above it.

He exhaled once through his nose.

“That must have been here the entire time,” he thought. “I was looking only at the exam counters and never even saw it.”

He crossed the lobby and came to a stop in front of the desk.

The staff member on duty, a man in standard Academy colors, was writing in a logbook. He did not look up right away. When he did, his expression was flat, the kind of face that had already answered too many simple questions that morning.

…“Um… excuse me,” Elrond said, stopping just short of the desk.

The man lifted his eyes only partway from the logbook.

“Yes?” he replied.

“I… think I’m supposed to be here for orientation,” Elrond said. “For new students.”

The man gave him a brief, uninterested once-over, then let out a quite heavy sigh before his gaze dropped back to the page as if that settled it.

“General orientation for new students will be held in three days,” he said without even looking up. “You’re early. Come back then.”

For a second Elrond wondered if he had misheard. His fingers pressed against the letter inside his pocket before he drew it out.

“But... My letter says my orientation is today,” he said, placing it on the counter. “T-They told me to come to the Academy this morning.”

He laid the letter on the counter.

The staff member reached for it with the same bored movement he had used a moment ago. His eyes moved over the lines in a routine way, until they reached the part that listed the assigned class.

First Year – S Class.

Something in his face shifted. His back straightened by a small degree. His eyes went back and read the line again, slower this time.

“…Mr Elrond von Astrea,” he said.

“Yes,” Elrond answered.

The man turned the logbook toward himself and ran a finger down one column. He found the right page, then the right entry.

There it was, the line for S Class orientation on that day with Elrond’s name written beside it.

“My apologies,” the staff member said as he straightened a little and closed the logbook. “You are scheduled for a separate S Class orientation and your name is clearly written here so I should have checked it first.”

After he closed the logbook he stepped out from behind the desk and gave a small proper bow.

“If you would come with me,” he said. “I will take you to the meeting room.”

Elrond gave a small nod so he would not make a fuss here and then he followed after the man.

They walked along one of the side corridors that led away from the main lobby. With each step, the noise of the crowd behind them faded into the quieter echo of their footsteps and the distant murmur of classrooms. They passed stairs and closed doors and tall windows that looked out over internal courtyards.

Elrond kept track of the turns in his head as they walked.

After a short climb up one flight of stairs and another turn, the staff member stopped in front of a door set slightly apart from the others. The wood was polished, the handle metal rather than simple iron.

"Here," the man said. "This room has been reserved for your orientation."

He opened the door, checked the inside for a moment, and then turned back to Elrond.

"Please wait in this room for a little while," he said. "I will go and call the person who will guide you."

Elrond stepped inside and the staff member closed the door behind him.

The room was not large, but it was bright. Light came in from tall windows on one side and fell over two couches that faced each other with a low table between them for placing food or drinks. Beside the windows there was a simple table that could be used for writing, and along one wall stood book racks filled with ledgers and thinner volumes. There was no one else inside.

Elrond sat down on the couch, and while he waited he traced the path they had taken in his head and made sure he could still recall each turn.

After a short wait, there was a knock on the door.

"Excuse me," a calm voice said from the other side.

The door opened and Lacia stepped into the room wearing the formal attire of Academy staff. She looked around once and when she saw him her expression softened into a small, composed smile.

"Welcome back, Elrond, we meet again," Lacia said. "I am glad you made it on time. For today, I will be in charge of your orientation."

When she greeted him so naturally, he sat up a bit straighter without thinking, the same way he used to when a teacher called on him in his previous life.

“Hello, um… Lady Roosevelt,” he said. “I didn’t expect you would be guiding me personally.”

Lacia let out a short breath that was close to a laugh.

“There is no need for such formality,” she said. “When it is just the two of us, you can call me Lacia.”

Elrond hesitated. Calling an examiner by her given name felt too familiar. In his previous life he would at least have added a title. This world had its own rules, but the instinct to leave a small distance was the same.

“…Then, Lady Lacia,” he said. “If that is acceptable.”

“That is fine,” Lacia replied with a small nod. “In that case, let us begin.”

Lacia walked over to the small table beside the window, took a thin notebook and a pen from the stack there, and then sat down on the couch opposite him with the notebook resting on her knees. Elrond shifted his seat a little so he faced her more directly while still keeping the door in his sight.

“As written in your letter, this is an individual orientation for S Class students,” Lacia said. “The Royal Academy’s regular classes follow a fixed pattern, but S Class does not simply repeat that.”

“Normally, students attend lectures that build their foundation step by step. In S Class, we assume you already have that foundation. The lessons review what you have learned up to now and then focus more on practical application and self–improvement. The learning style is more open and flexible compared to the regular classes.”

Elrond listened without interrupting and marked the important parts in his head, letting the explanation settle.

'So this is to decide how that ‘flexible’ part will look like for me,' he thought.

“That is why this individual orientation is necessary,” Lacia continued. “Rather than placing you into a completely fixed schedule, we ask you directly which areas you feel you are lacking in. After that, we adjust your timetable inside the S Class framework.”

She raised her pen, ready to write.

“First, I will explain the broad areas the Academy covers,” she said. “Then you can tell me where you want to focus.”

Elrond gave a small nod.

“At the Royal Academy,” Lacia said, “you will study magic, physical training, general knowledge, natural studies, arithmetic, etiquette, and political and social affairs. There are also sub–branches under each of these that may appear on your schedule depending on your needs.”

As she spoke, she drew seven short lines down the page and placed a simple heading on each one.

Magic. Physical training. General knowledge. Natural studies. Arithmetic. Etiquette. Affairs.

For the Academy, each of those headings had more weight than the simple word written on the page. Magic was not only the spells a student could already cast but also how safely they handled their mana, how steady their control stayed under pressure, and how well they adjusted a spell when the situation changed in front of them.

Physical training covered the body that had to carry that power. It meant weapon drills and basic forms, but also balance, stamina, and the habit of moving together with other people instead of fighting alone. A student who collapsed in armor before the day was over failed this part no matter how sharp their sword work looked at the start.

General knowledge gathered everything that did not fit into a single discipline. History of the kingdom, the shape of the land, the names of neighboring countries, and the basic customs and laws that everyone in the capital assumed “people already knew” even though many commoners had never been taught them properly.

Natural studies focused on the land itself and the things that lived on it. Monsters, animals, and plants, the way they reacted when mana in an area thickened or thinned, the signs that showed a habitat was about to break, and which places should never be entered without preparation because one wrong step there meant not coming back.

Arithmetic looked simple at a glance and turned cruel when someone treated it lightly. It handled coin and trade, but also rations, distances, and days on the road, how many people a wagon could support, and how many potions or bandages had to be ready before a unit moved out. One wrong number there meant supplies that arrived too late or not enough medicine when people needed it.

Etiquette decided whether a meeting ended in a bow or in quiet resentment. It covered greetings, posture, behaviour at a table, how to address someone above or below in rank, and even how to write and fold a letter when sending it to a person of higher status so the paper itself did not become an insult.

Affairs was the Academy’s short way of naming the web behind all of that. It meant how the royal family, the great houses, the ministries, the church, and the guilds held and traded their power, how decisions actually moved from one place to another, and how to listen when people chose not to say everything directly in front of others.

Elrond’s gaze moved down the list until it stopped on the last two headings. Out of everything on the page, those looked the most unfamiliar to him.

“Those last two are the problem,” he thought.

He could picture his father drilling him with a wooden sword in the yard and his mother correcting his casting when his mana wobbled, but there was no memory of anyone telling him which fork to pick up at a noble table or how to answer if a lord asked a question that was not really a question.

“Up to this point, which fields have you studied on your own or with your parents?” she asked. “And which do you feel are lacking?”

Elrond took a moment before answering, arranging his thoughts.

“In terms of magic and physical training, I have been taught the basics,” he said. “My mother handled magic, and my father handled the sword. I have also studied arithmetic and some general knowledge.”

Those were the parts he could prove with action if someone asked. He drew a slow breath before he touched the parts he could not.

“But I was born as a commoner in a frontier town,” he continued. “I have almost no experience with etiquette or with political and social affairs. I think those are the areas I lack the most, and I will need them if I am going to deal with nobles and higher society in the future.”

He remembered the way people had glanced at him at the Academy gate and the way conversations at the inn had shifted when nobles were mentioned.

Lacia did not look surprised or confused by his answer. Many first–years asked for stronger magic or more sword drills, but for a commoner coming from the frontier, admitting that etiquette and affairs were his weakest fields was the most natural thing in the world, and the fact that he understood that from the start only made her take his request more seriously.

She turned the notebook a little toward herself and, on the lines for etiquette and affairs, wrote a short note that would tell any instructor who saw the page later that those subjects could not be treated as extras.

Etiquette – priority. Affairs – priority.

“I understand,” she said. “We will make sure your schedule reflects that.”

She underlined both notes once for emphasis.

Elrond’s eyes went back to the notebook, but a corner of his mind circled around the same thought.

“When am I supposed to ask about the scholarship,” he wondered. “If I bring it up at the wrong time, it will sound like that was the only reason I came.”

For now, he pushed it down and waited.

Lacia closed the notebook and set it on the low table between them.

“Next, I will explain the layout of the Academy,” she said. “It will be easier if you can picture the grounds before we walk through them.”

She stood, crossed to the table by the window, and returned with a folded sheet. When she spread it out on the table, Elrond saw a simple map drawn in clear lines. Buildings, courtyards, and training fields were all marked with neat letters.

He shifted forward on the couch so he could see.

“This is the main building,” Lacia said, tapping the center. “Most of your lectures and indoor lessons will be held here.”

Her finger moved to one side.

“Over here is the magic training area,” she continued. “Outdoor spell practice, barrier exercises, and anything that might damage the surroundings will be done there.”

She traced a short line to the opposite side.

“And this section is for physical training,” she said. “Weapon drills, formation practice, and general conditioning. You will become familiar with both of these places very quickly.”

Her finger slid to the back of the map, where a group of rooms was drawn together.

“This wing is reserved for instructors and other staff,” she said. “If you are called there, it will usually be for meetings or evaluations.”

Elrond followed each point and fixed the positions in his head, linking them to the path he had already taken from the gate.

“After this briefing, I will walk you around the grounds,” Lacia added. “We will visit each of these areas in person so you do not have to rely on the map alone.”

When she said that, Elrond felt his chance to ask about the scholarship slip a little further away.

“If I stop her now, it will slow everything down,” he thought. “Maybe after we finish with the buildings.”

Lacia’s finger moved again and came to rest on a block of rooms marked a little apart from the rest.

“And this is the dormitory area,” she said.

The dormitory building was drawn with several floors marked. On the lowest one, a smaller section had been outlined and labeled more carefully than the others.

“For first–year students, rooms in this building are prepared in advance,” Lacia explained. “Within it, S Class has its own section on the lowest floor.”

She tapped the outlined part.

“This part is separated from the rest of the dorm by a locked door,” she said. “It is reserved for S Class students only. However, most S Class students are nobles from the capital or from houses that keep a residence here. Many of them live with their families instead of using the dormitory, so this floor is usually very quiet.”

She looked up from the map.

“If you choose to live there, it may feel a bit lonely,” she said. “There are not many students who stay in that section.”

Lonely was not the first word that came to Elrond’s mind.

“If I can stay there, I don’t have to keep paying for the inn,” he thought.

He ran the numbers in his head without meaning to. The cost of one night at the inn, multiplied by weeks, then by months, compared to a bed that was already waiting for him inside the Academy.

The surprise at being offered a place there came first, followed quickly by a quiet relief that settled in his chest.

Lacia went on, as if she had seen that calculation pass across his face.

“The S Class dormitory includes breakfast in the common room on that floor,” she said. “On certain occasions, there are formal dinners prepared only for S Class students. The Academy calls them gala dinners, and they are used when announcements or invitations that concern only S Class must be made.”

“Gala dinner…”

For a moment, Elrond pictured a long table set with silverware and glass, nobles in formal clothes speaking in low voices while servants moved between them. The image lasted only a breath before it turned into a list of things he did not yet know how to do.

“Another reason to learn etiquette quickly,” he thought.

Lacia folded the map halfway, leaving the dormitory section still visible.

“Of course, there are rules for using that dormitory,” she said. “I will tell you the most important ones now.”

She held up a hand, counting them off with her fingers as she spoke.

“First, there is a curfew,” she said. “At night, after the bell that marks the end of evening study, the doors to the dorm are locked. Leaving the dorm after that without permission from a staff member is treated as a violation.”

“Second, students who are not assigned to S Class are not allowed past the door that separates your floor from the rest of the dormitory,” she continued. “If you wish to meet friends from other classes, you may use the common rooms on the upper floors or the shared spaces on the grounds, but not the S Class corridor itself.”

“Third, you are not allowed to practice combat magic or weapon drills inside the dormitory,” she said. “For that, you must use the training areas we saw on the map. The dorm is for resting and study, not for testing how strong your spells have become.”

“Fourth, you must keep noise to a reasonable level at night,” Lacia went on. “Voices, instruments, and any other sound that might disturb other students should be kept low after curfew, even if your own floor is quiet.”

“Fifth, your room and the shared areas must be kept in proper condition,” she said. “If something breaks, you are expected to report it instead of hiding it. Repeated damage or disorder will affect how the Academy evaluates your conduct, not only your scores.”

She let her raised hand fall back to her lap.

“These are the main rules that concern you,” Lacia said. “There are others written in more detail, but if you follow these, you will not have trouble.”

Elrond went over them once in his mind. Curfew. No guests on the floor. No training in the dorm. Quiet at night. Do not break things.

Compared to the rules he had lived under on the frontier, they felt strict in some places and strangely generous in others.

“A bed, breakfast, and even the chance to stand in the same room as nobles at a formal dinner,” he thought. “If this is part of what they already planned to give S Class, can I still ask about the scholarship on top of it?”

The question returned stronger than before. This time, it stayed at the front of his thoughts as he looked at the map.

Elrond was still looking at the dormitory section on the map when Lacia lightly tapped the paper with the back of her finger, as if remembering something she had almost skipped.

“There is one more thing I should explain before we go outside,” she said. “These are the general rules of the Academy. If you keep these in mind, you will avoid most trouble.”

She folded the map the rest of the way and set it beside the notebook.

“First,” she said, “you must attend the lectures and practical lessons that are marked as required. If you cannot attend because of illness or some other unavoidable reason, you must report it. Simply disappearing from class without a word is treated as negligence.”

Elrond thought of how Selene had handled his studies. If he had tried to skip a lesson by vanishing somewhere, she would have found him within the hour.

“Second, you may not start fights on Academy grounds,” Lacia continued. “Duels and sparring are only permitted in the proper places and under supervision. If you raise your hand or your magic against another student outside those conditions, it will be treated as an offense, even if you say it was only practice.”

He remembered the training yard in his hometown and how quickly things could get out of hand when pride was involved. In a place filled with nobles, that warning felt heavier.

“Third, the use of magic is restricted in certain areas,” she said. “Inside the main building, the dormitory, and the streets around the Academy, you are not allowed to cast offensive spells unless there is a clear emergency. Normal training belongs in the designated fields.”

She raised another finger.

“Fourth, cheating on written exams, altering records, or using magic to interfere with evaluations is forbidden,” Lacia said. “If someone is caught doing that, the Academy will not protect them.”

That one was simple enough. If he needed to rely on tricks just to pass an exam, then his place in S Class would be a joke anyway.

“And fifth,” she finished, “you may not use your status as a Royal Academy student to involve the school in personal business. That includes making promises in the Academy’s name or acting as if the Academy supports a private deal or dispute.”

Elrond thought of Darius’s faction and the nobles who wanted to pull students into their own circles. It was easy to see why the rule existed.

“These five are not the only rules written,” Lacia said. “But as long as you remember them and use common sense, you should have no problems.”

She gave him a moment, then looked toward him.

“Do you have any questions so far?” she asked.
