Elrond pulled his thoughts away from the map and the rules. The scholarship question burned at the back of his mind, but something else came out first.

“Um…” he said, raising his hand a little out of habit. “How about the lecture scheduling system? You mentioned it briefly, but I still don’t quite understand.”

“I see,” Lacia said. “Then I will explain that in more detail.”

She reached for the notebook again and opened it on a fresh page.

“For S Class,” she said, “your schedule is built in three layers. The first layer is the default timetable. These are the lessons that every S Class student takes together. If you do nothing, you simply follow that.”

Her pen drew a simple grid as she spoke.

“The second layer is made from the fields you told me you are lacking in,” she went on. “For you, that means additional lessons in etiquette and in political and social affairs. These will be placed into your schedule as fixed sessions, just like your core classes.”

Elrond watched her mark two slots on the page with short notes.

“And the third layer,” Lacia said, “consists of open spaces. During those times, you may choose to attend extra lectures, ask for guidance, or use the time for self–study. S Class students are trusted to decide how to use those hours. That kind of freedom is not given to other classes.”

So, if he used the empty spaces well, he could stretch what the Academy gave him. If he wasted them, no one would stop him from falling behind.

Elrond rested his hand lightly against his chin for a moment while he put the pieces together in his head.

“That sounds good,” he said at last. “You can continue, Lady Lacia.”

“Very well,” she said.

She closed the notebook again, leaving the rough grid visible, and drew in a quiet breath.

“Now,” Lacia said, “that brings us to the next topic: tuition.”

The word hit harder than he expected.

She did not circle around it.

“Normally, the tuition for a student in S Class is twenty–five gold coins per term,” she said.

Elrond felt the air catch in his throat. His shoulders tightened before he could stop them, and a chill ran down his back. Twenty–five. That was more than double what he had even brought with him.

His reaction must have shown on his face, because Lacia did not continue right away. His fingers curled against his knee, and he had to force them to relax.

“But,” she said, “in your case, the Academy has agreed to grant a scholarship.”

Elrond’s head snapped up before he could stop himself.

“A scholarship…?” he said.

“Yes,” Lacia said, as if answering that unspoken word. “You are a special case. You come from a commoner background, and your exam results were exceptional. Because of that, the tuition will be reduced.”

Some of the tension drained from his shoulders. The breath he had been holding slipped out of him slowly.

“Reduced to seven gold coins,” she said.

The relief stopped halfway.

Seven.

Elrond felt his thoughts begin to race again, this time in cleaner lines. He had brought ten gold coins to support himself through three years. The nights at the inn and the meals he had eaten had already cut that down to a little over nine. If he paid seven gold for tuition, he would be left with less than three.

Less than three gold to cover everything else until he found a way to earn more.

He tried to keep his face still, but the weight of that number pressed against his chest. Lacia’s eyes narrowed slightly, watching him.

“Is there any problem?” she asked.

Elrond swallowed once.

“Um…” He gathered his thoughts, then forced the question out. “Is there any scholarship that completely removes the tuition?”

For a moment she simply looked at him. The surprise on her face was small, but it was there. When she answered, her voice had lost some of its earlier firmness.

“I am afraid there is no such scholarship,” Lacia said. “The reduction to seven gold is already the maximum support the Academy can offer under the current rules. I am sorry. There is nothing more I can do about the tuition itself.”

The apology sounded honest, not formal.

“It is all right,” Elrond said, more quickly than he felt. “I will find a way to manage.”

If he stayed in the S Class dormitory, he could at least cut the cost of lodging. He would have to be careful with food and anything else he bought. Even so, three gold over three years was thin enough to make his stomach tighten.

There was one more thing he needed to know before they left the room.

“In that case,” he asked, “am I allowed to take a side job to earn money? As long as it does not interfere with my studies.”

“That is possible,” Lacia said. “The Academy does not forbid students from working, as long as it does not harm your grades or the Academy’s reputation. If you choose to take a job, you must make sure it does not keep you from attending classes or draw you into anything… questionable.”

Elrond nodded slowly.

“In other words, if I fall behind because of it, that will be my own fault,” he thought.

“Understood,” he said.

They both rose from the couch.

“In that case, let us begin the tour,” Lacia said.

Elrond followed her out of the room and back into the corridor. The air outside felt a little lighter now that the question of tuition had at least been given a shape, even if the answer still pressed on his chest.

They started with the closest place.

“This side holds the teachers’ rooms,” Lacia said as they walked. “If you are ever summoned for an individual meeting or evaluation, it will usually be here.”

The doors they passed were plain, each marked with a small nameplate. Elrond fixed the corridor and its turns in his memory. From here, it would be a short walk back to the meeting room he had just left.

From the teachers’ wing they moved toward the main lecture buildings. All of the structures were connected by open hallways with stone balustrades. Light and wind flowed through them easily, and the roofs above kept off the sun.

As they walked, Lacia pointed out each building and gave a short explanation. Which one held first-year lectures, which floors were used for upper years, where the examination rooms were, and which doors students did not need to use unless they were called.

For Elrond, seeing each place once was enough. He linked the halls and turns together in his head and watched the map he had seen on the table settle into something solid.

Next, Lacia led him toward the magic buildings.

“This is where most magic lectures and training are held,” she said.

Classrooms lined the corridors, doors half-open here and there as voices drifted out. At the end of one hallway, Elrond saw the familiar long room where the magic exam had taken place. From this angle it looked even more like a shooting range, with targets lined up behind thick glass. The traces of practice spells had already been cleaned away.

Beyond that room, the corridor opened into the magic practice field.

Elrond stopped for a moment at the edge.

The field was a wide, open space, surrounded on all sides by partitions and low walls. Simple spectator seats rose in tiers along one side, enough for an entire class to watch. The size was hard to grasp at first glance, but as he followed the lines of the walls he guessed it was at least three times larger than a soccer field from his previous life.

Several students were already practicing inside. Flashes of light and short bursts of wind appeared and vanished as spells struck the practice targets. The sound came to him muted and steady.

“Official magic duels are sometimes held here as well,” Lacia said. “When the Academy needs to judge a formal match, this is one of the places we use.”

He pictured the same field with the seats full and noble students watching from the shade, then stored the image away and followed her back into the hallway.

They crossed an open corridor that curved around the outside of the magic field and approached another building set a little apart.

“This is the physical training area,” Lacia said.

It was smaller than the magic field, but still large. Inside, Elrond saw students sparring with wooden swords and shields, moving across marked squares on the floor while an instructor watched. Racks of practice weapons lined one wall. There were sandbags, wooden dummies, and enough open space for drills and formation practice.

From a quick look, it had everything needed to train a person for real combat.

Lacia gave a brief explanation of the kinds of lessons held there, then they circled the building and returned along the corridor toward the main hall.

Walking this loop, Elrond had the sense that the entire Academy had been laid out with a purpose. The lecture halls, the magic buildings, the practice field, and the training area all connected in a way that made sense. There were no wasted paths that led nowhere. Once he drew the full shape in his head, it felt strangely natural.

They had gone through the places he would be using most often. That left one last destination.

“The dormitory is next,” Lacia said.

From the main hall they took the route that led back toward the front of the Academy. The dorms were close to the entrance gate. At one intersection, going straight led toward the exit, while turning right led deeper into the dormitory area. They turned right and followed the path.

From the outside, the dormitory building looked almost like a small noble residence. The area around it was lively but orderly, with a small park, a fountain, and trees casting shade over benches where students sat talking.

They stepped inside.

The entrance hall was bright, with a counter set against the far wall. The receptionist behind it raised her head at the sound of the door and smiled when she saw Lacia.

“Good morning,” Lacia said. “We are here about the room for Elrond von Astrea. First year, S Class.”

The receptionist checked a prepared ledger, nodded, and stepped out from behind the counter.

“His room is ready,” she said. “Please come this way.”

The entrance to the S Class section was directly behind the wall at the back of the reception desk. From the lobby it looked like part of the decoration, but when they moved closer, Elrond saw a set of grand doors there. The doors were carved and framed with metal, the kind of design he would have expected at a noble estate rather than a dorm.

When they passed through, the change in atmosphere hit him.

A large chandelier hung from the ceiling above an open hall. The floor beneath his feet was polished granite, smooth enough to reflect the light. To Elrond, it felt almost like stepping into a small royal palace.

“This hall is for S Class students only,” the receptionist explained. “The other dormitory floors are separated on the opposite side.”

They moved toward the stairs at the side of the hall.

“Breakfast and, on certain days, dinner are served through that door,” the receptionist added, indicating a wide doorway to the right that led into what looked like a dining room. “You may use it from tomorrow morning.”

On the second floor, a corridor ran along the edge of the hall, with a railing instead of a solid wall. From there, Elrond could look down and see the chandelier and the lobby below as if he were standing on a balcony.

At the far end of the corridor, facing the hall, one door stood open.

“This is your room,” the receptionist said.

Elrond stepped through the doorway and stopped.

His jaw loosened before he caught himself.

The floor was made of white granite tiles that matched the hall below. Against one wall stood a bed so wide he wondered for a moment if it was meant for more than one person, then pushed the thought away. On another side there was a desk with a large mirror above it, and beside that a comfortable-looking couch. A tall window opened onto a small balcony, and heavy curtains hung neatly at the sides.

A wardrobe stood ready along the wall, and there was a door that led into a private bathroom. When he glanced inside, he saw a clean basin and a bathtub large enough for a full soak.

It was more than anything he had imagined when he heard the word “dormitory.”

“As part of the service here, the room will be cleaned regularly,” the receptionist said. “Your laundry can also be collected and returned. If you have any problems with the room, you may inform the staff at the front desk.”

In Elrond’s mind, a simple thought formed in clear lines.

“If this is included, the seven gold might actually be worth it.”

Lodging, cleaning, laundry, and breakfast, all in a place like this. If he added the chance to be this close to the Academy itself, it changed the weight of the number he had been carrying.

The receptionist walked over to the desk.

“Your prepared items are here,” she said.

Laid out in order were his Academy uniform, folded carefully, a spare key for his room, another key for the gate to the dorm section, and a set of basic necessities for a first-year student. Writing tools, notebooks, and a small booklet that, from the cover, looked like a summary of school rules.

Elrond followed her explanation and checked each item with his eyes. Everything he would need to start his life here was lined up in front of him.

“With this, the dormitory explanation is complete,” the receptionist said, stepping back with a polite smile.

“Thank you for your help,” Lacia replied.

They left the room as it was and walked back down the stairs, out through the grand doors, and through the dormitory lobby. The receptionist bowed them out, and the noise of the park outside met them again when they stepped into the light.

From there, they retraced their path toward the main hall. The Academy grounds already felt different now that he could attach rooms, windows, and corridors to the lines on the map.

At the entrance to the hall, Lacia came to a natural stop.

“This concludes your individual orientation,” she said. “In three days, the standard first-year orientation will be held in this hall. You are allowed to join it as well if you wish, but it is optional for you.”

Elrond turned to face her fully.

“Thank you for everything today, Lady Lacia,” he said. “For the explanations and for guiding me around.”

“You are welcome,” she said. “I hope your time at the Academy will be a good one.”

She gave him a small bow, and he returned it.

With that, Lacia turned back toward the teachers’ wing, and Elrond headed toward the exit at a calm pace.

The main hall felt different now compared to the day of the exam. The doors and corridors were no longer just part of a test site. They were places he would be walking through every day as a student of S Class. That thought stayed with him as he stepped out through the Academy gate and into the noise of the city.

On the familiar street leading back to the inn, his hand went to the inside of his shirt. The folded letter from the Academy was still there, and next to it were the two small keys he had just received. One for a room that looked far beyond anything a frontier commoner should have, and one for the dorm gate that marked his place in S Class.

“Seven gold for tuition and a dorm like that on top of it,” he thought. “I really cannot waste this chance.”

With that quiet resolve set in his mind, Elrond walked on toward the inn, his fingers resting on the weight of the letter and keys as the first day of his new life at the Academy came to a close.

### Chapter 18: 14 – Seeking a Better Life

#### Scene 1

The next morning, Elrond sat on his bed and stared at the ceiling.

The room at the inn was the same as always. The same worn beams, the same small window, the same faint smell of wood polish and old dust. The only thing that had changed was the weight sitting in his head.

“I already have a room in the dorm,” he thought. “So when am I actually going to move there…”

He glanced toward his pack in the corner, then toward the small wooden receipt the innkeeper had given him. He had already paid for ten days in advance when he arrived in the capital. There were still a few days left on that payment, and it felt wasteful to walk away from it while he still slept well here.

On the other hand, there was now a room waiting for him in the Academy dormitory. A proper bed, a desk, a place that belonged to S Class.

He weighed both sides for a while, then let out a quiet breath.

'…I will stay here for now,' he decided.

The streets around the inn were closer to the places he had in mind for today, and he already had one thing he needed to start on as soon as possible.

;If I cannot secure my living costs, the rest of my plans will fall apart,' he thought.

He ran through the simple options he had thought about last night.

Working as a waiter. Helping in a shop. Carrying goods for a warehouse.

On paper, those sounded safe and ordinary. In his head, it became a very clear picture of himself standing in front of a shop owner and trying to explain that he was a fifteen–year–old from a town far away, with no family in Arbalest and no proper references, asking them to trust him with a real job.

'Even if they listened,' he thought, 'would they really hand proper work to someone like that?'

He imagined the polite smile that hid refusal and the way the conversation would end. The more he pictured it, the more unrealistic it felt.

So he set that idea aside.

What remained was the Adventurer Bureau.

Elrond stood up and changed into the clothes he used to wear on patrol back in his hometown. The fabric felt different from the neat shirt he had used for the Academy. It was thicker, tougher, and his body remembered the way it moved in it. He strapped his sword into place on his back so it sat where his hand could reach it easily, and he pulled on a pair of good leather gloves he had not used in a while.

When he finished adjusting the straps, he flexed his fingers once.

'This looks more like someone who actually goes outside the city walls,' he thought.

He left the inn and headed toward the street he remembered.

The last time he had walked that way, he had only watched the Adventurer Bureau from a distance, more to understand the flow of people than to do anything with it. Today he was going there as a proper visitor, and that simple difference made his steps feel heavier and more focused at the same time.

After a decent walk, the familiar open hall came into view.

The building faced the street directly, without a closed front door. The wide opening led straight into a hall that was almost an extension of the road. Voices and footfalls spilled out into the street together with the smell of leather, metal, and dust.

Elrond crossed the threshold.

Inside, the place was crowded. Adventurers moved in and out in small groups, some talking quietly as they checked notices on the boards, others carrying bundles that looked like monster materials. The noise was restless but not chaotic. It felt like a place where people came because there was work to do.

Elrond did not stop to look around for long. He walked straight toward the reception counter that stretched along one side of the hall and picked an empty section where a receptionist was not yet busy.

The woman there lifted her head as he approached.

“Welcome,” she said with a warm smile. “My name is Kaira Denholt. What can I help you with today? I do not think I have seen you around here before.”

Her tone was open and easy, like someone used to dealing with all kinds of people without letting any of it show on her face.

“Yes,” Elrond said. “I just got here not long ago.”

He paused for a beat, then continued.

“I wanted to ask if it is possible for me to register and take jobs as an adventurer,” he said.

He chose his words carefully and tried to keep his voice steady. He did not have any recommendation to lean on, so he could only be honest.

Kaira’s expression shifted a little, the way someone’s face did when they wanted to help but already knew the answer would not be simple.

“I am truly sorry,” she said gently. “At the moment we cannot take any more new individual adventurers. For now, only Companies are allowed to register with this Bureau.”

“Companies…?” Elrond repeated.

He had seen the word in passing, but he had never seen it applied to people in this world yet.

Kaira gave a small nod.

“Yes,” she said. “A Company is a group of adventurers who decide to work together and register themselves with the city’s civil office. They choose a leader, set up their own internal rules, and come here as one unit instead of as separate people.”

She spoke in a way that made it sound as normal as registering a business.

'In that case,' Elrond thought, 'it is closer to a corporation than to a loose party.'

At the same time, the way she described it, with leaders and members and shared rules, made it feel like the guilds he had seen again and again in games and stories.

Kaira went on before the quiet between them could grow heavy.

“One of the reasons we only accept the Company system,” she said, “is that it makes things easier for the city. Each member’s information can be linked to the civil registry through the Company, and their taxes can be tracked properly. It keeps the work clean for both us and the offices that handle records.”

She folded her hands lightly on the counter.

“Because of that,” she said, “we are not accepting any more solo adventurers for the time being. Only new Companies can register right now.”

Elrond felt something inside him sink.

He had come here dressed for work and ready to start, and in a few sentences the path he had chosen closed in front of him. If even the Adventurer Bureau was full for individual people, there was no place for someone like him in their normal system.

“I see,” he said.

He lowered his eyes for a moment and stepped back half a pace. His body was already turning a little away from the counter, as if it had decided that the conversation was over even while his mind was still catching up.

“Thank you for telling me,” he added.

He was ready to leave and look for some other path, even if he did not know yet what that would be.

Kaira watched the way he moved and did not let him walk away so easily.

“Wait a moment,” she said.

Her voice stopped him more quickly than a hand on his shoulder would have.

“There is another option,” she said. “If you are all right with something a bit different.”

Elrond turned back toward her.

“Another option…?” he asked.

“Yes,” Kaira said. “You can work as a freelance monster hunter.”

She let the term hang there for a heartbeat so it had room to settle.

“In that case, you do not register as a full adventurer,” she explained. “However, you are still allowed to take monster subjugation requests that are marked as monster hunt from the job board and bring back materials from the monsters you defeat.”

She pointed lightly toward one of the boards, where several sheets were posted in neat rows.

“Only the subjugation requests with the monster hunt mark can be taken by freelance hunters like you,” she added. “The other monster subjugation requests can be taken as usual by registered adventurers, whether they work alone or as part of a Company, but those are outside the range of what we can assign to you.”

“You would not receive a formal completion reward from that,” she said. “The official rewards for those requests are only paid out to registered adventurers in this Bureau, whether they work alone or as part of a Company. However, the materials themselves can be sold by anyone. If you bring back usable parts from a Monster Hunt request you chose, you can sell them directly to us here, and we will pay you for them based on their size and condition.”

So there would be no fixed sum waiting at the end of a job, only whatever he could pull out of a hunt and carry back. For someone with no entry in their books, that was still better than being turned away.

In Elrond’s chest, the feeling of a blocked path shifted into something else.

'If I hunt monsters and manage the risks myself,' he thought, 'I can still earn money.'

It was not the clean, guaranteed income of a formal job, but it matched the skills he already had. He did not need to convince anything. He only needed to bring back proof.

“If that is possible, I would like to take that option,” Elrond said.

Kaira’s smile returned, a little brighter than before.

“I thought you might say that,” she said. “In that case, I will register you as a monster hunter affiliated with the Arbalest Adventurer Bureau.”

Kaira reached to the side of the counter and pulled out a thin wooden board with a sheet clipped to it. The page was neatly ruled and already printed with simple headings.

As he watched her set the board down, Elrond reminded himself that this was not the same as becoming a full adventurer. Proper adventurers registered in the Bureau could take a wide range of work: monster hunts, long expeditions, escort jobs, gathering trips, and many kinds of special requests that flowed in from the city every day.

What she was giving him now was a much narrower role. A monster hunter was someone the Bureau pointed almost entirely at subjugation work. There were so many monster requests coming in from trading companies, artisans, procurement offices, and even from the country itself that the Bureau had carved out this specific job just to handle them. Instead of juggling every kind of task, a monster hunter existed to cut down monsters and bring back parts that still had value.

“This is the monster hunter registration form,” she said. “Please fill in your name, age, place of origin, and any previous combat experience you can write down.”

Elrond accepted the board with both hands.

The questions were straightforward. He wrote “Elrond von Astrea” in the first space, then filled in his age and his hometown. For combat experience, he described patrol work under the town guard and regular monster subjugation around the outskirts, keeping it as simple as he could while still being honest.

When he finished, he checked the lines once more, then slid the board back across the counter.

Kaira took the form and read it quickly. Her eyes moved from the name to the notes about patrol work, then she gave a small, satisfied nod.

“Very well,” she said. “The fee is fifteen silver. After that, I will mark you as registered.”

Elrond reached for the small pouch at his belt. When he loosened the string, the weight in his hand felt lighter than before. He counted out fifteen silver coins one by one on the counter so they formed a neat line, then he pushed them toward her.

Kaira took the form and read it quickly, then checked the coins with a quick, practiced glance and drew them in.

“Thank you,” she said. “In that case, I will proceed.”

She set the form on a square stone plate near her elbow and pressed a small metal tool into one corner of the sheet. There was a brief, soft sound as the seal sank in. When she lifted it away, a clear mark of the Bureau’s crest was left in the paper.

Only after that did she move for a moment with the practiced ease of someone who had done this many times before. After a short exchange at the counter that did not need to be spoken out loud on the hall floor, she reached under the desk and brought something up.

“Here,” she said.

Resting on her palm was a simple necklace. A small tag hung from the cord, engraved with a clear mark.

“This will be your proof,” Kaira said. “As long as you wear it when you bring in materials, we will treat you as a recognized monster hunter under this Bureau.”

Elrond reached out and took it carefully.

The metal was cool against his glove. It was just a small piece of engraved work, but it carried an official shape that the inn, the street, and even the Academy letter did not. It was the first thing in this city that named him as someone who could stand in front of a counter like this and talk about work.

“…Thank you,” he said.

He closed his fingers around the tag for a moment, feeling its weight.

'This is my start,' he thought. 'If I use this properly, I can make the seven gold stretch.'

With the tag in his hand and the noise of the hall around him, Elrond took his first clear step toward earning the money he needed for the life waiting at the Academy.

After that smooth registration, Elrond stepped away from the counter with the necklace in his hand. The light feeling of having some kind of status did not completely erase the dull weight in his chest. He had wanted a clear, formal path like the registered adventurers had, and instead he had ended up a half step to the side of the system.

Even so, life would not wait for his mood to catch up.

“I still have to earn money,” he thought. “If I do not fix that, everything else will stop.”

He slipped the necklace into an inner pocket for now so it would not swing around, then turned toward the job board.

On the way there, his eyes moved over the hall again. Adventurers came and went, some alone and some in groups. Earlier, Kaira had mentioned solo registrations and Companies, and now the flow of people matched her explanation more clearly in his mind. There were people who acted on their own, and there were groups that looked like they always moved together.

“The structure is really solid,” he thought.

He went back over what he had heard at the counter. The Bureau worked with the city’s civil office to manage registrations and taxes. Trading companies and the country issued requests, and the Bureau stood in the middle, linking work, materials, and records in a way that kept everything clean.

“In my old world, this would be something like a properly designed agency,” he thought. “Whoever set this up did not do it halfway.”

The thought left him with a small sense of admiration before he pushed it aside and focused on the board in front of him.

Several people were already standing there, reading notices and talking in low voices. It was not crowded enough to block his view, so he slipped into an open spot and started scanning the papers from one side.

There was a dedicated section for monster subjugation. In that section, several sheets were marked clearly as Monster Hunt. The mark was the same one Kaira had pointed out earlier, the one that meant freelance hunters like him were allowed to take the request.

One of those notices caught his eye.

It was a request to collect Lizardian scales.

Elrond’s mind immediately pulled up the information from the Monster Knowledge book he had read before. A Lizardian was a C-class monster, roughly the size of a crocodile and sometimes even larger. Its body was like a giant lizard with thick scales that were hard to penetrate. When they were young, they lived in caves away from people. When it was time to reproduce, they moved toward the coast and the rivers that led there.

Their scales were valuable as materials. Armor craftsmen used them for reinforcement, and artisans liked them for certain kinds of work that needed both toughness and a particular surface pattern.

He checked the details on the sheet.

The request said the Bureau would purchase a minimum of five back scales in perfect condition. There was no fixed reward listed for completing a hunt. Instead, the Bureau would pay between one and ten silver coins per scale, depending on the size and the condition of each one.

The numbers lined up quickly in his head. Five scales at the lowest price already meant a noticeable amount. If he chose his targets properly and took better pieces, the return could be much higher.

Without meaning to, he felt the corner of his mouth lift.

“There is room to work with this,” he thought.

The feeling of having his path blocked eased a little, and a thin line of hope came back into his chest.

He took the request sheet from the board and turned back toward the counter.

Kaira was free again by the time he approached. When she saw him return with a notice in hand, she gave a small welcoming smile, then her gaze dropped to the text on the paper as he set it down.

Her smile faded into a more careful expression.

“Lizardians?” she said.

Her eyes moved once from the sheet to Elrond’s clothes and the way he carried himself. This was his first hunt as a registered monster hunter in Arbalest, and the request he had chosen was for a C-class monster right from the start. For most new hunters, that was not a simple choice.

Elrond understood what that look meant.

“ Yes. I am already familiar with Lizardians,” he said.

He kept his tone steady and matter of fact rather than defensive.

“Back in my hometown, I helped my father with patrols,” he went on. “When I was thirteen, we had a case where a pack of Lizardians settled near the outskirts. I joined the subjugation and we wiped them out. Dealing with Lizardians is not new to me.”

He did not add any extra weight to his words. He simply stated what had happened.

Kaira watched his face while he spoke and searched for any sign that he was exaggerating. What she saw lined up with the way he had written “regular monster subjugation” on the registration form earlier. After a moment, the tension in her shoulders loosened a little.

“I see,” she said.

The hesitation in her eyes eased and turned into acceptance.

“In that case, I will register this request under your name,” she said. “As a freelance monster hunter, you may take this Monster Hunt request. Please remember to bring back the back scales in good condition if you want the higher evaluation.”

She made a small note on the sheet, then looked up again.

“Be careful out there,” she added. “Even if you have dealt with them before, they are still C-class monsters.”

“I understand,” Elrond said with a small nod.

With the approved request in hand and a clearer goal in front of him, he turned away from the counter. The disappointment from earlier had not vanished completely, but now it shared space with a quiet, focused resolve.

He had a target, a way to turn his skills into money, and a first step toward making his life in the capital hold together.

With the request sheet folded and tucked safely into his pocket, Elrond stepped out of the Adventurer Bureau and back into the street.

The hall’s noise faded behind him as the open air of Arbalest wrapped around his ears again. Carts rattled past, and people moved in steady lines along the stone road. For a moment he simply followed that flow, then he adjusted his grip on his sword’s strap and turned his feet toward the city’s main gate.

The closer he came, the more the view opened.

The grand city gate rose ahead, heavy and solid, with its thick wooden doors set open to frame the road. People walked in and out in a constant stream. Some led pack animals, some pushed handcarts, and others simply carried bundles on their backs. Carriages rolled through in an orderly line, one after another, while guards checked each one as it passed over the glowing magic circle set into the ground.

Elrond watched a wagon’s wheels pass across the circle. The light stirred faintly in response, then calmed. The guards nodded and waved the driver on. It was a simple motion and a simple system, yet it kept the flow moving without breaking.

He stepped through the gate with the others and only then stopped walking.

Just outside the gate, he pulled a folded map from his shirt pocket. The paper was already worn soft at the creases. He opened it carefully and traced his finger along the markings, starting from the symbol for Arbalest and moving outward.

“Lizardians like wet caves and come out to hunt nearby,” he thought. “Father always said to watch for water and hollow ground at the same time.”

He searched the map for that kind of place. After a short scan, one spot stood out. There was a small mark for a cave near a stream, a little way off the main road. Judging from the scale, it was around a dozen kilometers from the gate.

Walking all the way there would eat a good part of the day. He could still do it, but it would mean more time spent moving on the road and less time actually searching and hunting.

“If I ride part of the way, I can keep more strength for the hunt,” he thought.

He folded the map again and slid it back into his pocket, then turned to the side, where carriages waited in a loose line near the entrance.

The staging area was busy but not disorderly. Drivers leaned against their carts or adjusted harnesses while they called out destinations from time to time. Passengers came and went in small groups. Elrond approached the closest driver who did not seem busy with someone else.

“Excuse me,” he said. “Is there a carriage that passes near this area?”

He unfolded the map just enough to point at the region he had chosen.

The man glanced at the spot, narrowed his eyes for a moment in thought, then raised his chin and gestured toward a carriage a little farther down the line.

“That one,” he said. “The carriage heading to Radras. It goes along the main road and stops at a staging post near there. That is as close as you will get by wagon.”

Elrond gave a small bow of thanks, then walked toward the carriage the man had pointed out.

The driver of the Radras carriage was tightening a strap when Elrond approached.

“How far do you go on this route?” Elrond asked. “And what is the fare to the nearest staging post to this place?”

He showed the same mark on the map again.

The driver studied the map, then nodded as if he had matched the point in his mind.

“We stop at a post about there,” he said. “Fare is two silver.”

Two silver was not a small amount, but with seven gold sitting in his savings and a hunt ahead of him, it was well within what he could spend.

“Understood. I will ride to that stop,” Elrond said.

He took two silver coins from his pouch and placed them in the driver’s hand. The man checked them with a quick glance, then jerked his thumb toward the back of the carriage.

“Find a seat wherever you like,” he said. “We leave when it is full enough, so do not stray.”

Elrond climbed up and found a space on one of the benches. Little by little, more people boarded. Some carried bundles, while others had the look of traders or small-town visitors returning home. He kept to himself and listened to the low murmur of conversations without joining any of them.

Before long, the carriage was almost full. The driver called out once more to the street, then took his place at the front. The horses started forward, and the city began to slide slowly away behind them.

The road they followed was part of a main route, so it was wide and well-maintained. Even with the weight of the carriage, the wheels met few real bumps. Elrond watched the fields and scattered trees pass by and occasionally caught sight of distant patrols or other travelers, which told him that this stretch truly was considered safe.

In less than an hour, the carriage slowed. The driver guided the horses toward the side of the road and brought them to a halt at a wider stretch of packed earth. A little farther ahead, Elrond could see a modest staging post—a small building, a watering trough, and a few hitching posts where other wagons sometimes gathered.

The driver glanced back over his shoulder.

“This is as close as we go to the place you showed me on the map,” he said.

Elrond nodded, stood up, and stepped down from the carriage. He adjusted his sword strap once, then moved away from the wagon as other passengers got off or stayed seated for the longer ride to Radras.

He opened his map again and turned his body so the markings lined up with the direction of the main road.

'Gate is back that way,' he thought. 'The cave should be off to this side.'

He traced his approximate position from Arbalest’s symbol to the staging post, then from the post toward the cave mark. It was not exact, but it was enough to tell him which direction he needed to take.

He lifted his eyes and looked around.

From the road itself, there was no visible path leading straight toward the cave. There were only open ground and a line of trees that slowly thickened into a small forest.

'There is no proper trail,' he thought. 'Then I will just have to cut straight through.'

He folded the map carefully and put it away again, then left the safety of the road and stepped into the trees.

The forest here was not truly dense. Sunlight still reached the ground in broken patches, and the undergrowth was only waist-high in most places. Even so, after only a few minutes of walking, the feeling around him changed.

The sound of the road faded until it was only a faint background. In its place came the soft rustle of leaves, the occasional crack of branches under his boots, and the distant calls of unseen creatures. The air felt cooler and heavier, even though the trees were not thick enough to block the sky.

Elrond slowed his steps and let his senses stretch outward.

He had grown up walking patrols in places like this. His eyes scanned the ground for tracks and disturbed grass while his ears picked up small shifts that did not match the wind. Beneath that, there was the constant awareness that he could not name easily, the one that told him where danger tended to gather even before he saw anything.

'There are things moving in more than one direction,' he thought. 'They are not close yet, but this place is definitely alive.'

That was expected. A place that suited Lizardians would also suit other monsters and animals.

He looked up again and searched the treeline.

Farther ahead, above the tops of the trees, a hill rose gently. Its outline matched the one drawn on the map, sitting just to the side of the cave symbol.

“If I head toward that hill, I will pass close to where the cave should be,” he thought.

He adjusted the position of his sword so he could draw it more smoothly if needed, then took a breath and fixed the hill as his next point.

Step by step, he began moving toward it, threading his way deeper into the woods while the safe, orderly world of the main road faded behind his back.

As he moved deeper into the forest, the trees began to thin out around one side, and a small patch of open grassland appeared between the trunks.

Elrond checked his surroundings once more, then decided to take a short detour. He stepped out into the open ground and walked to the shade of a large tree that stood near the edge of the clearing. Some of its thick roots rose above the soil like low wooden ridges. He sat down on one of them and let his legs rest for a moment.

He took out his water and drank slowly.

The air here was still and quiet. Birds called from somewhere in the distance, and a faint breeze moved the top leaves, but nothing seemed to press on him directly. It was the kind of pause that made it easier to think about the next steps without his body pulling for attention.

When he finished, he capped the container and slid it back into his pack.

He was just about to stand up when he heard an oink and the rustling of trees.

At first, he thought it was just a wild boar wandering nearby. The sound fit. Then the noise changed. The rustling grew louder and harsher, more like something heavy was striking against a trunk. There were creaks and sharp cracks, the kind that came when branches snapped under force.

Elrond’s body tightened before he even finished straightening his back.

His hand moved to the hilt of his sword. The oinks turned into higher, more desperate squeals. They sounded like an animal that could not escape. A moment later, a loud, heavy snort cut through the forest, followed by a deep, rough huff that did not belong to any simple boar.

He drew a slow breath and let it out.

'That is not just a boar running,' he thought. 'Something big is chasing it.'

Gathering his focus, Elrond moved toward the noise. He kept his steps light and stayed near the trunks, closing the distance in a curve instead of walking straight in. When the sound was close enough that he could feel the vibration of the bear-like snorts in his chest, he stopped behind a tree and leaned out just enough to see.

In the space between the trees ahead, a large monster bear was crouched over a boar’s body.

It was a Spiky Bear.

Thick, dark fur covered its bulk, but in several places, long hardened spikes grew out along its shoulders and back, angled backward like crude armor. Its jaws were buried in the boar’s side, tearing flesh and bone apart with each bite. The ground beneath it was already stained, and each movement sent wet sounds through the air.

The Spiky Bear was classified as a low C-class monster, strong enough that a careless hunter could die from one bad step.

Elrond let his eyes follow the way it shifted its weight and how its forelegs pressed into the earth. The spikes on its back moved slightly with each breath, catching bits of light between the leaves.

He stepped out from behind the tree.

The bear lifted its head at once. Blood smeared its muzzle. For a heartbeat it only stared at him, then it turned fully, planting all four legs on the ground and lowering its body in a warning stance. A deep growl rolled out of its chest.

Elrond answered by drawing his sword.

The blade came free in one smooth motion. He set his feet, let his shoulders relax, and pulled a breath into his lungs. There was no chant. Instead, he pushed his will directly into the flows of mana inside his body.

Strength, three times. Agility, two times.

The magic wrapped around his muscles and bones in a familiar way. His limbs felt lighter and more responsive, while his grip and stance gained a firm, controlled pressure.

The Spiky Bear bared its teeth and charged.

For its size, it moved fast. One massive forepaw swung out in a horizontal arc, claws aiming to tear through his torso.

Elrond stepped in rather than back.

With his enhanced agility, the bear’s arm felt slow. He slipped under the path of the claws by a narrow margin, boots digging into the earth as he shifted his weight. As the bear’s body was still turning with the

force of its own attack, he dashed forward and drove his sword into its side, aiming for the gap behind the front leg where the ribs were softer.

The blade punched through fur and flesh.

The bear roared, a burst of sound that shook his ears. Elrond pulled his sword back out at once and moved away in a low step, not letting his feet stick to one place.

The Spiky Bear reared slightly and raised its other foreleg to strike again.

By then, Elrond was already in position.

As the claw came down, he swung his sword in a full arc toward the elbow joint, matching his movement to the angle of the limb. His enhanced strength drove the cut through muscle and bone in a single, decisive line.

The bear’s left forearm separated and hit the ground.

Enraged and in agony, the Spiky Bear began to flail. It slashed with its remaining arm, stomped heavily, and twisted its body in wild motions that ignored any thought of balance. Each step crushed earth and leaves, sending grit and dust into the air, but the pattern of its attack broke down into something rough and easy to read.

Elrond did not trade blows.

He simply kept moving, slipping outside each wild swipe and letting the storm of its panic pass close without touching him. His eyes stayed on its shoulders and hips, watching for the point where its weight would shift too far in one direction.

After one particularly heavy stomp, the bear’s head dipped low and its body pitched forward.

For a heartbeat, its guard opened.

Elrond stepped in and drove his legs upward, using the full strength of his enhancements. His sword traced a rising line from below, cutting up toward the underside of the bear’s head.

The impact ran through his arms and into his shoulders.

The Spiky Bear jerked once. Then its strength went out of it, and its huge body collapsed onto the forest floor with a heavy, final thud.

Elrond held his stance for a moment longer, listening for any sign of movement. When none came, he let the tension ease out of his muscles and released the enhancement spells, allowing his body to settle back toward its normal state.

“To this extent,” he thought, “it really is just a warm-up.”

His breathing was steady. The weight of his sword in his hand felt normal, not heavy. Compared to the times he had stood in front of a Monster Wolf, a higher C-class monster, on a winter patrol with its pack circling in the dark behind it, this had been simple. Compared to the tension of watching a lower B-class Basilisk move while he kept his eyes away from its gaze, this had been almost relaxed. Compared to the night when an S-class Amarok’s howl had rolled over the outskirts and every mistake could have meant a dead patrol, a single low C-class Spiky Bear on open ground did not even reach the edge of his limits.

The fight had sharpened his senses and reminded his body what it felt like to move at those numbers, but it had not come close to bringing out everything he could do.

He looked down once more at the fallen Spiky Bear and the ruined boar beside it, then wiped his blade clean and returned it to its sheath. His thoughts were already turning back to the real purpose of today’s hunt.

Lizardian back scales were still waiting somewhere near the hill and the cave beyond.

He did not leave the body as it was.

Elrond stepped closer again and crouched near the Spiky Bear’s back. From this distance, the spikes jutting out of its shoulders and spine looked even more unnatural. They were like bone that had grown outward in the wrong direction, hardened into pale, rough spines that broke the line of the fur.

He reached out and grabbed one of the larger spikes near the shoulder, testing how firmly it was attached.

'Even if they only bring in a bit of silver, it is better than leaving them here,' he thought.

With steady, practiced motions, he worked his blade in at the base and cut the spike free. One by one, he removed several of the bigger pieces, always choosing the ones that looked most solid and intact. The work took a little time, but he did not rush it. Carrying the whole bear was impossible, and carrying too many parts would only slow him down when he had not even reached the Lizardians yet.

When he had gathered a small armful of the larger spikes, he returned to the tree where he had rested earlier.

Near its base, one thick root rose and then curved back into the earth, leaving a narrow gap underneath. Elrond knelt there and used his hands to clear away loose leaves and small stones, making just enough space to hide what he had taken. He stacked the spikes in the hollow and covered them again with the natural debris so they would not be visible at a glance.

'I will come back for them later,' he thought. 'No point dragging extra weight if a fight breaks out.'

He stood, brushed the dirt from his gloves, and took one last look at the spot so he could find it again. Then he turned away from the clearing and headed deeper into the woods.

The trees slowly grew thicker again, and the ground underfoot changed from dry leaves to patches of softer soil. After a while, another sound began to reach his ears under the normal forest noise. It was low at first, then became clearer as he walked.

Running water.

He stopped and listened to fix the direction, then angled his steps toward it. With each dozen meters, the sound of water flowing over stones became sharper, until finally the trees opened just enough to reveal a river running through the landscape.

It was not huge, but it was wide enough that crossing it carelessly would be a mistake. The current moved steadily, and the surface broke around rocks and fallen branches in small white lines.

‘If any Lizardians are out to hunt, they should not be far from this river,’ he thought.

He walked slowly along the riverbank, eyes scanning the opposite side and the shadows under the overhanging ground. Nothing obvious moved there. No scales, no heavy drag marks that screamed of a large reptile hauling itself out of the water.

So he closed his eyes.

He drew his focus inward and called up mana from within his body. Without any spoken chant, he compressed that mana into a single, steady point in his center. Then he released it in a slow, controlled pulse that spread outward in a low wave.

It flowed through the ground and the air around him, brushing against trees, rocks, and the river. As it moved, it carried back faint impressions of the mana it touched. Small things flickered at the edge of his awareness. Animals. Insects. The distant echo of something that might have been another monster far away.

He let the first pulse fade, then repeated the process. Each time, he listened more carefully for a particular pattern.

Eyes still closed, he sorted through the returning signals. Weak, scattered mana patterns that matched ordinary beasts he discarded at once. He looked for clusters, for shapes that had both weight and a certain hard, layered feel around them.

After a couple of minutes of sending pulses and adjusting his attention, something finally stood out.

There was a group of signatures gathered in one direction, not too far away. Their mana felt dense and solid near the surface, with a more fluid strength beneath. The shapes matched almost exactly what he remembered from the last time he had faced Lizardians near his hometown.

'That should be them,' he thought.

A small, sharp satisfaction rose in his chest.

“Jackpot,” Elrond muttered under his breath.

He opened his eyes and fixed the direction firmly in his mind. Without wasting time, he called up mana again and cast a two times Agility enhancement on himself. His body grew lighter and his muscles responded more easily.

Then he pushed off the ground and dashed toward the source of those mana signatures, following the invisible line his detection had drawn through the forest.

### Chapter 19: 15 – A Better Life

#### Scene 1

Elrond dashed forward at high speed, weaving between dense trees and the exposed roots that rose like low walls from the ground. His body felt light under the double agility spell, but he kept his steps measured so he would not catch his boots on anything hidden under the leaves.

As the mana signatures he had sensed drew closer, he began to slow.

'If I rush in carelessly, they will notice me before I am ready,' he thought.

He let the enhancement do the work of softening his footsteps instead of using it only for speed. When the pressure of the mana ahead settled into a clear direction, he shifted into a crouch and moved the last part on quieter feet.

Branches overlapped above him, leaving only narrow lines of sky. Elrond picked a tree with a thick trunk and low limbs, then bent his knees and jumped. His fingers caught a branch and he used the momentum to pull himself up, climbing higher with small, controlled movements until he reached a place with a clear view through the leaves.

He pressed his back lightly against the trunk and eased one shoulder forward.

From there, he could see them.

A group of Lizardians moved near the riverbank. There were probably a dozen of them in all. Most of them were smaller, with thinner bodies and scales that had not finished thickening, which marked them as young. Among them he counted seven adults, heavier and broader, with darker, harder plates along their backs.

They were not arranged in any strict pattern. Some were standing on their hind legs to pull at leaves and branches. Some were down at the water’s edge, dipping their mouths in and drinking in short, careful stretches. A few of the adults were gathered around a deer’s carcass. They tore at the flesh with their jaws, then chewed slowly as they looked around between bites.

'So they really are omnivorous,' Elrond thought.

The scene in front of him was almost peaceful. It looked more like a herd at rest than a pack of monsters. For a moment, he watched them in silence, feeling the thin line between his role today and the world they lived in.

He did not stay on that thought for long.

Elrond drew a slow breath in and sent his mana flowing.

First he strengthened his body. He wrapped his muscles in a three times Strength enhancement, then laid a two times Agility enhancement over it. His limbs grew lighter and his grip and stance gained a solid weight.

After that, he shaped the mana into a thin defensive layer that covered his body like a second skin, a shield meant to blunt the first impact if anything reached him.

All of it was done without a single word spoken.

Charging straight in now would only break the balance in the worst way. If he simply jumped down and attacked, some of the Lizardians would scatter, while others might rush him in panic. That kind of half- broken formation was harder to handle than a clean line.

'I need to cut down as many as I can before they understand what is happening,' he thought. 'A single move that can reach multiple targets at once.'

His eyes traced the positions of the adults and the young.

He raised his hand slightly and pulled mana into the air in front of him. Five fist-sized rocks formed there, solid and compact, hanging in a loose cluster. Above them, he gathered more mana and shaped it into a tight fireball. Heat rolled off it in waves as he fed it more power.

The fire sank into the stones, washing over their surfaces. Bit by bit, they changed color, dark at first, then red as the heat built. Elrond watched the Lizardians below and chose his targets.

'Five at once is my limit for precise tracking,' he thought. 'It is not that my mana cannot handle more. I just do not want this to miss.'

He picked five adult Lizardians, spacing them out so the deaths would cause the most confusion. His awareness settled on each of their heads in turn until he could follow their movements even when they shifted slightly.

The rocks glowed a brighter red.

He started them spinning, each one rotating in place. The air around them warped faintly as they picked up speed. Once he was sure the heat and momentum were high enough, he lined up his arm and tilted his hand, linking the direction of his motion with the path he wanted them to take.

'Now,' he thought.

The five heated stones shot forward.

They cut through the air like bullets, leaving faint trails of disturbed air behind them. In the blink of an eye, each rock found its mark. One after another, they smashed into the heads of the five chosen Lizardians.

There was no time for a proper reaction.

Skulls cracked. Bodies jerked and collapsed where they stood or fell sideways into the river. The sound of impact overlapped with the wet thuds of heavy bodies hitting the ground.

For a heartbeat, the riverside went silent.

Then the pack erupted in roars.

The remaining Lizardians whipped their heads around, hissing and bellowing, tails lashing against the earth. The young ones shrank back in confusion and fear, while the adults’ eyes snapped from the fallen bodies to the trees around them, searching for the source of the attack.

Elrond had still not been seen.

'This is the opening,' he thought.

He pushed off the branch and dropped.

Branches blurred past as he fell. Just before he hit the ground, he bent his knees and absorbed the impact, then he used his enhanced legs to launch himself forward, straight out of the tree line and toward the clearing by the river.

The sudden movement drew the attention he had been waiting for.

Two of the remaining adult Lizardians fixed their eyes on him at once. Their pupils narrowed. The muscles in their legs tightened and their bodies lowered into a forward stance.

His sudden charge did not scare them.

If anything, it provoked them.

They let out rough, rumbling roars, then started to move to meet him head-on.

Elrond tightened his grip on his sword.

'So it is a direct fight after all,' he thought.

Elrond shifted his stance as the two adults came for him and let his eyes run over their bodies.

For him, fighting Lizardians was not particularly difficult. The only real problem was their scales, especially on the adults. He remembered how, back in his hometown, one of the new patrol members had rushed in and swung straight at a Lizardian’s back. The blade had bounced off without even making the monster flinch.

Their scales were incredibly tough, probably thicker and denser than a turtle shell. It was closer to hardened bone with metal-like properties. Some of the plates carried small spikes and their color blended with the creature’s skin, which was what made them valuable. Blacksmiths used those plates to forge lighter but durable swords or to reinforce armor, and artisans turned them into accessories or decorations.

But Elrond knew where they were weak.

The main weakness lay between the plates of the shell. On some adults, the gaps between the scales were still exposed, so it was easier to stab or slash into the skin directly. Fully grown ones had much tighter coverage and far fewer openings. Other weak spots were the lower body, where the skin was closer to that of a normal reptile, and the head, where the scales were not as thick as on the back or the sides.

He took all of that into account as he moved.

Elrond kicked off the ground with his full strength and aimed his first strike at the nearest Lizardian’s head. His sword flashed toward its eye line, but the Lizardian twisted away at the last moment. Its heavy body spun and its tail lashed out at full speed.

He had barely any time to react.

Elrond brought his sword up across his body. The tail slammed into the blade and the force ran straight through his arms and into his legs. The impact hurled him backward and he slid across the ground, boots digging into the soil as he fought to keep his balance.

Pain shuddered through his arms, but the defensive shield around his body dulled the worst of the blow.

'If I did not have that up, my ribs would be gone by now,' he thought.

He had no time to rest. The younger Lizardians that had been hesitating at the edge of the clearing were now rushing toward him. Their movements were clumsy compared with the adults, but there were a lot of them and they were already closing in.

He glanced over their bodies once and then dismissed them.

Their scales were not what he needed.

Elrond snapped his free hand up and called mana into the ground in front of them. Several pillars of fire erupted from the earth, rising in straight lines that swallowed the charging youngsters. Heat washed over the clearing as the flames roared. The younger Lizardians barely had time to scream before they were burned to a crisp and collapsed as blackened shapes.

The bodies dropped one after another.

It showed how easily he could defeat them, but the request this time required perfect back scales from adults. If he damaged those plates, the value would fall sharply.

'I cannot waste effort on targets that will not pay for this risk,' he thought.

He shifted his focus back to the adults.

Elrond rushed forward again. One of the remaining adult Lizardians faced him directly and opened its mouth. Mana gathered there in a tight, rippling mass. For a split second, he wondered what it was shaping, then a high speed, high pressure ball of water blasted out toward him.

He was genuinely surprised.

'So they can fire that kind of spell,' he thought.

He twisted his body sideways and stepped out of the line of fire. The water shot past him and tore into the ground behind him, gouging a deep line into the soil and scattering mud and stones.

He used the force of his sidestep to push himself forward again.

In the same motion, he closed the distance and slashed across the Lizardian’s neck. The creature jerked and tried to stomp him flat or bite at his upper body, but he read the pattern of its movements and slipped past each strike. When it lunged in to bite, its head came low and its weight shifted.

There was the opening.

Elrond spun to the side and, at full speed, poured mana into his sword. Fire wrapped around the blade in a tight layer. He cut into the Lizardian’s neck again, this time driving the flaming edge deep into the flesh between the scales. The fire caught along the wound and spread outward.

Elrond pulled back and stepped away, then fed more mana into the flames to strengthen them. The fire sank under the scales and began to burn from within.

The Lizardian staggered, roared, and thrashed, but its movements were already losing strength.

At that moment, the other adult Lizardian charged in from the side with a heavy stomping attack. Its body loomed over him as it tried to crush him under its full weight.

'That was stupid,' Elrond thought as he saw how much it exposed its underside.

He moved a fraction of a heartbeat before the stomp landed. He slipped out of the direct path and felt the rush of air along his shoulder as the heavy limb slammed into the spot where he had just been. At the same time, he rotated the sword in his grip and twisted his body, driving the point into the Lizardian’s side in one clean motion.

The flames from his previous enchantment still clung to the blade. When his sword sank in, he sent another surge of mana through it. Fire burst out inside the wound and spread along the creature’s inner flesh.

The Lizardian convulsed.

Its front legs buckled, then its back legs followed. It collapsed onto its side and the ground shook under the impact. A short distance away, the first Lizardian that he had cut at the neck finally toppled, its body already losing strength as the flames finished their work from within.

Both adults stopped moving.

Elrond kept his stance ready for a few breaths longer. When nothing else rushed him and the clearing grew quiet again, he slowly let the tension in his shoulders ease.

He moved to the nearest corpse and checked the back with careful eyes. The large plates along the spine and sides were intact. There were no cracks, no burns, and no deep cuts running across them. The same was true for the second body.

'Good grief. I actually did not damage the back scales,' he thought.

He went around the clearing and checked the rest of the adults that had fallen from his earlier attack. All of their backs were in good condition as well. Once he was sure, he took out his knife.

Elrond began to remove the plates one by one, cutting the skin around the edges and easing each scale free without tearing it. Each back plate came off as a curved rectangular piece that matched the shape of the Lizardian’s body. That shape made them easier to stack and organize.

By the time he finished with all seven adults, he had collected twenty one back scales.

He looked down at the small pile.

'From seven bodies, this much is more than enough,' he thought. 'This should come to around forty silver.'

For a freelance hunter working alone, that was a very good haul.

He pulled out a sack he had prepared in advance from the small bag at his hip. He packed all twenty one Lizardian scales inside and adjusted their position so they would not crack against each other, then he tied the sack closed and slung it over his back.

To be completely honest, for Elrond it had gone a little too smoothly.

He walked through the trees with the sack over his shoulder and replayed the fight in his head. From his past experience, hunting monsters usually needed planning and coordination, and most of the effort went into finding the targets in the first place. Sometimes it took days just to confirm a trail.

Finding Lizardians this quickly felt like hitting a jackpot on the first try.

'Good grief. If it is this easy every time, the older patrol members will start complaining,' he thought. 'No, that is exactly why I should not get used to this.'

The uneasy feeling sat in his chest like a small stone, but he pushed it aside for now. Thinking too hard about luck he could not explain would not change anything while he was still in the forest.

On his way back, he cut across to the small patch of open grassland where he had fought the Spiky Bear earlier. The ground still bore the marks of their clash. He moved to the spot where the spikes had scattered and began picking them up one by one.

He did not know how much they were worth, but the material looked solid and nasty enough that someone would want them. He pulled out another empty sack and put the Spiky Bear’s spikes inside so they would not get mixed up with the Lizardian back scales.

Now carrying two sacks full of monster materials on his shoulders, he started walking again.

Under normal circumstances, this much weight would have been a real burden. The sacks dragged at his shoulders and pulled at his balance a little every time his boots left the ground.

'If this were a game, I would just dump all of this into an inventory window and be done with it,' he thought. 'Too bad this world does not come with quality-of-life features.'

He let out a short breath that was close to a quiet laugh and adjusted the straps so they sat more evenly across his back. His enhancements had already worn off, so every step was just his normal strength and stamina, but it was still manageable.

He kept walking in the direction he had memorized earlier. This time he was not going deeper into the forest, so there was no need to slow down to check for ambushes between every tree. The return trip felt shorter because each landmark matched the image in his memory.

Before long, he stepped out from between the trees and emerged back onto the road where he had first started.

The light was a little different from when he had gone in, but the gentle bend of the road and the familiar line of trees on the opposite side matched what he remembered. From the map he had studied, he recalled that the carriage staging post was to the south along this road.

He shifted the weight of the sacks once more, turned to face the correct direction, and began walking toward the staging post.

After about an hour of walking, he finally saw the outline of the staging post up ahead. The sun was still high enough that the road and wagons were clearly lit, and the heat pressing down on his shoulders made the sacks feel a little heavier than before.

A couple of wagon carriages were waiting there, some already hitched to their horses and some with drivers leaning against the wheels. Elrond shifted the weight of the sacks on his shoulders and walked toward the nearest driver.

'First I need a way back, then I can worry about counting silver,' he thought.

“Excuse me,” Elrond said. “Which carriage is heading to Arbalest?”

The driver he had approached jerked his thumb at his own wagon.

“That’d be me, lad. Arbalest run. It’ll be three silver—two for the ride, one for all that you’re carrying.”

He had expected the fare to cover his bags as well. However, when he thought about how much he was carrying, it did not sound unreasonable. Two full sacks of monster materials took up space and weight, and the carriage was already half filled with other passengers.

'It would be strange if they did not charge extra when I am basically loading half a cargo crate,' he thought.

“That is fine,” Elrond said. “I will take it.”

He paid the three silver, then followed the driver’s instructions and loaded his sacks into the storage space under the seats. The smell of worn wood and old leather greeted him as he climbed up to sit with the other passengers. Once everyone was settled and the driver had checked the harnesses one last time, the carriage rolled out toward Arbalest.

The sun slid lower as the wheels rattled along the road. By the time the city’s walls and familiar skyline came into view, the sun was already at the horizon and the sky had turned a deep orange, with the first hints of red spreading across it.

When they arrived at the city gate, Elrond climbed down, collected his sacks, and made his way straight toward the Adventurer Bureau.

He stepped in through the wide open front, where the street simply continued into the hall. The familiar mix of voices, steady footsteps, and the dry smell of leather and metal washed over him as he walked inside. Kaira, who was standing at the counter, noticed him almost immediately.

“Oh, you are back already,” she said. “Welcome back.”

“Hi, Miss Kaira. Yes, I just returned,” Elrond said with a small nod. “I would like to turn in materials. Twenty one Lizardian back scales and four Spiky Bear spikes.”

Kaira paused for a moment, then stared at the sacks he was carrying.

“Twenty one?!!” she repeated. “From a single hunt?”

Her expression shifted into open surprise. Normally, one monster hunt would not produce that many usable parts, especially not in good condition.

Elrond adjusted his grip on the sacks.

“I just happened to run into a full pack of Lizardians,” Elrond said. “The Spiky Bear showed up while I was still looking for them.”

Kaira let out a small breath through her nose that sounded somewhere between a sigh and a quiet laugh.

“You call that ‘lucky’, huh,” she said. “All right. Come with me. We will have them checked at the cargo counter.”

She stepped out from behind the counter and led him toward the back section of the Bureau. There, a male staff member in a work apron waited behind a wide table that already had scales, fangs, and other monster parts laid out in neat rows.

Kaira explained the contents of Elrond’s sacks, and he hauled them up onto the table.

The man untied the first sack and began to inspect the Lizardian plates one by one. He checked for cracks, burns, and cuts, and he ran his fingers along the edges to confirm that none of them were chipped. After that, he moved on to the Spiky Bear spikes and examined their condition as well.

The cargo staff member finished checking the last piece and straightened up. “Back plates are clean, no cracks or burns,” he said. “Spikes are in good shape too.”

He made a few notes on a board, then looked up at Kaira and Elrond.

“For this lot, we can offer forty two silver,” he said. “That includes the Spiky Bear spikes.”

Elrond did not even think about haggling. The number was already higher than his earlier estimate.

“I will take it,” he said.

The staff member nodded, wrote down the final amount, and prepared a small pouch with the payment. Elrond felt the weight of the coins as it dropped into his hand.

With that, he had earned about twenty silver in profit in a single day. At least, that was the case for today, because he still had to account for the monster hunt registration fee and what he had already spent. Even so, it was more than enough to cover food for at least a week.

The request sheet for the Lizardian hunt was stamped as completed. The cargo staff then gathered the materials and carried them into the back storage area. Kaira and Elrond turned away from the counter and headed back toward the lobby.

On the way, Kaira glanced at him.

“So,” she said, “how did you manage to find that many monsters in one go?”

Elrond did not try to turn it into anything more dramatic than it was.

“I really was just fortunate,” he said. “I followed what I had sensed earlier, and the area I chose happened to have a lot of monsters. There was a full pack of Lizardians there.”

Kaira nodded slowly.

“That area has been flagged a few times already,” she said. “This is why we put up monster hunt jobs in the first place. Even with the current number of adventurers, monster numbers are still dense.”

She folded her arms lightly and continued in a more thoughtful tone.

“Most adventurers prefer other kinds of work,” she said. “Exploration quests, for example. Companies often ask for escorts or support when they want to survey mines or old tunnels, and those places are usually still packed with monsters. Others focus on escort quests along the roads, which are safer, or on extermination requests in areas that are already marked and partially controlled, where monsters or bandits keep coming back.”

She looked at him out of the corner of her eye.

“Monster hunts like the one you took are usually picked by people who want to train or test themselves. The risk is higher, and the pay is not that impressive if you compare it to some of the other jobs.”

Elrond turned that over in his mind.

In his previous life, he had imagined things like “dungeons” as places where monsters simply appeared again and again, like in video games. Here, it clearly did not work like that. Monsters did not just spawn from thin air.

'So that is how they see it here,' he thought. 'Monsterization from high magic density and natural mutation, not some endless respawn point.'

Animals could change when the magic density in an area rose too high, and some species mutated over time into something entirely different. Certain environments, like caves or the deeper parts of forests, encouraged monsters to gather and settle. Their instincts pushed them into those places and kept them there.

That was why extermination requests were so valuable. They offered profit and also a chance to build influence and connections with people who cared about keeping those areas safe.

Their conversation faded as they stepped back into the lobby. The noise of the Bureau wrapped around them again.

Kaira stopped near the main counter and turned to him.

“In any case, good work today,” she said. “If you keep this up, you will build a solid reputation. I hope you will continue to work hard.”

“I will do my best,” Elrond said. “Especially since I will be at the Academy soon. I need the money to survive there first.”

Kaira smiled faintly at that and nodded, then turned back to her duties.

Elrond tightened his grip on the small pouch of coins.

With enough money to last him at least a week, he could finally shift his attention to the next step. Now he could focus on preparing to move into the Royal Academy dormitory the next day.

The next morning, Elrond packed everything he owned into one place.

He folded his clothes and stacked them as neatly as he could, checked his equipment one more time, and made sure the dorm key was in his pocket. Once he confirmed that nothing was left in the drawers or under the bed, he hoisted his backpack onto his shoulders and picked up the remaining luggage by hand.

When he stepped out of his room and went downstairs, the weight of everything he carried made his steps a little slower than usual.

At the reception counter, the innkeeper looked up. His eyes moved from Elrond’s face to the bags and then back again.

“Whoa,” the innkeeper said. “What is all this? You running away already?”

Elrond set one of the bags down so he would not drop it.

“I would like to check out,” he said. “I am moving to the Royal Academy dormitory today.”

The innkeeper watched him for a moment, then let out a low hum and nodded.

“So that is how it is,” he said. “In that case, hurry up and get going. Do not drag your feet.”

He waved his hand in a casual shooing motion, like he was chasing Elrond out, but there was a small smile on his face when he did it.

As Elrond was finishing the formalities, Lila came out into the lobby from the back.

She froze for a heartbeat when she saw him fully loaded with bags.

“Elrond? Where are you going with all of that?” she asked.

He straightened up a little.

“I am moving to the dorm today,” he said. “I want to get settled as soon as possible. Thank you very much for all the breakfasts you made for me every morning, Miss Lila.”

Lila’s expression softened. Her eyes lowered slightly, and for a moment there was a trace of sadness in her face.

“So it really is time,” she said. “You worked hard every day, even before your exam. Make sure you eat properly over there too, all right?”

“I will,” he said, and gave a small nod.

He said goodbye to the innkeeper and to Lila, then adjusted the straps of his backpack and stepped out of the inn.
