The road to the royal district was already busy. People moved in both directions, and carts rattled past with goods piled high. Elrond kept his pace steady as he walked, careful not to bump his bags against anyone.

When he reached the entrance to the royal district, he could feel eyes turning toward him.

Some of the people on the street glanced at him and then quickly looked away. A few of the guards near the checkpoint watched him more openly. He followed their gaze down to himself.

Plain clothes, a big backpack stuffed full, and extra bags in his hands.

'…Ah. Right,' he thought. 'I already have the Academy uniform and I still walked all the way here in plain clothes. So much for photographic memory. Of course they will stare.'

If he had worn the uniform, he would probably have blended in with the other students who were already moving in and out of the district. The realization slid in late, like an answer he should have seen from the beginning. He had memorized the route, the time it would take, even the layout of the royal district, yet the simplest thing—that he could just wear his Academy uniform—had slipped straight past his mind. Even with photographic memory, there were still things he could miss.

He kept going anyway.

By the time he arrived in front of the Royal Academy, he could feel even more attention on him. Students in neat uniforms, staff members, and guards at the gate all stood out clearly against the buildings and paved grounds.

As he stepped toward the entrance, one of the guards raised a hand.

“Hold it,” the guard said. “What business do you have here?”

Elrond stopped at once and set one of his bags down so he could reach into his pocket.

“I am a new student,” he said calmly. “I came to move into the dormitory today.”

He took out his acceptance letter, with the S Class marking clearly visible, and the dorm key he had received before. The guard took both, checked them carefully, and compared the name and seal with whatever he already knew.

After a short wait, the guard returned the letter and the key.

“Everything is in order,” he said. “You may pass. The dormitory is the same as you were told before.”

“Thank you,” Elrond said, then bowed his head slightly before picking up his bag again.

He crossed the grounds and headed straight for the dormitory building.

When he stepped inside, he immediately noticed that the receptionists were not the same as the ones he had seen on his last visit. Two women were behind the counter, and both of them watched him with expressions that clearly held some doubt when they saw him walking in with heavy luggage and plain clothes.

Elrond did not stop at the counter. He turned in the direction of the S Class area, just as Lacia had described to him before.

One of the receptionists quickly stood up and moved to block his path.

“Excuse me,” she said, holding out a hand. “That area is restricted. Only authorized students can go in there.”

Elrond felt a small wave of embarrassment rise in his chest. From her point of view, it probably looked like a random boy was trying to wander into the wrong place with all his belongings.

He shifted his luggage so he could free one hand.

“Ah, excuse me,” Elrond said. “I am an S Class student. I have access to that area.”

He took out his acceptance letter again, making sure that the line with “S Class” was visible, and placed the dorm key in her hand as well.

The receptionist read through the letter, then checked the engravings on the key. Her eyes flicked back to him, then to the letter again.

“I… understand now,” she said in a low voice.

She straightened her posture and gave a small bow.

“My apologies,” she said, bowing her head a little. “I did not recognize you as S Class. Please go ahead.”

“It’s all right,” Elrond said. “I did walk in looking like this. Thank you.”

She stepped aside at once, and he continued down the corridor toward the S Class dormitory section.

He found the stairs and climbed up to the floor where his room was located. The hallway was quiet. A few doors were already marked as occupied, but he did not see anyone else outside.

Elrond walked to his own door and unlocked it with the key.

The moment the door swung open, he saw the room again.

It was the same as when he had first been shown it: more spacious than anything he had expected to receive as a student, with clean floors, a large bed, a desk, and the red couch along the left wall.

Even though he had already seen it once, the feeling was still the same.

'Good grief,' he thought. 'I really am allowed to live in a place like this.'

He stepped inside and closed the door behind him. Then he moved over to the red couch and set all of his belongings down there, one by one, until his shoulders finally felt light again.

After that, he walked to the bed.

This time, he did not just look at it from a distance. He sat on the edge first, then let himself lean back until he was lying on it fully. The mattress supported his weight evenly, and the feeling of a proper, well-made bed sank into his body.

'If I am not careful, I will fall asleep like this,' he thought.

He stared up at the ceiling for a while, listening to the quiet of the room. Compared with his small inn room and the noise of the city outside, this space felt separated from everything.

He had finally reached a point where he could live a slightly more relaxed life, at least on the surface. He had a stable place to sleep, enough money in his pouch to last a short while, and a room that was clearly prepared for someone the Academy considered important.

But the next step was already clear in his mind.

'Next is the first day at the Academy,' he thought. 'I need to be ready for that before anything else.'

He sat up again slowly.

There were still things to organize, uniforms to lay out, and supplies to check before morning came.

The next day, Elrond woke up with one clear plan in mind.

Lacia had told him there would be a breakfast buffet, so he got ready and decided to wear the best shirt he owned, the same style he had used for the entrance exam. He fastened the buttons carefully and checked his reflection once.

'If I want to blend in here, I should really buy proper clothes,' he thought. 'Later, when I actually have the money for that.'

He stepped out of his room and walked down the hallway. A few students were already outside, talking in small groups, their voices low and relaxed. The door that led toward the buffet area stood wide open. Elrond followed the faint smell of food, went down the stairs, and entered.

Inside, there were far more options than he had imagined.

Lacia and the receptionist had both told him that the S Class dorm was usually quiet, but the scene in front of him felt more lively than that. Dozens of students were already there. Some were sitting at tables and eating with steady, polished movements. Others were calmly choosing food from the buffet, while a few were speaking with staff at the counter to arrange meals to take away.

As he walked in, the contrast hit him at once.

Even though Elrond was wearing what he considered his best clothes, they looked plain next to the well- tailored outfits and clean lines the other students had. He could feel the difference in quality just by looking around. A few students glanced his way, their eyes sliding over his shirt and worn trousers with something that felt vaguely like contempt before they turned back to their own plates.

'So this is the gap just from clothing alone,' he thought. 'I really will stand out if I am not careful.'

He felt a small tightness in his chest. In this world, he barely had any etiquette training. He had some experience from formal dinners in his previous life, sitting at long tables with senior researchers and sponsors, but that was a different culture and a different set of rules. Here, he did not even know which gesture might be considered rude.

Because of that, and because the looks in his direction bothered him more than he wanted to admit, Elrond decided not to sit down in the hall.

He would take his breakfast back to his room and eat there instead.

The procedure was simple enough. He only needed to choose what he wanted, tell the counter that it was for takeaway, and give them his room number.

He moved along the buffet line and decided what he wanted. He chose some bread, a portion of something that looked like beef steak, soup, and a few vegetables to go with it. For his drink, he simply chose water. After that, he went to the counter, told the staff it was for takeaway, and gave them his room number. They told him to return to his room and wait there.

Elrond headed back upstairs.

He had barely stepped into his room and closed the door behind him when there was already a knock.

He paused for a moment, then opened the door again. The waiter stood there with his breakfast neatly arranged on a tray.

'That was fast,' he thought.

He thanked the waiter, took the tray, and set it down on the small table. Since he was alone and there was no one to watch his every move, he did not worry about etiquette. He simply sat down and ate at a

comfortable pace, focusing on the taste and on filling his stomach rather than on which hand should move first.

Once he finished, he carried the empty dishes over to the special shelf in the corner of the room, the one that Lacia had mentioned before.

It was meant for dirty dishes and laundry. He placed the plates and cup there, then added some of the clothes he had worn yesterday on the lower part of the shelf. Part of it was simple convenience, and part of it was a test. Lacia had told him that someone would come by every afternoon to collect everything.

'So if I leave them here, they should disappear on their own later,' he thought.

After doing that, Elrond stepped back and looked around his room.

He was starting to get a clearer sense of how life in this dorm worked. Food came to the room if he asked for it properly. Dishes and laundry were handled if he placed them in the right spot. There was a rhythm here that he could follow once he learned the rules.

'Once I learn proper etiquette in this world, I should try eating in the dining hall with everyone else,' he thought. 'It will be easier to blend in if I can sit there without worrying about every small movement.'

Done with breakfast, Elrond leaned back in his chair for a moment and thought about what he should do today.

The regular student orientation would be held tomorrow. For him it was optional, which meant he had a full day with nothing fixed on his schedule.

He decided to use it to blend in a little better.

First, he took out the school uniform from the closet and tried it on properly. The moment he buttoned it up and looked down at himself, the difference was obvious.

'This is so fancy,' he thought.

The design was simple but elegant. Most of it was white, with a blue stripe running straight down from the collar. The cloth felt light and firm at the same time. It was still easy to move in, especially if he did not attach the semi cloak. Even when he put the semi cloak on his shoulders to test it, his range of motion did not feel restricted.

'With this, at least I will not stand out for the wrong reasons,' he thought.

After checking his appearance once more, Elrond decided to take a walk around the Academy and see how far the preparations had gone for orientation.

The event was scheduled to be held at the magic training field, since it was the largest outdoor space in the Academy. He headed there, following the route he had already memorized.

When he arrived, he could see that work was almost finished.

In the center of the field, many rows of chairs had already been lined up in neat blocks. At the corners of the open area, several magic crystals were set on stands. He did not remember seeing those during his last visit.

'They must have been added recently to form a barrier,' he guessed.

In the distance, guards were lined up and receiving a briefing. Near the other side of the field, a few students were still using a small section for light training, swinging their weapons or practicing simple spells without getting in the way of the setup.

It looked like everything was nearly ready for tomorrow.

Elrond watched for a short while, then turned away and walked out of the magic training area, thinking about what to do next. The day was still mostly open, and he had plenty of time to spare.

He remembered that there was a large library in the Academy and another one in the city. Both of them were places he wanted to visit at some point. However, he knew his own habits. If he went into a library now, there was a good chance he would get absorbed in the shelves and lose track of the entire day.

'If I start reading now, I might not notice the time until it is already evening,' he thought.

So he chose something else.

Instead of going to the library, Elrond decided to head to the Adventurer Bureau again and look for an easy monster hunting job he could handle within the day.

### Chapter 20: 16 – Fate’s Reunion

#### Scene 1

Before heading anywhere, he turned back toward the dormitory building.

If he was going to the Adventurer Bureau, he could not go empty handed. He climbed the stairs to his floor, unlocked his room, and stepped inside. The quiet air greeted him together with the neat bed and the red couch where he had left some of his things.

He went to the closet and pulled out a small hip bag. After that, he took a large foldable pouch, pressed all the air out of it so it would lie flat, and stuffed it into the hip bag. Finally, he fetched the plated gloves he used for protection and checked the metal on the backs of the hands.

"With nothing but this uniform on, I would look like I am out for a walk," he thought. "If I am going to hunt monsters, I should at least look ready for that."

He strapped the hip bag around his waist so it sat securely at his side. Then he picked up the gloves and hooked them where he could reach them quickly.

Once he was satisfied that everything was in its place, he left the room again, locked the door, and headed down through the dorm.

From the Royal District to the Adventurer Bureau, the route was already fixed in his memory. He crossed the Academy grounds, passed through the gates, and walked along the main streets. The uniform drew a few glances, but this time he did not feel like an out-of-place boy with a backpack. At least from a distance, he blended in as one more student who had some business in the city.

Walking outside the Academy in full uniform felt different from any other day.

The white fabric sat clean against his shoulders, and the blue stripe that ran down from the collar drew the eye directly to the crest on the upper right of his chest. The Royal Academy emblem caught the light when he moved. It was not heavy in weight, but it carried a weight of its own, the kind that came from how people looked at it.

"So this is what it is like to walk around with the Academy’s name on my chest," Elrond thought.

The quiet pride that rose in him came with a small warning at the same time. The crest said he belonged to a place with rules and expectations. That alone was enough to remind him not to do anything strange while he was wearing it.

The Academy had provided five sets of uniforms. Knowing that made it easier for him to use one like this. Even if it got a little dusty while he was out, he could change into another set later.

It did not take long for the Adventurer Bureau to come into view.

The wide open front of the building faced the street in the same way as before. Today, the air felt thinner. It was still fairly early in the morning, so the usual flow of adventurers had not yet built up. The open hall was not empty, but the voices were fewer, and the receptionist counter looked bare in a way that made the difference clear.

Elrond stepped inside.

He glanced toward the section of the counter where Kaira had stood yesterday.

She was not there.

"Maybe it is her day off. Or a different shift," he thought.

There was no reason for him to linger at the counter when he did not need to talk yet. He turned away and walked straight toward the request boards.

He headed directly to the part he wanted.

The monster hunt section was marked clearly. Sheets of paper were pinned there in neat rows, each one listing a target, a location, and the conditions for completion. Elrond let his eyes move over them with the same steady focus he used when reading patrol reports.

One request caught his attention at once.

Ferocious Wolf Hide.

The title was simple and familiar. The note below it listed the usual location of the wolves’ den. It was not far from the city gate, on a hill to the northwest. The words brought up a clear image in his mind.

He remembered the map and the way the land rose in that direction. There was a trail that led up toward the hill from near the road. He had seen it from a distance when he first came through the gate, and he had matched it against the map later.

"So it really is that hill," he thought.

Ferocious Wolves were nocturnal.

The line on the sheet did not need to spell that out for him. He already knew the basic habits of monsters in this region from what he had studied before coming to the capital.

That gave him two options.

He could go to their nest during the day and strike while they were resting. Or he could wait until night and hunt them while they were active, moving between the trees and the slopes.

He weighed both in his head for a short moment.

Waiting until night would mean spending half a day doing nothing. The wolves would be alert, and the risk of being surrounded in the dark was not small. If he went now, he could use the fact that they were nocturnal against them. It would be more dangerous if any of them woke up early, but it would still be better than wasting time.

"I do not want to sit around until evening just to start moving again," he thought. "If I can finish this before night, that is the best."

He reached up, took hold of the Ferocious Wolf Hide request, and pulled it cleanly from the board.

With the sheet in hand, he walked back toward the receptionist counter.

The staff member on duty this time was a man in light work clothes, not Kaira. He looked up when Elrond approached, his gaze going first to the uniform, then to the paper in Elrond’s hand.

For a second, his expression froze.

The crest on Elrond’s chest was clearly visible at this distance. The receptionist’s brows lifted slightly, and the look in his eyes turned into something close to open surprise.

A Royal Academy student taking a monster hunt request was clearly not something he saw every day.

Elrond noticed the reaction, but he did not mention it. He simply placed the request sheet on the counter.

"I would like to take this monster hunt," he said.

The man cleared his throat once, then pulled the sheet closer and checked the details with a more focused face than before. His eyes moved down to the name section that would record the hunter.

He glanced at Elrond again.

"Understood," the receptionist said. "We will process this as a monster hunt request under your name. Please be careful. Ferocious Wolves travel in packs, so do not underestimate their numbers."

His tone had shifted into something more formal, as if the uniform alone required that.

Elrond gave a small nod.

"I will keep that in mind," he said.

The receptionist stamped the sheet to mark it as taken and handed the part that Elrond needed back across the counter. Elrond folded it once and slipped it into his hip bag.

With that, there was nothing more to do inside the hall.

He turned away from the counter and walked back through the Adventurer Bureau’s open front. The morning light outside felt a little brighter after the dimmer interior.

He headed straight toward the city entrance.

The road from the Bureau to the gate was already familiar. He moved at a steady pace, his steps light in the uniform, his hand resting lightly near the hip bag where he had placed the request.

"First the city gate," he thought. "Then the hill to the northwest. If I do not waste time, I can reach the den while the sun is still high."

The city walls came into view, along with the guards and the flow of people passing through in both directions. Elrond adjusted his pace slightly and walked toward the gate, already tracing the path to the wolves’ hill in his mind.

He walked out through the city gate and followed the flow of the road for a while. After about thirty minutes of steady walking, an intersection came into view ahead of him.

There was a wooden signpost standing at the fork. One arrow pointed straight ahead toward the next main settlement along the highway. The other pointed to the right.

Elrond slowed his steps and looked at the right arrow.

“Shortcut to Calderidge,” he read quietly.

Calderidge. A small hub town for travelers, known for its agricultural products. The name matched what he had seen on the map when he was planning his route.

He turned right toward the northwestern hill.

The road here was not as wide as the main road he had been using until now. The packed earth narrowed to something closer to a long path, and the stone markers that lined the main highway became fewer and farther between. It was also much quieter. The sounds of the city and the larger road faded behind him, and only the faint rustle of leaves and the light crunch of his own footsteps remained.

As he followed the trail, he could see the hill on the horizon.

It was not towering, but it rose clearly above the surrounding land in a gentle slope. The path did not go straight toward it. It wound around clusters of trees and small rises in the terrain, bending left and right to avoid obstacles like thicker trunks or smaller hills. From a distance the route might have looked simple, but from here it was a string of turns that guided him through the uneven ground.

He walked in silence for a while.

That was when the feeling reached him.

Something felt off.

Elrond lifted his gaze from the path and slowly looked around.

He did not see a single person using this road.

No adventurers with weapons at their belts. No merchants with carts. No farmers moving goods toward Calderidge. The trail stretched ahead and behind like a line drawn only for him, as if someone had emptied it on purpose.

His eyes went back to the memory of the sign at the intersection.

The arrow had clearly stated that this was a shortcut to Calderidge, a town that many travelers passed through, a place that was known for the produce that flowed out from it. A road connected to a place like that should have seen at least a few people, even at this hour.

Even so, the road felt completely empty.

He approached a bend in the road.

As he drew closer, the silence finally broke. The sharp sound of metal striking metal rang out from somewhere beyond the turn. It was not the dull clatter of tools. It was the clear, harsh ring of blades clashing.

The sound of steel meant a fight between people.

Elrond’s body reacted before the thought finished forming. He pulled mana into his legs and spine and activated a 2x Agility spell. His muscles felt lighter at once, and the ground seemed to come toward him faster as he pushed off and rushed toward the source of the noise.

He closed the distance to the bend in a few long strides.

Earlier, on the other side of that turn:

The carriage had been forced to stop in the middle of the narrow road.

Four figures stood ahead of it, blocking the way. They did not spread out randomly. Their positions were too clean, as if each one had already chosen their role.

One held a staff, clearly a magician. One carried a sword alone. Another had a sword and shield. The last one gripped a spear.

The guards escorting the carriage tightened their formation at once. Shields shifted, blades were raised, and the front line formed in front of the horses.

“Identify yourselves!” one of the guards shouted.

The four did not answer.

They simply stared back with blank expressions. Two of them, the swordsman and the spearman, had unnaturally pale skin and dead-looking eyes. There was no tension in their faces, only a strange emptiness.

The guards’ grips tightened.

The enemy magician lifted her staff.

She began to chant, her voice steady as mana gathered at the tip of the staff. A magic circle formed above the carriage, lines of light spreading out and locking into place. The hairs on the guards’ arms prickled as the air around them began to charge.

When the chant reached its final word, she slammed the staff into the ground.

The enemy guardian stepped in front of her at the same time, shield up, braced to absorb any arrow or spell that might be thrown back at her.

Multiple bolts of lightning crashed down toward the carriage.

The world flashed white for a moment. The explosive noise tore at the air. The smell of burned wood and scorched leather mixed with the sharp scent of ozone.

Fortunately, one of the carriage guards—a magician assigned to the escort—had already begun forming a defensive barrier the moment he noticed the magic circle appearing overhead. His shield was not large, and it did not cover everything, but the glowing plane of mana was enough to blunt the worst of the strike.

Lightning slammed into the barrier and split around it. Some arcs still pierced through and struck guards who were not fully covered. They cried out and fell to their knees, but their burns were shallow enough that they did not die on the spot.

As one of the front-line guards tried to push himself back up, he realized something was wrong.

The enemy swordsman and spearman were no longer in front of them.

“Defensive position!” he shouted.

His warning came just in time.

They attacked from above.

The spearman descended first, his spear wrapped in wind. He drove the point straight down into the ground, and the impact sent a shockwave bursting out along the road. The compressed air tore at legs and balance. Several guards were knocked off their feet as the ground seemed to jump under them.

Before they could recover, the spearman swept his spear sideways. The remaining wind clung to the weapon and lashed out, knocking more guards away and throwing the line into chaos.

The swordsman followed up like a shadow behind that movement.

He fell on the guards whose shields were not in position yet. His blade moved in fast, efficient cuts. One, two, three guards without shields went down under his strikes, their armor sliced open where they were slow to raise their guard.

A guard with a shield saw this and threw himself forward.

He forced his way between the swordsman and the next target, shield raised to take the incoming blow. Steel met reinforced wood with a heavy impact. He managed to block, but he had misjudged the weight behind the enemy’s attack.

The enemy swordsman shifted his stance.

He thrust the tip of his sword straight into the shield with focused strength. The force drove the guard back and staggered him, opening the angle of his defense. His stance broke for an instant.

In that instant, the swordsman moved again.

His blade swept upward from below with frightening speed. The angle would have gone straight through the guard’s throat or chin—

—but the strike did not land.

Another sword met it first, catching the blade and pushing it off its path.

A blonde girl had stepped between them.

Her sword met the enemy’s upward slash and diverted it. She used the deflection to force him back a step, then followed immediately with another swing. The swordsman brought his own weapon up to block. Steel rang again, and their blades slid against each other.

The exchange was brief, but it broke his momentum and drove him away from the guards.

The shield-bearing guard stared for a heartbeat, stunned, then found his voice.

“Lady Cestina, thank you!” he cried.

The blonde girl—Cestina Ludwell—did not look back at him. She wore light armor suitable for battle, and her eyes moved quickly, measuring the battlefield in front of her.

In a single glance, she understood that the guards alone would not be enough to win against these attackers.

“Form up and protect Lady Emilia!” she ordered.

Her voice cut through the noise and gave the scattered guards a clear purpose.

The enemy spearman was already being held off by the guard captain. Their weapons met again and again as the captain kept him from breaking through toward the carriage. It was not an easy fight, but for now it was enough.

The enemy magician stood slightly behind her guardian, staff still in hand. Lisoletelle and the other carriage magicians watched her closely with their own staves ready. If she tried to unleash another major spell, they were prepared to counter it, or at least blunt its impact.

Emilia, unwilling to hide inside the carriage, stood in front of it.

She held her sword and used ice magic whenever she saw an opening, sending shards and spikes to support the guards. Her magic did not dominate the field, but every spell that hit slowed an enemy step or forced them to adjust their movement.

The horses lay still on the ground. They had already been killed in the first strike, which meant escape by carriage was no longer an option.

Cestina judged the situation quickly.

It was dangerous, and losses had already occurred, but as long as the lines held and their magicians kept the enemy caster in check, it was still winnable.

Then the enemy magician began chanting again.

This time, the signs were different.

Mana spread out from her in multiple streams and linked to her allies. Cestina saw the patterns of light stretch toward the swordsman, the spearman, and the guardian. The words of the chant were clearly the names of enhancement spells.

Strength. Agility. Defense.

Glow settled around the enemy fighters. Their movements grew sharper even before they took a step. The guardian’s armor seemed to gain an extra layer of weight around it, an invisible shell that clung to shield and plate.

“Prepare enhancement spells!” the guard captain shouted.

Liso and the other magicians answered at once.

They chanted their own enhancement magic, sending Strength and Agility buffs to the guards who could still stand, and reinforcing the defenses around the front line. Lines of light wrapped around arms and legs and shields.

The enemies charged.

What followed was brutal.

The enemy swordsman shot forward with his new speed. Before the enhanced guards could fully adjust, he cut into them. All six front-line guards who had recovered from the first assault went down under his blade one after another. His sword found gaps between plates and seams in armor with terrifying precision.

“Damn you!” the guard captain roared.

He tried to break away from the spearman to reach the swordsman, but the spearman moved to intercept. The enemy’s spearwork, now boosted by magic, locked the captain in place and refused to let him leave. Every attempt to disengage opened a risk of being skewered, and he was forced to focus entirely on the opponent in front of him.

Cestina saw the slaughter.

Anger burned in her chest. She wanted to run straight for the swordsman and cut him down before he could reach anyone else. She tried to force her way past, but the moment she shifted, the swordsman turned his attention to her, and their blades met again.

She attacked him relentlessly whenever she caught an opening.

Her sword traced sharp, precise lines, and she pressed him without holding back, but he blocked or dodged with an ease that made her grit her teeth. Even when she thought she had finally drawn out a real gap in his guard and lunged into it, she realized too late that another threat was already coming.

A blade came in from the side.

The enemy guardian had closed in.

His sword cut toward her at an angle that would have bitten deep if she had not twisted away at the last second. She barely managed to dodge, feeling the wind of the swing pass close to her. The force of the near miss and the need to reset her footing forced her to pull back.

The guardian did not give her room. He pressed forward immediately, sword and shield working together to keep Cestina occupied and away from his allies.

That left Emilia.

The enemy swordsman began walking toward her.

Emilia felt his presence before he reached her.

His steps were not rushed, but every one of them carried confidence. She could feel the weight of his skill and power the same way she had felt it when fighting against her brother during training. In fact, the pressure now might have been close to that level.

He was strong. Possibly on the same level as Gilbert.

But she could not back down.

She raised her sword in front of her and gathered magic in her other hand. Fear sat cold in her chest, but she did not let it push her backward. She chose to face him head-on rather than hide behind the remaining guards.

Liso watched from behind, lips pressed tightly together.

She could not leave her position. The enemy magician still stood across from her, staff at the ready. If Liso turned away now, a single unchecked spell could wipe out what was left of their formation.

Her fingers tightened on her staff until they hurt. She could only watch Emilia and grit her teeth.

This attack was clearly deliberate.

On Liso side, Liso try to move first.

She and the other magicians raised their staves at almost the same time. A fireball shot out toward the enemy magician from the line, bright and fast, meant to force a reaction.

Liso did not stay in place.

She charged in, feet pounding the ground, staff held low. Close-range magic had always suited her better, and fast chanting came to her as naturally as breathing. Several mana blast spells gathered above her as she ran, the spheres of compressed mana circling and tightening with every word she spoke.

When she reached what she judged to be the right distance, she released them all toward the enemy magician.

The enemy had already seen it coming.

The enemy magician raised her staff and finished a shorter chant that she had prepared in advance. A specialized barrier flared to life in front of her, clear and rigid. Liso’s mana blasts slammed into it one after another.

The barrier held.

The blasts exploded against it and scattered light and shock, but the shield did not break. The fireball from the other magicians weakened it, yet it was not enough to shatter the defense outright.

Now that she was in range, Liso switched spells without hesitating.

She chanted a weapon enhancement spell. Power gathered around the tip of her staff until it began to glow. She gripped it with both hands, stepped in, and swung it down toward the enemy magician’s head.

The enemy moved at the very last moment.

Her body slipped to the side. The enhanced staff missed her and crashed into the ground instead. The impact triggered the spell that had been packed into it, and the earth burst upward with a sharp explosion.

Dirt and fragments of stone flew out, and smoke billowed between them.

The enemy magician used that instant.

She kicked off with a powerful leap and rose into the air. As her feet left the ground, she began chanting again, and her body steadied in midair instead of falling back down right away. She glided forward, as if the air itself was carrying her.

Glide magic? Liso’s eyes widened.

She recognized the pattern of the spell at once. Glide magic was an advanced technique. Even she had not learned it yet. She knew what it was, and that was exactly why she understood how bad the timing was.

It was already too late to form a proper shield.

Before the enemy could finish what she was building, one of the other magicians fired off another fireball. It hit the enemy magician in the middle of her chant. The blast forced her to twist away, and her aim went off.

The spell she was casting missed Liso.

Even so, the exchange made one thing completely clear. The caster floating in front of them was on a different level. She was a powerful magician, and she had not been pushed into a corner yet.

The enemy’s eyes slid over the battlefield, toward the cluster of staves and robes.

The backline casters were troublesome. Their counters and support spells had already blunted more than one of her attempts.

She decided to remove them first.

A magic circle formed under her feet. She kicked off from it, her body rising higher as if pushed by an unseen hand. Hovering above the magicians now, she began to glide over their line.

Liso saw the movement and rushed back, trying to get under the enemy’s path and force her down again, but she was a step behind.

The enemy magician finished her chant.

A massive volley of magic spheres rained down on the magicians.

The escorts on the ground tried to respond. They began chanting defensive barriers as fast as they could, but the spells descending on them were faster. The first spheres hit before most of the shields were complete.

Explosions tore through the back line.

Light and sound swallowed them. The blasts ripped into the formation and flung bodies aside. When the explosions faded, smoke and dust hung thick in the air.

Liso stared, her stomach turning cold.

Three of the magicians lay motionless on the ground, their robes burned and their bodies twisted in ways that did not belong to the living. From the injuries alone, it was obvious that they were dead.

Anger flared up and burned through the shock.

Liso raised her staff and unleashed everything she had at the enemy magician. She threw magic balls, sent out mana blasts, and called up elemental spells, pushing fire and raw force into the air with no thought of conserving power.

The enemy answered with calm movements.

She blocked and deflected with precise timing, her staff and barriers knocking Liso’s spells aside or dulling them until they lost their bite. Every attack that looked like it might land was turned aside just before it did.

Liso bit down hard and made a decision.

As a last resort, she closed the distance again.

She surged forward, chanting enhancement magic over and over while she moved. Power wrapped around her staff. When she reached the enemy, she did not hold back. She slashed and struck relentlessly, her staff moving like a heavy blade.

Blow after blow hammered into the enemy’s defenses. For a brief moment, the rhythm broke. A gap appeared that was barely wide enough to reach.

Liso took it.

Her enhanced staff connected with the enemy magician’s body. The spell packed into the blow triggered on impact and set off another explosion at close range.

Smoke burst out between them.

When the blast cleared, the enemy magician had been wounded. Her outfit was burned and torn in places, and there were marks on her skin where the spell had bitten in.

Her expression did not change.

Her eyes remained flat and calm. If anything, the way she held her staff now felt different in another way.

She seemed to get serious.

She raised her hand and began to cast again. Magic spheres formed one after another around her, lining up like a string of glowing orbs. They shot out toward Liso in an unbroken barrage.

Liso already had a shield spell active in front of her.

She poured what power she had left into it and held on as the spheres crashed against it. Every explosion shook her arms and sent cracks spiderwebbing across the barrier. The next blast deepened the fractures. Another one widened them.

Then one of the magic blasts slipped through.

It struck the ground close to her and exploded. The shockwave lifted Liso off her feet and hurled her backward. Her body hit the earth hard and rolled.

For a few seconds, she could not move.

Pain screamed through her limbs. Blood trickled down from her head, running past one eye and dripping off her chin. Her mana felt almost completely drained, like an empty well.

Even so, she tried to get up.

Her arms trembled as she pushed against the ground. She forced her body up, one breath at a time, refusing to stay down.

As she raised her head, she saw it.

Another magic blast was forming in front of the enemy magician, larger and more focused than the earlier ones. Its aim was locked straight on her.

The spell was coming for her, and she had nothing left to stop it.

On the other side of the battlefield:

Cestina was still furious.

The images of the slaughtered guards would not leave her mind. She continued to press the attack against the enemy guardian, sword flashing as she tried to break his defense and escape his range.

No matter how hard she hit, his shield remained solid.

Every thrust and slash met a wall of steel and reinforced stance. Her blows made him slide back, and sometimes a heavy strike forced him a step away, but none of it was enough to open a path past him.

She finally landed a hit that drove him back more than before.

His boots slid across the dirt, and for a heartbeat he had to reset his balance. Cestina shifted her weight, ready to use that moment to run past him and head toward Emilia.

Before she could take the step, he was already back in front of her.

He raised his shield and restored the barrier between her and the rest of the field, as if he had never been moved at all.

Cestina gritted her teeth.

That was when she noticed it.

A wave of dizziness washed over her, as if the ground had suddenly tilted to one side. Her vision blurred for a moment. She forced herself to focus, pushed the feeling away, and kept attacking. The guardian’s sword and shield clashed against her blade again as she aimed for every opening she could see.

With each clash, the lightness in her head grew worse.

Her timing felt slightly off. Her arms were still moving, but the world around her seemed to slow and darken at the edges.

She swung one more time.

The guardian caught her sword on his shield and answered with a straight stab. She managed to bring her weapon back in time to block the thrust, steel scraping against steel.

Then everything went dark.

In that darkness, there was no battlefield. No shouts. No ringing steel.

Only a strange woman’s voice, whispering clearly in her mind.

You are under my command.

Cestina felt as though chains had closed around her entire body.

Her limbs no longer moved according to her will. Something cold and heavy coiled around her thoughts and pulled them down.

Outside, her body collapsed.

She fell to the ground for a moment, motionless. Then she stirred, pushed herself up, and stood.

Her eyes had lost their light.

They were as empty as the attackers’ eyes. Her expression had gone completely blank. Side by side, the controlled Cestina and the enemy guardian began slowly walking toward Emilia.

On Emilia’s side, the battle had narrowed down to a single line.

She was still facing the enemy swordsman. Their blades met again and again. In terms of pure swordsmanship, she could tell that she held the advantage. Her forms were cleaner, her swings more precise, and her footwork more stable.

The problem was not technique.

The difference in raw strength and physical buffs pushed her into a corner every time. She had cast 3x Strength and 2x Agility on herself, and her body responded well, but the enemy’s enhancements and physical power were still heavier.

Whenever she saw an opening, she added ice magic.

Ice spears formed and shot toward him. Ice bind spells reached for his legs and arms. She used them to interrupt his flow and carve out space, yet the swordsman dealt with them with frustrating ease. He broke the ice, stepped around it, and cut through her spells without losing his rhythm.

Their blades crossed again in a hard clash.

At last, Emilia managed to create a real opening.

She turned his weapon aside with a twist of her wrist and stepped in, her sword cutting across his body. The impact knocked him backward. He hit the ground, armor scraping against the dirt.

She moved to finish it.

She raised her sword and rushed in, ready to strike before he could recover.

A shield slid into her path.

Her blade crashed against it instead of flesh and armor. The shock ran up her arms. She leapt back a step on instinct and reset her stance, eyes snapping toward the one who had intercepted.

The guardian from before was there.

The same man who had been holding Cestina back now stood in front of the fallen swordsman, shield raised between them.

Emilia’s gaze shifted quickly.

She spotted Cestina nearby.

Something was wrong.

Cestina’s eyes were empty, just like the attackers’ eyes. There was no recognition in them. No anger. No fear. Only a flat, hollow stare.

Without any warning, Cestina charged.

She closed the distance and attacked Emilia with the same sharp swordsmanship she had been using against the enemy moments earlier.

“Cestina!” Emilia called out.

Steel rang as she met the blows. She called her friend’s name again and again while she tried to read her movements.

“What is going on? Answer me!” Emilia demanded.

Cestina did not respond.

Her sword strikes did not falter. They kept coming, one after another, forcing Emilia to defend instead of push forward.

Confusion and alarm twisted inside Emilia’s chest.

She created distance the moment she saw a chance. She chanted even as she moved and cast an ice wall between them, using it to slow Cestina down and give herself a breath of space. The spell rose and hardened while her sword still moved, the chant woven into the clash of blades.

At that moment, on the other side, the guard captain had begun to overpower the enemy spearman.

Their duel reached a turning point. The captain pushed his advantage, struck the spearman off balance, and finally managed to break away. He did not waste the opportunity. He ran to Emilia’s side and took in the scene with a quick, experienced glance.

Emilia told him what had happened in short, clipped words.

“Cestina suddenly turned on us,” she said. “Her eyes are like theirs.”

The captain’s expression darkened.

“It might be some form of long-range puppetry magic,” he said. “I do not know the exact cause, but her body is probably being controlled from a distance.”

Before they could say anything more, another sound crashed across the battlefield.

A massive explosion roared nearby.

Both of them turned toward the backline where the magicians had been positioned.

The air was filled with dust and smoke. When it began to clear, Emilia saw it. A huge magic blast had formed and was now racing straight toward Liso’s position.

In that moment, it felt as if the world narrowed down to that single sight.

Emilia moved without thinking.

She jumped and screamed, her voice raw.

“NO!! LISO!!!”

It sounded like the cry of someone about to lose her own life, not just her friend’s.

The magic blast rushed toward Liso.

Just before it reached her, another explosion erupted. This time the sound was different. It was the impact of power striking a solid defense.

The blast had been blocked by something.

When the dust from that impact settled, a single figure stood in front of Liso, between her and the point of impact.

A man held his sword raised in a guarding stance. Around him, the fading traces of a powerful defensive shield shimmered and then vanished from the air.

It was Elrond, who had rushed into the battle.

He spared a brief glance over his shoulder.

“Are you alright?” he asked.

Liso’s face was pale. Her body shook slightly, and her eyes were wide. From the way she looked at him, it was clear that a moment earlier she had already resigned herself to dying. The fact that she was still alive had not fully caught up to her yet.

Now that Elrond was on the field, he turned his attention forward and began to read the situation. Even so, it did not take long.

From one look, it was already obvious who was on which side.

Elrond glanced back.

The girl behind him was still on her knees. Her breaths were shallow, and blood that had run down from her head was already drying on her cheek. He raised his hand and cast a healing spell on her, letting gentle light sink into her injuries and stabilize her body. There was no time to ask her name.

As the spell settled, he looked past her.

On the other side of a massive ice wall, he saw another part of the battlefield. A dark-haired girl and a man stood together, facing off against two men and a blonde girl. The formation was uneven. The air around them felt like a taut string pulled close to breaking.

He did not stay where he was.

Elrond picked the red-haired girl up in his arms and leapt. With one jump, he crossed the ruined ground and moved to regroup with the dark-haired girl’s side.

He landed behind the ice wall and set the girl down carefully.

“It is alright now,” he said.

His voice was calm, and it cut through the panic for a moment. The dark-haired girl—Emilia—turned to look at him. The man beside her, the guard captain, assessed him in a single sharp glance.

Elrond did not waste the opening.

He cast clairvoyance, focusing it not on the enemy this time but on the people around him. Lines of information slid into his awareness. He saw that the red-haired girl and the dark-haired girl had almost completely drained their mana. Their reserves were like nearly empty vessels. The man beside them, on the other hand, still had enough strength left to fight.

Elrond turned to him.

“Can you keep fighting?” he asked.

“Of course,” the captain answered without hesitation. “That is my duty.”

The words were simple, and the way he spoke them left no doubt.

So this wolf hunt turned into an assassination rescue, Elrond thought.

He faced the battlefield again, ready to move.

Before he could charge in, Emilia stepped forward in a rush. Her eyes were fixed on the blonde girl beyond the ice wall.

“Please do not hurt the blonde girl,” she said quickly. “Her name is Cestina. She is my friend. She is being controlled by someone.”

Elrond gave a short nod.

He cast clairvoyance again, this time on the girl Emilia had pointed out. When he looked at Cestina through the spell, he saw it clearly. Thin strands of mana were connected into her body, like threads woven into her limbs and head. They stretched out from her and led somewhere far beyond the immediate field, out of sight.

That was enough to confirm Emilia’s words.

Without wasting another moment, he turned inward and drew mana into his muscles.

He cast 4x Strength and 3x Agility on himself.

Power flooded his body in layers. His limbs felt lighter and heavier at the same time, packed with force that waited to be released.

“I will deal with the enemy magician first,” he said. “She is the biggest nuisance.”

He did not wait for an answer.

In the next instant, he leapt forward. The ground behind him cracked under the force of his takeoff. To the people watching, his figure blurred. In the space of a blink, he moved in front of the enemy magician.

Her eyes widened for a fraction of a second.

By the time that reaction reached her face, he was already behind her.

His sword drew a hard line across her back. The impact of the strike bit into her and broke her stance. She staggered, and her body pitched forward.

He stepped in to finish it.

At that moment, the guardian intervened.

He hurled his shield between Elrond and the magician. Metal and mana collided. The impact sent a harsh vibration up Elrond’s arm and forced him to pull back a step. The blow also bought the magician the opening she needed.

She leapt away.

Her feet touched a glowing magic circle that rose beneath her, and she kicked off from it. Her body moved up into the air again, and she began to glide while chanting, her voice building into the words of a powerful magic blast.

Elrond watched her for a brief beat.

He had already thought ahead.

Before closing in, he had prepared several compressed fireballs in the air, each one aimed precisely at her expected escape path. The spheres waited, small and dense, fixed on her position.

The enemy magician saw them.

She did not bother to dodge. She did not cast a full defensive spell. She continued her chant without breaking rhythm, confident that her barriers and endurance would be enough to withstand a few attacks while she completed her own spell.

Elrond raised his hand slightly.

He fired the compressed fireballs at high speed.

They streaked through the air and detonated midair around her. The explosions swallowed her in heat and light. The blasts tore at her balance even as she tried to maintain her glide.

He did not have time to confirm the full extent of the damage.

He sensed killing intent from behind.

A sword swing was coming straight for him from that direction. The guardian again.

Elrond twisted aside, and the incoming blade missed his body and slammed into the ground. The impact drove the steel deep into the earth and sent up a burst of dirt.

The guardian adjusted quickly.

He wrenched the sword free and shifted his stance for another thrust, aiming straight for Elrond’s center.

Elrond jumped slightly and brought his own sword down beside him.

Steel met steel just in front of his body. The clash stopped the thrust cold. The force of the collision traveled through both blades and locked them together for a brief moment.

That was all he needed.

He turned his wrist and knocked the guardian’s sword aside, breaking the line of attack. In the same motion, he stepped in and swung his weapon. The blow struck the guardian’s sword hand and tore the weapon from his grip.

The blade spun away and fell to the ground.

The guardian’s hands were now empty.

Elrond did not slow down. He infused his sword with fire, doing it without any chant. Flames wrapped around the steel in a tight layer.

He drove the burning sword straight into the guardian’s armored chest.

The impact carried all the force of his enhancements. The guardian’s armor deformed under the strike, and the blow lifted the man off his feet. His body flew backward and crashed to the ground.

He did not get up again.

It had all happened in an instant.

Just as Elrond finished with the guardian, another presence cut in from the side.

Cestina, still under control, closed in on him with her sword raised. He barely noticed in time. He twisted his body and brought his weapon up. Their blades clashed with a sharp ring.

Emilia’s plea flashed through his mind.

He held back the lethal edge of his counters. He kept his strikes focused on defense and control, trying to find a way to subdue Cestina without causing serious harm. Every swing she made, however, was aimed to kill. There was no restraint in her movements.

Their swords collided again and again with heavy force.

For Elrond, it was troublesome. He had to block killing blows while also limiting his own options. As the exchange continued, he began to study the rhythm of her attacks.

Her sword style was different from most he had seen on the frontier.

It resembled a Western fencing style. Her thrusts and slashes were fast and precise, with footwork that kept her at the most efficient distance. Her blade always seemed to aim for vital lines rather than broad cuts.

As they traded blows, he started to see the pattern.

He decided to take the offensive.

Several times, he tried to end it by striking the back of her head with the hilt of his sword. Each attempt came at the end of a parry or a deflection. Every time, Cestina’s body moved just enough. She avoided the blow, or her blade intercepted his arm and pushed it aside.

He waited.

Finally, the opening came.

Cestina leapt at him with a downward slash, putting her weight and momentum into the strike. Elrond met it head-on. He blocked the blow, letting the force travel down his arms.

He used that impact.

He turned with it, spinning and stepping in closer instead of being pushed away. The movement took him to her side. Using that momentum, he brought the hilt of his sword around in a tight arc and struck the back of her head.

The blow landed cleanly.

Cestina’s body stiffened. Her sword slipped from her fingers. Then she collapsed and lost consciousness.

With the three of them—the magician, the guardian, and Cestina—down, Elrond turned.

His eyes went to the last part of the battlefield. The guard captain was already at his limit. His breaths were ragged, and his guard was beginning to open as he barely held on against the enemy swordsman.

Elrond dashed in.

He closed the distance in a heartbeat and leapt toward the fight, sword ready to intercept.

A moment later, he stood between the captain and the enemy.

Now, only Elrond and the swordsman remained.

When he faced the enemy swordsman head-on, Elrond felt it at once.

Mana was surging through the man’s body, swelling and twisting as it wrapped around his limbs and blade. The air around him felt heavier, like the pressure before a storm.

The guard captain noticed it as well.

“That is Berserk,” he said sharply. “It is a technique from the northern highlands, tied to the Sieghart household. He is drawing natural mana from the surroundings to enhance himself, both physically and magically. He can turn his slashes into pure mana strikes with terrifying impact.”

Elrond’s expression hardened.

He decided to push himself closer to his limit.

He cast 6× Strength and 5× Agility on himself, layering the spells over his muscles and nerves. On top of that, he added a Body Defense spell that would not completely nullify attacks, but would blunt their impact and keep a fatal blow from tearing him apart. As always, the spells settled into his body without a single chant.

“Stay behind me,” he told the others.

Then both he and the swordsman moved.

They dashed forward, and their swords collided with a heavy clang. In the next moment, they had already separated and clashed again. For ordinary eyes, their movements would look like blurs that appeared and vanished in different positions, almost like teleportation. People like Emilia and the guard captain could still follow, but only just.

For Elrond, this was the most serious fight he had faced since sparring with his father.

Every block felt heavy. Each time steel met steel, the weight behind the swordsman’s blade pushed numbness into his arms. On top of that, he had to deal with the man’s mana slashes.

When those blade-waves cut through the air and hit trees, they carved halfway through the trunk. Chunks of wood fell away, and deep scars opened in the bark. Elrond did not want to imagine what would happen if one of those waves hit him directly.

For now, he managed to block them with focused defensive magic, forming small but dense barriers exactly where the waves would pass. It worked, but it ate away at his concentration and stamina.

The swordsman’s movement was wild and chaotic.

It felt as if his body was being pushed forward by something that did not care about rhythm. Steps were irregular, swings came from unexpected angles, and his attacks did not follow the usual patterns that came from training.

Elrond narrowed his eyes. He tried to read the flow and find a clear pattern, but nothing lined up the way he wanted.

The guard captain shouted between clashes, raising his voice over the ringing steel.

“For someone who cannot control Berserk, they sometimes lose their mind!”

So that is what is happening, Elrond thought.

Even as he accepted that, something else began to press at the edge of his awareness.

A wave of dizziness hit him.

It was not the simple dizziness of fatigue. It felt as if something was trying to slip into his head, like fingers pushing against the inside of his thoughts. He gritted his teeth and forced himself to focus. He continued trading blows, meeting the swordsman again and again, but the sensation grew worse every time he closed in.

He did not know what it was at first.

The feeling did not fade. It only grew clearer, and that made his irritation rise together with his caution.

Finally, he snapped to a realization.

In the middle of the fight, Elrond cast clairvoyance on himself and the space around him. Information flooded into his vision and senses. He saw it then.

A magic thread was linking both him and the swordsman to something far away.

He leapt back at once to create distance, dodging a slash as he moved away. When he stopped, he focused on the mana thread tied into his own body. He gathered his power and poured a massive surge of mana into the link.

The mana inside him felt like it was about to explode. Pressure built at the point where the thread entered him, as if something was trying to hold the line from the other side.

Then the thread snapped.

Somewhere far away, in a place hidden from the battlefield, a mysterious woman stood in the shadows.

Her hand, which had been extended in the middle of a spell, lowered slightly. She had tried to cast her puppet magic on Elrond through the link.

Her lips curved in a faint smile instead of a grimace.

The attempt had failed.

With that issue dealt with, Elrond refocused on the fight in front of him.

He charged again and resumed trading blows with the swordsman. This time, he kept his mana and senses on high alert, ready to attack any new thread that tried to latch onto him before it could settle.

At one point, their swords clashed in mid-air.

The force of the impact pushed both of them back. They landed apart from each other. Elrond came down near his group, boots skidding slightly on the dirt before he steadied himself.

Emilia and the guard captain could only stare for a moment.

How is he still fighting like that after dealing with three of them? Emilia thought. He stepped in and saved everyone I could not.

Her grip on her sword tightened without her noticing. The images would not leave her alone—the guards cut down one by one, Liso thrown through the air, Cestina’s empty eyes turning toward her like a stranger’s.

At the same time, another thought gnawed at her.

I am still too weak, she thought. In the end, I could not protect anyone.

Elrond fixed his grip on his sword.

He decided he could not rely on swordsmanship alone.

He charged in again. His blade flashed toward every opening he could find. The swordsman either blocked or dodged, his Berserk-enhanced body still fast and strong. Now, whenever Elrond created even a slight gap, he added something else.

He used magic blasts from behind the swordsman.

He timed the spells so that the explosions would go off just as the swordsman committed to a movement. The blasts staggered him, shook his balance, and forced openings that Elrond tried to follow up on with slashes.

The hits were not fatal.

The enemy was sharp, and his enhanced body was tough enough to keep going. Even so, each successful strike and each blast chipped away at him. Little by little, Elrond wore him down with a mix of sword and magic.

For the finishing setup, Elrond decided to recreate the “bullet” trick he had used before with earth and fire magic.

He pulled back slightly to gain space.

He conjured three dense stone bullets in the air and then heated them with fire magic until they glowed red. The compressed stones hung behind him, hovering above and slightly to the rear, ready to follow his movement.

Then he dashed in again.

The bullets moved with him, tracking his path from above as he closed in on the swordsman.

When he finally forced an opening, he fired them one by one.

The first shot grazed the swordsman. It carved a shallow path along his side and exploded behind him.

The second missed entirely as the man twisted away, reacting at the very last moment.

The third hit dead-on, but not where Elrond had aimed.

Instead of piercing the torso, it struck the swordsman’s left arm.

The superheated stone did not just pierce. It exploded on impact.

The man screamed and grabbed at his shoulder. His left forearm was blown clean off, and blood poured from the ruined stump. Both of them pulled back, Elrond to observe and the swordsman to try to stabilize himself.

As he watched, Elrond noticed movement from another direction.

The blonde girl—Cestina—was waking up.

For a moment, he hoped she had regained her senses. That hope disappeared almost immediately. When her eyes opened fully, they were still empty.

She was still under control.

Cestina began moving toward him, posture steady and blade ready. It was clear that she was preparing to join the fight again.

“No way…” Elrond muttered under his breath, stunned for a moment.

He hesitated. He did not know how much longer the controller would keep using her, and he did not want to keep striking down the same person without thinking ahead.

He turned his head slightly toward Emilia and, with genuine concern, asked for forgiveness in advance.

“What if I… accidentally kill her?” he said.

Emilia’s fingers tightened.

“If that happened,” she answered, her voice tight, “I would be devastated. I might even lose my sanity. Cestina is one of my closest friends.”

That was enough.

Elrond immediately discarded the idea of landing a killing blow on her. There had to be a way to subdue her without killing.

He came up with one.

Knock her out through blood loss and then heal her at once before it became fatal.

He did not have time to refine the plan.

Cestina charged.

Elrond met her head-on. Compared to the earlier chaos, the flow now was different. His body was still fully enhanced, and he had already seen her style. He dodged and blocked her attacks with ease. They traded blows, but this time he was clearly in control of the exchange.

When he finally saw a clean opening, he moved.

In the middle of a clash, he drew a small dagger from his belt with his free hand. He stepped to the side, guided her momentum past him, and stabbed her in a non-vital spot. The strike was deep enough to make her lose consciousness, but not in a place that would kill her quickly.

She staggered, her sword slipping.

Then she collapsed again.

Right after, Elrond scanned the battlefield and realized something else.

The other three enemies he had fought—the swordsman, the magician, and the guardian—were gone. They had vanished while he dealt with Cestina. Only the enemy spearman remained, lying defeated where the guard captain had brought him down.

Elrond immediately cast healing magic on Cestina.

Light sank into the wound he had made. He closed it before the blood loss could become dangerous. Once he was satisfied that she was stable, he carried her over and laid her gently in front of Emilia.

He took a slow look around.

From what he could see, the fight was finally over. The primary attackers had escaped, but there were no signs that they were still nearby. To be certain, he expanded his senses and unleashed a wide-range mana detection pulse over the area.

Nothing resembling their mana signatures remained.

They were gone.

Elrond let out a quiet breath and released his enhancement spells.

His body felt heavy all at once. The weight of his own muscles returned to normal, and the fatigue that the magic had been holding back came rushing in.

Emilia leaned forward, anxiety clear in her voice.

“Will Cestina be alright?” she asked.

“Not yet,” Elrond replied. “She is still linked.”

He explained, briefly but clearly, how puppet magic worked.

“The caster repeatedly trades blows through the ‘puppet’ and keeps pouring mana into the target,” he said. “Little by little, that builds a link. Once the link is solid, the caster can override the target’s will and move their body however they want.”

“She tried the same thing on me earlier,” Elrond added. “I will use the same method I used on myself to break it.”

He focused on the mana thread still attached to Cestina. He gathered his power and poured mana into the connection point, more and more, pushing against the foreign control that held the line.

After a moment of resistance, the thread snapped.

He cast clairvoyance once more to confirm.

The thread was gone. The connection had been severed.

With that, the immediate crisis was finally over.

The guard captain took a step closer, exhaustion written across his face. He bowed his head slightly.

“Thank you,” he said. “May I have your name?”

“I am Elrond,” Elrond answered.

He deliberately left out his family name.

Not long after, the sound of wheels and hooves reached them from the distance. A carriage appeared on the road, bearing the Alfrost emblem and flag. The sight was clear even from where they stood.

Elrond recognized it.

He remembered what that implied. Nobles, questions, and attention.

Then another thought surfaced.

He still had a monster subjugation request to finish.

He did not want to get dragged into noble politics or interrogations that would pull him deeper into their affairs.

“I am leaving,” he said simply.

Without any further conversation, he turned away from the road and quietly slipped out of the scene.

Emilia, still in shock, could barely process what was happening.

She was alive. Her friends were alive. All of that was because of a stranger who had appeared, fought, and then walked out of her life without even giving a surname.

Reinforcements from House Alfrost arrived at the battlefield and were stunned by what they saw.

Only three regular guards, the guard captain, Liso, Cestina, and Emilia were still alive. Six guards had been killed. The bodies of the fallen and the dead enemy spearman were collected with grim care.

Emilia and the others were escorted to the second carriage.

They climbed aboard while the bodies were loaded as well. The carriages then turned and left the ruined stretch of road behind.

From a distance, Elrond watched them go.

If I stay, it will just draw too much attention. Too much trouble, he thought.

He turned away and continued his original plan.

He headed toward the northwest hill to hunt Ferocious Wolves.

The rest of the work was almost simple compared to what had happened before. He tracked the den, dealt with the monsters while they were still sluggish from daylight, and successfully collected six hides that met the request’s conditions.

Later, he returned to the Adventurer Bureau and sold them for twenty-four silver.

After everything that had happened, he finally made his way back to the Academy dorm.

The sun had already set. The sky over the capital was slipping into full night. Inside the dorm, the quiet felt heavier than usual.

He soaked in the bathtub for the first time, letting the hot water ease the strain in his muscles while he replayed the day’s events in his mind from beginning to end.

After the bath, he went out to a tavern for dinner and ate in steady silence.

Then he returned to the dorm, went to his room, and collapsed onto the bed.

Quite a “free day” before orientation, he thought.

Sleep took him soon after.

### Chapter 21: 17 - Unsettled Feeling

#### Scene 1

The battle ended, but the weight of it did not leave.

Inside the carriage, the air felt heavy and stale. The wheels rattled over the road back to the capital, yet to Emilia it felt as if they were barely moving at all.

It was the first assassination attempt in three years.

She remembered the last time, when she had been twelve and could not do anything. She had only watched and endured while the adults around her acted and fell in front of her. Now, even after all her training and even after holding one of the attackers back, that same memory pressed hard against her chest because, in her mind, nothing had changed.

She had still failed to protect the people beside her.

Lisoletelle was slumped against her, completely drained. Liso’s head rested on Emilia’s shoulder, her face pale and slack with exhaustion. Every small jolt of the carriage made Liso’s body sway, and Emilia had to brace her gently so she would not slide off the seat.

On the opposite side, Cestina lay stretched out, armor still on, eyes closed and unresponsive. Her breathing was shallow but steady. That simple rise and fall was the only proof that she was still there.

This was far worse than Emilia had imagined.

A simple, short trip to Calderidge had turned into a disaster. She had thought it would be a small duty, something she could handle easily with the strength she had trained so hard to gain. Now she sat in the dim carriage with blood still on the floor and could not even keep her hands from trembling.

Ahead and behind them, the escort formation was thinner. The remaining guards rode in stiff silence. The other carriage, following behind, carried the bodies of the fallen guards, along with the three survivors and the guard captain who had somehow kept everyone moving.

When they reached the capital of Arbalest, the guards at the main gate only had to see the crest and the state of the escort. The carriages passed through without inspection and went straight toward the royal district. No one tried to stop them, and no one dared to slow them down.

They turned into the grounds of the Alfrost mansion and did not stop at the front entrance. Both carriages were driven directly to the backyard, where there was more space and fewer eyes from outside. As soon as the wheels ground to a halt, word began to spread through the mansion like a gust of wind.

Gilbert heard it and ran.

He cut through the corridors without bothering to hide his haste, then pushed through the doorway that led to the backyard. The evening light hit his eyes for a moment, and then he saw them.

Two carriages were lined up. One had already been opened and was being unloaded. The bodies of the dead guards were laid out carefully on the ground in a neat row. Mansion guards had gathered around them. Some lifted the cloths that covered the faces of the fallen and checked their features. Others wrote names on slips of paper with rigid, controlled movements.

The sight pressed a cold weight into Gilbert’s stomach, but he did not stop there.

As he approached, the guards straightened and bowed. One of them quickly stepped forward and told him, with a tight voice, that Lady Emilia’s carriage was the one at the front.

Gilbert did not waste a second. He moved past them and went straight to the first carriage. His hand closed around the door handle more tightly than he intended, and he pulled it open.

Inside, he saw three exhausted girls.

Lisoletelle was leaning sideways, still half collapsed against Emilia. Cestina lay motionless on the opposite seat. However, his eyes went first and immediately to the girl in the middle.

“Emilia…” he breathed.

She lifted her head as if it took all the strength she had left. When her gaze met Gilbert’s, something inside her broke. Tears rose so quickly that she could not hold them back. They spilled over her lashes and ran down her cheeks before she even realised she was crying.

She pushed herself to her feet and stepped down from the carriage. The moment she reached him, the tension left her legs. She threw herself into her older brother’s arms and clung to him, fingers clutching at his clothes as her knees gave out.

“I couldn’t protect anyone…” Her voice came out in a ragged sob.

The words stabbed straight into Gilbert’s chest.

For a heartbeat he could only hold her, feeling how small and how heavy she was at the same time. This was not the confident younger sister who carried herself like the future pillar of a great house. This was the twelve-year-old girl he remembered from three years ago, shaken and helpless, only now with fresh blood on her hands as well.

He forced himself to move. With one arm he supported Emilia and eased her weight against him. With the other, he braced himself on the carriage frame and looked inside again.

Lisoletelle’s eyes were closed, and her shoulders rose and fell with tired, uneven breaths. Cestina lay pale and still, but her chest moved. Both of them were clearly worn out, yet they were undeniably alive.

“What are you talking about?” Gilbert said, keeping his voice as steady as he could. “They are alive. You did your best.”

He could feel Emilia trembling against him. She shook her head, tears still streaming down.

“It was just luck,” she choked out. “An unknown man saved us. If he hadn’t been there, then…”

Her words faded into another sob. The way she said it made it sound as if her own efforts meant nothing at all. To her, everything that had happened was only proof that she was still the girl who could not protect anyone.

Gilbert pressed his lips together. There were questions he wanted to ask. Who that man was. How he had appeared. What exactly had happened on that road. He swallowed them all.

“Enough for now. Save the explanation for later,” he said quietly.

Right now, they needed rest and treatment. The details could wait until Emilia’s hands stopped shaking and until the colour returned to her face.

Footsteps hurried across the stone. Eira came running into the backyard, her apron slightly disheveled and her breathing uneven. The moment she saw Emilia clinging to Gilbert, she stopped, then rushed forward.

She dropped to her knees to bring herself level with Emilia’s eyes and grabbed her hand with both of hers.

“Lady Emilia, you are safe… thank goodness,” Eira said.

Relief flooded her expression so strongly that it swept away her usual composure. Tears gathered at the corners of her eyes and spilled over as she squeezed Emilia’s hand more tightly, as if to confirm that this was real.

She began to cry as well.

Gilbert waited a moment, then gently shifted Emilia toward Eira.

“Eira, take Emilia to her room,” he instructed. “Stay with her. Make sure she rests.”

“Yes, young master,” Eira replied at once, bowing her head. Her voice trembled, but her grip on Emilia’s hand was firm.

Gilbert turned his head and called out to another maid who had hurried into the yard.

“Help Lisoletelle inside and see that she receives treatment,” he said. “Put her with Emilia for now.”

The maid nodded quickly and moved toward the carriage.

Gilbert climbed back into the carriage himself. Up close, he could see that Cestina’s light armor was stained with blood. Some of it had dried and darkened, and some of it still looked sticky in places where it had not fully set.

His heart beat faster as he knelt beside her.

He reached out with careful hands and checked her pulse at her neck, then lowered his ear for a moment to listen to her breathing. Each slow, steady breath eased the pressure in his chest a tiny bit.

She was still alive.

Gilbert let out a breath he had not realised he had been holding. He took Cestina’s hand in both of his. Her fingers were cold, so he pressed them gently to his forehead and closed his eyes for a moment.

“Thank goodness… you are alright,” he whispered.

The words were barely audible, yet they carried everything he did not say in front of the others.

After that, he slid one arm under her knees and one behind her back. He lifted her slowly and carefully so he would not shake her. Her weight rested in his arms.

He stepped down from the carriage and turned toward the mansion.

Gilbert walked through the doorway with Cestina in his arms. On the way down the corridor, he raised his voice just enough to reach a nearby maid.

“Get a physician. Now,” he said. “Have them come to the guest room.”

The maid straightened at once and hurried away. Her footsteps faded down the hall as Gilbert continued on. He chose one of the guest rooms close to Emilia’s side of the house, then pushed the door open with his shoulder and stepped inside.

He laid Cestina carefully on the bed. Her clothes were still stiff with dried blood in places, and that alone made the room feel colder.

“Bring a change of clothes,” he said to the female maid who had followed him in. “Use something from Emilia’s for now, and wipe the blood off her as best you can.”

The maid bowed her head.

“Yes, young master.”
