She moved at once, fetching water and cloths, then slipping out to find suitable clothing. Gilbert stayed only long enough to see Cestina’s armor unfastened and set aside. The sight of her injuries no longer open helped a little, even if her skin was still pale.

Not long after that, a knock sounded at the door. A female physician entered, already in work clothes, with a small case and a calm expression.

“Where is the patient?” she asked.

Gilbert stepped back from the bed.

“Here. Her name is Cestina Ludwell. She lost blood in an attack,” he said. “The wounds look closed, but she has not woken up.”

The physician moved to Cestina’s side and began her examination. She pressed her hand lightly above Cestina’s chest and murmured a spell. A faint magic circle spread out under her palm, then faded. She repeated the process at Cestina’s head and along her arms, checking the flow of mana and the state of her body.

Gilbert watched every small movement. Each time the physician’s brow tightened even a little, his shoulders tensed.

After a while, the physician let out a slow breath and straightened.

“She is only exhausted,” the woman reported. “Her body has lost a fair amount of blood, and her mana is drained, but the wounds themselves are fully healed. There is no lingering damage.”

Gilbert felt his chest loosen.

“So she will recover?” he asked.

“Yes,” the physician replied with a firm nod. “With proper rest and food, she should regain her strength. Make sure she drinks water and eats light meals when she wakes. As long as she does that, she will be fine.”

The answer cut through the worst of his fear. He bowed his head slightly.

“Thank you,” he said.

He reached into his pocket and handed the usual fee to the maid beside him so it could be processed properly, then looked back at the physician.

“If anything changes, I will call for you again,” he added.

“I understand,” she said, and then she left the room.

Gilbert turned to the maids.

“Inform the Ludwell household at once,” he told one of them. “Tell them Cestina is safe, but resting here.”

The maid bowed and moved quickly toward the door.

He looked at the remaining two.

“You two stay with her,” he said. “If she wakes up, speak to her calmly and do not let her move around too much. Send someone to me in Emilia’s room immediately.”

“Yes, young master,” they answered in unison.

With that, Gilbert gave Cestina one last glance. Her breathing was still even. That alone was enough to push him back into motion.

He left the guest room and headed straight for Emilia’s quarters.

By the time he arrived, several maids and butlers were already gathered there. The air in the room was quiet and tense. Lisoletelle was lying in Emilia’s bed, tucked under the covers. Emilia had ordered it that way because Liso needed proper, deep rest more than anyone else.

Emilia herself sat on the couch nearby, with Eira close at her side. Eira’s eyes were still red from earlier, and she kept one hand near Emilia as if ready to support her at any moment.

Gilbert stepped into the room. The staff bowed and made space for him without being told. He walked over to the couch and stopped in front of Emilia.

“Eira,” he said.

Eira understood without needing more words. She rose from her seat so Gilbert could take the place beside Emilia, then stepped back but stayed within arm’s reach.

Gilbert sat down next to his sister. Up close, he could see how swollen her eyes were and how tightly she held her own hands together.

“Are you able to talk now, or do you need time to rest?” he asked.

Emilia’s fingers clenched harder for a moment. She drew in a breath, as if steadying herself, and lifted her head.

“I can talk,” she said. There was a slight tremor in her voice, but there was anger in it as well. “But… what I said before has not changed. I still could not protect anyone.”

The frustration behind the words was sharp. She had spent years training so she would not freeze like she had at twelve, yet the result felt the same in her heart.

Gilbert did not interrupt. He only waited.

Emilia began to speak, forcing herself to go through it step by step.

She told him about the four men who had appeared out of nowhere on the road. She described how their formation had cut through the escort, how the guards had been cut down one after another, and how the road had turned into a scene of slaughter in moments. Her voice grew tighter when she reached the part about Cestina.

“They controlled her,” Emilia said. “Cestina was turned against us. I could not reach her at all. I could only try to stop her from killing us.”

Gilbert’s eyes narrowed slightly. For a heartbeat, he said nothing. The idea that someone had seized Cestina’s will and used her as a weapon hit him harder than the rest.

Emilia went on. She told him how Liso had almost been killed, and how, at that point, an unknown man had suddenly jumped into the fight. He had stood alone against the three remaining enemies and held them back, buying time and breaking the flow of the attack.

“If he had not appeared then, we would all be dead,” Emilia said. “It was luck. Pure luck that he was there at that moment.”

To her, that fact cut deeper than anything else. It made all of her training feel small.

Gilbert listened in silence until she finished. When there was a pause, he asked the question that naturally followed.

“Who was he?” Gilbert asked. “Do you remember his name?”

Emilia shook her head.

“I… I do not know,” she admitted. “I could not focus on him. Everything was happening too fast. I cannot even remember his face properly.”

She sounded angry at herself for that too. In her mind, even failing to remember her saviour’s name felt like another failure.

“That is fine,” Gilbert said. His voice was calm. “We can find out who he is later.”

There were other ways to trace a person who had stepped into a battle like that. For now, forcing Emilia to recall details she did not have would only tire her more.

He looked toward one of the butlers standing near the door.

“Go to the backyard,” Gilbert ordered. “Check on the surviving guards. If they can talk, get any information they have about the attackers and about the man who helped. Bring it to me immediately.”

“Yes, young master,” the butler replied, then bowed and left the room at once.

That was all Gilbert needed for the moment. The rest of the answers could wait until the wounded were stable and the first reports came in.

He turned his gaze back to Emilia.

“You have done enough for now,” he said. “Rest. We will handle the rest from here.”

The words were simple, but the way he said them made it clear that the burden did not sit on her shoulders alone anymore.

That night, House Alfrost stood in mourning at the city cemetery once more.

Lanterns lined the path in a straight line, their light dim against the rows of stone markers. In front of six new graves, plain coffins rested with the Alfrost crest and the city watch emblem laid carefully on top. The air was still and cold enough that each breath felt thin.

They were “just” guards, but no one in House Alfrost had ever treated them that way.

Gilbert and Emilia stood at the front, facing the families. Husbands and sons had not returned. Mothers, wives, and children filled the space opposite them, some holding back tears, some already unable to stand without support.

When the rites ended, Gilbert and Emilia stepped forward together.

They bowed their heads deeply.

“We are sorry,” Gilbert said. His voice was steady because it had to be. “They fell while protecting us. House Alfrost will not forget that.”

Emilia followed his lead. When she tried to speak, only a small apology came out, barely louder than a whisper, to the coffins and to the families in front of them. In her head, it was an apology for being alive when those guards were not.

It was an unfortunate tragedy, and yet those men had fulfilled their duty to the very end.

After the last incense burned low and the families had been given time to say what they needed to say, the ceremony drew to a close. The coffins would be laid to rest, and the graves would carry their names. For now, the weight of the night followed the Alfrost siblings back to the carriage.

They rode in silence to the mansion.

Waiting inside, in one of the sitting rooms, were Armand Ludwell, Garrick Ashfeldt, and Rowena Ashfeldt.

Armand rose first when Gilbert and Emilia entered. His usual calm expression was tighter than usual.

“Lord Gilbert. Lady Emilia,” he said, bowing. “I am sorry our daughter caused you trouble, and that such a thing happened under your care.”

Garrick and Rowena bowed as well.

“We have heard the report,” Garrick said. “We are truly sorry for everything that occurred on this trip.”

Rowena’s eyes were red at the corners, but her posture stayed composed.

“We also heard that you took care of both our daughters until now,” she added. “Thank you very much for protecting them.”

Gilbert shook his head slightly.

“Really, there’s no need to apologize,” he said. “They’re technically still Emilia’s aides, and as for Cestina, she is my future bride. Of course I should be the one taking care of her.”

He let a small, wry smile soften the words and added, “Otherwise I will be scolded by my future father-in-law.”

For a moment, the heaviness in the room eased.

Armand gave a short laugh.

“No way I would do that,” he replied.

Gilbert had said it on purpose. Even if it could not erase what had happened, lightening the mood even a little was better than letting everyone drown in the same silence they had brought back from the cemetery.

Near them, Emilia stood quietly.

Her face was pale, and her gaze stayed on the floor. She had not spoken since greeting them. Guilt kept circling in her thoughts, no matter how many times she tried to push it down.

Gilbert noticed.

“It is alright, Emilia,” he said gently. “As long as they are alive, you have done enough.”

She bit her lip, fingers curling slightly at her sides. The words did not settle easily, but hearing them out loud kept her from sinking further for the moment.

Rowena stepped closer.

“Lady Emilia,” she said, her voice softer than before.

Emilia lifted her head a little.

“You should stop blaming yourself,” Rowena said. “You did what you could with what you knew and what you had. We are grateful for how much you cared for their safety, and we are grateful they are safe. So please, lift your spirits. Otherwise Liso will feel sad too.”

She spoke with a warm smile that did not ignore the pain, but tried to give Emilia a place to stand.

Emilia’s shoulders relaxed by a small degree.

“…Thank you, Lady Rowena,” she said quietly. “For saying that.”

Rowena nodded in response. To her, it was only natural.

After that, they went their separate ways.

Gilbert and Armand headed toward the guest room where Cestina had been resting. Emilia walked with the Ashfeldt couple toward her own room to check on Liso.

Cestina’s condition had improved. Her complexion was better, and her breathing was stronger, though her eyes were still closed. Lying there, she looked more like someone in a deep sleep than a patient who had just come back from the edge.

Gilbert stood at her bedside for a moment with Armand, then spoke.

“She should rest in her own home,” he said. “It will be easier for you to look after her there.”

Armand agreed.

Gilbert carefully picked Cestina up again, the same way he had carried her from the carriage. This time, her weight felt less like a desperate burden and more like something he could finally protect properly. They walked together out to the waiting Ashfeldt carriage, where he laid her down inside so she could be taken home.

They parted ways there, with the promise that they would be informed as soon as she woke.

As for Liso—

When Emilia opened her bedroom door, she found Lisoletelle snoring loudly in Emilia’s bed.

Liso was sprawled under the covers as if it were her own room, one arm sticking out in a completely careless angle. Her breathing was deep and completely unbothered, and every new snore made the maids at the side exchange helpless looks.

Rowena’s brow twitched.

“Honestly…” she muttered.

She walked straight to the bed and slapped Liso on the hip.

“Liso!!” Rowena raised her voice. “What do you think you are doing, sleeping like this in Lady Emilia’s room?”

Liso blinked awake, eyes unfocused. She looked around once, sluggishly, then rubbed her face.

“…Mm? Ah… Mother…?” she mumbled.

Rowena folded her arms.

“Well?” she pressed.

Liso stared at the ceiling for a second as if searching for the answer, then said with complete honesty, “Emilia’s bed is really comfortable and smells nice, so I got sleepy and… I fell asleep again.”

That only made Rowena angrier.

“So you were already awake once and decided to go back to sleep?!” she said.

Liso’s eyes went wide.

“Y-Yes…” she answered, voice small and panicked.

Rowena did not let that pass. She grabbed her daughter by the arm and yanked her out of the bed.

“You think this is your own room after everything that happened? Wake up Already!” she said as she dragged Liso toward the door.

Liso flailed, trying to pull back, and squeaked, “Wait, wait, I’m getting up!”

Garrick watched the scene unfold with a resigned expression. He bowed deeply toward Emilia.

“I am very sorry you had to see this, Lady Emilia,” he said. “Our daughter is… like this.”

Emilia could not help it.

She laughed.

The laugh came out lighter than she expected, and she felt herself relax a little for the first time since the attack. Seeing Liso flail and complain while her mother dragged her away told her that Liso had not been broken by what happened.

As Rowena hauled Liso out into the corridor, Liso twisted around and called back over her shoulder.

“I will come visit again tomorrow!” she shouted. “We will talk about everything then!”

The door closed behind her while Rowena kept scolding her in the hall, and Emilia watched the empty doorway for a moment as one of the tight knots in her heart loosened a little.

After both Lisoletelle and Cestina returned to their own mansions, House Alfrost began to slide back toward its usual.

Emilia returned to her room.

Eira was still there, standing near the table where a light meal had been cleared away. When she saw Emilia come in, she smoothed her apron and spoke carefully.

“Lady Emilia,” Eira said. “Tomorrow is the regular orientation. Attendance is optional for you, as before.”

Emilia blinked.

“Ah… I completely forgot about that,” she said.

The reminder pulled up the half-formed memory of the schedule she had been given before the trip. Compared to what had just happened on the road, the word “orientation” felt strangely distant.

“Thank you for telling me,” she added.

Eira bowed.

“Yes, my lady. Then I will take my leave,” she said, and stepped out quietly, closing the door behind her.

Emilia stood there for a moment.

Emilia stood there for a moment and thought about the next day. Sitting in a hall to listen to explanations and polite greetings did not match the day she had just gone through. Her body felt heavy from fatigue, and whenever she let her mind wander she saw the attack on the road again. So she decided she would skip the orientation this time.

She went to wash up. First she took a shower, then she sat in the bath. The hot water helped lift the smell of blood and dust from her skin, and her tense muscles eased a little, although the memory of the fight stayed clear in her mind. She stayed in the bath until the water began to cool, then she got out, dried herself, and went back to her room.

When she opened her closet to look for pajamas, something familiar caught her eye.

The Royal Academy uniform hung among her clothes.

It had been delivered ahead of time so she could have it adjusted if needed, and she had seen it before. Even so, as she looked at it now, she felt a faint sense that she had seen it in another place very recently. The feeling brushed her thoughts and then slipped away before she could catch it.

She was too tired to chase it.

Emilia closed the closet, changed into her sleepwear, and lay down on the bed. The moment her head touched the pillow, drowsiness pulled her under, and she let the unfinished thought go for the night.

—

The next day, Emilia woke later than usual.

There had been no knock at dawn. When she opened her eyes, light was already filling the room, and a tray with breakfast sat waiting on the table. Eira had clearly decided not to wake her early.

Emilia ate in quiet, the simple meal doing more to steady her than she expected. When she finished, she set the plate aside, washed her face, and went back to the closet to choose her usual clothes.

Her gaze stopped on the Royal Academy uniform again.

That uneasy feeling from the night before returned, stronger this time. She reached up and touched the edge of the hanging fabric, then brought her hand to her chin and closed her eyes, forcing herself to think it through.

Where had she seen it?

Not just in her room. Somewhere outside. Somewhere very recently.

A clear image rose in her mind at last.

On that road, in the middle of the chaos, the boy who had stepped between them and the assassins had been wearing that same style of uniform.

“…So that was it,” she murmured.

She opened her eyes fully.

The mysterious boy who had saved them had been wearing a Royal Academy uniform.

With that realization set firmly in her mind, Emilia changed into her casual clothes as quickly as she could. She did not bother sitting down afterward. She left her room at once and moved through the corridor at a half-run, heading straight for Gilbert’s room.

When she arrived, the door was already slightly ajar. Voices came from inside.

Gilbert was seated at his desk, and across from him stood the familiar figure of the guard captain, Dorian Kestrel. He was in the middle of giving his report about the previous day, his posture straight and his expression serious.

The sound of Emilia’s steps in the doorway made him pause.

Dorian turned toward her and bowed.

“Lady Emilia,” he said.

Emilia stepped into the room without going further in than she needed.

“Brother. Captain Dorian,” she said. “There is something I forgot to say yesterday.”

Gilbert looked up from the documents on the desk.

“What is it?” he asked.

Emilia drew a small breath.

“The man who helped us,” she said. “He was wearing a Royal Academy uniform.”

She had not been able to name the boy or describe his face clearly, but this was one detail she could now place. For her, it was the one concrete thread she could offer them.

Dorian’s brows lowered slightly as he thought back.

“…Now that you mention it,” he said slowly, “yes. I remember that. At the time I was focused on the attackers, so I did not pay attention to it, but he was indeed wearing the Royal Academy uniform.”

Gilbert stared at them both.

“A Royal Academy student?” he said. “You are telling me an academy student handled something even the guard captain struggled with?”

Gilbert frowned as he said it. Students could be talented, but what had happened on that road was not simple training or a school duel.

Dorian did not deny it.

“Perhaps he is a gifted student,” Dorian said. “Or a third-year S-Class student.”

“That is still strange,” Gilbert said. “If someone at that level already existed, he should not be completely unknown. Someone like that would normally be famous, or at least talked about.”

Emilia looked down for a moment.

“I still do not know his name,” she said quietly. “At the time I could not focus on him at all.”

Dorian glanced at her, then spoke up.

“When the fight ended, I asked for his name,” Dorian said. “He answered ‘I am Elrond.’ He did not give a family name.”

“Elrond…” Gilbert repeated.

The name did not ring any bells. For a noble family, for the Academy, or for the guard, it meant nothing by itself.

“So we only know a first name and the fact that he wore the Academy uniform,” Gilbert said. “No house, no background, nothing else.”

Emilia raised her head a little.

“…What if he is a new student, just like me?” she said, almost as if she were thinking out loud.

The room went quiet for a short moment.

Dorian and Gilbert both considered it. If the boy was new, his skill might not have spread by reputation yet. In that case, he could have come from a major house or a minor one, and no one outside his own circle would know him yet.

Gilbert rested his arm on the chair and narrowed his eyes in thought.

“If that is true, we need to know who he is,” he said at last.

He turned to Dorian.

“Captain Dorian,” Gilbert said. “Continue investigating this young man. Use what you can from the reports and from the surviving guards. If there is any sign of a Royal Academy student called Elrond who matches what we saw, I want to know.”

“Yes, young master,” Dorian replied. “I will look into it.”

Gilbert then faced Emilia again.

“As for you,” he said, “you will be at the Academy yourself soon. If you see him there, or if you recognize him from among the students, tell me immediately.”

Emilia nodded.

“I understand,” she said.

For now, that was all they could do. The boy had stepped in, changed the outcome of the attack, and then walked away with only the name “Elrond” and a Royal Academy uniform left behind as clues.

A knock sounded at the door just as their conversation reached its end.

One of Caelen’s personal aides stepped inside after a brief pause.

“Lord Gilbert,” the aide said, bowing. “Lord Caelen has returned from the palace and requests your presence in his room.”

Gilbert rose from his chair.

“I see,” he said. “Tell him I am on my way.”

The aide bowed again and withdrew.

Gilbert picked up the documents on his desk, then looked once at Dorian and Emilia.

“We will continue this later,” he said. “For now, do what you can on your sides.”

Dorian placed a hand over his chest.

“Yes, young master.”

Emilia gave a small nod in return.

With that, they parted ways—Dorian heading toward the guard wing, Gilbert going to answer Caelen’s summons, and Emilia stepping back into the corridor with the name “Elrond” and the image of the Royal Academy uniform now fixed clearly in her mind.

But just as Emilia was about to step back out into the corridor, Gilbert called out to her.

“Emilia. One more thing.”

She turned around.

“I just received a report,” he said. “Cestina has already woken up. I plan to visit her after I finish reporting to Father. You need to come with me to see him anyway, so let’s go together.”

Emilia gave a small nod.

“…Alright.”

They left the room side by side and walked down the corridor toward Caelen’s office.

On the way, Gilbert glanced at her.

“How are you feeling now?” he asked.

Emilia looked straight ahead.

“Better than yesterday,” she answered. “At least I can think clearly.”

“Good,” Gilbert said. “You did your best.”

He said it simply, without trying to press the point further. For him, it was enough to say it once and let her carry it at her own pace.

They reached their father’s office and a maid opened the door for them.

Caelen was already inside, standing near the window with his back to the room. He looked out over the estate grounds, but the moment he heard their footsteps he turned.

As soon as he saw Emilia, he moved toward her in long strides.

“Emilia,” he said, and pulled her into his arms.

It was a straightforward, tight hug, like any father who had just confirmed with his own hands that his child had come home alive.

“Good grief, you’re uninjured,” Caelen said. “God still protected you.”

Emilia’s shoulders stiffened a little.

“Father, please stop,” she said, pushing lightly at his chest. “I am not a child anymore.”

Gilbert, watching from the side, let out a quiet breath.

“But yesterday you jumped at me like a little kid,” he said.

Emilia flushed.

“T-that was…” she started, then trailed off, unable to find a proper answer.

Caelen released her and lifted one hand to his face. He rubbed at the corners of his eyes in an exaggerated way.

“So that is how it is,” he said. “Emilia doesn’t love me anymore.”

His tone was clearly playing it up, but he still made it sound just real enough that Emilia panicked.

“It’s not like that,” she said quickly. “I just… I just do not want to be treated like a kid all the time.”

Caelen lowered his hand again, the hint of a smile tugging at his mouth.

Gilbert let out a small laugh.

Moments like this, where worry and relief turned into light teasing, were what kept the Alfrost household warm, even when the weight on their shoulders never truly went away.

“Jokes aside, let’s talk properly,” Caelen said.

His joking tone faded, and Emilia straightened a little in front of him. She began to explain the incident again, this time in a simple outline. Caelen had already read the written report, so she focused on the main flow and the parts she had seen with her own eyes.

When she finished, Caelen folded his arms.

“In my perspective, they were not trying to kill you to begin with,” he said.

Gilbert and Emilia both stared at him.

“What?” Emilia blurted out. “How is it like that?”

Gilbert frowned as well. From where they had been standing on that road, it had looked like a straightforward attempt on her life.

Caelen looked at both of them. As a counselor at the Adventurer Bureau, he had already received a separate report. “I received some information before you did, Gilbert,” he said. “The attackers were most likely a platinum-rank party that went missing during an S-rank extermination mission.”

Emilia drew in a small breath. Gilbert’s expression tightened.

Caelen continued.

“I already have the report about the spearman’s corpse and its autopsy,” he said. “Judging from their rank and ability, their power exceeds that of imperial knights, and is at the level of senior magi. In other words, they had more than enough strength to kill you if they wanted to.”

Emilia remembered how the spear had moved and how the formation had cut through trained guards. Hearing it put into words from this side only made it feel heavier.

Caelen let out a slow breath.

“The fact that you are still alive and uninjured is truly a miracle, and must be deliberate” he said.

Gilbert shook his head.

“But she said those attackers were being controlled,” he cut in. “They also controlled Cestina.”

Caelen closed his eyes for a moment and put a hand to his chin.

“I see,” he murmured.

He opened his eyes again.

“Then that might explain why they went missing in the first place,” he said. “They were captured and turned into puppets like that.”

Emilia still did not look convinced.

“If they were not planning to kill me, then what was their goal?” she asked.

“Who knows,” Caelen replied. “My guess is they were trying to capture you and turn you into a puppet as well, just like that platinum party. But they clearly failed.”

The room grew quiet.

Emilia thought about Cestina’s empty eyes and about the way her attacks had come without hesitation. The idea of standing in that same state made her stomach turn.

Gilbert broke the silence.

“Whoever that Elrond is, the one who saved Emilia, we should thank him properly,” he said.

Caelen nodded at once.

“I agree,” he said. “I will also use my own connections to help find this brave young man.”

They did not need to say more than that.

All three of them understood very well that, for someone in Emilia’s position, being controlled by another will would be worse than death, because the damage that could be done through her would go far beyond the value of her own life.

With that report finished, Caelen let Emilia go.

He had only come back from the palace briefly to see her condition with his own eyes. The rest of what he needed to discuss with Gilbert was work that did not require her there, so she bowed and stepped out first, leaving her brother behind in the office.

As she walked out and entered the main hall of the mansion, she stopped in surprise.

Someone was sitting on one of the couches.

“Cestina?” Emilia blurted out.

It was indeed Cestina. She had come on her own and was sitting upright, hands folded neatly in her lap.

“Cestina!! What are you doing here? You should be resting,” Emilia said, worry clear in her voice as she hurried over.

Cestina looked up at her and gave a faint, easy smile.

“I just couldn’t stand being in my room all day,” she said. “I wanted to see everyone.”

Emilia let out a small sigh.

“But are you really okay moving around like that?” she asked.

In answer, Cestina stood up from the couch. She raised one arm over her head and bent her body to the side in a simple stretch, as if to prove nothing hurt.

“I’m okay, see?” she said.

Just then, Gilbert walked into the hall from the other side and caught sight of Cestina in that pose.

“…What are you doing?” he asked, one eyebrow lifting.

Cestina froze, then quickly lowered her arm and brought both hands up to cover part of her face. Her ears reddened.

“I just wanted to show Lady Emilia that I’m fine,” she mumbled.

Gilbert let out a quiet breath that was almost a laugh.

“If you really are fine, then that is good,” he said. “We were planning to visit you, but you decided to come here on your own. That was a dangerous move.”

Hearing that, Cestina straightened her back.

“…I am sorry,” she said.

Her voice was small, but she met his eyes properly as she apologized.

Watching the two of them, Emilia felt a prickling sense that she was standing in the middle of something she did not need to be in.

“I just remembered I left something in my room,” she said quickly. “I will go get it.”

Without waiting for an answer, she turned on her heel and moved toward the corridor that led away from the hall. However, when she reached the corner, she stopped and stayed just out of sight, back pressed lightly against the wall.

From there, she could still hear the hall and see part of it if she leaned a little.

Out in the open space, Cestina looked around to make sure there were no maids or other guards nearby. The hall was empty now except for her and Gilbert.

She lowered her gaze for a moment, then walked toward him with quick steps.

When she reached him, she wrapped her arms around him and held him tightly.

“I was so scared,” she said. Her voice trembled. “I was so, so afraid that I might hurt Lady Emilia back then. I saw everything, but I couldn’t move my body at all…”

The words broke as she spoke them, and she pressed her face against his chest, clinging to him as her body started to shake.

Gilbert did not pull away. He let her cling to him until her breathing steadied a little.

“It is understandable,” he said. “Anyone who was controlled and forced to fight her own friend would be terrified.”

He kept his tone calm.

“It is okay. That was outside your own will. You could not do anything about it,” he went on. “In the end, both of you are safe.”

Cestina nodded against him, as if she were trying to fix those words in place.

At the edge of the hall, Emilia watched from her hiding spot. From where she stood, it looked very much like the two of them were being openly lovey-dovey in the middle of the mansion. She pressed her lips together, unsure whether to sigh or smile.

Gilbert’s gaze shifted slightly. He glanced toward the corridor and met Emilia’s eyes peeking around the corner.

Emilia flinched.

Realizing she had been noticed, she drew back at once and stepped deeper into the corridor. This time she left the hall for real, leaving the two of them alone.

After a while, Emilia came back from her fake excuse.

When she returned to the main hall and peeked inside, Gilbert and Cestina were already sitting on the couch, facing each other. Their posture was relaxed enough that the earlier tension had faded, yet their expressions were still serious. It was clear they were talking about what had happened.

Noticing Emilia, Cestina shifted her body a little to include her.

“Welcome back, Lady Emilia,” Cestina said. “We were just talking about what I remember from… that time.”

Since Emilia had been gone, Cestina started over so she could hear it too.

“When I was being controlled,” Cestina said slowly, choosing her words, “it felt like I was chained in a dark room inside myself.”

She clasped her hands on her knees as she spoke, as if remembering the feeling.

“I could still feel and see and hear everything from the outside,” she continued. “I knew what I was doing. But I could not move my body at all.”

Emilia listened in silence. Hearing it from Cestina’s own mouth made the memory of her attacks feel even heavier.

“I could not control my emotions either,” Cestina added. “That is why my face looked so flat and empty. It was not that I did not feel anything. I just could not show any of it.”

Emilia remembered that expression very clearly. Knowing there had been fear and panic trapped behind that flat face made her chest tighten.

Cestina let out a quiet breath, then went on.

“I also remember some boy,” she said. “He came between us when I was attacking and stopped me easily. I only saw him for a short time, but he blocked me as if it was nothing.”

She frowned a little, trying to pull his image into focus.

“If I ever meet him again, I want to thank him properly,” she said. “I owe him that much.”

Emilia and Gilbert both knew who she meant, but neither interrupted.

“Lastly,” Cestina said, her gaze dropping, “just before I was fully controlled, I heard a woman’s voice inside my head. I did not see her, but I clearly heard her. I think that voice belonged to the one who did it.”

She stopped there and looked up again.

“That is all I remember,” she said.

For Gilbert, that last detail in particular stood out. It gave a clearer shape to the enemy than anything they had heard earlier.

“That helps a lot,” he said. “Thank you for telling us.”

After that, Cestina rose from the couch. She turned to Emilia, placed one hand over her chest, and bowed deeply.

“Lady Emilia,” she said. “I am very sorry I attacked you.”

Emilia stood up as well.

“There is no need to apologize,” Emilia said. “After hearing what happened, I know it was not your will. I do not mind.”

She met Cestina’s eyes as she said it, making it clear that she meant it.

Gilbert added his own words.

“Even so, you should strengthen your mental focus from now on,” he said. “According to the investigation report, that puppet-type magic needs the target to lose concentration first. If you can hold your mind and mana steady, it will be harder for something like that to catch you.”

Cestina nodded at once.

“…Understood,” she said. “I will work on it so I can protect Lady Emilia properly next time.”

Her answer was simple, but her face was firm.

Just then, the front door of the mansion opened with a familiar sound.

Lisoletelle stepped inside without knocking, moving as naturally as if it were her own house. When she looked toward the hall and saw Emilia, Gilbert, and Cestina already on the couch, she blinked.

Her gaze landed on Cestina and she raised her voice at once.

“Cestina!! What are you doing here? You should be resting,” Liso said, in almost the exact same tone Emilia had used earlier.

Cestina gave her the same faint smile she had given Emilia.

“I just couldn’t stand being in my room all day,” she said. “I wanted to see everyone.”

Liso opened her mouth to say something, then closed it again, apparently unable to argue with that.

Gilbert watched the three of them line up in front of the couch and suddenly felt like the odd one out.

“Well then,” he said, standing up. “Since you three are all here, I will leave you to talk. It would be awkward for me to sit here and get in the way.”

Without waiting for them to protest, he gave a small wave and headed out of the hall, leaving the space to them.

After he left, Liso plopped down onto the couch beside Cestina.

She narrowed her eyes and leaned in a little.

“Why do you look like you were crying, Cestina?” Liso asked.

Cestina stiffened for a moment and raised a hand to her face on reflex.

“Huh? No, it’s nothing,” she said. “It might just be your imagination…”

Liso gave her a doubtful look, so Cestina hurried to add more.

“I was sleeping all day,” she said. “So maybe my face just looks like that.”

Liso tilted her head.

“…Is that so?” she said.

She was a bit light-headed by nature and did not think too deeply about it. After a short pause, she accepted the answer as it was and moved on.

With that, the three of them slipped back into their usual flow.

They talked about everything that had happened, this time with all three present to fill in each other’s gaps. At one point Liso suggested going over to Claire’s mansion like they often did, but they ended up dropping the idea, since Claire was probably still at the palace on some business.

They also complained together about the regular Royal Academy orientation they had all skipped that day, wondering half-jokingly what boring speech they had avoided.

For now, it was just the three of them in the hall, talking and arguing and laughing in their usual way, and the mansion felt lively again, as if things were finally returning to normal.

### Chapter 22: 18 - It Started

#### Scene 1

Yesterday really had been too much.

Elrond sat on the edge of his bed in the S-Class dorm room and let out a slow breath. In one day, he had thrown himself into an assassination attempt on a noble girl, then gone right back to hunting Ferocious Wolves and stripping their hides for money. When he lined those events up in his head like that, they felt a little unreal.

‘Anyway. Money first.’

He untied the coin pouch he had placed on the small table and spilled the contents out. Silver and copper pieces rolled across the surface and stopped in a loose pile. He picked them up one by one and stacked them in neat rows.

Twenty-four silver from the Ferocious Wolf hides. On top of that, there was the money from the Lizardian hunt the day before. When he added those together in his head, he could see that it would be enough to keep him eating for about two weeks, as long as he was careful.

Next, he took out a different set of coins and counted more slowly.

This was the money from his parents. From the ten gold coins they had given him before he left home, there were now only two gold and five hundred sixty-six silver left.

He checked the number twice, then closed his hand around the coins.

‘These are savings,’ he said quietly. ‘Emergency use only.’

He decided that he would not touch that money unless it was truly urgent. In the capital, he would live only on what he earned by himself.

He put the savings back into the pouch and set it aside. The remaining silver on the table would be his daily money.

As he looked at the small stack, another thought slipped into his mind.

‘…Should I start bringing leftovers back?’

The breakfast in the S-Class dorm was almost too luxurious. Every morning, the dining hall prepared more food than he could reasonably finish. The plates were always full and the staff behaved as if that was normal. When he compared that to the simple meals he bought at the cheap tavern for dinner, the gap was obvious.

If he quietly wrapped up some bread or something similar and brought it with him, he could probably turn that into his dinner. His wallet would last longer that way.

The idea itself made sense. That was why it bothered him that he still felt reluctant.

It was hard to picture himself walking out of the dorm breakfast while carrying food in his hands. The image alone made him feel like he was doing something he should not do.

‘…I will hold that idea for later,’ he decided after a moment. ‘Until I really need it.’

Until he found a decent job or more stable requests, he would just have to endure the uncomfortable balance between rich breakfasts and plain dinners.

He gathered the coins, separated the savings and the daily money, and put everything away. When he stood up from the bed and turned toward the chair, his eyes fell on the neatly folded Royal Academy uniform.

‘Today is orientation,’ he reminded himself.

The regular Royal Academy orientation was meant for first-year students in the normal course, from Class F up to Class A. For those students, it was part of the schedule. For him, as an S-Class student, it was only optional.

He had already received a special orientation. That one had been quiet. A staff member had guided him around, explained the rules, and shown him the important places. It had felt more like a careful tour than the start of school life.

This time would be different.

This time, the first-year students would all gather together. The hall would be filled with people his age. There would be noise and movement and the kind of restless air that only appeared when many students were in one place.

He picked up the uniform jacket and ran his hand over the fabric once.

In his previous life, he had sat through more than one orientation in a crowded hall. Back then, it had only felt long and boring. Now, the memory of that time felt strangely warm.

‘If I can walk there and it is free, there is no reason not to go,’ he thought.

He began to put on the uniform piece by piece. Today, he wanted to sit among the others, listen to the speeches meant for regular students, and quietly enjoy that nostalgic feeling from his previous life.

The moment he stepped out of his dorm room, the hallway was much busier than usual.

On a normal morning, only a few students passed through at this hour. Today, footsteps and voices filled the corridor. Elrond moved with the flow and headed toward the dining room, letting the sound of overlapping conversations wash over him without really listening to the contents.

He picked out a simple breakfast and a drink, then returned to his room to wait for the food to arrive. For this morning, he chose beef soup with bread and some vegetables. It was plain compared to the full choices on the menu, but it was more than enough.

After finishing his food, he carried the empty plate to the washing tray near the door, as he always did. When he placed it down, he noticed that the dirty clothes in the laundry basket below the tray had already been picked up. The laundry from yesterday was gone without him noticing. He added the uniform he had worn the previous day to the basket and closed the lid.

With that done, he left the room again.

From the moment he opened the S-Class section door, the busy mood he had felt earlier only grew stronger. The reception area had more people than usual, and there was constant movement in and out of the building. When he stepped outside, the park in front of the dorm was already lively.

Some upper-year students sat on benches and talked in relaxed tones. Others read books in the shade. A few were just playing around, chasing each other or practicing light spells in the air. It was a very different sight from the quiet mornings he had seen before.

He passed through the gate and walked toward the magic training field, where the regular student orientation was being held.

From a distance, he could already tell how crowded it was. The lobby in front of the magic training field was packed with people. New students and older students mixed together, and there was no sign that the crowd would thin out soon.

Rather than try to push through that mass, Elrond turned and went directly to the entrance for the training field itself.

Before he could enter, a staff member stopped him and held out a hand.

“Student card, please.”

Elrond took his card from his pocket and passed it over. The staff member glanced at it once and raised an eyebrow.

“S-Class,” the man said. “You can sit anywhere on the field, but there is also a special S-Class seating area in the upper spectator stands. The regular students’ seats are in the center of the field.”

“I see. Thank you.”

He took the card back.

For now, he wanted to feel the atmosphere in the center instead of watching from above. So he followed the flow of people and entered through the same path as the others.

Inside the training field, the seats were already filling up. Many students had formed small groups and talked with each other. Judging by the number of heads he could see, there were probably around three hundred people gathered.

To avoid getting pulled into a conversation, Elrond chose a seat with no one directly to his left, right, front, or back. For a brief moment, it looked like he had successfully created a small empty space around himself.

It did not last.

More students kept coming in. The empty seats were taken one after another. Before long, the places in front of him, behind him, and on both sides were occupied. By the time the staff finally closed the entrance, not a single seat on the field was empty.

He waited quietly.

About thirty minutes passed before the orientation finally began.

A man in formal clothing stepped forward to the front of the field. When Elrond saw him, he immediately understood who he was.

The head of the academy, Grand Master Marius Edevane.

He looked exactly like the kind of noble Elrond would have pictured from his old world. He was middle-aged, with a pronounced potbelly and soft cheeks. A neatly groomed mustache sat above his lips. His heavy- lidded eyes gave him a calm, almost sleepy expression.

‘So a noble like that really exists in this world,’ Elrond thought.

Grand Master Marius began to speak.

His voice carried easily across the wide field as he talked about what it meant to study at the Royal Academy. It was not only about showing off talent, power, or strength. It was also about building relationships, learning new things outside one’s comfort zone, thinking about a future path, and preparing to stand in society after graduation. He spoke of responsibility, pride, and effort, and the rhythm of his speech made it clear he had said these things to many first-year classes already.

Elrond listened and quietly agreed. The content was general, but each point fit neatly with how he had decided to use this place.

After the speech, they moved on to the rundown of the event.

One by one, the main subjects for first-year students were introduced. Magic. Physical Training. General Knowledge. Natural Knowledge. Each instructor gave a short explanation about what their class would cover and what kind of attitude they expected from the students.

As Elrond listened, he compared it in his mind to the explanation Lacia had given him a few days ago. Some of the subjects she had mentioned did not come up at all this time.

He thought about it for a moment and reached a simple conclusion. Those missing subjects, like Arithmetic and Etiquette, were probably counted as more specific topics. Today’s orientation only covered the general curriculum that everyone would share.

The explanations took time. By the halfway point, nearly two hours had passed.

Here and there, Elrond noticed students who could not endure it. A few nodded off where they sat. Some tried to hide it, and some did not even bother.

‘Can’t believe some nobles would do something like that,’ he thought.

From where he sat, it looked like almost everyone around him was a noble.

After that, they moved into the closing part of the event. The staff explained how the school tours would work for each class. Groups would be formed and guided around the grounds, and each group would receive a basic explanation of the buildings and facilities.

Elrond listened, then quietly took that part as information only.

He had already gone through his own tour. There was no need to join another one.

When the four-hour orientation finally ended, he let out a small breath and stood up. The mass of students began to move at once, and the inside of the training field turned noisy again.

On his way out, he lifted his eyes toward the upper spectator stands.

That was where the S-Class seats were. As the staff member had said, the section was only partially filled, and when he counted quickly he could see about twelve people sitting there. They were far away, but it was not enough to hide their faces from him, so he memorized each one, since they would be his classmates, after all.

With that done, Elrond left the magic training field and stepped back out toward the park. He planned to return straight to the dorm and rest a little before thinking about what to do next.

He managed only a few steps before a familiar voice called out from the side.

“Oi, Elrond!”

When he turned his head, he saw Ryn Halber, the first guy he had met at the entrance exam, jogging over with the same easy energy Elrond remembered.

“How you doin’?” Ryn called out casually.

His voice was loud enough that a few students nearby turned their heads.

“I–I’m in good condition,” Elrond answered, a bit stiff.

He could feel the eyes on them and it made him uncomfortable. By nature, he preferred to stay out of sight, and this kind of attention was the exact opposite.

“You know what? I got accepted into Class B. How cool is that, Elrond!” Ryn said, his face bright with excitement.

Elrond froze for a heartbeat.

He was happy for Ryn, but at the same time, hearing him say the class name out loud made Elrond feel out of place. His own placement was something he would rather not talk about here.

“Wow, t-that’s cool. I’m glad you got such a high class,” Elrond replied, forcing himself to match the mood.

Ryn puffed out his chest a little.

“Hehe… well, it was worth it. A commoner like me getting into B–Class is pretty rare. Even C–Class is already hard,” Ryn said.

“That’s right,” Elrond answered, keeping his voice low and his expression as neutral as he could manage. He did not want to stand out any more than he already had.

“So, how about you, Elrond?” Ryn leaned in with a grin. “Don’t tell me we’re in the same class? If we are, I’d be really happy. But if not, don’t worry—I’ll still be friends with you.”

He slapped Elrond on the back with a friendly thump.

Elrond hesitated.

“Well… it’s around that,” he said vaguely.

“Hey, hey, why are you being so secretive?” Ryn complained. “Just tell me already, you don’t need to be embarrassed.”

Elrond shifted his weight slightly, and at that moment Ryn’s gaze dropped to his hand and stopped when he noticed the student card Elrond was still holding.

“Ah—”

Before he could react, Ryn reached out and grabbed his wrist.

“Let me see that for a second.”

Elrond’s fingers tightened in surprise, but Ryn had already brought the card close to his face, so it was too late to hide it. As Ryn read it clearly, he froze in place, unable to believe what he was seeing.

“Are you kidding me? You’re S–Class?? That’s so cool…!!” Ryn shouted, so loud that people around them started murmuring.

“S–Class…?” “Ηim?” “Who’s that S–Class?”

Seeing people react one after another, Elrond quickly covered Ryn’s mouth with his hand and dragged him toward a quieter spot.

Ryn let out a muffled “Mmff—?!” as he stumbled after him.

“Quiet,” Elrond said.

He pulled Ryn away from the main path and into a slightly less crowded corner of the park. He did not let go until they were out of the center of attention. When he finally released him, Ryn sucked in a breath, his eyes still shining with excitement.

“I knew you were amazing, but S–Class? Seriously? That’s insane. I can’t believe I’m actually friends with an S–Class student. This is—”

“I know, I know, so stop being so loud, okay?” Elrond cut in, his voice mostly calm but clearly strained. “I don’t want to attract more attention.”

Ryn straightened his back and raised his right hand in a mock salute.

“Understood, sir. I won’t tell anybody,” he said in an exaggeratedly polite tone.

Elrond grimaced. Being called “sir” made him uncomfortable.

“Stop that. Just act normal. We’re both first–year students,” he said.

Ryn dropped the act and smiled instead.

“Please don’t forget about me, okay, Elrond?”

Elrond gave a small smile in return.

“Understood. I’m not going to forget you. Don’t worry.”

After standing there for a moment longer, they naturally went their separate ways, with Elrond turning toward the dorms while he planned out the rest of his day in his head, and Ryn waving once before heading off in the opposite direction, back toward the city where his home waited.

──────────

In the near desert of the northern buffer, the capital of Roxarea shone like a polished stone set into sand.

Caravans from human kingdoms rolled in along the southern roads. From the west, elven traders arrived with pale wood and glassware. From the east and southeast, beastkin mercenaries and hunter bands came and went, and from the north, adventurers returned with dust on their cloaks and monster blood on their weapons. For a country so small, Roxarea carried the weight of a crossroads.

Fields and orchards surrounded the city in carefully carved strips of green. Irrigation channels glittered under the sun, feeding rows of pomegranate-like trees whose fruit would become the liquor nobles fought over in distant courts. Beyond those strips, the land broke again into harsh winds and monster territory, where rare materials hid behind claws and fangs and the economy of the city was built on the simple fact that people were willing to risk their lives to get them.

At the very center of all that movement stood the royal palace.

White stone walls rose above the lower roofs, not overly tall, but solid in a way that did not invite testing. Inside, the throne hall opened like a calm pool. Banners hung in steady rows. Stained glass caught the light and laid red and gold across the floor.

On the throne sat Serelis Thalanor.

Her hair fell like a sheet of white silk over her shoulders. Her ears were long and sharp, yet today they were partly hidden by the way her hair lay, so that from a distance she might pass as human if one did not look too closely. Her skin held no sign of age, and her clear blue eyes watched the hall with a quiet that had nothing to do with softness.

She ruled a nation of mostly humans, along with elves, beastkin, and others who had drifted to this crossing point and decided to stay. Some of them called her queen. Some called her ruler. Others knelt in front of her like supplicants before a temple statue and whispered prayers for protection.

She did not encourage that, but she did not stop it either.

If they asked for safety and order, and if their voices did not interfere with her real goal, then it did not matter what name they gave her. What she sought was not worship. It was justice.

Justice meant absolute power.

That belief had never changed. Not in the age when heroes still walked openly, not in the wars that shattered kingdoms, and not in the long centuries afterward.

She had watched more than one era of heroes rise and fade while she kept walking forward. In age after age, she fought alongside them when their battles aligned with the order she wanted, pushing back monsters, demon forces, and anyone who disrupted her goal. In the last great age, she lived through the

time when the True Demon Lords and the hero of that era destroyed one another, and the world changed around her as their deaths erased both sides.

To the world, the hero and the True Demon Lords were spoken of as opposites. One was called light, the other darkness.

In Serelis’s eyes, both of them had been candidates.

If either of them had survived long enough to reach the shape she wanted, they might have become the absolute power she sought, a single point strong enough to enforce justice without question. Instead, both of them died. The hero fell. The True Demon Lord was crushed. The world broke again into smaller strengths that could be argued with and overturned.

Their deaths left a crack inside her.

For the first time, the idea that someone else might carry the weight she demanded simply vanished. If no one else could reach absolute power, then there was only one path left.

She would become it herself.

Not long after the True Demon Lords and the hero of that era were both gone from the world, another name remained in the shadows people whispered about: The First Witness. The last servant said to have stayed close to the True Demon Lord until the very end.

Serelis sought that presence out. Despite thousands of years she had lived and honed her power up to this point, when she finally stood in front of the First Witness, she carried all that time in the magic wrapped around her. She challenged the First Witness directly, not for land or border, but to prove that she herself could stand as the core of absolute power.

Even so, she was defeated.

The defeat was clean and undeniable. If it had been anyone else, she might have risen and tried again out of simple pride, but she was not interested in pride for its own sake. She was interested in the result. In that moment, the First Witness looked at her, saw the shape of her belief, and spoke of an ambition that was almost identical to her own.

The First Witness saw the ideology within Serelis and understood that the goal she was reaching for was the same as its own. Serelis accepted that and chose to join forces with the First Witness, and from then on the two of them moved together with one shared ambition: to one day bring forth absolute power as true justice.

The throne hall was quiet now.

Afternoon light filtered in through the glass, softening the red carpet that ran up to the throne. A few officials waited at a distance, quills and tablets in hand. Guards stood still near the pillars lined up accordingly

A messenger knelt at the center of the hall.

“Rise,” Serelis said.

The woman stood, still bowing her head slightly as she spoke.

“Your Majesty. A force has been sighted moving inside the northern buffer.”

The officials’ hands tightened on their writing tools for a heartbeat, then steadied again. Only Serelis’s gaze sharpened.

“Where,” she asked.

“Approximately three days’ march from our northern watchtower, Your Majesty,” the messenger replied. “The advance scouts report organized formations, supply wagons, and a clear standard. The banner matches that of Bene.”

Bene.

That name belonged to a demon state beyond the desert fringe. So did the name of its ruler.

“Azazeal,” Serelis said.

“Yes, Your Majesty,” the messenger answered. “It appears to be a demon army from Bene. There has been no advance unit crossing our border yet, and no emissary has been detected. They are still within the buffer.”

Her voice stayed steady, because she had been trained to deliver this kind of report without showing fear. In Roxarea, people relied on the ruler on the throne to face danger, so there was no point in panicking in front of her.

Serelis took in the report. A demon army from Bene under Azazeal’s banner was inside the buffer, and it was close enough that Roxarea’s northern watchtowers could see their movement when the wind shifted.

“We have had no demon army at our border for decades,” she said.

“Yes, Your Majesty.”

That much was simple fact. Conflicts and skirmishes still happened in the outer zones, but an organized military movement under a Demon Lord’s flag had not come this close in a very long time. The buffer was supposed to take that weight, to absorb it in raids and monster tides before it reached any stable crown.

If they had decided to move now, then they had a reason.

A provocation? A test? Or some other piece in a pattern that reached beyond Roxarea’s line.

“Current disposition at the northern forts,” Serelis asked.

“Standard garrisons at all three watchtowers, Your Majesty,” the messenger said quickly. “The border patrol rotations are operating under the usual schedule.”

Serelis rested her elbow on the arm of the throne and set her fingers lightly against her cheek. Her posture looked relaxed, but the officials closest to her knew that she only held that pose when she was arranging shapes in her head.

“Send orders,” she said. “Quietly. Reinforce the northern watchtowers. No banners, no visible change in routine. Rotate in more mages and scouts, and extend the range of our eyes. I want a continuous record of their movement.”

The messenger bowed deeply.

“As you command.”

“Inform trade inspectors as well,” Serelis continued. “If any caravans arrive with news from Bene, they are to be questioned politely and thoroughly. Do not detain them unless they carry direct military symbols. We will not close our roads yet.”

──────────

Three days passed after the regular Royal Academy orientation, and the first proper day of class finally arrived.

In those three days, Elrond’s life had settled into a comfortable rhythm.

He slept in a soft bed that still felt wasteful and woke to the quiet of the S-Class dorm. He ate meals that were far above what he would have chosen for himself. Sometimes he went down to the physical training area and swung his sword until his breathing turned rough. Other times he walked out into the city, tracing the streets and corners until the layout settled into his memory.

If he had nothing else to do, he simply sat and went over what he had seen, fixing routes and landmarks in his head. For him, that kind of work was as natural as breathing.

On the morning of the first day, he buttoned up his Royal Academy uniform in front of the closet.

As he reached in, he noticed something and frowned slightly. There were fewer uniforms hanging inside than there should have been. The two he had worn on the previous days still had not come back from the laundry. That meant he only had three left, including the one he was putting on now.

‘Should I pick it up myself?’ he wondered.

He looked toward the door for a moment, then remembered what had been written in the dorm booklet. Laundry would be collected and then sent back to each room.

‘Probably it needs more time,’ he added silently.

Since he was already wearing a full set of uniform, complete with the half-cloak resting on his shoulders, he decided to leave it at that. When he checked his reflection in the closet door, the dark cloth of the cloak fell neatly down his back.

‘Still looks kinda cool,’ he thought.

He closed the closet and let his eyes move once around the room, checking that nothing else needed fixing. Since it was already morning and his stomach felt light, the next step was simple.

He took the room key from the small table near the door and reached for the handle, planning to head straight to the dining hall to request his meal like always.

When he opened the door to step out, he stopped after a single step because something new was sitting in the corridor.

Right outside his room, next to the door frame, there was a small rack he did not recognize, and on top of it rested a closed woven wooden basket. The rack looked like it belonged to the hallway, yet he knew it had not been there yesterday.

Elrond glanced left and right along the corridor. No one was there, and all the other doors were still shut, so there was no one he could ask.

Since the basket was placed directly in front of his room, there was only one reasonable guess in his mind.

He lifted the lid.

Inside were the two uniforms and two sets of clothes he had put into the laundry basket inside his room before. Each one was folded so neatly that it almost looked like a display.

‘So they send it back like this,’ he murmured.

He carried the stack inside and returned the clothes to their place in the closet, feeling the small confirmation that the dorm really did handle these details for him without being asked. After that, he set the empty basket back on the rack and quietly closed the door.

After that, he headed down the corridor toward the dining hall.

As usual, he requested his breakfast there, then brought himself back to his room to wait. When the food arrived, he finished it without rushing, the same way he had done for the last three days. Once he had set the empty plate back on the washing tray near the door, he checked the time in his head and turned toward the chair.

Now that breakfast was done, it was time to get ready to leave.

After that, he picked up the suitcase-like bag that the Academy had prepared for students.

The bag was not heavy. For today, he had only packed the Academy booklet and one empty notebook. The first day would most likely be introductions and explanations in the classroom, so there was no need to bring anything more.

He checked once that the shoulder strap was properly set, then stepped out of the room and locked the door.

The air outside the dorm carried a different kind of energy compared to the orientation day. There were fewer crowds than there had been at the training field, but more students were moving with clear purpose, heading toward buildings they already knew.

Elrond walked directly toward the Academy lobby.

He passed through the familiar entrance and crossed the hall without stopping, making his way into the main building. The S-Class homeroom was in the middle section, at the far end of the corridor. According to the map he had already memorized, it was technically still part of the main building but separated by an open hallway that created a small gap.

When he reached the end and saw the doorway, he let out a short breath.

‘At least it’s not that far to walk,’ he thought.

He adjusted his grip on the bag and stepped inside.

The classroom opened up in a semi-circular shape, with rows of seats rising step by step toward the back. From a glance, it looked like it could hold around thirty people without feeling cramped.

There were only a few students present.

Elrond had come a bit early on purpose, and the room reflected that choice. Most of the seats were still empty, and the low hum of conversation that had filled the field during orientation was nowhere to be found.

He scanned the room once.

Then he walked straight up the steps and headed for the back row, aiming for the inside seat beside the aisle on the highest level. From there, he would be able to see the entire room easily, and at the same time he could reach the exit quickly if he needed to.

He set his bag down and sat in the back row seat. No one sat directly beside him, and with the aisle on his left and an empty seat on his right, it really was a perfect spot for a loner.

Before long, more students started entering the classroom.

One after another, they came through the door and walked up the steps, filling the empty rows. As Elrond watched them, he began to notice familiar faces mixed among the new ones. They were the same faces he had seen in the spectator seats during the orientation, in the S–Class area above the field. He still did not know their names, so he simply matched them in his mind and left it at that.

While he was doing that, a voice suddenly came from the side.

“Yo, is that seat beside you empty?” the boy asked.

Elrond turned his head. The question had arrived without any warning, and it took him a moment to answer.

“Y–yes, it’s empty,” Elrond said.

His voice carried a bit of hesitation, just like his expression.

He slid his own chair forward slightly so the boy could pass behind him. The boy moved through the gap, then sat down in the seat on Elrond’s right and put his bag on the desk in front of him.

“My name is Leon. Leon Sieghart,” he said.

“Uhm, I’m Elrond von Astrea,” Elrond said, a little shy.

As soon as he heard the name ‘Sieghart’, a thought rose up in his mind.

‘Sieghart? That famous swordsman family?’ he wondered.

Sieghart frowned a bit.

“Heh… von Astrea. I’ve never heard that name,” Leon said. “Means you are non–noble. You must be very amazing for being able to reach S–Class.”

Hearing that made Elrond nervous.

“Probably,” Elrond replied.

It was the only answer he could manage while feeling that kind of gaze.

“Can’t wait to see it,” Leon added.

Elrond blinked.

‘Huh? See it? Like, what does he mean, see it?’ he thought.

He could not tell what, exactly, Leon expected to watch.

Just after that, another boy walked up the stairs in their direction, and Leon looked over and spoke to him at once.

“Whoah! You are Garfield, right?” Leon said, his voice full of spirit.

The boy stopped and looked surprised.

“Yes, I am. You are?” he asked.

“Oh, you are Sieghart. I’m sorry for my rudeness,” Garfield said.

His tone shifted from casual to polite the moment he understood who he was talking to.

“Nah, just drop the formality,” Leon replied. “We’ve met each other a couple of times, and I don’t really mind talking casually like this.”

He brushed the politeness aside as if it was unnecessary.

Leon then noticed that Elrond seemed a little confused about what was going on.

“Oh, sorry, I haven’t introduced you,” Leon said. “This is Eiden Garfield. He’s a very talented magical craftsman and blacksmith. He and his family are very well known all over the country.”

“Ohh, I’m Elrond von Astrea. Nice to meet you, Sir Garfield,” Elrond said.

“Sir? You don’t need to do that, Astrea,” Eiden replied. “I’m also not noble, so you don’t need to worry about formality towards me. And also for Sir Sieghart, that sounds a bit exaggerating. It just happens we became official Arbalest supplier.”

“Come on, of course that’s because you and your old man are geniuses,” Leon said immediately.

“You make me embarrassed,” Eiden answered.

“That’s very amazing,” Elrond said, trying to react.

After that short exchange, Eiden looked at the nearby seats and chose the one across the aisle from Elrond. He sat down there, so that Leon was on Elrond’s right and Eiden was on the other side of the aisle to his left.

While they had been talking, more students had arrived.

The classroom was now almost full, and the noise of small conversations filled the room. At that moment, a man stepped to the front of the class, drawing Elrond’s attention.

Elrond recognized the man at the front as Julian Roosevelt, the examiner who had tested him during the entrance physical exam.

“Please, silent and take your seat,” Julian said.

His voice carried through the room, and the murmur of the class began to fade as the students settled down.

Murmurs began to spread through the room the moment Julian stood at the front of the class.

“I can’t believe Sir Julian became our private teacher…” someone whispered.

“This is Sir Julian… the genius Sir Julian…” another voice added, full of excitement.

The whispers overlapped one after another, and the room, which had just quieted down, started to grow noisy again.

“I said silence. I will start the explanation now,” Julian said.

His calm voice cut through the noise, and this time the students actually settled. The conversations faded, and everyone turned their attention to the front.

Once the room was quiet, Julian looked over the class.

“First of all, congratulations on being accepted into S–Class,” he said. “You were already selected from among many excellent candidates, and from that group, you were chosen again as special students. It is only natural that I acknowledge that achievement.”

For a moment he let that sink in, then he added the one detail that tied him directly to their position.

“I also once sat where you sit now. I graduated from this very class.”

A small wave of surprise ran through the room. Several students straightened in their seats, because the distance between “famous instructor” and “student” suddenly felt much smaller. Elrond simply listened and fit that fact together with what he already knew about Julian’s record.

Without lingering on it, Julian shifted to the main topic.

“Next, I will explain the rules and schedule for this class,” he said. “As S–Class, your timetable will differ from the regular classes.” He moved straight into the details.

“Each of you has areas that were identified as lacking during the orientation interviews,” Julian continued. “Based on that, you have been assigned individual lesson slots. These personal lessons will be held on the first and third days of the week, during the final time slot.”

“There is also a self–improvement slot scheduled for the last period on the second, fourth, and fifth days of the week,” he added.

At that point, most of the students in the room reopened the schedule sheets they had brought with them and checked the details again, tracing the lines with their eyes.

Elrond did not reach for his schedule sheet, because he had already memorized it when he first read the booklet, so he only listened and confirmed that Julian’s explanation matched what he remembered.

Even so, one part still caught on his thoughts.

‘What should I do during that time? Should I just go to the library to read books?’ Elrond wondered.

Self–improvement sounded flexible, but it also felt a bit vague, and he was not sure yet what would be the best way to use it.

After finishing the basic explanation, Julian added one more point.

“I will also be the one teaching your physical training,” Julian said. “As you may have already read in the schedule details in your booklet, I will be your trainer.”

The room filled with murmurs again at once.

“For real… Sir Julian himself…?”

“We’re getting physical training from that swordsman genius…”

“He graduated from the swordsman academy in just one year, right…?”

“And then he attended the Royal Academy and became an instructor at twenty–one…”

Fragments of admiration and rumor spilled out in low voices from different parts of the classroom. Most of the students looked a mixture of impressed and tense as they realized they would be trained directly by Julian Roosevelt, the swordsman whose name they had already heard long before coming here.

Julian set the schedule booklet aside and picked up another sheet.

“I’ll be calling all of you one by one,” he said. “It seems a couple of students are still missing today, but that’s understandable. They are people with important duties.”

He lowered his eyes to the list and started reading.

Each time Julian called a name and someone stood to bow, Elrond linked it to the faces he had seen in the S–Class spectator seats during orientation, fixing them one by one as people he would share this room with.

“Cestina Ludwell.”

Elrond’s hand twitched on top of his desk.

A girl in the middle rows stood from her seat and bowed toward the front.

“Wow, she’s so beautiful…”

“She’s so cute…”

“I’m going to ask her out…”

The boys nearby watched her like she was some rare ornament that had been dropped into the classroom.

Elrond’s gaze wasn’t on her face.

In his mind, her figure went straight back to that day when he took a detour during a Ferocious Wolf hunt and crashed into the assassination attempt at the carriage.

‘Good grief… she’s in good condition already. And I didn’t expect we’d be in the same clay.**ss,’ Elrond thought. ‘If she’s here, then the other girls might be here too. I was too busy talking with those two to notice them earlier.’

Julian’s voice went on without pause.

“Claire von Arbalest—she cannot attend today due to palace matters.”

The Arbalest name settled over the class like a quiet bell. No one spoke up, but Elrond stored it. Even if she wasn’t physically here, she was still part of this class on paper, and that alone meant trouble if things went wrong.

“Emilia Alfrost.”

When Julian called “Emilia Alfrost,” Elrond found her at once.

A girl with a calm expression stood and bowed toward the front. When he heard the family name “Alfrost”, several scenes surfaced at once in his memory. He remembered the girl who had stepped in front of the carriage during the attack, the Alfrost carriage that had stopped in front of his house, and the brief glimpse he had caught of a girl watching him from inside it.

‘She’s the one who stood in front of the carriage during that attack,’ he thought. ‘Come to think of it… is she the same girl I saw inside the carriage at my house back then? No way… right?’

The pieces did not fit tightly enough to be certain, so he left it as an open question.

‘I hope we can be good classmates,’ he added, even though part of him still tensed at the thought of getting pulled any deeper into noble affairs than he already had.

Julian read several more noble names before he finally reached Elrond’s.

“Elrond von Astrea,” Julian said.

Elrond rose, bowed toward the front as the others had done, then sat again. It was the same gesture everyone else made, but hearing his name spoken in the middle of all those noble houses drew a thin line between where he came from and where he was sitting now.

“Lisoletelle Ashfeldt.”

When Julian called her name, the reply that came back was nothing like the quiet bows before.

“Yes! Liso here!” she said.

She answered in a bright, clear voice instead of bowing in silence. Several students turned their heads in her direction automatically.

‘She’s the one I saved from that massive magic blast,’ Elrond thought.

In his mind, “Lisoletelle” still pointed first to that moment when a magic construct had almost swallowed her and she had looked like she had run out of options. Compared to that, the tone she used now sounded like someone who had already climbed back onto her feet.

‘Looks like that despair on her face back then is already gone.’

The realization loosened a small knot he had not noticed he was carrying.

Julian read on.

Elrond listened and tried to keep track, especially of the names attached to faces he remembered from the S–Class spectator seats during the general orientation. The list of “people in S–Class” that had just been numbers before now had voices and reactions attached.

Then a call from the front changed the air in a more obvious way.

“Rowan Kael.”

As soon as Julian called his name, whispers spread about the commoner magic genius who had been taken under noble patronage and was said to handle high-level grimoires long before most nobles ever touched them.

“Is he that the magic genius…?”

“He’s just a commoner…”

“He’s just a bookworm—probably nothing special…”

The word “commoner” came out in the same tone some nobles used when they talked about cheap goods. After hearing Ryn proudly say that a commoner reaching B–Class was rare, and after watching how much work went into that, the way the word was thrown out now scraped against Elrond’s nerves.

‘What’s wrong with a commoner being special?’ he thought, irritated.

Beside him, Leon leaned slightly closer, eyes still fixed on the front.

“They say that Rowan guy already mastered all the grimoires at the age of twelve,” Leon said in a low, excited voice.

Watching Leon stare at Rowan with that excited look, Elrond could guess the reason easily.

‘He probably just wants to fight him,’ Elrond thought.

The idea fit Leon too neatly to be anything else.

### Chapter 23: 19 - Assessment

#### Scene 1

When Julian finished reading the list, three seats in the room were still empty.

He lowered the paper and glanced over the class.

“Three students are absent,” he said. “One of them is Claire von Arbalest. In her case, it is most likely palace duties.”

No one was surprised by that. Even Elrond could imagine that a princess would be pulled into work at the palace on the first day instead of sitting in a classroom.

With the people in front of him confirmed, Julian moved on.

“Now then,” he said. “I will explain how we will start.”

He set the list aside and rested one hand on the desk in front of him.

“Let us run an assessment today,” Julian said. “To be clear, most of you were not accepted through the entrance exam. You did not get in by taking the normal tests. I have only read the documents you submitted, so I cannot judge your current ability from experience. I only remember a few of you who actually took the exam.”
