Julian’s explanation was straightforward enough. Most of the students here were nobles or invitees, and many of them had probably never had the time or the need to sit through an entrance exam. Their households sent written assessments and recommendations instead, and the Academy accepted them off that.

As he said it out loud, the room went still. A few students shifted in their seats, and some who had been looking at Julian a moment ago turned their eyes away, as if they did not want that fact pointed at too directly. Only Julian could throw that kind of reality in their faces without softening it.

Before he could continue, a voice cut across the room in a rough tone.

“Oy. You called all our names, but you haven’t even introduced yourself,” the boy said.

Elrond knew the voice belonged to Bram Veller because Julian had just called that name a short while ago. When Elrond turned his eyes toward him, he saw a student sitting with his body half slouched in the chair, as if the uniform did not quite belong to him yet. His black hair was left as it was, and his amber gaze met the front without flinching. From this distance, Elrond could see the calluses on his fingers where his hand rested on the desk.

The rudeness in his words was obvious enough that even someone with poor manners would have noticed it.

Julian did not frown and he did not raise his voice.

“Ah, you are right,” he said. “I forgot, because most of you already seem to recognize me. My name is Julian. Julian Roosevelt. I am from the Roosevelt household. Any questions?”

When he said “Roosevelt household,” the air in the room tightened. Everyone in S–Class knew Roosevelt stood beside Arbalest and Alfrost as one of Althania’s Three Founding Families. Even Bram, who had just raised his voice at a teacher, closed his mouth there.

Next to Elrond, Leon leaned over with his usual restless energy.

“They say that Bram guy is a swordsman genius and an ex-mercenary,” Leon whispered. “He can use a lot of sword stances.”

Elrond glanced at Bram again. The way he sat loose in his chair and the rough skin on his hands did match that kind of story.

“O-oh… good information,” Elrond replied hesitantly.

Leon’s eyes were bright in a way that Elrond already recognized, and from that alone he could tell Leon wanted to fight Bram someday.

‘Someone who can use multiple sword stances,’ Elrond thought. ‘That could be exciting to fight.’

Julian led them out of the classroom a few minutes later.

He picked up the attendance sheet again, then turned toward the door.

“We will move to the physical training area,” he said. “Follow me.”

He stepped into the corridor without waiting for a reply. The students rose in a soft scrape of chair legs and followed in a loose column. The murmur that had started after his assessment explanation dulled into a low buzz that ran through the hallway.

Elrond walked beside Leon, keeping half an eye on the backs of the nobles in front of them.

“This should be good,” Leon muttered under his breath. “We finally get to see how everyone moves.”

His tone was almost light, but his gaze stayed sharp on the people ahead. For Leon, this kind of assessment was closer to entertainment than obligation.

They stepped out into the light.

The physical training grounds were a wide stretch of hardened earth divided into several stone–marked rings. Low barriers of pale stone and metal railings framed each field, and practice dummies lined one side beneath a long roof with neatly arranged weapon racks. Rows

of wooden swords and spears rested there in order, the faint smell of oil and dust mixing with the distant sounds of other classes training.

Julian stopped at the edge of one of the marked rings and faced the class.

First,” he said, “we will confirm your current physical skill through light sparring.”

Julian swept his eyes over the rows of students and checked which faces lit up at the word “sparring” and which ones tightened.

“After that, I will divide you into three groups based on what I see,” he continued. “These groups are only for today’s sparring. I want each of you to have opponents at a roughly suitable level.”

He stated it like a simple fact, so no one could mistake it for a ranking or a verdict on their worth.

“Before we begin,” Julian said, “we need referees.”

Julian checked the attendance list in his hand once more, then started calling names.

“Lord Aeric Valemont. Lady Nyssara Corvine. Rowan Kael. Step forward.”

Three students separated themselves from the others.

Aeric moved with the composed air of someone who believed the ground belonged to him by default. Nyssara’s steps were neat and measured, her posture straight as if even the training grounds were a stage. Rowan looked the most neutral of the three, his plain uniform and quiet eyes giving him the air of someone who had simply been pulled forward by chance.

They did not look like people who spent most of their time with swords.

Rowan lifted a hand slightly.

“Instructor,” he said, “I am not confident with a sword. Are you sure I should act as a referee?”

His voice did not wobble, but it held the careful tone of someone who preferred precise work over swinging wood at people.

“It does not matter if you are not skilled with a sword,” Julian replied. “For now, you are not being tested as fighters. You will watch and give your judgement on how both sides fought. That is all.”

He spoke as if he had chosen them for that exact reason. For Julian, people who were not busy comparing themselves to the fighters would likely see more clearly.

“Understood,” he said.

Before Julian could say anything more, another voice cut across the ring.

“Oy.”

Bram’s voice carried without effort. He stepped half a pace forward from where he had been standing, shoulders loose, hands in his pockets as if the training field was just another alley.

“Seems like no one here is good enough to fight me,” he said. “Roosevelt Teach, you fight me first.”

He did not add any title beyond that rough “Teach.” To most nobles in the row, that was already more than enough to scrape across their nerves.

Several of them turned toward him with visible displeasure. For them, a commoner from the slums calling a Roosevelt instructor out in public sounded less like courage and more like insolence.

Leon’s eyes lit up.

“He really said it,” Leon whispered, almost pleased. “This is going to be fun.”

For Leon, the lack of respect toward rank mattered less than the promise of a strong clash.

Elrond watched Bram’s back.

‘He is serious,’ he thought. ‘He does not care who is in front of him as long as they are strong.’

Julian did not show any irritation.

“Very well,” he said. “If you are willing, Bram Veller, I will accept.”

He set the attendance sheet on a nearby stand and walked toward the weapon rack.

“This will serve as a demonstration,” Julian added. “Referees, watch closely. The rest of you as well.”

His tone did not change. He treated Bram’s challenge as one more piece of the assessment rather than a disruption.

Bram clicked his tongue softly, but he followed.

They each picked up a wooden sword. The weight was lower than steel, yet enough to leave bruises if swung carelessly.

Julian stepped into the ring and took his stance.

His feet set at a modest width on the packed earth, and his shoulders settled as if he had done this motion a thousand times. At a glance, it looked like a standard form any swordsman could

learn, but his center of balance did not settle in one fixed place. The line from his heel to his hand flowed almost too smoothly, like water that had already chosen several paths ahead.

Elrond recognized that feel.

‘That is the Roosevelt way of standing,’ he thought. ‘A stance that looks simple until the blade starts moving.’

Across from him, Bram rolled his shoulders and lifted his sword one-handed, then brought his other hand up to grip properly. The lazy posture fell away, leaving something narrower and sharper in its place. His gaze stayed on Julian’s hips and shoulders, not on the sword.

“Heh,” Bram said. “I’ve seen that kind of stance before.”

He did not say where, but the angle of his mouth showed confidence. Bram was used to pulling apart other people’s styles and stitching pieces into his own.

On the edge of the ring, Aeric shifted the wooden sword in his hands as if it were an inconvenient prop.

“Ready when you are,” Julian said.

He did not add any formal call. He simply looked at the referees.

Rowan took the hint.

“Both sides ready,” Rowan said. “Begin.”

Bram moved first.

He shot forward with a speed that did not match his earlier slouch, bringing his wooden blade down toward Julian’s side. To anyone who did not know better, it looked like a direct, full-commitment strike.

Julian did not even raise his sword to block.

As Bram closed the last step, Julian’s blade snapped out in a straight thrust toward Bram’s chest.

Bram’s eyes widened. The downward swing that had been bait suddenly became a burden. He pulled his sword back with a rough jerk, his feet skidding as he twisted his body away from the incoming point. He barely slipped past the thrust and stepped to the outside, swinging his sword toward Julian’s blade to knock it off line and create space.

Wood smacked against wood in a sharp sound.

Julian turned with the rebound as if he had been waiting for it.

His leading foot drew a smooth arc on the ground, and his torso rotated with controlled force. His sword came around in a horizontal cut that aimed for Bram’s ribs.

Bram brought his blade up with both hands.

The impact ran up his arms and pushed him back three full steps. His heels carved shallow grooves in the dirt before he found his weight again.

“Tch…!”

He clicked his tongue, then kicked off the ground and charged again.

This time, he tried to press first. His blade darted out in a series of quick cuts and thrusts that chased every small gap he saw. He leaned in and out of range like someone who had learned to fight in tight spaces, where one misstep meant a wall or a body.

For a moment, it looked like he was dragging the pace along by sheer force.

Then Bram realized Julian was no longer directly in front of him.

In the middle of one exchange, Julian’s sword met his and guided it aside. Julian stepped across Bram’s line of sight rather than away from it, and his body slid past the edge of Bram’s vision. By the time Bram corrected, Julian’s presence was already at his back.

A wooden point pressed toward the back of his head.

Bram ducked low on instinct, feeling the thrust cut the air just above where his skull had been. He twisted and brought his sword around in a tight circle, forcing Julian to step out instead of landing a clean follow–through.

They traded several more blows.

Bram’s eyes sharpened with each clash. His shoulders began to move in a rhythm that answered Julian’s flow instead of chasing it. He was already learning when Julian liked to turn his hips, when the blade rose as a prelude to a cut, and when that smooth stance seemed to favor a thrust.

“He’s adjusting even while he’s being pushed back,” Leon whispered, voice low and fast. “That’s why they call him a genius.”

Elrond watched the line of their swords.

‘He is starting to read the outer shape,’ Elrond thought. ‘But the inside is still Julian’s pace.’

Julian’s stance did not change on the surface, yet the points where he placed his weight kept shifting in response to Bram’s choices. When Bram tried to force a pattern, Julian let it form for one or two exchanges, then stepped somewhere Bram did not expect and broke it.

At one moment, Bram saw Julian’s blade angle off to the side.

He set his guard to catch a side slash, muscles ready to meet the impact.

The slash never came.

Julian’s wrist turned, and the arc collapsed into a direct thrust that lined up with Bram’s face. The wooden tip stopped just short of the bridge of his nose.

For a heartbeat, only the faint hiss of their breathing sounded inside the ring.

“That is enough,” Rowan said. “Match over. Instructor Julian wins.”

His tone carried a touch of annoyance, but it was directed at the way the match had forced him to track every movement, not at the result itself.

The tension around the ring eased. A few nobles let out breaths they had not noticed they were holding.

Bram straightened slowly.

“Oi,” he said. “You used magic just now, didn’t you?”

He narrowed his eyes at Julian as if trying to catch a trace of mana in the air.

Before Julian could answer, Rowan raised his hand slightly.

“I used clairvoyance magic from the start of the bout,” Rowan said. “I did not sense any mana flow from Instructor Julian. Only physical movement.”

His magic was simple, a spell that traced the presence and movement of mana in a fixed area. For someone like Rowan, who lived in grimoires, tracking that kind of thing was closer to breathing than effort.

Bram clicked his tongue again.

“…Seriously,” he muttered. “So that was all just your stance and footwork.”

His eyes stayed on Julian’s sword, but the tone had shifted. There was no more accusation in it, only a rough, honest frustration at the gap he had just felt.

He lowered his sword and gave a short nod.

“Fine,” he said. “Next time, I’ll win.”

For Bram, that was the highest admission of respect he knew how to give. He only bothered to promise a rematch to people he accepted as real opponents.

Julian rested his wooden sword on his shoulder.

“I will look forward to that day,” he said. “When it comes, bring everything you have.”

The answer was simple, yet it left no doubt that he took Bram’s words seriously.

Bram snorted once and walked back to the side of the ring, dropping down into his previous place as if the match had been nothing more than a warm–up.

Leon leaned closer to Elrond.

“Did you see that?” he whispered, eyes still on Bram. “He kept getting up even while he was being toyed with. I really want to fight him.”

Elrond watched Bram’s back again.

‘A swordsman who can follow Julian that far on the first day,’ he thought. ‘And he still wants more after losing.’

He felt a quiet thrill in his chest that had nothing to do with noble names or Academy rankings.

‘This class will be noisy,’ he thought. ‘But it will not be boring.’

Julian turned back to the rest of the students.

“Now then,” he said. “As I mentioned earlier, we will separate into three groups.”

He stooped to pick up the attendance sheet from the stand.

“When I call your name, step forward and stand in the ring I indicate,” Julian said. “First group.”

Julian looked down at the list and began to read. In the end, Elrond’s name came under the second group, and Leon’s followed right after his.

“Second group will use the center ring,” Julian said. “Nyssara Corvine will serve as referee.”

Nyssara stepped forward with quiet steps and took her place at the edge of their ring. She held a wooden sword in one hand, but she rested it like a pointer rather than a weapon.

Farther down the list, Bram’s name went to a different group. Julian sent him to the ring under Aeric’s referee.

Leon let out a low click of his tongue.

“So the moment came faster than I thought,” he said, smiling a little as he moved toward the center ring. “But I still wanted to fight Bram first.”

Elrond fell into step beside him.

‘So I am in the same group as Leon,’ Elrond thought.

He glanced toward the ring where Bram was heading.

“How about Bram?” Elrond asked. “Who is in his group?”

Leon followed his line of sight for a moment.

“He seems to be pointed out with some other great swordsmen,” Leon said briefly. “That ring will be noisy too.”

Julian finished the last names and stepped back.

“Groups, take your positions,” he said. “You will fight within your group. No magic. Only swordplay.”

Today’s assessment was to see their bodies and technique, and everyone already knew that much. Nyssara raised her voice so the whole center ring could hear.

“We will go in order,” she said. “When I call your names, step forward.”

The matches began.

Each time Elrond’s name came up and the opponent was a noble, the same pattern repeated. The noble would glance at his plain surname and at his simple way of standing, and the look in their eyes would sink by half a step.

“Tch. A commoner who’s not worth fighting,” one noble boy said under his breath as they faced each other.

Three moves later, he was on his back, staring up at the sky with his wooden sword knocked out of his hand.

Nyssara did not raise her voice.

“Win. Elrond von Astrea,” she said.

The boy pushed himself up with a red face and walked off the ring without looking at Elrond again.

The next noble changed the way he held his sword as soon as he heard Elrond’s name.

“So you are that commoner,” he said, as if that explained everything.

Five exchanges later, his guard broke open and Elrond’s wooden blade rested against his neck.

“Elrond von Astrea,” Nyssara said. “Win.”

That was how it continued.

Elrond did not need to show anything fancy. A clean guard, a sharp step, a cut that arrived faster than the opponent believed it would. Against people who had trained in safe practice halls, that was enough.

At the same time, Leon was moving through his own matches in the group.

The nobles who faced him often tried to meet him head-on once. Most of them did not try a second time. Some dropped their swords after a single heavy clash. Others lost the will to continue when a one-strike difference turned into an overwhelming line of pressure.

Nyssara’s announcements began to sound almost like a rhythm.

“Leon Sieghart. Win.”

“Leon Sieghart. Win.”

For Elrond, that only confirmed what he had already seen when they walked together.

‘Leon is strong even without magic,’ Elrond thought. ‘And he is not serious yet.’

Sooner than he expected, Nyssara called their names together.

“Elrond von Astrea. Leon Sieghart. Step into the ring.”

A low murmur ran through the watching students. The nobles had seen both of them crush their earlier opponents, and they leaned in a little without thinking.

Leon turned to him with a grin that did not reach his eyes yet.

“Elrond, you better go all out against me,” Leon said. “Or else I will kill you.”

It sounded like a joke, but the way he said “kill” did not feel light.

Elrond held his wooden sword a little tighter.

“O-oh, I will try,” he said. “But please do not kill me.”

Leon’s grin widened into something satisfied.

They walked to opposite sides of the ring.

Nyssara watched them for a moment, then nodded once.

“Begin when you are ready,” she said.

They started moving.

Elrond and Leon both began to circle, stepping carefully, searching for an opening instead of rushing in blindly. Neither of them wanted to be the first one to be read.

Elrond had already watched Leon fight several times. Leon did not break a sweat even when nobles swung with all they had. That was not only technique. That was the way his body had been built.

Leon Sieghart came from the Sieghart household, a swordsman family tied to the Highlander tribe in the northeast mountain range. People said those Highlanders trained in thin air and harsh cold from a young age. Because of that, their bodies grew in a way that most humans could not match.

A Highlander’s natural strength could rival a human who used triple Strength Enhancement, even if they had not cast any magic. They lived long as well. There were stories of Highlanders who reached two hundred years of age. Some people whispered that their origin lay with half-elves, because they traded and trained with elven settlements in the highlands more closely than any other humans did.

None of that required magic because it was simply the way they lived.

With enough training, humans could still touch that height. Julian stood as one proof of that.

Right now, Leon stood in front of Elrond as someone who had been born and raised inside that kind of strength.

‘If I block him carelessly, I will lose the match in one blow,’ Elrond thought.

Elrond moved first, kicking off the hardened ground and closing the distance as fast as he could without using any enhancement, bringing his wooden blade in a low line toward Leon’s side. The cut was only a feint, and in the next instant it flowed up into a top-down strike meant to catch Leon as his guard rose.

Leon read the change and brought his sword across to cover his side before lifting it to meet the descending blow, and their blades crashed together overhead with a solid sound. The weight of that clash ran through Elrond’s arms, so he let the contact go and slid back out of range.

‘Too heavy,’ he thought. ‘If I try to win in a contest of power, I will lose.’

Across from him, Leon’s expression had already changed.

The earlier smile that carried light excitement faded. His mouth flattened into a straight line.

“Is that all?” Leon asked.

Leon did not wait for an answer and he shot forward, so for a moment Elrond lost sight of him from the front as Leon’s presence slipped to his side and a heavy wooden blade came cutting in from there.

Elrond barely managed to bring his sword up in time.

The impact ran through his bones and almost numbed his fingers. He took the blow on his blade, let his feet move with it, and stepped away to keep his balance.

Leon did not stop.

Slash after slash fell toward him. Each one had a weight that would have broken a normal student’s guard in two or three hits. Elrond met some of them with his sword and moved away from others, but even blocking correctly felt like catching a falling rock.

He forced a deflect on the next cut, turning Leon’s blade aside and using that small window to create distance.

“I see,” Elrond said, breathing a little faster. “You are still playing around, Leon.”

Leon’s lips lifted in a small, sharp smile.

“Of course I am,” Leon said. “I told you to be serious and go all out. If you cannot do that, I will seriously hurt you so badly you cannot stand.”

Elrond blinked.

“You lowered your threat,” he said. “You said you would kill me before.”

“Right now, you do not deserve that much effort,” Leon replied. “If you disappoint me this badly, you are not worth my attention.”

There was no malice in his voice, only a matter-of-fact judgement.

Elrond let out a slow breath.

‘He is not trying to insult me,’ Elrond thought. ‘He is just saying what he sees.’

He tightened his grip again and stepped forward.

This time he did not bother with feints. He ran straight at Leon, bringing his sword down in a direct cut that aimed for Leon’s guard.

Their blades met.

From that point on, they traded attacks in rapid succession. Elrond stopped trying to block every strike and began to slip his body around them instead, stepping to the side whenever he could, ducking when the line allowed it. He only brought his sword up when there was no other choice.

Leon’s expression changed back into a smile.

“Good,” Leon said. “Now it looks like you are trying to fight me.”

Even without magic, Leon’s steps were fast. His swings were heavy, but he did not waste movement. For a short stretch, Elrond began to feel the pattern of his shoulders, hips, and feet. He slipped past one swing that would have knocked him flat and answered with a clean cut that scratched Leon’s uniform at the arm.

It did not hurt Leon, but it proved something.

Nyssara’s eyes narrowed slightly as she watched.

‘If I keep this up, I can see more of his timing,’ Elrond thought.

Leon’s smile deepened.

His next steps changed.

The rhythm he had just started to show disappeared. His sword came from angles that did not match the weight of his feet. His hips turned at moments that did not match his shoulders.

To Elrond, the feeling pressed against something familiar.

‘This is close to Father,’ Elrond thought. ‘A stance that moves in ways my eyes can follow, but my prediction cannot catch.’

His mind tried to grab patterns and found nothing solid. In the end he had to block more often, because the new lines of attack stepped into places where there was no time to dodge cleanly.

His arms began to feel the strain.

He remembered another training.

Aldric had stood in front of him with triple Strength Enhancement active, while Elrond stayed unenhanced. The lesson then had been simple. Against someone stronger, you mostly lived by dodging. But there was one move Aldric had forced him to practice again and again.

A quick deflect that used all his strength at the moment of impact, and an immediate counterattack that followed the enemy’s power back into them.

Elrond had never landed it cleanly in a real match.

Now he searched for that one opening.

Their swords kept meeting. Leon chased him like a hunter, and Elrond moved like a cornered animal that refused to fall. The ground under their feet showed thin lines from sliding steps and sharp stops.

Then Leon’s shoulders set in a way Elrond recognized.

A powerful swing came from Leon’s right, heavy enough that if it landed, the match would end at once.

Elrond stepped in instead of away.

He brought his sword up with both hands and put everything he had into the guard. Their blades crashed together. For an instant, the impact locked their bodies in place.

Elrond let the force run through him, then turned his body with it.

He let his arm loosen just enough at the right moment, let Leon’s strength carry his blade aside, and used that flow to swing his own body around. His sword came back in a short arc toward Leon’s open side.

Leon caught it in time, but the impact rang up his arms.

His eyes widened a fraction.

“That one was good,” Leon said.

Leon answered with a sudden thrust, and Elrond bent his body and slipped past it. When their chase resumed, the gap between them was even clearer—Leon still held the upper hand.

Elrond’s breathing grew rougher, and his steps grew a little heavier. Leon’s swings did not lose weight. He pressed in, and Elrond found fewer and fewer safe places to stand.

Finally, Leon changed his height.

He dropped his center and swung low, catching Elrond’s guard from below. The strike did not knock Elrond’s sword away completely, but it broke his stance enough that his feet stumbled.

In the same motion, Leon stepped around him.

By the time Elrond caught his balance again, a wooden blade rested at the back of his head.

Nyssara raised her voice.

“That is enough,” she said. “Leon Sieghart wins.”

Elrond let out a short breath and lowered his sword. He turned around with a small, tired smile.

“It is my loss,” he said. “Hehe…”

Leon laughed once, full of energy that had not burned out yet.

“That was amazing, Elrond,” Leon said. “I never thought you would pull off that kind of move. You surprised me.”

He stepped forward and dropped an arm around the back of Elrond’s neck like they had known each other for years.

Elrond blinked at the sudden closeness, then relaxed a little.

‘So this is how he treats someone he accepts,’ Elrond thought.

The assessment still had more matches to go, but for Elrond, this was the point where his friendship with Leon Sieghart truly began.

Even after that match, the assessment did not stop.

Nyssara continued calling names, and wooden blades kept clashing in each ring. The referees were the ones giving decisions, but Julian did not sit back and leave it to them. He stood where he could see all three groups, his gaze moving from ring to ring as he watched who kept their composure, who broke, and who hid more strength than they showed.

In Elrond’s group, the ones that stood out were obvious. Elrond, who had cut through noble opponents with clean, efficient swordplay, and Leon, who had crushed them with sheer strength and speed.

In the first group, Emilia Alfrost drew the eye in a different way. Her footwork and blade work were precise in every match, and the way she handled distance made it clear she had already been shaped by Julian’s training before today. On technique alone, she was one of the best in the class.

In the third group, Bram’s presence was as rough as ever, but the results were simple. The nobles in his ring looked down on him just as they had on Elrond, and he still beat every single one of them. Even without magic, he pushed through each match with the kind of stubborn, violent rhythm that came from real fighting.

Julian watched, and a shape of the class began to settle in his mind.

After another round of matches, he raised his voice.

“Everyone, return to the edge of the field,” Julian said. “We will hold one final match.”

The noise around the grounds dropped as the students stepped back from the rings and formed a loose circle at a distance.

“For this last part,” Julian continued, “the strongest from each group will fight together. One versus one versus one. It is not a common form in the Academy, but in reality, there are times when three different sides cross blades at once. Think of this as practice for that.”

He let that sink in.

“From the first group, Emilia Alfrost,” he said. “From the second group, Leon Sieghart. From the third group, Bram Veller. Step forward.”

All eyes turned to the three of them as they moved toward the larger central ring.

──────────

On another part of the grounds, Emilia tightened the strap at her wrist as she walked.

She was usually the type who checked every detail around her, from footing to the people watching, yet during the earlier matches she had barely looked beyond the edge of her ring. Her world had narrowed to the opponent in front of her, the next step, and the angle of the next cut. Because of that, she had not noticed Elrond’s fights at all, even though his performance would have stood out to anyone who cared about the sword.

Someone else had noticed.

From the watching students, Cestina had been peeking toward Elrond since they were still in the classroom. When he stood at the back near the window, when he answered Julian, when he moved in the sparring ring, she had been trying to fix his shape in her eyes.

‘Is that the boy who saved us during the assassination?’ Cestina thought. ‘It has to be him.’

At a distance, her vision made people blur together if she did not focus. In the previous world, someone would have called it myopia. Here, it was just a problem that made far things fuzzy unless she squinted or used a tool.

This world knew about lenses in other forms. There were binoculars and telescopes for scouts and sailors, but the idea of fitting glass in front of a person’s eyes as daily tools had never spread. No one would think of eyeglasses when they saw her narrow her eyes.

Even so, Elrond’s outline, his black hair, and the way he moved matched the savior in her memory. His name matched as well.

‘There is no mistake,’ she thought. ‘It should be him.’

She still had not had a proper chance to confirm it with Emilia or Liso. The matches had not stopped long enough, and it was hard to approach someone while referees were calling names.

‘I will talk to them after this assessment is over,’ Cestina decided.

For now, she kept watching.

──────────

The larger ring was clear, and the boundary lines were easy to see. The rest of the class stood back so they would not get drawn in if someone lost control of their movements.

Nyssara walked to the edge of that ring and took her place as referee. Julian stood a short distance away with his arms folded, watching in person.

Emilia, Leon, and Bram faced one another, each standing on a different side of the circle.

“Prepare,” Nyssara said. “Then fight.”

She raised one hand and held it for a moment, then cut it down to signal the start.

For a few breaths, none of the three moved.

They watched one another instead and measured who would make the first mistake. Emilia tracked the other two from behind her guard, Leon leaned lazily with his sword tip resting on the ground, and Bram’s eyes moved between them with an impatience that could not last long.

Bram’s temper broke first.

“Tch,” he said. “You are not worthy to fight me, little girl.”

He launched himself toward Emilia.

His charge was rough and direct. To many swordsmen, it would have looked reckless, yet for someone like Emilia, who had honed her form toward perfection and elegance, that kind of wild movement pulled at the edges of her rhythm.

Bram knew that. He attacked that way on purpose.

Even so, Emilia’s blade came up to meet him.

Their swords met with a hard sound, and they began to trade blows. Emilia’s movements were sharp, her feet stepping on precise lines, and her cuts followed clean paths that any instructor would praise. Bram’s swings were irregular and seemed to come from strange angles, but his power and timing came from real battle, not drills.

“You are an open book, little girl,” Bram shouted as their wooden blades struck and slid apart.

The words dug under her skin in a way that had nothing to do with technique.

Emilia’s jaw tightened. Her movements shifted. The smooth, predictable rhythm of her swordplay broke apart and grew jagged. She wove an inner swing into the next exchange, then turned it into a feint and pushed through with a straight thrust that went for Bram’s center.

The point drove in hard enough to jolt his guard.

“Tch. Not bad, little girl,” Bram said.

He was still saying “little girl,” even though Emilia was not little at all, and his tone had shifted from pure dismissal to a rough praise wrapped in his usual way of pushing people down.

At the third side of the ring, Leon watched with his sword still resting on the ground.

He did not move to join them. His weight stayed relaxed, and he seemed content to let the other two clash first.

Bram noticed.

“Oy,” Bram shouted, switching his attention for a moment. “Are you not going to do anything?”

Leon glanced at him.

“Why should I?” Leon said. “Watching is more entertaining for now. I will wait until both of you have settled.”

His voice was calm, and the confidence in it sounded like something everyday for him rather than arrogance thrown in anyone’s face.

Outside the ring, Elrond could not help thinking about it.

‘He was so fired up to fight Bram before,’ Elrond thought. ‘Now he is acting like this.’

Bram could not stand being treated as part of the scenery.

“Watching is more entertaining, you said?” Bram retorted. “Then at least take a taste of this.”

He kicked off the ground and dashed toward Leon at full speed, swinging his wooden sword with an attack that would have smashed most students.

Leon lifted his sword from the ground and met the swing with a simple block.

The shock of the impact ran up Bram’s arms. He felt at once that if he pushed that clash any further, the result would be his immediate defeat.

He pulled back at once.

“What is that strength? That is clearly cheating!” Bram shouted.

Leon tilted his head slightly.

“I am sorry, but I was born and trained to be like this,” Leon said. “There is nothing I can do about it.”

While the two of them spoke, Emilia moved again.

She charged Bram with a flurry of thrusts. The repeated points of attack came in fast from slightly different lines, and Bram struggled to both block and dodge. He did not take a direct hit, but he was forced to give ground, step after step.

Emilia did not stop there. When Bram retreated to a safer distance, she changed direction and went for Leon instead.

Their swords met. Emilia’s attacks came in sharp and fast, but Leon did not step away from his place. He blocked every single one, his feet staying on the same patch of ground as he shifted his arms and adjusted his stance just enough to catch each strike.

“Damn it,” Bram muttered under his breath.

He grit his teeth and rushed back toward Leon as well. Without saying it out loud, he and Emilia became a two–sided pressure on Leon, blades coming from different directions.

Even then, Leon’s boots barely moved.

He rotated his body, raised or lowered his guard, and shifted his sword line in ways that turned both sets of blows aside. When he finally swung with full force, Bram and Emilia met it together.

The impact knocked them both back.

Bram slid but caught himself and kept his feet under him. Emilia lost her footing and fell, landing hard on the packed earth.

Leon did not let the chance slip.

He drove toward her at once.

Emilia pushed herself up with a wince and threw her body to the side. Leon’s blade cut the air where she had been a moment before.

She had felt the difference in that clash as clearly as anyone watching.

Against someone that much stronger, meeting a direct blow head-on was foolish. Dodging at the last possible moment was the only way to stay in the match.

Her dodge was clean, but Leon’s smile when he straightened looked more like mocking amusement than joy at a good fight.

Emilia bit down on her frustration. She tried to force her mind away from it and searched for an opening instead. She launched into a series of rapid attacks, aiming for small gaps, testing any line where she might land a counter. Every time she came close, Leon turned or raised his blade and dismissed it.

Bram saw an opening and swung at Leon’s back.

Leon noticed the shift in pressure and stepped back at the last moment.

Because of that movement, Bram’s full–force swing did not hit Leon. The wooden blade crashed into Emilia’s shoulder instead.

The sound of the impact cut through the field.

Emilia’s body jerked with the blow. Pain ran across her face for a moment before she could suppress it, and she dropped to one knee with her free hand pressed against the place where the hit had landed. Her uniform dented and bruised the skin underneath. The strike had not broken bone, but anyone watching could see she would not be able to keep swinging without making it worse.

Nyssara’s eyes flicked to her, and she raised her hand once.

“Emilia Alfrost is out,” Nyssara said.

Emilia drew in a breath, then exhaled slowly and forced herself to stand up straight enough to step back from the ring. She kept her hand on her shoulder and did not look at Bram or Leon as she walked away.

Only Bram and Leon remained.

“This is irritating,” Bram said, more to himself than anyone else. “I win that with some accident. It is not satisfying at all, you know.”

Leon’s mouth curved in a small smile that did not soften his eyes.

“A win is a win,” Leon said. “You took Lady Alfrost square and fair.”

Bram clicked his tongue.

He charged again, swinging at Leon like before.

Leon still did not advance. He waited.

Bram tried to read him. He watched Leon’s shoulders, the tilt of his hips, the angle of his wrists. The longer he watched, the more frustrating it became. There was no clean line he could call a “style.” Leon’s movements felt like pure speed and reaction wrapped around a body that did not know what weakness meant.

‘What is with this guy?’ Bram thought. ‘He is utter chaos. No straight line to follow.’

He pulled back to change something.

He shifted his grip and stance, trying to imitate the way Julian had moved earlier. He charged again, this time with steps and swings that tried to draw a pattern around Leon instead of smashing straight in.

It did create small openings. Leon chose to dodge a few of the attacks rather than block them directly, and that only made Bram more irritated.

‘I have already thrown everything I have,’ Bram thought. ‘Even that last piece I stole from Julian.’

Leon watched him for a moment.

“It looks like you are out of tricks, Bram,” Leon said.

He moved.

This time, Leon did not wait for Bram to come. He stepped in and swung. Bram did everything he could, blocking, dodging, parrying. Each clash sent a jolt up his arms. Every time he tried to change the flow, Leon’s blade was already there.

‘If only I could use enhancement magic,’ Bram thought. ‘Things would not turn out like this.’

The match did not drag on.

In a few more exchanges, Leon brought his sword up from below in a hard swing. The angle caught Bram’s grip in a way that knocked his hands open. The wooden sword flew out of Bram’s fingers and landed outside the ring.

By the time he realized his hands were empty, Leon’s blade was already in front of his face.

“I thought you would be more interesting,” Leon said. “But I was wrong.”

Bram stared at the wooden tip for a moment, then clicked his tongue without answering.

Nyssara raised her voice.

“The winner is Leon Sieghart,” she said.

For a breath, the training grounds were quiet. Then voices burst out one after another.

“Whoaa!”

“Sieghart is amazing!”

“Well, of course. He is from Sieghart.”

Excitement and a certain kind of acceptance mixed together in those reactions. For them, this outcome fit the story they already knew.

Leon let his sword drop to his shoulder and walked back toward his group.

Elrond stepped forward to meet him.

“Good fight,” Elrond said. “You really are amazing, Leon.”

Eiden nodded hard beside him.

“It was something else,” Eiden added.

Leon scratched his cheek lightly, as if the cheers were more awkward than pleasing.

“It was nothing,” Leon said. “Besides, it helped that we were not allowed to use magic. If we used magic, the table would turn.”

His words sounded simple, yet there was a small tightness around his eyes when he said it. Even Leon knew that once spells and enchanted bodies entered the field, his natural advantage would not stand alone forever.

Elrond had seen enough of magic to understand that thought without saying it.

Today, with no magic involved, Leon Sieghart’s victory was the natural result of his nature. Tomorrow, the shape of the class might look very different.

──────────

With that, the assessment was over.

Julian called an end to the matches, and the students began to relax. Some stretched their arms, some sat down where they stood for a moment, and some rubbed at places where wooden blows had landed harder than expected. Three hours of fighting had left its mark even without serious injuries.

Julian had already seen what he needed. He knew who moved on drilled lines and who moved like they had fought for real. He knew who broke under pressure and who held together. The referees would still submit their observations later, but his own picture of the class was clear.

“Return to the classroom,” Julian said. “Homeroom will continue there.”

They filed back inside.

On the way and as they entered the room, Elrond kept to the rear as usual. Leon and Eiden matched his pace without making anything of it, letting the noisier nobles fill the front rows while the three of them stayed near the back. Elrond simply could not stand being in the middle of a crowd.

They were about to step out with the others when Julian’s voice stopped them.

“Elrond,” Julian said. “Can you stay a bit?”

Elrond, who had been about to leave the room with Leon and Eiden, turned around.

“Yes, of course. What is it, Teach?” he asked, curiosity rising.

Julian’s eyes moved to Leon and Eiden.

“Both of you can go first,” Julian said. “It is a private talk.”

The three boys looked at one another. Leon gave a small shrug, and Eiden nodded once.

“We will wait outside later,” Leon said. “Do not get scolded too hard.”

They stepped out and left the scene to the two of them.

When the door had closed and the last of the footsteps in the corridor had faded, Julian faced Elrond properly.

“Could you please come to my room after this homeroom ends?” Julian asked. “It is the same room where you and Lacia talked before. That is my personal room, actually.”

‘So that was his room from the start,’ Elrond thought. ‘I did feel there was something similar about the two of them, but I let it slide.’

“Oh. Of course,” Elrond said. “Do you have anything to talk about that you cannot talk here and now?”

He wanted to affirm that this really needed to be kept for later, in private.

“Yes,” Julian said. “There is a lot to talk about. We will talk about it later. For now, stay silent about it. You can go back to your classroom, and do not make me wait too long later.”

His tone was calm, yet the demand in it was clear.

That only made Elrond more curious.

“Understood, Teach,” Elrond said. “I will not make you wait later.”

Julian gave a short nod.

Elrond returned to the classroom and took his seat again beside Leon and Eiden to continue homeroom.

It was not much that remained. It was a two–day homeroom schedule, and Julian told them that tomorrow the agenda would be magic, just like today had focused on assessment without magic, so they needed to prepare themselves.

### Chapter 24: 20 - Equal Footing

#### Scene 1

As homeroom finished, the light outside the windows had already turned heavy and bright. It felt like the middle of the day, and if he compared it to the time sense from his previous world, it was probably around two or three in the afternoon. There was no proper clock in the classroom, so it was only a guess. The only thing close to a timekeeper was the sand clock on the teacher’s desk, its last grains already settled at the bottom.

Emilia and the girls began to pack their things.

Everyone started packing up and getting ready to leave. Emilia reached for the pen on her desk, but her fingers bumped it by mistake, and it rolled off the edge.

“Ah…”

The pen fell and rolled under the desk, so Emilia leaned down to grab it, and her hair slipped forward in her face.

While she was reaching, Elrond walked past their row, and she only caught the edge of his uniform and the shadow crossing the aisle. When her fingers finally closed around the pen and she straightened up, he was already at the front door, and it was closing behind him.

She caught only the faintest glimpse of him at the edge of the doorway.

It felt, in a small way, like the world itself was avoiding their first proper meeting. As if the timing refused to let them face each other this early.

Next to her, Cestina leaned in.

“Lady Emilia,” Cestina whispered. “Did you see that boy who just passed by?” Her voice had the tone of someone who already knew the answer she wanted.

Emilia slid the pen back onto the desk and glanced toward the door that had just shut.

“I saw him,” Emilia said. “Why is that?”

She had only seen his back and the shape of his shoulders as he left. It was not enough to fix a face in her mind.

“Did you not notice at all?” Cestina pressed, puffing her cheeks a little as if she were bragging about something only she had caught.

Emilia frowned slightly.

“Wait, what is happening, Cestina?” she asked. “Of course I saw him, but I do not know who that is. It was only a glimpse.” Cestina let out a small exhale and shook her head.

“He is Elrond,” Cestina said. “The one who saved us. Does that name not ring a bell?” The name settled over the desk.

Before Emilia could answer, Liso turned from the other side.

“Elrond?” Liso said. “You mean Elrond, that guy, Cestina?” Her voice rose half a step, full of excitement.

“I am still not completely sure,” Cestina admitted. “But his appearance and his name match what I remember. I think it is him.” Cestina was never good at seeing things from far away, so faces blurred unless she squinted. In another world, Elrond would have called it myopia, the kind of problem that could be fixed with simple everyday lenses. But in this world, lenses were made for telescopes and binoculars used by scouts and scholars, not something people wore day to day. Because of that, she could only say his outline “resembled” their savior, but the way he moved and the name she caught were enough for her to connect it.

Emilia stayed quiet for a moment, her eyes still on the door as if she was replaying the brief glimpse in her head.

“Heh. Is that so?” she said.

Her tone was light, almost too casual for what Cestina had just said.

Cestina hesitated, confused by how little reaction Emilia showed.

“What is happening, Lady Emilia?” Cestina asked. “Do you not want to meet the boy who saved you and thank him?” “That is right,” Liso added quickly. “We should talk to him.” Emilia did not look at either of them. Her gaze dropped to the pen on her desk instead.

On the surface, it might have looked like she simply did not care. Inside, the feeling that turned in her chest was nothing like indifference.

For the past few days, that feeling had been weighing on her, heavy and stubborn. It was not excitement at the thought of finally meeting the person who had saved her. It was something closer to disappointment that pointed straight back at herself.

It was true that he had saved her. That part was not in doubt.

Yet every time someone mentioned “the boy who saved us” and every time the name Elrond came up, the first thing that rose in her mind was the fact that she had not been able to protect the people beside her. An unknown person had stepped in where she had failed, and that simple truth did not sit well inside her.

She had trained for years. She had been taught, guided, and shaped so that she could stand on the front line and shield the people she cared about. That was what it meant to be Emilia Alfrost.

And still, when it mattered, she had been the one who needed saving.

Because of that, she could not accept the idea of walking up to him now with a simple “thank you.” It felt too light. It felt like admitting that the gap between them was fixed and that she had nothing to put on the other side of the scale.

She was grateful. She understood that much. If Elrond had not been there, things would have gone much worse.

Yet she could not bring herself to face him while she was still standing this far below him.

The fact that she could not protect her dear friends when the blades came out only showed her how far above her league Elrond stood. Every time she thought about that difference, it pressed on her chest.

So knowing him, in this moment, was not a source of pride or happiness.

It felt much closer to envy that had nowhere to go, and Emilia had no intention of letting that show on her face.

“Well, if you two want to meet him, let us go,” Emilia said.

She smiled when she said it.

To Cestina, the smile was hard to read. She could not tell if Emilia was happy about meeting him, or if Emilia was only trying to go along with Cestina and Liso so they would not feel bad.

They finished packing their things.

Chairs moved back. Bags were lifted. The last few students walked out. When they were ready, Emilia, Cestina, and Liso stepped out of the classroom together.

By the time they reached the corridor, it was already too late.

Elrond was gone.

They could not see him anywhere. They did not know which way he had gone after he left the room. Even so, they tried to look for him.

“Maybe he went this way,” someone said, and they started walking.

Without knowing it, they chose the wrong direction. Elrond had gone the other way, so every step they took only made the distance between them wider.

After a short while, Cestina stopped.

“Seems like we cannot find him today,” Cestina said clearly.

Liso let out a breath.

“Yeah,” Liso said. “I was already this excited to meet him properly. Seems like not today to celebrate that.” She sounded disappointed, but it was the simple, honest kind of disappointment.

Emilia looked at the two of them.

Her face did not change much. She did not look upset, and she did not look especially relieved either. To Cestina and Liso, it just looked like she was not very interested.

“Well, there is still tomorrow,” Emilia said. “Let us go home for today.” Her voice was calm.

Cestina watched her.

The more she looked at Emilia’s quiet face, the more something inside her felt wrong. It felt like Emilia was ignoring what had happened back then. A brave person had saved them. Guards had died to protect them. To Cestina, that was not something you could treat lightly.

Right now, it did not feel like Emilia was grateful at all. Cestina wanted to ask why she was acting like this and tell her it was not like her, but the hallway was still busy and this was not the time or place. She swallowed the words and, for now, let it go.

When the girls went back home, Elrond was already standing in front of Julian’s room.

He took a small breath and knocked on the door.

“Get in,” Julian’s voice came from inside, calm as always.

Elrond opened the door and stepped in.

He had expected to see only Julian. Instead, there was another person sitting on the couch. A gentle looking man with light blue hair sat there in a neat white noble suit. A half cloak hung from his right shoulder, held in place by a golden chain and a blue crystal that caught the light when he moved.

They seemed to be in the middle of a conversation.

“Sorry, am I interrupting your business?” Elrond asked.

He stayed near the door for a moment. It felt like he might have come at the wrong time.

“Do not worry,” Julian said. “You are the business.”

“O–oh…”

Elrond’s reply came out a little stiff.

“Please sit down, Elrond,” Julian said, and motioned toward the couch opposite the man.

Elrond walked over and sat where he was told. Julian took the single seat between them so that the three of them formed a cross shape when viewed from above.

The gentle man’s eyes stayed on Elrond the whole time. When their eyes met, the man gave him a soft smile.

It made the back of Elrond’s neck prickle.

‘What is with this guy, smiling like that?’ he thought.

Julian sat back and folded one leg over the other.

“So, for starters, Elrond, I would like to introduce you to this man,” Julian said. “He has been searching for you for a couple of days. From the crest on his half cloak, you can already tell he is Alfrost. He is Gilbert. Gilbert Alfrost.” ‘Alfrost, huh. I thought it would be about time they finally found me,’ Elrond thought.

From his point of view, it was not strange at all. Even though he had kept his face and origin hidden during the assassination attempt, he had still given his name. He had been in a Royal Academy style uniform as well. At the time, he had not planned that far ahead. He had simply tried to save people.

The man leaned forward a little.

“Yo. Elrond, is it not? It has been a long time, no see,” Gilbert said.

‘Long time no see? What is this guy talking about? Did I meet him before?’ Elrond thought.

“Excuse me,” Elrond said. “Have we ever met before?”

Gilbert nodded once.

“I see,” he said. “Of course you would forget. We were still very young back then. We never met properly. We only saw each other briefly in your hometown.” A picture rose up in Elrond’s head at once. He remembered the carriage from that day, with a boy inside waving through the window and a girl beside him sitting still and shy.

“Ah,” Elrond said. “Are you the boy that was waving at me back then?” Gilbert gave a light smile.

“Precisely,” he said. “I am glad that you remember. It saves time for explanation.” “So, what would you need from me, Sir Alfrost?” Elrond asked.

His tone stayed polite. Inside, he already had a rough idea of why Gilbert was here.

“Well,” Gilbert said, “there was a recent attempted assassination on my little sister. The girl who was with me in the carriage that time.” He paused for a moment, then continued.

“And it happens that an unknown boy saved her very gallantly. So we are currently searching for him.” That alone was clear enough.

“And apparently,” Gilbert added, “it happens that both of them are in the same class with Julian here as their homeroom teacher. So it was pretty easy to find him.” He really hit the point.

Elrond tried to escape anyway.

“I see,” Elrond said. “I hope that you can find that boy.” He looked slightly to the side as he spoke.

Gilbert’s mouth curved into a small, knowing smile. He understood Elrond’s intention at once. That was why he still had not said the name directly. This was simply how Gilbert liked to talk. Teasing, making it a little fun.

“That is right,” Gilbert said. “Julian senpai, did you catch the boy?” In this world, “senpai” was just another way to say “senior.” In Elrond’s head, it still rang like the word from his previous life in Japan.

“Do not throw the responsibility back to me,” Julian said. “I already gave you the package.” Elrond’s shoulders stiffened.

Being called a package felt strange.

“You are not fun at all, senpai,” Gilbert said, quick as ever.

Julian did not answer that. Gilbert let out a small breath and straightened his posture.

“Well, enough with the chit chat,” Gilbert said.

He paused for a brief moment, then looked straight at Elrond.

“So, Sir Elrond,” Gilbert said, “I would like to express my gratitude toward you for saving my sister. It was truly a fortunate event that you were heading toward that direction and were able to save her.” With those heavy, polite words, Gilbert stood up from the couch and bowed slightly.

Elrond immediately stood as well.

“Please raise your head, Sir Alfrost,” Elrond said. “It is just as you said. It was only coincidence that I was passing by. I…” Before he could finish, Gilbert lifted his head again.

“But it is very, very fortunate,” Gilbert said. “And it just happened to be you, Sir Elrond. I believe this is what you can call… fate.” His voice was soft. It sounded genuine.

To Gilbert, it really did feel like fate. Emilia kept getting targeted. Now the one who had saved her was the same boy tied to that old carriage memory from years ago.

“First we were attacked by a wyvern long ago, and it was your father who saved us,” Gilbert said. “And now, it was you who saved my sister. I am truly grateful toward you.” Julian watched the two of them without saying anything. His eyes were open and calm, taking in every word.

Elrond felt his throat tighten a little. He could only stand there and accept what Gilbert was saying.

“Elrond,” Julian said, “I can tell that you might not really think that far, but you were a hero, and you should be proud.” A small warmth rose in Elrond’s chest at those words. He did not let it reach his face.

“What Julian senpai said is true, Elrond,” Gilbert added. “You might not think much of it, but you just saved a whole lineage. You probably saved this country, if the worst had come and she had fallen into enemy hands.” It might have sounded dramatic, but it was not wrong. If Emilia had died, House Alfrost would have lost another direct heir, and if she had been captured, any faction that took her could have turned her into a puppet.

“I never thought that my action would be that significant,” Elrond said. “I was just trying to save people.” Gilbert let the silence sit for a moment, then spoke again.

“I would never imagine what would have happened if you had not come to save them,” he said. “Elrond, you might have just saved two lineages of Alfrost.” ‘Two lineages? What does he mean by that?’ he thought.

Only Julian understood the meaning at once.

“What do you mean by that, Sir Alfrost?” Elrond asked out loud.

Gilbert’s smile returned, a little wider now.

“If you noticed a beautiful blonde with purple eyes, with a magnificent smile and perfect demeanor,” Gilbert said, “she is my fiancée.” He said it in a way that sounded like he was praising her on purpose.

“Oh,” Elrond said. “If I remember correctly, her name is Cestina Ludwell, is it not?” “Yes,” Gilbert replied. “That is her.”

‘Well, that makes sense,’ Elrond thought. Someone with beauty like Cestina would obviously have a fiancé like Gilbert.

“I think that is all from me for now, Elrond,” Gilbert said. “I would like to invite you to the Alfrost mansion. When are you able to come?” Elrond already understood what this meant.

Nobles did not like to feel indebted. They would try to balance the scale. If it came in the form of money, then he needed it. That alone was enough reason for him to accept.

“I can come any time you like,” Elrond said. “Just not during school time.” “Then how about the day after tomorrow,” Gilbert said. “Around the same time as this.” “Yes,” Elrond answered. “That is possible.”

“Good,” Gilbert said.

He gave one last polite nod to Elrond, then another to Julian.

“With that, I will take my leave,” Gilbert said. “I still have other matters to handle.” Julian watched Gilbert walk to the door and let himself out, the latch clicking softly behind him. The room fell quiet, leaving only Julian and Elrond.

Julian watched Gilbert walk to the door and let himself out, the latch clicking softly behind him. The room fell quiet, leaving only Julian and Elrond.

For a moment, Elrond did not know where to look. It felt strangely heavy now that it was just the two of them.

Julian was the one who moved first.

“There is also something that I want to talk about,” Julian said. “I told you in the entrance exam that I chose you to become my own disciple.” He restated it on purpose, as if he wanted to make sure there was no misunderstanding.

“Yes, you said something like that,” Elrond replied. “I am still not quite sure what to do.” He wanted to be sure he understood what he was getting into.

Before Julian could answer, the door suddenly opened and Lacia stepped in without knocking.

“Lacia, how many times have I told you already. Knock before entering,” Julian said. His voice was more like a tired scolding than real anger.

“I apologize, dear brother. I saw Sir Alfrost already leaving the room,” Lacia replied.

She did not look at either of them. She walked straight to the bookshelf and reached up for one of the books on the upper shelf.

“Wait, dear brother?” Elrond said, surprised.

Lacia turned her head as if she had only just noticed him.

“Oh, Elrond. Long time no see. I did not notice you were here,” she greeted him, carefree.

She felt different from the Lacia he had seen before. Back then, she had been calm and polite and very insightful, but now she barged in with an easy, relaxed air just because she saw that Gilbert had already left.

“Yeah… good to see you again, Lady Roosevelt,” Elrond said.

“Wait… Roosevelt. Is that also Julian teach’s family name?” he added in a low voice, but it was still easy to hear.

“You have not noticed it yet?” Julian said. “She is my younger sister. Well, step sister, to be exact.” “That was rude, dear brother,” Lacia said at once. “No matter what, you are still my dear brother, and I am your precious little sister.” Julian sighed a little.

“Sorry, Elrond,” he said. “This is what she actually looks like when she is not in her workplace. She is very attached to me.” “That is totally fine,” Elrond said. “I think I can understand that. Everyone has their own serious side.” Lacia hugged the book against her chest.

“Well, since you already know how I look, it means you are going to be tied to me and dear brother in the future, Elrond,” she said, as if she were sealing an agreement all by herself.

In truth, her cheeks felt a little warm. Calling him “dear brother” in front of other people was embarrassing, so she doubled down and kept her tone cool. Elrond did not really mind it.

After taking the book she needed, Lacia left the room and went back to her workplace.

“Hah… anyway, let us get back to the point,” Julian said when the door closed. “You becoming my disciple means that every personal schedule slot in your class schedule will be occupied by me personally.” He spoke as if the decision was already made. Julian was also trying to push the agreement one sided. In that way, he and Lacia felt very similar in personality.

Even though Julian and Lacia were brother and sister, they had different mothers. Lacia was born from a concubine who was raised into an official wife after the death of Julian’s real mother, which made Lacia and her mother part of the official heir line. They had known each other since they were three years old, and Lacia had always been attached to Julian. With her Divine Blessing, Clairvoyance, she could see Julian as a warm and reliable person with powerful magic inside, so she felt safe when she was with him.

“I see, but I do feel a bit disagree about that,” Elrond said.

He tried to push back, because it felt too one sided.

“Because it says personal improvement, so I should be the one who chooses that.” Julian replied without any hesitation.

“You should be honored to become my direct student,” he said. “I get a lot of invitations to become a personal trainer, but I never take them.” He said it with pride, thinking it would be enough to convince Elrond.

Elrond remembered how it felt to fight Julian firsthand and how amazing Julian had been. Under Julian’s training, he could clearly improve, yet he still hesitated.

‘Well, he is indeed strong, but I still want to do something else, like reading books in the library or something,’ Elrond thought.

Julian watched his face.

“Or do you wish to do something else, Elrond?” Julian asked. “Tell me what you really want.” “I… I actually just wanted to read books and learn more magic that I do not know yet,” Elrond said directly.

“Oh. Is that all?” Julian replied. “Then that is perfect.” Elrond blinked.

“You can use my permission to get as many books as you want anywhere in the city,” Julian said. “That includes the forbidden section.” He continued in the same calm tone.

“You can bring as many books as you want here and read them here when we are not training,” Julian added.

A bright smile appeared on Elrond’s face before he could stop it.

“Is that true? I can get any books I want? Then I will accept that,” Elrond said.

He accepted at once.

Then it was settled.

“Starting from the day after tomorrow, in the last slot of your class schedule, just come here,” Julian said, giving clear directions.

With that, their discussion settled.

For Elrond, it was a satisfying result for a single day. In the end, he had gained far more than he expected, from access to books to a direct tie to the Roosevelt family, a firm connection to House Alfrost, and a promised reward from Alfrost waiting in the near future.

The next day, the magic assessment was held in the magic training area.

Just like the sword test, the class was split into three groups. Each group had its own practice zone, and in the center of every zone stood an armored golem. The golems waited without moving, metal plates fitted over their bodies, ready to receive whatever spells the students cast at them.

In simple terms, people in this world often broke magic into three parts, imagination, chanting, and mana control.

The first part was imagination. Before anything else, the caster had to see the spell in their mind. For a spell like fireball, the name alone already gave a picture, a ball of flame leaving the hand and flying toward a target. The clearer and stronger that inner image was, the easier it became for the spell to form the way the caster wanted.

Then came chanting. Chanting was the spoken part, the words that guided the mind and pushed the image into a fixed shape. When Elrond first learned fireball under Selene’s guidance, he stood in front of the practice target and recited the fireball spell out loud.

*“Flame that answers my call, gather and grow, become the fire that follows my will.”* Those spells were written in the ancient tongue. In Selene’s notebook, that single line was split by small marks into three parts, and each part shifted the caster’s unconscious one step further along the spell.

The first part, “Flame that answers my call”, narrowed the caster’s focus and breathing. The old words pushed the unconscious so that they reached only for fire that would answer them and no one else. The mana in the body reacted to that and began to gather as if it had been given a name.

*“Gather and grow”* nudged that flow forward. The sound of the old language told his body to keep drawing mana in and squeezing it around that point instead of stopping at a thin spark. When he had practiced it under Selene, he could feel the weight build up in his palm, tight and hot.

*“Become the fire that follows my will”* was the last part of the line, and it closed the spell. Those words pressed down on the picture in his mind so the flame would not wander or lash out at random. Once that part was spoken, the shape and the path were fixed, and from that moment on the fire had to move according to his intent or the spell would break.

In the end, the ancient tongue and the steps meant nothing if the amount of mana did not match them. Too little and the fireball that came out would be small and weak. Too much and the shape would swell, distort, or break apart before it reached the target. What mattered was that each word, each step, and the flow of mana all lined up.

In the end, everything still depended on mana control. Imagination and chanting could both be good, but if the caster could not control how much mana they poured into the spell, the result would not match what they pictured. Too little mana and the fireball would come out small and weak. Too much and it might swell up, lose shape, or break apart before it even reached the target. What mattered most was balance, a clear image in the mind and a steady hand on the flow of mana, so that the finished spell sat as close as possible to what the caster had imagined.

Julian walked a few steps closer to the front practice zone and turned to face the class.

“Your assessment today is to destroy that golem using your strongest magic,” Julian said. “It is that simple. Any damage you deal will remain until it breaks. You will work on it as a group.” The students focused on the construct in front of them.

The golem itself was a rough humanoid made from hardened brick. Its shoulders were broad, its arms thick, and even standing still it gave the impression of weight. If someone had stacked a wall into the shape of a person and set it in the middle of the yard, it would have looked like this.

Any single basic spell, or even an advanced one, would barely take effect on that golem, let alone break it. That was the point. Against a target like this, people who only knew how to repeat textbook magic would be exposed, and people who could really drive their power would stand out.

Some students looked excited. They would probably throw everything they had at the golem just to show off.

Others were more careful.

For nobles, magic was tied to their house. Some families had spells that were almost like their own signature. The Alfrost family’s ice was one clear example. Their ice could freeze and shatter things in a way other houses could not easily copy, so people often thought twice before showing that kind of magic too openly.

“There will be no separate referee for each group,” Julian continued. “You will decide the order yourselves, and everyone must take at least one turn.” He did not raise his voice. He did not need to. People were already listening closely.

The three golems waited in their own zones while Elrond checked who was standing where, matching the written group list with the people in front of him. This time he was not with Leon, and just knowing that made his shoulders feel a little lighter.

‘Well, there was never supposed to be a competition to begin with,’ he thought.

Even so, not having to stand right next to Leon in this kind of test still helped.

What caught his eye more was his own group.

Lisoletelle was there, already peeking past the others to look at the golem. Emilia stood nearby as well, calm as always. On the other side, he saw Rowan Kael in the group where Leon was. People had started calling Rowan a magic genius after seeing his earlier scores, so that combination made sense.

Elrond let his gaze move over the other zones and watched how everyone prepared.

He paid attention to their hands and to the air around them. Each time a student gathered mana, he checked whether there was any sign of a spell forming without words. No matter how he looked, he could not find anyone who used chantless magic. Everyone moved their lips. Some whispered, some chanted clearly, but they all spoke.

‘So chantless magic really is that rare,’ Elrond thought. ‘Just like Mother said.’ With that, his mind settled.

‘In that case, I will chant normally when it is my turn,’ he decided.

There was no reason to put another strange mark on himself in front of the whole class.

A small stir of voices came from the second practice zone.

It was Leon’s turn.

He walked up to the front with his greatsword resting on his shoulder and a wide, confident grin on his face. The people in his group stepped back to give him space. Even students from the other zones glanced over.

“Teach,” Leon called out. “There is no restriction on how we use magic, right. Using a weapon is still fine?” Julian looked at him from the edge of the zone.

“Do as you like,” Julian said. His answer came out light, almost lazy.

Leon’s grin widened.

Mana began to gather around him at once.

It did not take the neat shape of a spell. It did not form a circle or a clear pattern. It swelled and pressed against the air, thick and heavy, as if the space around him could not quite hold it steady.

In Elrond’s eyes, it was clearly visible.

‘That is pure mana control,’ Elrond thought.

The flow reminded him of something he had already seen. It was the same feeling as the Berserk technique he had seen during the assassination attempt on Emilia Alfrost. Back then, the swordsman who had used Berserk had become stronger and faster, but his movements had been wild because he was being controlled like a puppet.

The pressure now was weaker than that enemy’s, but the shape of it was more solid. Leon’s eyes stayed sharp. His expression stayed clear.

‘He can hold that state without losing his mind,’ Elrond thought. ‘He is using Berserk, but he is keeping control.’ Leon lowered the sword from his shoulder and let the tip touch the ground for a moment. Then he drew it out to his side and settled into a wide slash stance. Another layer of dense mana wrapped around the blade and clung to it. The air hummed faintly, as if it did not like how tightly that power was being packed.

“Hiiiyaaaa…!” Leon shouted.

He swung the sword sideways with all his strength.

The mana that had gathered on the blade tore away and shot forward in a horizontal line. It looked like a cut in the air itself, a compressed wave moving straight toward the golem’s chest.

The impact landed with a deep, cracking sound.

Stone dust burst out from the golem’s torso. When the dust settled, a thick horizontal crater line had been carved across its body. Brick fragments had fallen to the ground under its feet.

Leon clicked his tongue.

“Tch. I was trying to cut it into two. Seems it is stronger than I thought,” he muttered.

He did not raise his voice, but the people near him could still hear it.

The class stared at the mark.

The slash had not been clean enough to split the golem in half, but the damage was clear and deep. If a person had been standing there instead of that construct, there would have been nothing left in that line.

Even the students who liked to brag fell quiet for a moment.

Elrond watched in silence and adjusted his view of Leon’s strength.

That was not a neat, shaped spell. That was raw mana being forced into a path and released through a weapon, closer to the way warriors risked their own bodies in battle.

‘So this is what Leon can do when he stops holding back,’ Elrond thought.

The next interesting display was Lisoletelle.

She stepped forward and took a slow breath, then she started chanting quietly. One magic ball formed near her hands, then another, then another. She did not fire them and kept them hovering close, holding them in place on purpose.

Then she started forcing them together.

It took time because she had to keep several magic balls stable at once, and she also had to force them to merge without letting any of them collapse. The longer she kept chanting and compressing them, the more it showed how much focus it demanded.

When the last ball finally fused, she released the combined spell in one straight blast like a laser, and it punched a hand-sized hole into the golem. It was deep, but it still did not reach the back.

Lisoletelle stared at the damage for a second, then stepped back with disappointment and sighed.

Next was Emilia.

She raised her right hand and opened her palm, then she aimed straight at the hole Lisoletelle had made. She started chanting, and a thin ice spike formed in front of her palm before she sent it directly into the opening.

The moment it plunged inside, mist burst out of the hole like an explosion.

Emilia tightened her fingers into a grip, like she was crushing something.

‘Wow, using additional hand sign for explosion activation is quite impressive,’ Elrond thought.

As the mist scattered, it quickly turned into a massive ice burst that spread through the golem and wrapped it from the inside, and then the structure gave way under the pressure until the whole thing crumbled.

That was also the case because body movement could act as the catalyst for activation, and it was one of the ways a magician could push imagination into something real. Certain actions gave feedback to the caster’s own senses, so the intention stayed clear instead of drifting.

In Emilia’s case, she wanted the mist to explode even more, and she wanted it to turn into a burst of interconnected blocks of ice that penetrated the golem’s structure and made it crumble. That result was intentional, and it was already written into the spell and already fixed in Emilia’s imagination before she even released it.

The classmates around Emilia fell silent for a moment, and then they started whispering as they stared at the crumbled golem.

“woah...”

“so amazing,”

“of course, that was alfrost ice magic...”

“it also looks scary...”

Emilia stepped back and lowered her hand, and the last bits of mist and ice finished dispersing around the broken golem.

After that, the staff moved in and cleared the remains, and a fresh golem was brought into the practice zone and set in place.

“Good job,” Julian said.

On the other side, a boy raised his hand as if he had been waiting for the timing to be right.

“Excuse me, teach, could you also please replace my group golem?” he asked.

It was Rowan Kael, the commoner boy people kept whispering about, and the one they had already started calling a magic genius. He looked ordinary at first glance, short black hair, sun-browned skin, and light green eyes that stayed quiet even when everyone else was making noise.

He asked on purpose because the golem was already too damaged, so he wanted a fresh one to test his magic at full power and end it in a single attack.

“The golem is still standing, we will replace it after it destroyed,” Julian replied, trying to refuse.

Rowan did not reply, and he just started chanting right away. The words flowed out smooth and efficient, and then he fired a magic ball so fast it almost looked instant. It hit the already-damaged golem, and the whole thing exploded in a single blow.

‘The speed and the way he chanted were smooth and efficient,’ Elrond thought.

“How about now, teach, can I request a new golem?” Rowan asked.

Julian sighed and had a new golem prepared, and Rowan faced it without wasting time, ready to try and obliterate the next one.

Elrond fixed his eyes on Rowan, watching the supposed genius magician.

Rowan raised his right hand in a casual motion as he began chanting, and a large circular spell formation opened in front of him while the chant went on far longer than any normal Academy spell, and from the way his lips moved and the pattern on the circle kept shifting, Elrond could tell that the structure was on the same level as the high-tier and forbidden grimoires Rowan was rumored to have already mastered.

About fifteen seconds passed.

Black lightning began to crawl around the edge of the circle. It flickered in tight, controlled arcs, pulled inward instead of spilling out. The next instant, a huge black ray shot out from the circle toward the fresh golem.
