The ray hit in a straight line and the impact was heavy enough to be felt even from the edge of the practice zone. The shock spread outward along the path of the ray, and the golem did not have time to tilt or stagger. Its body simply broke. The brick frame that the staff had just brought in was crushed and scattered at once, and only boulders and shattered pieces remained on the floor where it had been standing.

For normal Academy standards, that level of pure destructive output had already stepped into the territory that old books quietly grouped under forbidden magic. It was a kind of spell that demanded too much from anyone who was not born with the talent and mind to hold it together.

Julian watched the whole thing from afar with his hands folded, and he did not say anything. His eyes stayed on Rowan until the last fragments of the golem finished rolling to a stop.

Before the assessment even began, Elrond had already cast Clairvoyance so he could observe anyone he was interested in, and he focused it now on Rowan’s magic, yet he still could not grasp the spell at all. The chant was long even for Rowan, and Elrond could tell that if a normal magician tried to copy it, the casting time would stretch even further and most of them would lose control before they finished the chant.

'I cannot understand that magic at all. I should befriend him and ask about it,' Elrond thought. The feeling inside him was a mix of amazement and clean curiosity.

Most of the students here would only be able to nick the golem at best, even if they used everything they had, and the commoner boy they had been calling a magic genius had just obliterated a fresh one in a single attack.

No one spoke right away, and the room stayed quiet because no one could find anything to say.

### Chapter 25: 21 - Strongest Will

#### Scene 1

The remains of the golem that Rowan had destroyed still lay scattered across the practice zone. It had been an earth golem roughly as tall as an elephant, with simple steel plates strapped over its brick body, and now it was nothing but broken stone.

Even with Clairvoyance active, the black ray that had erased it had only looked to Elrond like a single mass of pure mana, pressed so tightly together that he could not see where one part of the spell ended and another began. He knew he would not understand that magic at all unless he could read the spell itself, but Rowan had cast it almost as a whisper, and from where Elrond stood he could not hear a single word.

Around him, his classmates kept their eyes on Rowan and on the broken stones, and no one even tried to make a joke. A few shoulders were still stiff, and nobody wanted to be the one who had to stand in front of the next fresh golem after that.

However, Elrond did not have time to keep watching everyone’s reactions, because Julian called the next turn, and the golem in Elrond’s group stood waiting in front of them. The earth golem assigned to his group was still relatively intact, with only nicks and dents on the steel plates and a few scraped bricks where earlier spells had hit and stopped.

Elrond stepped forward and stopped at the front of his group. In his heart, he felt like asking for a replacement golem so that he could show his magic against a clean target, but he swallowed that thought because it would only trouble the staff and drag out the test.

In reality, he already stood far above most of the students behind him in pure magic study. From the time he was small, he had studied magic from basic to expert level using the books his mother kept at home, and he had gone through them so many times that he could recall most of the spells and their structures without opening a page. He did not stop at copying them, because he kept poking at the way each spell was built until he could twist and combine them in ways that made the result look like something new.

The fire–earth bullet was the clearest example in his mind. Once he had learned how to use fire and earth at the same time, and once he understood how each of them behaved on its own, he had started to imagine small stone bullets hardened by earth magic, then heated from the inside by fire until they were ready to burst on impact. He had used that spell during the monster hunt job, and even then he had felt that it was a terrifying thing to throw at a living target.

On top of that, he could perform that kind of magic without chanting at all. As long as he had a clear image of what he wanted and enough mana control to match it, he could build the spell with imagination alone, guided by the knowledge he carried over from his previous life about how things should move and break.

To other people, that might have looked like he was manipulating the nature of the world itself through imagination and mana, but to Elrond it only felt like understanding how fire and earth wanted to behave and forcing his mana to follow that behavior.

Elrond closed his eyes for a moment.

‘I will use that magic… but to avoid suspicion, I will cast it properly now,’ he thought.

He opened his eyes again and raised his right hand straight up toward the training yard ceiling. He moved his lips and muttered random gibberish that only sounded like a proper chant from a distance, while the real spell formed through his imagination and mana control as magic circles appeared one after another around his raised hand.

Each circle drew in mana, and small stones began to appear in the air around his raised hand, each one starting at about the size of a man’s head. He narrowed his focus and squeezed them down. One by one, the stones shrank until each of them was only about as big as a palm.

Then he added a second layer of fire magic to the stones, and heat built up inside each one until the bullets glowed a deep, dull red like metal left too long in a forge, and the air near his hand wobbled from the heat.

To anyone watching, it probably just looked slow because he stayed in one place and built the spell step by step. In truth he usually put the same thing together while he was running or already in the middle of a fight, and he did it while keeping other spells and his opponent’s movement in mind at the same time. Having to split his focus that far would make most magicians lose control, but for Elrond that kind of focus had already become normal and it was exactly what made him exceptional.

The only reason he stood still today was because too many eyes were on him and not because he needed the extra time, and around him voices started to leak out.

“It’s just a small stone.” “Small stones, what can they even do?” “As expected from a commoner.” “He thinks stones like that will do something.”

Elrond did not look back. He only checked the color of the bullets and the way the heat sat inside them.

‘That should be enough,’ he decided.

He dropped his hand forward and aimed at the waiting golem.

The five bullets tore away from the circles and shot out in a straight line, so fast that the air rippled along their path and a sharp cracking sound followed behind them, and in the next blink they were already at the golem.

The armor plates on the golem’s chest and shoulders, already dented from earlier spells, shook hard when the bullets hit. Cracks ran across the metal, and then the plates broke apart as the bullets punched straight through and buried themselves deep inside the brick body. For a moment, nothing else happened.

Then the bullets went off.

Fire burst out from inside the golem’s torso and shoulders at the same time, as if something had exploded in several places at once. The brick body swelled and split from the inside, and the whole golem blew apart in a cloud of broken stone and heat. Shattered pieces rained down around the spot where it had stood, and a wave of hot air washed across the front row.

Compared to Rowan’s black ray, the range was small and the blast stopped at the edge of the shattered body, but for one practice golem it was still far more than anyone had expected from a “small stone” spell.

Some of the students who had been talking a moment ago took half a step back, and the ones who had laughed at him went quiet. Julian was not surprised at all and he had already seen enough in the entrance exam to expect this level from Elrond.

Elrond stared at the empty spot where the golem had been.

‘I messed up. I did not think it would explode that badly,’ he thought.

He had used the golem’s body as a container without thinking too far ahead, and the pressure inside had pushed the explosion harder than it would have been in open air. The logic was simple when he thought about it now, and it made him realise that his scientific approach from his previous life had already started to fade away bit by bit, but the time to correct it had already passed.

Rowan, who had been standing a little distance away, had stopped moving at some point during the blast. His eyes followed the last bits of stone as they dropped to the ground, then he shifted his gaze briefly to Elrond.

‘Who is that guy?’ Rowan thought.

His face did not change much, but for once his attention was clearly pulled away from his own spells.

On the other side, Liso leaned closer to Cestina.

“So that was Elrond’s magic…” she whispered.

Cestina answered in the same low tone, her eyes still fixed on the broken remains.

“Rowan and Elrond in the same class. That is not normal at all,” she said.

Emilia stood beside them with her hands at her sides. Her fingers curled in for a moment and pressed against her palm. She had frozen a golem and shattered it earlier, and she knew her ice had impressed people, but seeing Elrond blow one apart from the inside still pressed on the same place in her chest as before.

She kept her face steady and did not say anything.

“Whoah… amazing…” Leon muttered from his group, a grin starting to show on his face.

It was the simple way he reacted whenever he found someone worth chasing. His sword slash had carved a deep line through his own golem before, and now he had one more person in the class he wanted to test himself against.

Elrond let out a small sigh.

There was nothing he could do to take the spell back now. He turned away from the shattered stones and walked back to the rear of his group. He could feel that several people were watching him, but he kept his head slightly lowered and did not try to meet anyone’s eyes.

After that, the assessment moved on.

Not long after Elrond’s turn, Lady Rhiannon Astervale of House Astervale stepped up in. Counted among the Great in both magic and sword, she wore her auburn hair in a tight braided crown, and her uniform was neat and properly fitted. The seams of her gloves hid the fine calluses from years of sword work along her fingers. She raised her hand once and released a single spell at the golem’s neck. The stone head snapped off and hit the floor, and the body stayed standing only long enough to topple over on its side.

In a different group, Lady Nyssara Corvine of House Corvine faced her own golem. Her long black hair, pale skin, and clear teal eyes made her stand out even before she cast, and the faint perfume she always wore still clung to the air around her spot on the line. A Great Magician, she drove her magic through one side of the golem until half of its torso lost shape and broke away in heavy chunks, as if she were cutting an unwanted name out of a guest list.

On the far side, Lord Aeric Valemont of House Valemont stood in front of his target. He was tall and pale, with neat platinum blond hair, and his uniform and cloak pin were precisely arranged so that he almost looked more like a critic judging the exercise than a student taking it. Another Great Magician in their class, he cut down the upper half of his golem with a tight line of blasts and left the lower part standing like a stump in the middle of the practice ground.

When their turns were over, the remaining attacks finished without anything unusual. The staff started clearing the rubble.

“That is all for today’s magic assessment. We will return to the classroom,” Julian said.

The students gathered their things and lined up again. The groups broke apart, and they began to walk back toward the building, still talking in low voices about Rowan’s black ray, Elrond’s explosion, and the handful of names that had clearly stood out.

By the time they got back to the classroom, Elrond had already decided he would not talk to anyone if he could help it.

He walked to his seat with Leon and Eiden and sat down in his usual spot. He could feel eyes on his back. When he glanced around once, here and there he saw the same thing: classmates looking at him, then looking away again as soon as their gazes met.

Some of them had flat, doubtful faces, as if they were still deciding whether what they had seen was real or just a fluke. Others looked at him with open curiosity, as if they wanted to ask something but did not know how to start. Either way, it was attention he did not want.

Julian stood in front of the teacher’s desk for a moment.

“I need to go to the staff room. Stay in your seats,” he said.

He picked up a stack of papers and left the room. The door closed behind him, and the classroom noise jumped immediately.

Voices spread from every direction.

“Did you see that black ray earlier…” “The stones exploded from the inside…” “Rowan, Elrond, the others…”

Even without listening to the words, Elrond could tell from the energy that almost all of it was about what had happened in the training yard. Rowan’s black ray, his own explosion, and the small handful of students who had stood out. He let it wash over him and stared at the top of his desk instead.

Leon leaned forward with his arms crossed over the back of Elrond’s chair.

“You’re really amazing, Elrond. You literally obliterated that whole thing,” Leon said, his eyes bright with honest excitement.

Eiden nodded next to him.

“That’s true,” Eiden said. “I was shocked watching you. What kind of magic was that, anyway?”

Elrond scratched his cheek.

“T-Thanks…” he answered. “It was just super-heated rock magic.”

Leon’s eyebrows went up, and Eiden gave a low whistle, but before they could push for more, movement from the front aisle caught their attention.

A red-haired girl was walking toward them from the front, her steps quick and her face full of curiosity. Behind her came a blonde girl with a calm, collected expression, and next to them a blue-haired girl whose hair color and presence reminded Elrond of Gilbert.

He understood immediately. He already knew who they were.

They were the three girls he had dragged clear on that road, when assassins broke through the Alfrost escort and the carriage line started to collapse, Liso almost erased by a stray blast, Cestina’s magic turning wild, and Emilia forced to hold the front while the guards fell around them.

“Excuse me…” the red-haired girl said when she reached their row.

The three boys turned toward her.

“My name is Lisoletelle Ashfeldt. You must be Elrond, right?” she asked.

“Y-Yes… I am,” Elrond replied.

“Wahh… I’ve been looking for you this whole time…!” Liso said, suddenly brightening.

She grabbed his hand in both of hers and shook it with all her strength. Her grip was firm enough that he felt his arm move with it.

“Oy, Liso. You’re being way too pushy,” Leon said from behind her.

“Hmph. Shut up, musclehead. I’m not talking to you,” Liso shot back without even turning around.

The way they spoke made it clear they knew each other well already. After that one exchange, she finally let go of Elrond’s hand.

“So… what is it?” Elrond asked.

He kept his tone light, like simple small talk, even though he already knew the real reason they had come.

“Please forgive my loud friend, Sir Astrea. My name is Cestina Ludwell,” the blonde girl said, stepping forward a little. Her voice smoothed the mood Liso had stirred up as she gave a small, proper bow.

“And this is Emilia Alfrost,” Cestina added, gesturing toward the blue-haired girl.

Emilia bowed as well, just a slight movement of her upper body, but she did not speak yet.

“The reason we are here is because we would like to express our gratitude for saving us the other day,” Cestina said, making their purpose clear.

She took a slow breath and met his eyes more directly.

“Especially from me, Sir Astrea,” she continued, her tone turning more serious. “I nearly hurt you, and I nearly hurt my friends here. If you had not been there, we truly do not know what would have happened.”

“That’s true,” Liso said, cutting in. Her voice was still lively, but this time it carried more restraint. “I almost got obliterated, and you suddenly appeared and protected me. Thank you so much for saving me, Sir Astrea.”

Emilia lifted her head a little.

“Yes,” she said, quiet but firm. “They are telling the truth. If you did not intervene, I might have hurt Cestina as well. From the bottom of my heart, I am grateful you saved us.”

As she said it, the scene from the training ground came back to her. She had frozen her own golem from the outside until it shattered, while Elrond had blown his apart from the inside in a single strike, and the gap between them pressed on her mind.

As she thanked him, Emilia held onto the one simple fact that mattered to her. Because he had stepped in, Cestina and Liso were still standing here with her.

All three of them bowed together.

Around them, some of the nearby students stopped pretending not to look and stared openly. Others bent over their desks and whispered to each other while their eyes kept sliding back to the noble girls and Elrond.

“A-ah… I appreciate your gratitude,” Elrond said quickly.

He raised both hands a little.

“But please raise your heads,” he added. “It was just luck that I happened to be there. I only acted on instinct when I saw someone in danger. It’s not something you need to treat as a huge debt.”

He hesitated for a moment, then continued.

“And I already met someone from your household,” he said. “Gilbert Alfrost. He invited me to come tomorrow.”

“I see,” Emilia replied.

She straightened and met his eyes properly for the first time.

“He is my older brother. If that is the case, then we will await your visit at our mansion, Sir Astrea,” she said.

Cestina looked at Elrond with a careful seriousness that did not feel heavy, but did feel precise.

“I know simply saying thank you is not enough, Sir Astrea, especially from me,” she said. “Is there anything you would like to ask of us? Of course, within our limits.”

“No, no…” Elrond answered, shaking his head. “I’m grateful for the thought, but you don’t need to go that far.”

“But…” Liso began, a worried look on her face as if she hated leaving things uneven.

“It’s fine,” Elrond said, cutting her worry off before it grew. “Knowing you’re all okay is enough for me. And I already have the invitation from House Alfrost, so I don’t think you need to add anything on top of that.”

Emilia and Liso, and after the three of them traded a brief look as if to confirm they agreed, she let the matter drop without pressing him further.

“I understand,” Cestina said after a short pause, giving a small nod as she let the matter drop without pressing him further.

“In that case, we will simply remember this,” she said. “If you ever need anything, please do not hesitate to reach out to us, Sir Astrea.”

“Then please excuse us,” Cestina added.

With another slight bow, the three of them turned and walked back toward their desks. The soft sound of whispers followed them as they went.

He let out a quiet breath of relief, because it was finally settled and that was enough for him, since the last thing he wanted was to be dragged any deeper into noble houses through favors.

He understood very well how nobles handled pride and debt, because they hated owing anyone, so if they felt like they owed a debt they would try to pay it back, and if that still was not enough they would look for a way to tilt the balance to their side instead, and once favors started to pile up the strings came next in the form of invitations, requests, and expectations.

Accepting Gilbert’s invitation was one thing, because that was already a line he had agreed to cross, but taking anything more on top of that, especially directly from the girls, would only drag him further into their world, so for now a simple thank you was more than enough.

Leon and Eiden stayed quiet until the three girls had fully returned to their seats, and Eiden only leaned in a little once the whispers around the room started to mix with other topics, as if he had been holding back the whole time.

“Sorry, Elrond. I was just… observing,” Eiden said. His brow was still tight. “But what was that exactly? Why would those high nobles bow towards you?”

Elrond rubbed the back of his neck.

“T-That was…” he started, then stopped.

“I just happened to help them killing some rats,” he said. “That’s all.”

Eiden stared at him.

“Rats,” he repeated.

Leon clicked his tongue.

“Stop with your humble, Elrond,” Leon said, pushing his chair a bit closer. “You must have done something to them. They literally said ‘life and death’ right there. That’s not ‘killing some rats’.”

Elrond let out a small breath and looked at the two of them.

They had seen him fight. They had stood in the same class line and taken the same test. If he was going to trust anyone in this room with that story, it would be them.

“…Fine,” he said. “I’ll tell you. But just you two.”

He spoke in a low voice.

As he talked, Eiden’s expression shifted step by step, from simple curiosity to tight shock. Leon’s grin faded for once, replaced by a steady, serious look as he followed each piece. By the time Elrond finished, neither of them looked like they could treat it as just another school story.

Eiden let out the breath he had been holding.

“T-That was… quite a story, isn’t it,” he said.

Elrond glanced to the side again, checking that nobody was sitting close enough to catch details.

“B-but please don’t tell anybody about it, ok?” he said. “I already trust you guys. I don’t want this spreading.”

Eiden straightened.

“Of course,” he said at once. “I’m not going to talk about that to anyone.”

Leon snorted.

“I already knew you were amazing from the first time I saw you, Elrond,” Leon said. “Hearing this doesn’t really shock me.”

He leaned back with a grin that now looked half like he was proud of Elrond and half like he was proud of himself.

“If anything, it just proves my eye is perfect,” Leon went on. “You should be proud that I reached you in the first place.”

Elrond had no idea how he was supposed to be proud of that, so he let the comment pass.

Leon tapped a finger on the desk.

“But you mentioned one of those swordsmen used berserk, right?” he asked. “The one you fought near the end.”

“Yes,” Elrond said. “His mana pattern felt similar to yours.”

“Similar?” Eiden asked, looking between the two of them, and Elrond gave a short nod as he remembered how both auras had pulled raw mana into the body in the same way, only Leon’s had held its shape while the other one shook itself apart.

“When he went into berserk, I could feel how much raw mana he was forcing through his body,” Elrond said. “It was the same kind of thing I sense from you when you get serious, but his was shaking all over the place. Yours is… stable.”

Leon’s mouth pulled up at one corner, clearly pleased that Elrond had noticed the connection.

“Hmph. Of course,” he said. “I’m Sieghart, you know. That’s our speciality,” and he folded his arms with the easy confidence of someone who had been told since childhood that his body was built to hold that kind of power.

“But to make it clear,” Leon added, “I can confirm that guy couldn’t be a Sieghart. Probably some random Highlander, or someone from our Brandh family. To prove you’re Sieghart, you have to train hard to control the berserk.”

Elrond listened while Leon spoke, and his own thoughts lined up the pieces.

For most people, the mana they used in spells was mana their bodies had already made safe. A person could only hold a certain amount inside at once. They filled that amount slowly, by absorbing mana from nature over time or by taking it in when someone else pushed it into them.

The mana outside, in the air and the ground, was different. That was raw mana, the mana of nature itself.

Raw mana did not sit in neat shapes and it was still in chaos, so it did not flow into a person’s body just because they wished for it and instead had to be absorbed naturally, and because Elrond’s body and mana control were already trained far beyond a normal student’s, he could absorb much more of that raw mana at once and convert it into normal usable mana inside his body.

There were exceptions.

Some magicians could work with raw mana before it settled inside them by gathering it from the air and turning it straight into a spell outside their bodies. It demanded very high focus, because they had to sense and control mana in the air instead of inside themselves, and the more raw mana they tried to handle at once like that, the easier it was for their control to slip and for the spell to fall apart.

The other exception was the Highlander tribe, because an abnormal trait in their bodies let them manipulate raw mana much more directly and even wrap it around their muscles and bones to harden their bodies, boost their strength and speed, or change its shape as a weapon.

That was where berserk came from, because when a Highlander forced too much raw mana into their body at once, they started to lose control and attacked on instinct until the excess raw mana ran out and their movements returned to normal.

If a normal person tried the same thing, their body would probably tear itself apart before they ever reached that state, while Highlanders who had grown up training in thin air and harsh cold until their natural strength rivalled a human using triple Strength Enhancement could survive being filled with that much raw mana, and that was the difference.

Elrond had in mind when he looked at Leon and remembered how Leon’s slash had carved a deep line through the practice golem with one swing, the feeling of berserk there but held tight inside his movements instead of spilling everywhere.

From what Elrond knew, the Sieghart household had spent generations training the Highlanders’ berserk state until they could enter it and leave it on purpose without losing control, and that was exactly why people called them dangerous even among Highlander-blooded warriors.

On top of that, Sieghart bloodlines had already spread across Althania and Radras as proxies for the Highlander tribe, so whenever someone needed Highlander-type berserk power but could not move a full Highlander clan, they turned to a Sieghart branch instead.

Further to the north, beyond the main settled lands, the Highlander tribe’s own territory lay in the highlands near the elven regions, still inside the borders of Althania and Radras but rough and hard to reach.

“So that guy was forcing raw mana through his body like you do,” he said, “but without the control.”

“That’s right,” Leon said. “If you force raw mana without training, the berserk just runs wild. That’s why I said he couldn’t be Sieghart. We have to learn to hold it down from the time we can walk.”

Eiden’s eyes flicked to Leon’s arms for a moment, as if picturing the kind of strength it took to handle that much raw mana, then he looked back at Elrond.

“So you fought someone like that and still came out alive,” Eiden said quietly. “No wonder they bowed.”

“It wasn’t just me,” he said. “The guards held as long as they could, and those girls fought to the end as well. I only did what I could in the middle.”

Even without listening, Elrond could tell that most of the energy in the room kept drifting back to the training yard and to his own name, so he let it pass and watched the surface of his desk instead.

Liso’s loud “musclehead” from earlier resurfaced in his mind, along with the grip of her hand on his and the way she had brushed Leon aside without hesitation. That was not how strangers spoke to each other after a first meeting in class.

‘Then what are those two to each other?’ he thought.

“It made me curious, Leon,” Elrond said, keeping his voice low so it would not carry. “You and Lisoletelle Ashfeldt seemed pretty close back there.”

Leon thought back to how easily Liso had stepped into their space and treated him as someone she already knew well, and he decided there was no point acting like they had only just met at the academy.

“Ah, that,” Leon said. “I actually grew up here in Althania. Back when I was a kid, my parents got along well with House Ashfeldt, so whenever I ended up at the Alfrost place or the Ashfeldt place, Liso was usually the one they pushed at me to play with.”

“So you have known each other since you were children?p” Elrond said.

“Yeah, sort of, In those days she clung to my arm whenever we were in the same room, and now she acts like she is embarrassed to even stand near me, like you saw earlier,” Leon said.

“Well, that sounds normal,” Elrond said. “Both of you grew up.”

The classroom door opened, and Julian came back in from the corridor with a stack of papers in his hands.

“Sorry. I got called out for a bit,” Julian said. “Anyway, I have already collected all of your assessment results. That is enough for today, so I will end homeroom here. After this, you are free to do as you like. Class dismissed.”

He set the papers down on the desk at the front and stepped out again, and as the door closed behind him chairs scraped and voices rose at once, making it clear that homeroom was truly over.

#### Scene 2

The night over Althania’s business district sat heavy and dull, even though the streets below were still bright. From the tall window, the man could see food stalls lined along the stone road and the smoke from their grills curling up into the air, and he could see performers drawing small crowds in the corners where the lamps shone the strongest.

He stood there in a neat royal suit, hands loosely folded behind his back as he watched the town’s busyness from above. The cut of the cloth and the fine crest on his cuff were the kind that only appeared inside the Royal Palace, never in a common merchant’s house.

“Not only did you fail, you dare to face me directly, Veyra?” he said without turning from the glass.

His gaze stayed on the view, but his voice carried the kind of steady irritation that did not need to be raised.

“Start explaining before I lose patience. My entire plan almost crumbled because of your failure,” he added.

“Ooooo… scary,” Veyra answered from behind him.

She sounded amused instead of nervous, and the curl at the edge of her lips did not show any respect for his position. That had always been her habit when she spoke to someone above her.

“Not only did you give me an almost impossible task, you gave me no time to prepare,” she went on. “And there was a hindrance during that attempt. I even lost one of my pawns because of it.”

The man exhaled once through his nose and finally shifted his eyes away from the street lights so he could look at her reflection in the window.

“You got what you needed,” he said. “I prepared a platinum rank party of adventurers. That should have been enough to capture a kid like them. You completely disappoint me.”

His face stayed calm, but the air in the room tightened as if his mood had pushed against it.

Without lowering his hand from behind his back, the man let mana rise around him. A dark pressure spread through the room like smoke from an unseen brazier, and the five men standing around Veyra stiffened at the same time.

“Vow Authority,” he said, and the spell caught.

The force of it pressed down on the ones bound by vow magic. The five men dropped to one knee in almost perfect unison, shoulders bent and heads lowered, their bodies answering the authority they had already accepted when they swore.

Veyra felt the weight of it as well, because she had given her vow to him long ago, but she did not let her knees bend.

“Oy, oy… emitting such an aura. Jeez,” Veyra said, clicking her tongue. “Sometimes you really can’t see how your underlings struggle. I did my best, you know. Controlling them over such a wide range is very tricky.”

She lifted one shoulder and let it fall again as she spoke, then let her hand drop back to her side.

“Like I explained earlier, I only had about half the preparation I normally would,” she said. “If I could have set up a barrier in advance, the result would have been different. I promise.”

“That is what you always say,” he replied.

He turned enough that the light from the window traced the frame of his glasses and the line of his jaw.

“But I understand your point,” he said. “If this was not the first time you had messed up, I would have already put a hole in your head and controlled you myself.”

“Not to mention I failed to cast my long-distance puppetcraft on those girls. I only managed to catch one of them,” Veyra said, making it clear why her control had slipped.

“They have very strong will and mana control, so indirect casting does not work on them. If I want a proper puppet, I need them in my hands,” she added.

Veyra’s Flesh Puppetcraft was not ordinary mind control. When it worked, it wrapped around a target’s will and locked it in place, as if their imagined body were chained inside their own mind so they could not move themselves at all. After that, their body moved according to her decisions while their subconscious reactions still coloured each strike. It worked on both the living and the dead, but living bodies fought her longer and dead ones moved more stiffly.

She had two ways to plant that control with her mana. The first was direct, which meant closing in and forcing her mana into the target in one heavy push. The second relied on clashes, as she drove one of her existing puppets against a new target again and again so that each impact pushed more of her mana across and built the imprint step by step. The direct way was fast but dangerous. The clash method was slower, safer, and more theatrical.

Even then, full control did not always come at once. If the target was alive, she might seize only an arm, their breathing, or their tongue at first and build toward full control as more of her mana settled in. Dead bodies yielded more quickly, but they did not adapt as well.He knew very well that Veyra did not only twist people through Flesh Puppetcraft. She was also the one he turned to when he needed barriers that could cut a space off from the outside world.

“You said there was a hindrance,” the man asked. “What is that hindrance?”

“It is not really that big of a deal,” Veyra answered. “If I had been allowed to kill those girls, it would have ended in an instant. But you asked me to capture them instead, so it was hard to go all out.”

She gave a short, annoyed breath and began to trace the events in order, because they both already knew which day she was talking about.

They were speaking about the attack on Emilia Alfrost’s carriage line on the road, which most people would report as an assassination attempt even though the true goal had been closer to a kidnapping. The ones in this room were the real culprits behind it. Mirelle Veyra, a high rank magician and master of Flesh Puppetcraft, known to some as the Marionettist of Flesh, and the man beside the window whose threads reached into the Royal Palace.

Their plan had been simple and poisonous. They would take Emilia alive and twist her into a puppet, then let her carry their will into House Alfrost from within. Once a noble family’s heir moved under another’s hand, every decision, every signature, and every command that came through her would turn into a blade pointed back at her own house. In time, the weight of those cuts would be enough to break them.

“Then why did you not kill him if he is not a big deal?” the man pressed.

“In that fight? How?” Veyra said.

Her displeasure showed plainly now.

“If I let my craft loose, it might not only kill that hindrance,” she said. “It might kill everyone at the scene.”

She shifted her weight and glared past him at the town outside.

“Hells, why did we do the kidnap attempt at that place and time anyway?” she went on. “You must have had a reason, did you not? That place was very risky. And it failed because of that.”

“Because based on my intel, that was the only moment when she had the least guard,” the man answered. “It should have been much easier to clean up or fake the scene.”

Veyra watched him in silence for a breath, as if she expected something more.

“Just that?” she said at last, letting out a small exhale.

“If that is the case,” she continued, “like I told you, as long as I have the chance to cast a barrier to isolate her, I can do it anywhere, anytime.”

For a moment the man said nothing. He touched his chin and let his eyes move away from her to the night beyond the glass, then he turned back again.

“I see,” he said. “If that is the case, I will give you one more chance to clean up your mess.”

The way he said it left no space for her to treat it as anything except an order.

“Understood. I will live up to your expectation,” Veyra replied.

Then she tipped her head slightly to the side and looked past him.

“But before that,” she said, “may I borrow that sweet lady over there?”

She pointed at the maid who had been standing near the wall the whole time. The young woman wore a simple, proper uniform, and her eyes had been closed as if she were only waiting for orders. At Veyra’s words, the maid opened them.

“Hoo. You have good eyes, do you not?” the man said, without surprise. “She is a high spirit. I have her inhabiting that maid.”

A high spirit was a higher form of spirit that had evolved from the lesser spirits that floated unseen through the world. Lesser spirits were said to be formed from pure mana, with no physical body of their own, and they drifted and fed on mana in the air until, after decades or even centuries, they became something more. When a spirit reached that higher state, it gained the strength to inhabit a physical body and to move and speak through whatever it had entered. A host that carried a high spirit inside them held far more mana than they would have on their own.

“Of course I noticed,” Veyra said. “A human maid should not have that much mana.”

She had been looking at the maid with clairvoyance since the beginning of their talk.

“Nana,” the man said, “go and help her. If you lose that body, inhabit any other dead body and come back.”

“Understood, master,” Nana replied with the maid’s mouth.

High spirits could not be killed simply by breaking the body they used. As long as the spiritual body remained, they could continue to exist and take hold of another vessel, whether it was living or dead.

“Then I will come back with good news,” Veyra said.

She turned and walked toward the door with the easy confidence of someone who believed that what she had claimed was not an empty boast.

The man did not answer her. He only watched the door close, then shifted his gaze back down to the lights of the town below as the night and his unfinished plan pressed in around the window.

#### Scene 3

The next day at the Academy moved at a slower pace than the one before.

The morning schedule started with general monster knowledge, followed by arithmetic. For Elrond, both subjects felt more like review than lessons. The teacher talked through classifications, common habits, and risk levels, and most of it matched what he had already seen on the written exam. The arithmetic period was the same, because the problems stopped at simple trade and tax examples he could solve without thinking very hard.

Because it was still only an introduction to the term, both teachers spent more time explaining how far the subjects would go and what kind of competence they expected than drilling anyone in detail. Students were asked to talk about what they were good at or where they had trouble, and Elrond listened while other people answered.

Between periods, Leon and Eiden settled near him as if that had already become normal. They traded short comments with him about the classes and about the way some students tried to show off even when the content was basic.

The atmosphere around Elrond had changed a little as well. The girls in sometimes greeted him when they walked past his seat. Liso was the most obvious, because every time their eyes met she lifted a hand in a broad, open wave and smiled as if there were nothing strange about greeting him that way at all.

Elrond answered with a simple nod in return and kept his expression steady.

Even with the lighter lessons, he knew this day would not end early.

The final shared period of the day is over.

“That’s all for today,” the teacher said as he closed the book in his hands. “Don’t forget to prepare what I asked you for next week.”

The bell that marked the end of the period had not rung yet, but the line was enough.

For S–Class, the last slot on the third day of the week varied from person to person. It was a block set aside for personal lessons based on the gaps the instructors had seen in each student, so the exact content was different for everyone.

In Elrond’s case, that slot had already been filled from the moment Julian decided to take him as a disciple.

He packed his notebook and pen into his bag and stood up with the others, then stepped out of the classroom and followed the corridor toward the teachers’ rooms. Leon and Eiden had their own plans for

the period and did not try to stop him, and the small clusters of other students heading out peeled away toward different directions.

Julian’s room was where Elrond remembered it from before. The door was closed. He stopped in front of it and knocked twice.

“Come in,” Julian’s voice answered from inside.

Elrond opened the door.

“Excuse me,” he said as he stepped into the room.

Julian sat behind his desk with several papers laid out in front of him. He set the top sheet aside and looked up.

“Come in, and take a seat,” Julian replied.

Elrond crossed the room and sat down on the couch set opposite the desk. The quiet in the room settled between them for a moment, and he became aware that he still had no clear picture of how this “disciple” lesson was supposed to start.

“Uhm… I actually don’t know what I’m supposed to do, so I came without bringing anything,” Elrond said.

“You don’t need to worry,” Julian answered. “I wasn’t expecting you to bring anything either.”

He pushed his chair back and stood up, then walked out from behind the desk and stopped near its corner.

“But for today, follow me to the private training room,” Julian said.

He turned toward the door as he spoke. Elrond rose from the couch and followed.

“Private?” Elrond asked once they were back in the corridor.

“Yes,” Julian said. “It’s a training room set aside for situations like what we’re going to do now. Students can only use it under a teacher’s permission.”

They moved through the corridors toward the part of the section that housed the physical and magical training areas.

Before they reached the main entrance to those places, Julian turned into a narrower side corridor that most students had no reason to enter. At the end of it, a single heavy door waited with no signboard hanging above it.

Julian took out a key and unlocked it.

Inside, the private room held all the tools Elrond expected from a training space and more. Targets stood lined against one wall. Training dummies waited in different positions. Racks of wooden swords, spears, and other weapons stood beside hooks that held real steel, and there was enough empty floor for several bouts to happen at once.

“Take a wooden sword. We’re starting immediately,” Julian said, his tone left no room to argue.

And with that, Julian’s training began.

### Chapter 26: 22 - Responsibility

#### Scene 1

“Take a wooden sword. We’re starting immediately,” Julian said.

Those were Julian’s words to Elrond in the private training room after he had finished the day’s lecture schedule, telling him to get ready for a sword bout.

It felt fast to Elrond. Julian had not explained what kind of lesson this was supposed to be or how it would run, but even so, Elrond moved to the rack and chose a wooden sword that matched his hand. The weight sat familiar in his grip.

Julian also took a wooden sword and walked to stand opposite him on the open floor.

He set the tip of his sword against the ground, rested his hand lightly on the hilt as if he might draw it up at any moment, and then drove the blade straight down. The wood struck the floor with enough force to make a short, hard sound as it bit into the surface between them.

Elrond flinched at the sudden impact.

“Since you are my disciple now, my goal is simple,” Julian said. “You are going to surpass me. In sword technique, or even in strength.”

Julian Roosevelt’s strength sat in a range normal humans were never supposed to reach. He had trained his body up to the height people usually only saw from Highlanders, the kind of raw power that matched a human under triple Strength Enhancement even before any spell, and if he did add magic on top of that, the gap between him and ordinary swordsmen only grew wider.

On top of that, he was a Roosevelt swordsman and magician both, raised in a house that treated magic and the blade as equal obligations, so his technique and control already sat far above ordinary knights. His Divine Blessing of Space Manipulation was a separate advantage on top of that, and using spatial magic came naturally to him, so when he stacked that blessing over a body trained to Highlander levels and that kind of sword skill, his overall strength moved to a place most people could not even approach, and that was the strength he meant when he told Elrond to surpass him.

“Back in your physical entrance, I noticed how quickly you adapted to every movement I threw at you,” he said. “That’s what caught my interest. It felt similar to Bram Veller, but the way you do it is more complex.”

He watched Elrond as he spoke, as if he were confirming that the person in front of him matched what he remembered.

“Bram copies what he sees and refines it by fighting,” Julian said. “You do that and, on top of it, you understand the stance itself. You’re not just copying shapes.”

Hearing that, Elrond froze for a moment.

To him, Julian Roosevelt was a genius whose skill and record were already far above what most people could reach. Being told to surpass someone like that did not feel like empty praise. It felt more like a simple statement of expectation.

There was nothing he could even complain about in that logic, so he swallowed any easy answer that came to mind.

Elrond shifted his grip on the wooden sword and set his feet where they were always most stable. Across from him, Julian raised his own sword with the same casual readiness Elrond had seen in the entrance exam, as if he could start or stop at any moment without wasting a breath.

They faced each other in a short silence. Neither of them moved or spoke. Elrond watched Julian’s shoulders, the angle of his hips, the weight on his front foot, and he could not see a single opening.

He moved first.

Elrond pushed off the floor and closed the distance in one clean step, his sword cutting in from the side. Julian slid away with a small shift of his body, just enough to let the strike pass him, and their blades met on the next motion, wood clacking hard in the air.

They traded blows in short exchanges. Elrond swung and adjusted, but every time Julian either caught his blade with perfect timing or slipped out of reach with an easy dodge. After a few clashes, Elrond could feel how wide the gap in their strength and control really was.

He did not feel a trace of mana from Julian.

If Julian was not using magic, then there was no reason for Elrond to keep holding back. He pulled his own mana together, casting Strength Enhancement and Agility Enhancement on himself so the magic wrapped around his muscles and joints.

Strength swelled through his body as he wrapped himself in a triple Strength Enhancement, and at the same time he sharpened his movements with three times his usual agility. Heat spread through his limbs, and the wooden sword no longer felt heavy in his hand.

He stepped in again.

This time, when their blades met, the clash jolted Elrond’s arms, but it didn’t knock him back. He pushed forward instead. For the first time, Julian’s sword didn’t blow through his guard, and they traded a short series of blows in the middle, wood striking wood in a blur.

Julian’s eyes narrowed. “So you decided to use that,” he said.

He shifted his stance, and the casual looseness vanished. When he stepped in again, his sword moved faster, and Elrond only just managed to catch the first strike on his guard.

As the tempo rose, Elrond tried to remember every motion from the physical entrance exam, especially the way Julian turned his wrist at the last moment and the way he stepped across the opponent’s line instead of retreating straight back. He used those memories to guess where the next blade would come from.

It was not enough.

Julian’s wooden sword moved in arcs that looked almost playful. Sometimes he leaned his weight into the cut from one side, and other times he pulled it back at the last instant and sent it in from a sharper angle instead, so whenever Elrond thought he had caught the pattern, the next strike came from a place he didn’t expect.

He judged the next attack would be a frontal slash. Julian’s shoulders faced him directly, and the sword’s angle pointed straight down the center line.

Then Julian vanished from his sight.

The floor did not shake and there was no burst of wind. From Elrond’s point of view, the space just behind Julian’s shoulder twisted for a heartbeat, and in the next blink Julian stood at his back, the wooden point hovering just short of his spine.

Elrond froze.

Julian stopped there and lowered his sword. “Again,” he said.

They reset their distance and took their stances once more.

They clashed again and again. In each bout, Elrond ended up on the losing side, either from a clean strike to his guard or from a sudden angle he could not follow. He did not complain, and the wooden blades rang against each other in steady rhythm, filling the training room more than their voices.

By the fifth bout, something in the feeling of the fight started to change.

Elrond focused on the way Julian stepped in and how his shoulders turned instead of trying to memorize every single swing. He noticed that when Julian carried his momentum through a slash the next attack always came from the same side, but when Julian was feinting his weight shifted a little earlier to the opposite foot.

‘At first, I thought I could sense that Julian’s attacks always relied on momentum. But sometimes he feints, or attacks from an unpredictable direction… I think I can follow this,’ Elrond thought, heat building in his chest.

The fight lasted longer this time, and Elrond’s wooden sword caught more of Julian’s strikes cleanly. Even when he missed, he could tell where his reading had gone wrong. Julian watched him, and a small smile appeared on his face as he saw Elrond improve.

Then Julian used one of his movements, his spatial blessing.

That blessing allowed him not only to slash through space but also to manipulate his own body. He could move in a way that looked like blinking, and the shift was limited to a short distance, probably around five meters at most, but even that was enough to distract an opponent.

Julian thrust his sword straight toward Elrond’s chest. In the middle of the attack, he blinked and his body jumped within that short range, so the motion of the thrust broke and his sword came out as a slash instead. The straight thrust turned into a horizontal slash from Elrond’s flank. That was the use of his blessing.

The fact that Julian had to push himself to use this in a bout was actually a fantastic sign for Elrond, but with that movement he once again took a defeat. Elrond tried to follow Julian’s movement, but he was still a moment late, and the wooden edge stopped just before his ribs.

“Wait a second, teach. What was that kind of movement?” Elrond asked, turning toward him with his brows drawn, more curious than angry.

Julian rested the wooden blade against his shoulder. “I had to use my blessing,” he said, his face still steady. “Fighting you is actually exhausting me. So instead of going all out, I decided to cheat a little.”

‘Cheating? That’s unbecoming of a teacher,’ Elrond thought.

“But that’s not fair… I tried my best, you know,” he said, stepping closer and confronting him with a small frown that did not quite hide his interest.

“Sorry, sorry. I won’t do it again next time,” Julian answered. A hint of amusement reached his eyes. “That was only because we already had five bouts, and I’m quite satisfied with your feat, Elrond. You’ll surpass me in no time. I’m certain.”

“And time is almost up too,” Julian added. “You need to go to the Alfrost mansion, right?”

“Well, that’s true,” Elrond said. He paused for a moment. “If that’s the case, then I have no other complaints, but…”

He lifted his head, and a thin smile touched his lips.

“…I’m curious about that technique. If you want me to surpass you, then I’m definitely going to surpass that too,” he said, his voice full of confidence.

“That’s the spirit. I’ll look forward to it,” Julian replied.

“Then, let’s pack ourselves,” Julian said as he stepped away and began to tidy the training area, returning the scattered practice marks on the floor to order.

Elrond bowed slightly. “Thank you for today, teach.”

They walked out together and parted in front of the training room door. When Julian turned back toward the faculty corridor, Elrond shifted the wooden sword in his hand and looked ahead.

He would be visiting the Alfrost mansion for the first time.

Elrond still had plenty of time, so he went back to the dorm to change out of his sweaty uniform after the drill with Julian.

His room in the dorm was quiet when he entered. Afternoon light slipped in through the window and fell across the small closet by the wall. Elrond opened it and stared at the contents for a while.

Inside were only a few outfits. The frontier clothes he had brought from home were folded on one side, the fabric sturdy but rough. Next to them, two sets of the Academy uniform hung from the rail. Compared to the clothes he used to wear in the south, the uniforms looked clean and sharp.

“Haah… there’s nothing else I can wear,” he muttered, looking between the frontier clothes and the uniforms.

The kind of place Gilbert had invited him to was what he thought of as a Noble Mansion. He could not imagine walking into a noble estate in the same worn clothes he had used to travel across the country. Even if the Academy uniform was only schoolwear, it was at least something people here recognized.

His freshly washed uniform had already been delivered back, folded neatly on the small table. He picked it up, checked that there were no stains, and began to change.

He took off the damp uniform and set it aside, then put on the clean one piece by piece. Shirt, tie, jacket, belt, and boots. When he finished, he brushed a hand over his sleeves to smooth out any small wrinkles and checked that the collar sat straight.

“This is still better than the others,” he said quietly to himself.

He closed the closet door and glanced once more around the room. The plain furniture and the small number of personal belongings only reminded him that he had just started his life here. If he was going to step into noble mansions from now on, this much was not going to be enough.

“I might need to buy better clothes. I’ll ask Leon later,” he decided.

With that thought saved for another day, he left the dorm and headed toward the Academy gates.

The air outside felt cooler than inside the training room. He walked across the courtyard at a relaxed pace, his shoulders loose after the bout.

He passed through the Academy entrance and stopped just beyond the gate. Ahead of him, the road stretched toward the royal district. He remembered what Gilbert had said before, that the Alfrost mansion was still within the royal district, near the central roundabouts, so he could walk there without any trouble.

“Central roundabouts… that means it’s that way,” he said to himself, looking to the right of the Academy entrance.

He turned in that direction and began to walk.

The path was straightforward. The further he moved away from the Academy, the more the scenery changed. School buildings and student dorms fell behind him, and the streets widened little by little.

Soon, rows of large mansions appeared on both sides of the road. High stone walls ran along the street, with tall gates set into them every so often. Some mansions showed a glimpse of small parks inside their walls, with trimmed trees and open lawns. Others had long driveways that led from the gate to a main building deeper inside the property.

At every gate, a flag or banner hung in clear view. Each one carried a different crest, telling anyone who passed which household lived within. Elrond let his eyes move from one crest to another as he walked, quietly memorizing the shapes and colors even though he did not know most of the family names.

Guards stood at many of the gates. Some stood straight and silent as they watched the street. Others spoke in low voices with their partners when no one else was nearby, but when people approached they straightened at once. The constant presence of those flags and guards made it clear that this part of the city belonged to nobles.

After walking for about fifteen minutes, Elrond reached the central roundabout Gilbert had mentioned.

A wide fountain stood in the middle, water rising and falling again and again. Around it, the road curved in a circle, and several streets joined it from different directions. Shops and restaurants lined the outer edge. Signs hung over their doors, and some had tables near the walls for people who wanted to sit.

The roundabout was not crowded enough to feel noisy, but it was far from empty. Pedestrians crossed the streets in small groups, and carriages moved along the circle without rushing. The sound of hooves, wheels, and flowing water mixed together into a constant background noise.

This area felt like a small market sub-district inside the royal district. People went about their daily business, talking as they walked or carrying wrapped packages from the shops.

He waited for a gap in the carriages, crossed the roundabout, and took the road on the other side.

Once the fountain and the shops were behind him, the scenery changed again.

The signs and storefronts disappeared, replaced once more by stone walls and quiet gates. Banners with house crests hung above many of them, moving only slightly in the breeze. Compared to the roundabout, this street felt calmer. Fewer carriages passed, and the people he saw here walked more slowly and carefully.

Elrond kept walking at the same calm pace. This was not the noisy part of the city or the frontier he had grown up in. Every gate here belonged to someone who stood closer to the crown.

As he walked, he checked each crest he passed, searching for the one he already knew.

He remembered the Alfrost carriage that had come to the Academy, the emblem on its door, and Gilbert standing nearby. The pattern of that crest was sharp in his mind, so he only needed to match it.

After he passed a couple more mansions, he finally saw it.

Above one of the gates, a banner hung with the Alfrost crest displayed plainly on the fabric. The wall behind it was high and well kept, and beyond the bars he could see part of a stone path and carefully arranged trees. The mansion itself stood further back, its lines neat and restrained instead of overly decorated.

Its position made sense to him. Being this close to the central roundabouts and in this part of the royal district fit what he understood about a house that worked closely with the crown.

Two guards stood outside the gate, one on each side of the entrance. Their uniforms matched the house colors, and their posture was steady as they watched the street. They looked serious, not hostile.

Elrond took a breath, checked once more that his uniform sat properly, and then walked forward toward the gate.

He approached the two guards in front of the Alfrost mansion.

“Excuse me. My name is Elrond von Astrea. I’ve been invited by Sir Gilbert Alfrost to discuss something. Does he live here?” Elrond asked.

He spoke politely and gave all the details at once. He did not want a slow back-and-forth where the guards kept stopping him to ask for his name or where he came from.

“Um… that outfit… are you from the Royal Academy?” one of the guards asked.

The guard studied Elrond for a moment, taking in the uniform. Then he leaned closer to his partner and whispered something the rest of the way.

“What was your name again… Elrond?” he asked, turning back.

“Yes. I’m Elrond, and I’m from the Royal Academy as well,” Elrond answered.

“Please wait a second…” the guard said.

He stepped through a smaller door beside the main gate and disappeared inside the wall. Elrond waited where he was and watched the street in front of the mansion, listening to the faint sounds from inside the grounds.

Before long, the small door opened again. The same guard returned, and this time another man in armor came with him. The second man moved with a calmer, heavier step that made it clear he was used to being in charge.

“This way, Sir Astrea,” the second guard said. “Sir Gilbert is already expecting you.”

Elrond gave a short nod. “Thank you.”

The second guard, Dolvar, turned and walked into the estate, and Elrond followed at his side.

From outside the walls, the mansion had only looked large and distant, but once he stepped past the gate, its full size came into view. A long path stretched straight ahead toward the main entrance. It was wide enough for a carriage to pass without trouble.

On both sides of the path, the grounds looked like a well-kept park. Trees grew in even lines, and patches of greenery were trimmed with care. A few benches sat under the shade, placed where people could rest and still see the front of the house.

Near the main entrance, the path broadened into a wide open area. The stone there was laid out in a way that made it easy to imagine several carriages stopping or waiting at once.

‘For multiple carriages to hold, perhaps,’ Elrond thought as he took in the shape of the space.

When he stood in front of the entrance, he could see the mansion itself up close. The walls were a clean white, and the lines of the building were simple but elegant. There were decorations, but nothing felt wasted or overly showy.

‘I feel the resemblance of the White House in the US,’ he thought, recalling his previous life. The design here was not the same, yet the feeling of “an important official residence” was close enough that his memories overlapped for a moment.

As they approached the front doors, a man in a butler’s uniform stepped forward. He had been waiting near the entrance and moved at once when he saw Dolvar and Elrond coming.

“Is there anything I can help with, Sir Dolvar, and this young man?” the butler asked in a polite, steady tone.

Dolvar stopped in front of him. “Yes, Sir Varrick. This young man is Elrond von Astrea. He is Sir Gilbert’s guest.”

“I see. Then please follow me, Sir Astrea. Sir Gilbert is already expecting you,” Varrick said. He turned toward Elrond and gave a small, formal nod.

Dolvar returned to his post, and Varrick led Elrond to the door.

“Understood,” Elrond replied simply.

They stepped inside the mansion.

The entrance opened into a wide lobby. The floor was polished, and couches for visitors were set out in a neat arrangement instead of being scattered at random. A large stained-glass window on one wall showed the Alfrost family crest. Light passed through the colored glass and fell across the room in soft shades.

Overhead, a chandelier hung from the ceiling and lit the space evenly. Two broad staircases stood on the left and right, each one curving up toward the next floor. Along the walls, there were framed pieces, small ornaments, and a suit of armor standing on a platform, there only for show.

“This way, Sir Astrea,” Varrick said again.

He walked toward the right side of the mansion, and Elrond followed.

The corridor there was just as clean as the lobby. As they moved along it, Elrond saw maids passing by, some carrying folded fabric in their arms, others pushing a trolley with covered items on top. They moved quickly, used to this kind of work.

Soon, they arrived at a large door with an arched top. The wood was darker than the walls around it, and the frame had more detail than the others they had passed. Just from the look of it, Elrond could tell this room mattered more than an ordinary guest room.

Varrick stopped in front of the door and knocked.

“Sir Gilbert, our guest has arrived,” he said.

“Bring him inside,” Gilbert’s voice answered from within.

Varrick opened the door and held it. Elrond walked past him into the room. The butler gave a small bow as Elrond went by, then closed the door behind him, leaving Elrond and Gilbert alone.

Inside, only Gilbert was present. The room was full of furnishings but still felt spacious. It looked like an office for house matters, with several racks of books along the walls, a desk for work, and a couch with a low table set nearby for talking face to face.

“Please, take a seat, Elrond,” Gilbert said, gesturing toward the couch.

“Understood,” Elrond replied.

He walked to the couch and sat down where Gilbert had indicated. Gilbert stayed in his chair for a moment, watching him with an easy expression. Then he leaned back and crossed one leg over the other.

“How are your Royal Academy activities, Elrond?” Gilbert asked. “You seem to be settling in.”

“Well… it is not that amusing yet,” Elrond answered honestly. “Most of the lessons are still introductory. From the syllabus, it looks like what you would expect from advanced knowledge, but right now it is still the basics.”

“I see. At your level, I suppose it is going to be boring, right?” Gilbert said, his lips curling in a small tease.

“No, no, it is not like that,” Elrond said quickly, lifting a hand. “I did learn most of it in the past, but only from books.” He paused for a moment. “And having someone else teach it might be a different experience,” he added, trying to soften what he had just said.

“I see. So you have learned all of that already. You are amazing, are you not?” Gilbert said.

The words sounded like praise, but the smug look on his face told a different story. He was cornering Elrond on purpose.

Elrond noticed it at once and tried to hide his reaction.

‘So he is purposely asking that to dig into me. He is really dangerous. I need to be more careful around him,’ Elrond thought. In this world, Gilbert was one of the sharpest people he had spoken to.

“Well…” Elrond tried to answer, but the rest of the words would not come out.

Gilbert let the silence linger for a few seconds, then chuckled and waved a hand.

“Haha, let us put that aside,” he said. “If I keep going, you will run out of excuses. Let us talk about the reason I invited you here instead.”

His tone settled into something steadier.

“I would like to offer you a reward for what you did for Emilia and the others,” Gilbert continued. “And I want to give you a proper reward. To me, money is not enough for something on this scale.”

Elrond listened quietly.

“You saved Emilia, my little sister, and you also saved Cestina, my future bride, from an assassination attempt,” Gilbert said. He spoke the words plainly, without trying to make them lighter. “That is not something we can treat as a small matter.”

Hearing it said that plainly made Elrond recall the wolf hunt that had turned into an assassination rescue, and the three girls he had pulled away from the carriage on that road when the assassins struck. For him, stepping in back then had been obvious. People would have died if he stayed away, so of course he moved.

“...To be completely honest, I have not decided what the reward should be,” Gilbert admitted after a short pause. “That is why I want to ask your opinion directly, Elrond.”

Elrond looked down at his hands.

It would not be strange to ask for money here. A large sum could help his parents in the frontier and make his own life in the capital easier. But Gilbert had already said money was not enough. If he named an amount now, it felt too close to putting a price on that rescue, and his pride did not like that.

“I do not have anything in mind either, Sir Gilbert,” Elrond said at last. “I only did what felt natural, so I will leave this matter to you. I will accept anything you offer, if it eases your feelings about repaying my action.”

“I see. You truly are something, Elrond,” Gilbert said.

He reached to the side and picked up several sheets of paper that had been set out on his desk. The edges were neatly aligned, and there were already small notes written along the margins.

“The reason I needed two days before inviting you here was to investigate you, Elrond,” Gilbert said calmly. “I prefer to be clear.”

Elrond felt his shoulders tense.

“Investigate… me?” he asked.

“Yes,” Gilbert said. “According to this document, you are registered as a monster hunter in the Adventurer Bureau. The fact that you accepted that position instead of becoming an adventurer yourself. There must be a reason behind that, is what I thought.”

Elrond stared at the paper.

‘Wait a second… he has all that on his desk already? Where is the privacy in this world?’ he thought, remembering his previous life, where having someone pull your records like this would have started a complaint or even a lawsuit.

Outwardly, he kept his face as steady as he could.

“But your answer just now was unexpected,” Gilbert went on. “I expected you to ask for a lot of money and then walk away. Instead, you gave me something more to think about.”

‘Well, I would not mind taking that, actually,’ Elrond thought. He made sure none of it showed on his face.

“Yes, I do earn money from monster hunts,” he admitted. “To be clear, I still have savings, but that is for emergencies.” He paused. “And you said yourself that money would not be enough, so I thought asking for money would not cut it.”

“I see. I like your approach, Elrond. You are an interesting guy,” Gilbert said. He rested his chin lightly on his hand and watched Elrond for a few seconds. “In that case, there is one thing I can offer you.”

“What is it?” Elrond asked.

“Be a noble, Elrond,” Gilbert said.

He said it casually, as if he were suggesting a change of clothes.

“Excuse me?” Elrond blurted out.

The words hit him harder than he expected. Becoming a noble was something he had never even pictured for himself. It felt too far away from the life he had lived in the frontier.

Gilbert seemed to notice the way Elrond’s eyes widened.

“Sorry, I did not explain it clearly,” Gilbert said, correcting himself at once. “I am not saying you will become a noble in the direct sense. What I mean is that you will work under House Alfrost directly, under me, as our guardian. It is a new position I want to prepare for you. A place similar to Cestina or Lisoletelle, as Emilia’s direct aide.”

“So… something like a bodyguard?” Elrond asked.

“No. I would not call it a bodyguard,” Gilbert replied. “Yes, you will help ensure this household’s safety, but it is not as simple as being a bodyguard.”

He sat up a little straighter.

“You can live here, eat here, continue your Academy life, and get paid by this household,” Gilbert explained. “In return, you will help us in the way you can whenever there is a threat. Because as you can see, and as our history shows, we have had more than a few assassination attempts over the decades, both in this mansion and outside it.”

‘I am still not sure about the workload, but… that sounds like a bodyguard to me,’ Elrond thought that because, to him, the way Gilbert explained it really did make it sound like a bodyguard’s job.

“To put it simply,” Gilbert added, “you would be here not as someone under someone else. You would represent yourself here. A bodyguard has a strict employer. You would not. Think of it that way. So you do not need to force yourself to do anything in this mansion.”

‘I understand now,’ Elrond thought. ‘He is saying I will stand on equal footing with people like his sister and Cestina. I do not need to overdo the formality. I think that is what he means.’

Elrond went quiet and thought carefully.

On one side, he had the simple life he had imagined for himself. He could study at the Academy, work as a monster hunter when he needed money, and send what he could back home. On the other side, he had this offer. If he accepted, he would be tied directly to House Alfrost. That would change his life, and it would also open a chance to raise the status of the Astrea household.

‘Is this really what my parents would want?’ he asked himself. ‘Would they be happier if I stayed a frontier boy who made his own way, or if I stood beside nobles?’

He did not know the answer yet.

Even so, he could not ignore the fact that Aldric had pushed for him to attend the Royal Academy. Looking back, it felt like that might have always been meant to give him a path like this, a path that led closer to people of higher status instead of away from them. It was only his own interpretation, but the thought stayed with him.

He returned his eyes to Gilbert.

Gilbert’s offer did not sound complicated. Live here, study as usual, and be ready when danger came. The details would probably grow more complex over time, but the base was simple enough to grasp.

Elrond took a breath.

“I have decided,” he said.

Gilbert raised an eyebrow. “Have you thought about it clearly, Elrond? I do not mind if you take longer.”

Elrond had already thought it through. He was not the kind of person who grabbed at the first choice just because it was in front of him. In his previous life he had worked as a researcher, someone who was used to weighing every condition before deciding, and that habit had not faded just because he was in a different world. While Gilbert explained his offer, Elrond had been quietly running through the risks, the burden on his family, and what kind of future this path could open.

“No,” Elrond answered. “I will answer now, Sir Alfrost.”

He met Gilbert’s eyes.

“I accept your offer as the Alfrost family guardian,” Elrond said. “This opportunity could lead to something bigger in the future, for my benefit and for my family’s.”

Gilbert watched him for a long second, his expression loosening with a mix of surprise and relief.

“I see. So you have been thinking it through,” Gilbert said.

Gilbert stood up from his chair and walked over to the couch. Elrond stood as well. When Gilbert held out his hand, Elrond reached out and shook it.

“Then it is settled,” Gilbert said. “From now on, you can start living in this mansion, Elrond. We will prepare a place for you. And also, please just call me Gilbert.”

“Gilbert… Your Highness?” Elrond tried.

The habit of adding a title came out on its own.

Gilbert sighed lightly.

“I am not a king, you know. Just Gilbert is fine,” he said.

“But that feels a bit strange,” Elrond replied. “How about Sir Gilbert?”

“Alright, alright. You can call me that,” Gilbert said. A hint of amusement touched his eyes. “But try to call me more casually later.”

“Understood,” Elrond said.

As he let go of Gilbert’s hand, Elrond knew he had just tied himself to the Alfrost household for real. The quiet life of only studying and hunting monsters on the side was over, but he had chosen this himself, so he would live with whatever came next.

Elrond liked to watch and learn, and living here would let him see the trouble around the Alfrost family from up close instead of hearing about it from a distance. He did not know what would happen next, but he had chosen this himself, so he was ready to take responsibility for it.

There was a short pause in the room. The feel of Gilbert’s handshake still lingered in Elrond’s fingers when a knock came from the door, followed almost at once by it opening from the outside.

A young woman stepped in without waiting for an answer.

“Sir Gilbert, why did you take so lo—” she began, but her complaint stopped halfway when she saw there was someone else in the room.

She had not checked the room first, and when her eyes found Elrond on the couch, she stopped and drew herself up.

“Ah—” She straightened her back. “I apologize for suddenly rushing in. Are you in the middle of an important discussion?” she asked, her tone turning careful as she glanced between Gilbert and Elrond.

Gilbert’s shoulders relaxed a little when he saw her. “No, feel free to come in,” he said with a small smile.

Cestina Ludwell was wearing a long-sleeved house dress in Alfrost colors, more relaxed than the formal gowns he had seen at the Academy yet still far above anything from the frontier. The fabric was soft and easy to move in, and her long blonde hair was half tied at the back instead of being gathered into a formal style.

Seeing her like that, Elrond finally understood why people called her beautiful.

‘She’s… unbelievably beautiful,’ he thought, his mind stating it plainly. Even out of formal wear, or maybe because of it, she looked even more striking to his eyes.

“You’re lovely as ever,” Gilbert said lightly. The smile on his face turned a little more playful as he looked at his fiancée.

“Please stop it, Sir Gilbert. We have a guest here,” Cestina answered. She was blushing as she lowered her gaze.

“Ah, sorry. Please don’t mind me,” Elrond said quickly, lifting both hands in front of his chest. “We’re almost done anyway. Do you two have plans or something? I can excuse myself if you have something to do.”

“Don’t worry, Elrond. It’s nothing that important,” Gilbert replied. “We just want to have lunch together.”

“I see,” Elrond said. The way Gilbert answered made it sound ordinary, like something they did often.

“Originally, I wanted to show you around the mansion myself,” Gilbert went on. “But if I do that now, Cestina will be the one waiting.” He glanced toward the door. “Is Varrick still outside, Cestina?”

“Yes, he is still in the corridor,” Cestina said. “Would you like me to call him?”

“Yes, please,” Gilbert said. “And ask him to guide Elrond around the mansion.”

“Understood,” she replied with a small nod.

Cestina gave Elrond a polite smile on her way out, then left to fetch Varrick, and the room went quiet again after the door shut.

“Well, I think that is all for today, Elrond,” Gilbert said, turning his attention back to him. “If there is anything you do not understand about this mansion, feel free to ask Varrick. He knows the place better than I do. I have a date to attend,” he added with a soft laugh.

“I will keep that in mind,” Elrond answered.

Gilbert rose from his chair and tidied the papers on his desk into one neat stack. Elrond stood as well, and together they walked toward the door.

When Gilbert opened it, Cestina was already there, and beside her stood Varrick in his butler’s uniform. Varrick stepped forward at once and bowed lightly toward Elrond.

“This way, Sir Astrea,” Varrick said. His words were polite, and his tone was steady.
